Consequences for your environment (decide these before coding)

  1. Kafka lessons need Flink 2.2.x (connector 5.0.0) until a 2.3-compatible connector ships. Chapter 1 needs no connector.
  2. Java 25 (your horizon-hem-telemetry modules) is not documented as supported by Flink 2.x. Your recorded plan for the processor is Flink 1.20 on Java 21, but the 2.x docs call Java 21 experimental. Resolve this with the official Flink compatibility info before any upgrade decision.
  3. State compatibility between 1.20 and 2.x: the Flink 2.0 release notes say state compatibility is not guaranteed between 1.x and 2.x (Chapter 9). Plan as if state must be rebuilt, and confirm with the Flink project before deciding.
  4. Flink JDBC connector: 4.0.0 is for 2.0.x and 4.1.0 for 2.1.x/2.2.x; none for 2.3 yet. From 4.0 it is split into flink-connector-jdbc-core plus per-database modules (latest 4.1.0-2.2), which is why flink-connector-jdbc itself stops at 3.4.0-1.20 on Maven Central (Chapter 26).
  5. Config keys, resolved from the 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 jars (Chapter 6): execution.checkpointing.unaligned.enabled is primary and execution.checkpointing.unaligned is a deprecated alias; execution.checkpointing.incremental is primary and state.backend.incremental is a deprecated alias (old names still work).

Chapter 1: Time, watermarks, late data, and lag

Goal: after this chapter you can explain what a watermark is, pick a delay with data, detect late events, and say which of three lags is hurting you. No Kafka needed.

1.1 Three moments per record

 event happened        stored in Kafka            Flink processes it
 (on the device)       (broker timestamp)         (wall clock)
      t_event ───────────► t_kafka ───────────────► t_now
        └─ ingestion lag ──┘└── consumer/processing lag ──┘
        └──────────────── end-to-end event lag ───────────┘
  • Event time: timestamp inside the record. Deterministic and replayable. Needs waiting for out-of-order data.
  • Processing time: wall clock of the task. Simple, fast, non-deterministic (depends on load and outages).
  • Rule: use event time for features, replays, backfills. Use processing time only when you truly mean "now".

1.2 What a watermark is

A Watermark(t) is a message that flows inside the stream, saying: "there should be no more elements with timestamp <= t". It is a heuristic promise by you, not a fact. Operators use it to advance their event-time clock, fire timers, and close windows.

Flink's own bounded-out-of-orderness generator emits maxTimestampSeen - delay - 1ms. The -1 exists because Watermark(t) covers timestamps <= t, so an event stamped exactly max - delay is still allowed. (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 BoundedOutOfOrdernessWatermarks.onPeriodicEmit computes maxTimestamp - outOfOrdernessMillis - 1.) Watermarks are emitted periodically (not once per record), so the "watermark after" column below is the value the generator would emit at its next periodic emit; a record read between two emits sees the older value.

Worked example (delay = 5 s, one source subtask, timestamps in seconds)

Arrival ts max seen watermark after Verdict on arrival
1 3 3 -2.001 on time
2 9 9 3.999 on time
3 6 9 3.999 out of order but on time (6 > 3.999)
4 20 20 14.999 on time
5 12 20 14.999 LATE (12 <= 14.999)
6 16 20 14.999 on time (16 > 14.999)

Trade-off: larger delay = more late events captured but higher latency. There is no free setting.

Figure 1.1: The worked example: only arrival 5 (ts 12) falls at or behind the watermark 14.999.

1.3 API (verified: docs 2.3 generating_watermarks page; signatures checked with javap on flink-core 2.2.1 WatermarkStrategy)

WatermarkStrategy<Event> wm = WatermarkStrategy
    .<Event>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    .withTimestampAssigner((event, recordTs) -> event.eventTsMillis)
    .withIdleness(Duration.ofMinutes(1));          // see 1.5
    // .withWatermarkAlignment("group-1", Duration.ofSeconds(20), Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // see 1.6
  • The old AssignerWithPeriodicWatermarks / AssignerWithPunctuatedWatermarks do not exist in the 2.2.1 flink-core / flink-runtime / flink-streaming-java jars (verified: class search). Use WatermarkStrategy.
  • WatermarkGenerator (onEvent, onPeriodicEmit) covers both periodic and punctuated styles (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1). withIdleness(Duration) and withWatermarkAlignment(String, Duration[, Duration]) exist on WatermarkStrategy (verified: javap).
  • With Kafka, watermarks are generated per partition and merged by taking the minimum. Pass the strategy to env.fromSource(kafkaSource, strategy, "name") so it applies per partition.
  • By default the Kafka source uses the Kafka record timestamp as event time (verified: docs Kafka connector 2.2 page; KafkaRecordEmitter calls ConsumerRecord.timestamp()). Override with withTimestampAssigner if the business timestamp lives in the payload (usually it does).

1.4 Detecting late data

Three policies: drop (window default), allowed lateness (re-fire windows, Chapter 2), or side output. Always count late events, even if you drop them. A minimal detector (sketch, not compiled):

public class Event {                       // public fields + no-arg ctor => Flink POJO
    public String key; public long eventTsMillis; public String payload;
    public Event() {}
}

public class LateSplitter extends ProcessFunction<Event, Event> {
    public static final OutputTag<Event> LATE = new OutputTag<>("late-events") {};

    @Override
    public void processElement(Event e, Context ctx, Collector<Event> out) {
        long wm = ctx.timerService().currentWatermark();   // this operator's current watermark
        if (e.eventTsMillis <= wm) {
            ctx.output(LATE, e);          // behind the clock we promised
        } else {
            out.collect(e);
        }
    }
}
// main.process(new LateSplitter()).getSideOutput(LateSplitter.LATE) -> counter / sink / alert

numLateRecordsDropped (verified: constant in flink-streaming-java 2.2.1 WindowOperator) counts events a window operator dropped as late. Caveat (verified: WindowOperator.processElement bytecode): the counter is incremented only when the window has no sideOutputLateData(...) tag; if you attach a side output, late records go to the tag and the counter stays flat. Count the side output yourself. It does not see lateness in your own process functions, hence the side output above.

1.5 Idleness: the classic production bug

Operator watermark = minimum over its input partitions/channels. If one Kafka partition is empty (or parallelism > partitions), its watermark never advances, so nothing downstream fires. Symptom: records flow, windows never close, watermark lag grows forever. Fix: .withIdleness(Duration). The docs say sources do not enter idle state automatically. Cost: an idle partition that wakes up with old timestamps produces late events. Pick the timeout deliberately.

Figure 1.2: One idle partition holds the minimum watermark, so nothing downstream fires.

1.6 Watermark alignment (changed in 2.3)

Problem: fast sources/partitions race ahead; downstream buffers state waiting for the slow one. withWatermarkAlignment(group, maxDrift, updateInterval) pauses sources that drift more than maxDrift ahead of the group's minimum. Flink 2.3 adds a watermark alignment buffer (ring buffer of recent announced watermarks, so alignment checks against the oldest of the last N values) to stop alignment from throttling backlog processing. Option pipeline.watermark-alignment.buffer-size, default 3 (= alignment is applied 3 update intervals late); 0 restores the pre-2.3 behavior. Sources may pause slightly later than in 2.2, so windowed/temporal state can grow a little. (verified: docs 2.3 release notes; default and key verified by javap on flink-core 2.3.0 PipelineOptions, absent in 2.2.1.)

1.7 The three lags and where to measure them

Lag Meaning Where to read it Status
Ingestion lag event time to Kafka append time Kafka record timestamp minus event time, computed in your job or a probe derivable by you, no special metric needed
Consumer/processing lag Kafka head to Flink position Kafka consumer-group lag; Flink source metrics source metric names verified (see below); records-lag-max unverified
Watermark lag wall clock minus current watermark currentInputWatermark / currentOutputWatermark (verified), then compute now - wm in your monitoring verified base metrics
Late rate share of events behind the watermark side-output counter (1.4); numLateRecordsDropped for windows verified
Saturation is Flink the bottleneck? busyTimeMsPerSecond, backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond, idleTimeMsPerSecond (verified) verified

Status of the source/Kafka lag metric names (settled in Chapter 13): currentEmitEventTimeLag, watermarkLag, pendingRecords and sourceIdleTime are registered as gauges by flink-runtime 2.2.1 InternalSourceReaderMetricGroup (verified: javap bytecode). currentFetchEventTimeLag is only a MetricNames constant there with no registration in that class (consistent with Chapter 13): do not alert on it. The Kafka connector 5.0.0 jar adds KafkaSourceReader metrics currentOffset, committedOffset, commitsSucceeded, commitsFailed, and (default on, register.consumer.metrics) forwards Kafka consumer metrics under KafkaSourceReader.KafkaConsumer (verified: javap + docs 2.2 Kafka page). records-lag-max is a Kafka-client metric name that is not defined in any Flink jar we have: [unverified] (needs a running consumer). Confirm in your own metrics endpoint before alerting on any of them.

Reading them together: - High ingestion lag, low consumer lag: problem is upstream of Flink. - Growing consumer lag with high backpressure/busy time: Flink is the bottleneck (parallelism, skew, sink). - High late rate but healthy lag: delay too tight (or an idle partition waking up). - Watermark lag grows while records still flow: a stuck partition holds the minimum (1.5). - Never compute your only SLA metric inside the data path: a stalled job emits nothing, so it cannot alert on itself.

Choosing the delay with data (replaces the article's guesswork)

  1. Measure arrival_time - event_ts per event over a representative week (include a bad day).
  2. Set delay near the p99 of that distribution; send the tail to the late side output.
  3. Review when the producer fleet changes (new SDK version, new region).

1.8 What the article got wrong here

  • It measured lag with CURRENT_TIMESTAMP inside a windowed aggregate (non-deterministic) and put CURRENT_WATERMARK in a GROUP BY. Chapter 25 rebuilds this properly.
  • It never mentioned idleness, per-partition watermarks, or late-event accounting.

1.9 Self-check

  1. Why is the watermark max - delay - 1ms and not max - delay?
  2. Two partitions: A at event time 10:00, B idle for an hour. What is the operator watermark, and what fixes it?
  3. Late events are 3% of traffic. Raise the delay or use a side output? What does each cost?
  4. Your job is stuck. Which of your metrics still tell you, and which go silent?

1.10 Open items for the next compile step

  • Build a runnable demo (bounded in-memory source, punctuated generator so output is deterministic) on Flink 2.2.x or 2.3.0 with Java 17.
  • Pin versions and confirm the Maven coordinates through the internal Artifactory (mvn -s settings.xml, see CLAUDE.md).

Chapter 2: Windows

Goal: after this chapter you can choose a window type, say exactly when an event-time window fires and when its state is deleted, handle late data with allowed lateness and a side output, and pick an aggregation style that keeps state small. Window TVFs are SQL, so we deliberately do not use them; this chapter is DataStream only.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, late data, idleness).

2.1 Mental model

A window is a bucket of records per key, defined by a WindowAssigner, closed by a Trigger, and optionally trimmed by an Evictor. Per (key, window) Flink keeps state plus a cleanup timer.

record --keyBy--> assigner: which window(s)? --> state[(key, window)] --> trigger: fire? purge? --> window function --> output

Windowing on a keyed stream is stream.keyBy(...).window(assigner). Non-keyed windowAll runs at parallelism 1; avoid it for anything but tiny streams (see Chapter 10).

2.2 The four window types (verified: docs 2.3 windows page; class names checked with javap on flink-streaming-java 2.2.1)

Type Event-time class Processing-time class Shape
Tumbling TumblingEventTimeWindows TumblingProcessingTimeWindows fixed size, no overlap; each record in 1 window
Sliding SlidingEventTimeWindows SlidingProcessingTimeWindows size + slide, overlap; each record in size/slide windows
Session EventTimeSessionWindows ProcessingTimeSessionWindows per key, closed by an inactivity gap; static gap or SessionWindowTimeGapExtractor
Global GlobalWindows n/a (time-agnostic; GlobalWindows.create()) one window per key, never ends unless your trigger says so

Notes: - Tumbling and sliding assigners (event and processing time) take an optional offset to align windows, e.g. to a time zone: TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration size, Duration offset), SlidingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration size, Duration slide, Duration offset) (verified: javap 2.2.1; tumbling also has a WindowStagger overload). Session assigners (withGap(Duration), withDynamicGap(SessionWindowTimeGapExtractor)) have no offset. Constraint: abs(offset) < size (verified: exception text in TumblingEventTimeWindows). - Sliding windows copy each record into several windows: state and CPU multiply by size/slide. A 1 h window sliding every 1 s is 3600 windows per key; use a coarser slide or a different design (Chapter 21). - Session windows work by creating a window per record and merging windows closer than the gap. Merging needs a trigger that supports merging (canMerge() / onMerge; otherwise Flink throws "A merging window assigner cannot be used with a trigger that does not support merging" (verified: flink-streaming-java 2.2.1)) and a merging window function (docs: ReduceFunction, AggregateFunction or ProcessWindowFunction), and means session state is more expensive than tumbling. Sessions are rebuilt in Chapter 20. - Global windows only make sense with a custom trigger (default is NeverTrigger). Often a KeyedProcessFunction (Chapter 3) is clearer than a global window with a custom trigger and evictor.

// (sketch, not compiled)
events.keyBy(e -> e.key)
      .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))   // of(Duration) (verified: javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1)
      ...

Flink 2.x uses java.time.Duration for window sizes, slides, offsets, gaps, allowedLateness(Duration), TimeEvictor.of(Duration) and intervalJoin(...).between(Duration, Duration). The old org.apache.flink.streaming.api.windowing.time.Time class is not present in the 2.2.1 jars (verified: class search), so older Time.minutes(1) examples do not compile.

2.3 Default triggers and how an event-time window fires

Assigner Default trigger
Event-time tumbling/sliding/session EventTimeTrigger
Processing-time tumbling/sliding/session ProcessingTimeTrigger
GlobalWindows NeverTrigger (you must supply a trigger)

EventTimeTrigger registers an event-time timer at the window's max timestamp (window end minus 1 ms, since window ends are exclusive). When the operator's watermark reaches that timestamp, the timer fires and the window function runs. The boundary is watermark >= maxTimestamp (verified: javap 2.2.1 InternalTimerServiceImpl.tryAdvanceWatermark fires every timer with timestamp <= watermark; EventTimeTrigger.onEventTime returns FIRE when the timer equals window.maxTimestamp()).

Worked example, 1-minute tumbling window [10:00:00, 10:01:00), watermark delay 5 s (see Chapter 1):

Event Watermark after What happens
ts 10:00:20 10:00:14.999 assigned to the window, nothing fires
ts 10:00:59.9 10:00:54.899 still open
ts 10:01:04.9 10:00:59.899 window still not fired
ts 10:01:05.1 10:01:00.099 watermark passed 10:00:59.999: window fires

Consequences: - Output latency for an event-time window is at least window end + watermark delay, and it depends on new data arriving to move the watermark. No traffic on any input partition means no firing (idleness, Chapter 1.5). - The watermark is the minimum over inputs, so one slow or idle partition delays every window.

2.4 Allowed lateness, side output, and when state is deleted

Verified (docs 2.3 windows page, and javap/bytecode of flink-streaming-java 2.2.1 WindowOperator): - allowedLateness default is 0: late elements are dropped. - With lateness L, an element arriving after the watermark passed the window end but before it passes maxTimestamp + L is still added to the window. Precisely, the cleanup time is window.maxTimestamp() + L = end - 1 ms + L (docs say "until their allowed lateness expires"; the 1 ms comes from bytecode WindowOperator.cleanupTime). The ASCII sketch below writes this as end + L for readability. - Window state is kept until that cleanup time, then removed. - sideOutputLateData(OutputTag) captures elements that are dropped as late. When a tag is set, numLateRecordsDropped is not incremented (verified: WindowOperator.processElement bytecode: side output OR counter).

 watermark:   ... < end ........ end ----------- end+L ........ >
 element ts in window:  on time      "late but allowed"    DROPPED -> side output
 firing:                1st fire     re-fire per late element     (state deleted)

Semantics you must plan for: - With EventTimeTrigger and L > 0, each late-but-allowed element makes the window fire again with an updated result. Downstream receives multiple results per window. The sink must be idempotent or upsert by (key, window) (Chapter 26). Verified: docs say late elements "may cause the window to fire again ... the case for the EventTimeTrigger", and EventTimeTrigger.onElement returns FIRE immediately when maxTimestamp <= currentWatermark (javap bytecode 2.2.1), i.e. one firing per late-but-allowed element. - State lives L longer. Large L on sliding windows with many keys is a state-size cost (2.7). - Dropped elements are counted by numLateRecordsDropped only when no side output is attached (Chapter 1.4); with sideOutputLateData attach your own counter on the late stream. Always attach a side output.

// (sketch, not compiled)
OutputTag<Event> lateTag = new OutputTag<>("late-window-events") {};

SingleOutputStreamOperator<Result> out = events
    .keyBy(e -> e.key)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
    .allowedLateness(Duration.ofMinutes(2))
    .sideOutputLateData(lateTag)
    .aggregate(new CountAgg());

DataStream<Event> late = out.getSideOutput(lateTag);   // count it, store it, alert on it

Figure 2.1: When a window fires, accepts late elements, and drops state (L = allowed lateness).

2.5 Triggers (brief)

Trigger methods: onElement, onEventTime, onProcessingTime, onMerge (stateful triggers on merging windows), clear (called when the window is removed). Each returns a TriggerResult:

Result Meaning
CONTINUE do nothing
FIRE run the window function, keep window contents
FIRE_AND_PURGE run the function, then clear contents
PURGE clear contents, no output

Typical custom triggers: early firing every N seconds for a long window (a dashboard that cannot wait an hour), or count-based firing. Purge clears the elements but window metadata remains, and new data can still be assigned to a purged window (verified: docs windows page, "Purging ... only refers to the elements in the window, and not the window metadata"). Trigger also has canMerge() (verified: javap). A custom trigger is also the standard way to use GlobalWindows.

2.6 Evictors (brief)

Built-ins (verified: classes exist in 2.2.1 jars; TimeEvictor.of(Duration)): CountEvictor (keep last N), DeltaEvictor, TimeEvictor (drop older than max timestamp minus interval). They run evictBefore (before the window function) or evictAfter. Warning from the docs: specifying an evictor prevents any pre-aggregation, so Flink must buffer all elements. Recommendation: avoid evictors in production; if you need "last N events per key", a keyed ListState/ValueState in a KeyedProcessFunction is cheaper and more explicit (Chapter 3, Chapter 5).

2.7 Window functions and state size

Function State per (key, window) Metadata (window, key) Use for
ReduceFunction one value, same type as input no (unless combined) sum/min/max where in and out types match
AggregateFunction<IN, ACC, OUT> one accumulator ACC no (unless combined) avg, count distinct sketches, any aggregate with a custom accumulator
ProcessWindowFunction alone all elements buffered yes: Context needs the full set (e.g. median, sort), or window metadata
AggregateFunction + ProcessWindowFunction one accumulator yes incremental aggregation, then attach window start/end and key

AggregateFunction methods (verified: GitHub release-2.2 flink-core-api source): createAccumulator(), add(), getResult(), merge(). merge is required for session windows and other merging windows (docs: a session window needs a merging window function). Window aggregate/reduce functions cannot be RichFunctions (verified: exception text in WindowedStream); use the ProcessWindowFunction variant if you need open()/state.

// (sketch, not compiled) incremental aggregation + window metadata
public class AvgAgg implements AggregateFunction<Event, long[], Double> {
    public long[] createAccumulator()            { return new long[2]; }          // sum, count
    public long[] add(Event e, long[] acc)       { acc[0] += e.value; acc[1]++; return acc; }
    public Double getResult(long[] acc)          { return acc[1] == 0 ? 0.0 : (double) acc[0] / acc[1]; }
    public long[] merge(long[] a, long[] b)      { a[0] += b[0]; a[1] += b[1]; return a; }
}

public class AddWindow extends ProcessWindowFunction<Double, Result, String, TimeWindow> {
    @Override
    public void process(String key, Context ctx, Iterable<Double> single, Collector<Result> out) {
        out.collect(new Result(key, ctx.window().getStart(), ctx.window().getEnd(), single.iterator().next()));
    }
}
// .aggregate(new AvgAgg(), new AddWindow())

Rules of thumb: 1. Default to AggregateFunction (+ ProcessWindowFunction for metadata). The Iterable then has exactly one element. 2. Buffering all elements (plain ProcessWindowFunction) is the number-one cause of window state blow-ups. 3. State estimate: keys x open windows x state per window. Open windows per key = ceil(size/slide) for sliding, plus windows kept for allowed lateness, plus sessions not yet closed. 4. Use a compact accumulator type with efficient serialization (Chapter 8); Chapter 17 turns this into capacity numbers.

Figure 2.2: Buffering all elements versus keeping one accumulator per (key, window).

2.8 Window vs KeyedProcessFunction

Need Use
Fixed-interval aggregates, simple lateness window + AggregateFunction
Early/speculative results, cleanup control, per-key custom lifecycle KeyedProcessFunction + timers (Chapter 3)
Dedup, hysteresis, "no event for N minutes" KeyedProcessFunction (windows are the wrong tool)
Sessions with custom close rules session window for the simple gap case; KeyedProcessFunction otherwise

2.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Windows never fire: an idle/empty partition holds the watermark back (Chapter 1.5). A stream with no timestamps at all makes the event-time assigner throw "Record has Long.MIN_VALUE timestamp (= no timestamp marker)..." (verified: TumblingEventTimeWindows bytecode), so that case fails loudly rather than silently.
  • Processing-time windows in a backfill: wall clock, not data time, decides the windows; replays produce nonsense. Use event time for anything that must be replayable.
  • Late results duplicated downstream after enabling allowedLateness: sink must upsert by (key, window start).
  • Sliding-window multiplication: state and CPU scale with size/slide; the checkpoint grows with it.
  • Evictor or bare ProcessWindowFunction on a hot key: unbounded buffering, GC pressure or RocksDB growth.
  • Key skew: a window per key still processes one key on one subtask (Chapter 10).
  • Window start in the wrong zone: tumbling windows align to the epoch unless you use offset; a "daily" window is UTC midnight by default (verified: docs windows page, windows align to the epoch; for China use offset = Duration.ofHours(-8)).

2.10 What the article got wrong here

The article leaned on SQL window forms for rolling features and used a time expression that is not a window (Chapter 21 and Chapter 25 rebuild these). Its sessionization showed Oracle-style syntax and no handling of late emission (Chapter 20).

2.11 Self-check

  1. A 10-minute tumbling window, watermark delay 30 s, allowedLateness 5 min. When does the first result appear, and when is the state deleted?
  2. Why does a plain ProcessWindowFunction cost more state than AggregateFunction + ProcessWindowFunction?
  3. 1-hour sliding window, 1-minute slide, 10 M keys: how many window copies of each record exist?
  4. Why can allowedLateness break a non-idempotent sink?
  5. When would you replace a window with a KeyedProcessFunction?

2.12 Open items / unverified

  • (Resolved, see inline evidence: of(Duration), offsets, firing boundary, re-fire per late element, epoch alignment.)
  • Whether session-window operator state changes under State V2 / ForSt (Chapter 28): data unavailable.
  • Process-time windows and ProcessingTimeoutTrigger / other built-in triggers: not checked.

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/operators/windows/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/time/

Chapter 3: Timers and KeyedProcessFunction

Goal: after this chapter you can write a KeyedProcessFunction with keyed state and timers, choose event-time versus processing-time timers, control timer cost with coalescing, and clean state up safely. This is the workhorse for dedup, hysteresis and custom sessions.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks), Chapter 2 (windows, for contrast). State types are covered properly in Chapter 5.

3.1 Mental model

A KeyedProcessFunction<K, I, O> gives you three things per key: state, timers, and output control (main output plus side outputs). It is a tiny state machine per key.

        keyBy(k)
records ─────────► processElement(rec)  ──► read/write state[k], register timer(k, t)
                                             │
 watermark / wall clock reaches t  ─────────► onTimer(t) ──► read/write state[k], emit, clean up

Verified (docs 2.3; javap flink-streaming-java/flink-core 2.2.1): methods are open(OpenContext) (inherited from RichFunction; the 1.x open(Configuration) is gone), processElement(I, Context, Collector<O>) and onTimer(long, OnTimerContext, Collector<O>) (all three may throw Exception). Timers and keyed state exist only on keyed streams.

Context Gives you
Context (in processElement) timestamp(), timerService(), output(OutputTag, X) (side output), getCurrentKey()
OnTimerContext (in onTimer, extends Context) the above plus timeDomain() (EVENT_TIME or PROCESSING_TIME)
(verified: javap KeyedProcessFunction$Context / $OnTimerContext 2.2.1)

TimerService (verified: javap 2.2.1): registerEventTimeTimer(long), registerProcessingTimeTimer(long), deleteEventTimeTimer(long), deleteProcessingTimeTimer(long), currentWatermark(), currentProcessingTime(). ctx.timestamp() returns a boxed Long (verified: javap), so it can be null when the record has no timestamp (e.g. processing-time programs); guard for it when not using event time.

3.2 Event-time versus processing-time timers

Event-time timer Processing-time timer
Fires when the operator's watermark reaches the timer timestamp wall clock reaches it
Needs traffic yes: with no new data the watermark stalls and nothing fires no
Deterministic / replayable yes no
Use for business rules on data time: windows, session close, TTL by event time, backfills "do something N seconds from now" (flush a buffer, heartbeat, timeouts on a real clock)
Behaviour on recovery fires when the restored watermark passes it verified (docs): processing-time timers that were due before restoration fire immediately on restore

Choosing: - Anything that must give the same result on replay (Chapter 24): event time. - "No event for 5 minutes" as an alert: event-time timer is blind if the whole input stalls (watermark stops); a processing-time timer fires anyway. Decide which question you are asking. Chapter 25 returns to this. - Never mix them casually in one state machine: a replay at 100x speed makes processing-time timers fire at the wrong data time.

Figure 3.1: Event-time versus processing-time timers.

3.3 Minimal sketch: per-key timeout with cleanup

// (sketch, not compiled) emit an alert if a key sends no event for 10 minutes of event time
public class IdleKeyAlert extends KeyedProcessFunction<String, Event, Alert> {
    private static final long TIMEOUT_MS = 10 * 60_000L;
    private transient ValueState<Long> lastSeen;      // event ts of last record
    private transient ValueState<Long> pendingTimer;  // timer we registered

    @Override
    public void open(OpenContext ctx) {
        lastSeen     = getRuntimeContext().getState(new ValueStateDescriptor<>("lastSeen", Long.class));
        pendingTimer = getRuntimeContext().getState(new ValueStateDescriptor<>("pendingTimer", Long.class));
    }

    @Override
    public void processElement(Event e, Context ctx, Collector<Alert> out) throws Exception {
        Long old = pendingTimer.value();
        if (old != null) ctx.timerService().deleteEventTimeTimer(old);   // replace, do not pile up
        long fireAt = e.eventTsMillis + TIMEOUT_MS;
        ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(fireAt);
        pendingTimer.update(fireAt);
        lastSeen.update(e.eventTsMillis);
    }

    @Override
    public void onTimer(long ts, OnTimerContext ctx, Collector<Alert> out) throws Exception {
        Long expected = pendingTimer.value();
        if (expected == null || expected != ts) return;          // stale timer: ignore
        out.collect(new Alert(ctx.getCurrentKey(), lastSeen.value(), ts));
        lastSeen.clear();                                        // cleanup: no state left for idle keys
        pendingTimer.clear();
    }
}

The ValueStateDescriptor and getRuntimeContext().getState(...) forms are still present in 2.2.1: RuntimeContext.getState(ValueStateDescriptor<T>) exists next to a state.v2 overload, and getRuntimeContext() / open(OpenContext) signatures match the sketch (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1). The sketch also passed a javac check against the 2.2.1 jars (best effort: some core-API classes came from 1.20.5 jars because flink-core-api 2.2.1 was not available locally).

Figure 3.2: The 3.3 sketch as a flow: replace the timer on every record, ignore stale timers, clean up on fire.

3.4 Timer rules, cost and coalescing

Verified (docs 2.3 process_function page): - The timer service keeps at most one timer per key and timestamp; registering the same timestamp again is a no-op (duplicates are coalesced). - Timers are checkpointed together with the application state. Many timers make checkpoints larger and slower. - Timer execution and processElement are synchronized: they never run concurrently for the same operator instance, so you do not need locks around your state.

Cost model: timers = keys x timers per key. One timer per event (distinct timestamps) means as many timers as events within the pending horizon. Cost is memory (heap timers) or RocksDB entries, plus checkpoint size.

Coalescing (from the docs) rounds timestamps to coarser granularity so many keys/events share fewer timer slots:

// (sketch, not compiled) processing-time: round DOWN to a full second (this is the docs example)
long t = ((ctx.timestamp() + timeoutMs) / 1000) * 1000;
ctx.timerService().registerProcessingTimeTimer(t);

// event-time: fire once per watermark advance, "as soon as the next watermark arrives"
long t2 = ctx.timerService().currentWatermark() + 1;
ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(t2);

Since timers are deduplicated per (key, timestamp), rounding bounds timers per key to one per second. Trade-off: the timer fires up to one rounding interval early relative to the requested time (the docs example rounds down; round up with ((x + 999) / 1000) * 1000 if early firing is wrong for you). Coalescing across keys does not reduce count (timers are per key); it reduces per-key timers and wakeups.

Backend note (from the docs): with RocksDB incremental snapshots and heap-based timers, asynchronous checkpointing has known limitations (tracked as FLINK-10026) (verified: docs). Timer storage with RocksDB is chosen by state.backend.rocksdb.timer-service.factory, default ROCKSDB (verified: GitHub release-2.2 RocksDBOptions; the other enum value, believed to be HEAP, and the 2.3 default were not checked: [unverified]). With the HashMap backend timers live on the heap. Check before running with millions of timers.

3.5 Ordering guarantees

What the docs state: onTimer and processElement are serialized per operator instance, so state is never modified concurrently.

Verified from the 2.2.1 implementation (bytecode of InternalTimerServiceImpl.tryAdvanceWatermark): - When a watermark arrives, all event-time timers with timestamp <= watermark fire, repeatedly taking the smallest timestamp first from the timer priority queue, so timers fire in ascending timestamp order (including for one key). Order among equal timestamps of different keys is unspecified. - The firing boundary is timer timestamp <= watermark. Timers fire when the watermark is processed, i.e. before records that arrive after that watermark. - Processing-time timer firing relative to record arrival: wall-clock based, inherently not reproducible (not testable by javap).

Practical rules: 1. Do not rely on any particular interleaving of timers and records of different keys beyond the watermark rule above. 2. Make onTimer idempotent and tolerant of stale timers: compare the timestamp to the one stored in state (3.3). 3. If a record can arrive with a timestamp at or behind the current watermark, decide explicitly: process it, drop it, or side-output it (Chapter 1.4). A timer registered for a past event-time does not fire inline; it fires when the next watermark is processed (verified: it sits in the queue until tryAdvanceWatermark).

3.6 Cleanup timers

State without TTL grows forever with key cardinality. The pattern: every key that can go quiet gets a cleanup timer that clears all its state.

  1. On each record, push the cleanup deadline forward: delete the old cleanup timer (or compare stored deadline in onTimer) and register a new one for eventTs + retention.
  2. In onTimer, if the stored deadline matches ts, clear every state object for the key.
  3. Clear in onTimer only; avoid forgetting a state object (a leaked MapState entry is a slow memory leak).
  4. Alternative: state TTL (Chapter 5). Differences: TTL is wall-clock (processing time) based and invisible to your logic; a cleanup timer can use event time, emit a final result and trigger side effects. Chapter 5 confirms TTL details.

Windows do the same internally: they register a cleanup timer at end + allowed lateness (Chapter 2.4).

3.7 Why this is the workhorse

Pattern Why windows fail KeyedProcessFunction approach
Dedup by event id window = fixed interval, boundaries leak duplicates ValueState<Boolean> per id, cleanup timer = retention (Chapter 18)
Hysteresis (alert on N breaches, clear after M OKs) needs state across arbitrary time per-key counter/state + timer to expire stale breaches (Chapter 22)
Sessionization with custom rules session windows only support a gap keep session state, one timer per session end (Chapter 20)
Timeouts / "missing heartbeat" no event means no window fires timer fires with no event (3.3)
Enrichment with cache expiry state per key + expiry state + timer (Chapter 4, 19)

KeyedProcessFunction is a state machine you own. The price is that you own correctness: late data, timer cleanup, idempotence and state size are your responsibility.

3.8 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Timer storm: a timer per event, no coalescing, a hot key with a huge backlog. Result: checkpoint size and duration balloon. Coalesce (3.4) or keep one timer per key.
  • Event-time timer that never fires because the watermark is stalled (idle partition, Chapter 1.5, or no data).
  • Processing-time timer in a replay/backfill fires based on the wall clock, mid-replay. Use event time.
  • Stale timers: you changed the deadline but did not delete or ignore the old timer, so onTimer acts on outdated logic. Always validate against state (3.3).
  • Forgotten cleanup: no timer or TTL clears state, and key cardinality is unbounded (device ids, session ids).
  • Heavy work in onTimer/processElement: blocking I/O stalls the operator and creates backpressure (Chapter 11; Async I/O is the answer).
  • Timer registered in a non-keyed context: not possible; timers exist only after keyBy.
  • Fire storm after restore: processing-time timers scheduled before recovery fire immediately (verified), which can emit a burst of output after a restart. Design for it (idempotent sinks, Chapter 26).

3.9 Self-check

  1. Why does an event-time timeout not fire if the whole input stops, and what would you use instead?
  2. What does "at most one timer per key and timestamp" imply for a timer registered on every event?
  3. Why is onTimer safe without locking, and what does that not guarantee across different keys?
  4. Write the cleanup logic for a key that holds three state objects.
  5. Compare TTL and a cleanup timer for expiring dedup state.

  • Default timer storage in 2.3 and the non-default enum value of state.backend.rocksdb.timer-service.factory (only release-2.2 default ROCKSDB verified).
  • (Resolved inline: ordering, boundary, ctx.timestamp() type, open(OpenContext) signature.)
  • Behaviour of timers under State V2 / async state (Chapter 28): data unavailable.

Chapter 4: Joins and enrichment without SQL

Goal: after this chapter you can choose between window join, interval join, coGroup, connect + CoProcessFunction, broadcast state, a CDC-fed keyed-state table, and async lookup; and you can re-create by hand the semantics that the SQL temporal join (FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF) gave the article for free.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, idleness). Chapter 3 (timers, KeyedProcessFunction) helps; Chapter 5 covers TTL in depth.

4.1 Why the SQL temporal join is not used here

This book deliberately does not use Flink SQL. The article's enrichment used an event-time temporal join (FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF). It hides five decisions that you must now make explicitly in DataStream code:

What the temporal join did implicitly What you must write by hand
Keep a versioned table per key from a changelog A ValueState (latest) or MapState<ts, row> / ListState (versions) per key
Treat insert/update/delete rows as upsert/retract Explicit handling of tombstones (4.6)
Pick the version valid at the probe row's event time Buffer probes until the watermark passes their time, then look up (4.5)
Wait for the versioned side's watermark Your own rule: hold probes, or accept "latest known" (4.7)
Clean up old versions Your own TTL or timers (4.9)

Decide first which semantics you actually need: - As-of event time (deterministic, replayable): the value that was valid at the event's timestamp. Needs buffering + watermarks. - Latest known (processing-order): whatever the reference state holds right now. Simple, but not replay-stable. Reprocessing yesterday's data enriches with today's reference. Assumption: most operational enrichments are fine with this, billing/audit ones are not.

4.2 Window join, interval join, coGroup (stream-stream)

Verified (docs 2.3 joining page; API names checked with javap on flink-streaming-java 2.2.1): - Window join pattern: a.join(b).where(keySelector).equalTo(keySelector).window(assigner).apply(JoinFunction). Tumbling, sliding and session assigners are supported. Inner join only: unmatched elements emit nothing. Pairs are formed per window; in sliding windows one element can join in several windows. Result timestamp is the largest timestamp that still lies in the window (window end minus 1 ms), not the larger of the two element timestamps (docs quote; corrected from an earlier draft). Session window joins are inner joins too. - Interval join: a.keyBy(..).intervalJoin(b.keyBy(..)).between(lower, upper).process(ProcessJoinFunction); matches b.ts in [a.ts + lower, a.ts + upper], bounds inclusive unless lowerBoundExclusive() / upperBoundExclusive(). Event time only, inner join (verified: docs; between(Duration, Duration) takes java.time.Duration; inProcessingTime() exists but between then throws "Time-bounded stream joins are only supported in event time", javap bytecode). Result timestamp is the larger of the two element timestamps (verified: IntervalJoinOperator uses Math.max + setAbsoluteTimestamp). - coGroup: gives you both sides' elements per key and window as two iterables, so you can emit for unmatched sides (left/outer semantics by hand). Verified: a.coGroup(b).where(..).equalTo(..).window(..).apply(CoGroupFunction) with coGroup(Iterable<IN1>, Iterable<IN2>, Collector<O>) (javap), and the window function fills both lists from the window contents then calls coGroup, so one list is empty when a side has no elements (bytecode of CoGroupedStreams$CoGroupWindowFunction). The docs joining page itself has no coGroup text.

Window join:   |---- window ----|  every a x every b in the same window
Interval join: a@10 with bounds [-2s,+5s] matches b with ts in [8s, 15s]; no window alignment, per-element
Need Use
Events of two streams close in time, both "fact" streams interval join
Aligned batches (per minute totals of A with B) window join
Left/outer semantics, or custom handling of misses coGroup, or connect (4.3)
Reference data that lives for days NOT a stream-stream join: 4.4 to 4.8

Interval/window joins buffer both sides in state until the watermark passes the bounds. Both sides need healthy watermarks (Chapter 1.5). Late-data side output for interval join exists: sideOutputLeftLateData(OutputTag) / sideOutputRightLateData(OutputTag) on the object returned by between(...) (verified: javap KeyedStream$IntervalJoined; not mentioned in the docs page; exact lateness rule: operator isLate(long) not read in detail).

4.3 connect + CoProcessFunction

a.connect(b).keyBy(ka, kb).process(new KeyedCoProcessFunction<K,A,B,Out>() {...}) (after keyBy, use KeyedCoProcessFunction; plain CoProcessFunction has no timers/keyed state; both process overloads exist on ConnectedStreams, verified: javap): two inputs, one keyed state namespace, processElement1 / processElement2, plus timers. This is the general tool: you write the join. Both inputs are keyed by the same key, so state is partitioned and scales with parallelism. Ordering between the two inputs is not guaranteed; design for either arriving first. This is the correct replacement for the article's connect usage in anomaly detection (see Chapter 22).

Skeleton for "latest reference + buffer probes until reference exists" (sketch, not compiled):

public class Enrich extends KeyedCoProcessFunction<String, Fact, RefRow, Enriched> {
    ValueState<RefRow> ref;            // latest reference for this key
    ListState<Fact> pending;           // facts that arrived before the reference
    ValueState<Long> timerTs;

    public void open(OpenContext c) { /* getRuntimeContext().getState(descriptors...) */ }

    public void processElement1(Fact f, Context ctx, Collector<Enriched> out) throws Exception {
        RefRow r = ref.value();
        if (r != null) { out.collect(Enriched.of(f, r)); return; }
        pending.add(f);                                       // reference not here yet
        ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(f.ts + MAX_WAIT_MS);   // give up later: emit unenriched / DLQ
    }
    public void processElement2(RefRow r, Context ctx, Collector<Enriched> out) throws Exception {
        if (r.deleted) { ref.clear(); return; }               // tombstone: 4.6
        ref.update(r);
        for (Fact f : pending.get()) out.collect(Enriched.of(f, r));
        pending.clear();
    }
    public void onTimer(long ts, OnTimerContext ctx, Collector<Enriched> out) { /* emit leftovers as "unknown ref" */ }
}

OpenContext is the 2.x open parameter (verified: javap RichFunction.open(OpenContext) 2.2.1; this sketch compiled with javac against the 2.2.1 jars, apart from unrelated missing-transitive-class noise).

4.4 Broadcast state pattern (slowly changing reference data)

Mental model: the reference stream is replicated to every parallel task of the fact stream. Each task keeps a full copy in broadcast state and looks up locally. No shuffle of facts, no key needed.

MapStateDescriptor<String, RefRow> desc = new MapStateDescriptor<>("ref", Types.STRING, TypeInformation.of(RefRow.class));
BroadcastStream<RefRow> bc = refStream.broadcast(desc);
facts.connect(bc).process(new BroadcastProcessFunction<Fact, RefRow, Enriched>() {
    public void processElement(Fact f, ReadOnlyContext ctx, Collector<Enriched> out) throws Exception {
        RefRow r = ctx.getBroadcastState(desc).get(f.refKey);   // read-only here
        ...
    }
    public void processBroadcastElement(RefRow r, Context ctx, Collector<Enriched> out) throws Exception {
        ctx.getBroadcastState(desc).put(r.key, r);              // only this side may write
    }
});

(sketch, not compiled)

Verified constraints (docs 2.3 broadcast_state page; BroadcastProcessFunction / KeyedBroadcastProcessFunction / DataStream.broadcast(MapStateDescriptor...) checked with javap): - Only the broadcast side writes; the fact side gets a ReadOnlyContext. - No cross-task communication, so every task must apply the same updates. State updates must not depend on the order of incoming events, because order can differ across tasks. - All tasks checkpoint their broadcast state (not just one). Restore redistributes with no duplicates or loss. - Held in memory at runtime; provision for it. RocksDB is not supported for broadcast state. - KeyedBroadcastProcessFunction exists for a keyed fact side (gives timers on the keyed side; docs: timers can be registered in processElement, not in processBroadcastElement).

When to use: reference set that fits comfortably in heap on every task (rules, small dimension tables, tenant config). Memory cost = size x parallelism. Not for millions of rows.

Ordering trap: a fact can arrive before the reference version that applies to it, on one task but not another. Same job, same data, different tasks can enrich differently on a race. Buffer (4.3 style, needs KeyedBroadcastProcessFunction or own buffering) or accept it explicitly.

Figure 4.1: Broadcast state (left) versus connect plus keyed state (right).

4.5 Rebuilding "as-of event time" by hand

Store versions: MapState<Long, RefRow> (validFrom to row) per key, or a sorted list. For each fact at event time t: 1. Buffer the fact (ListState) and register an event-time timer at t. 2. When the timer fires, the watermark has passed t; the reference side (if its watermark also progressed) holds all versions <= t. 3. Pick the greatest validFrom <= t, emit, and prune versions older than the oldest buffered fact.

Cost: latency = fact lag behind reference watermark; state = versions + buffered facts. This is the part SQL did for you. The reference watermark must be combined into the operator's input watermark: in connect, the operator watermark is the minimum of both inputs (consistent with Chapter 1.5).

4.6 Keyed state fed by a changelog / CDC topic (upsert semantics)

Pattern: reference topic (compacted, key = business key) is read as a second source; connect with facts keyed identically (4.3). Treat records as an upsert stream:

Record Action on ValueState<RefRow>
value, key update (replace; last write wins)
tombstone (null value) or CDC op = delete clear(); later facts get "no reference"
update with older version/LSN than stored drop (guard with a version field; Kafka reorder across restarts/partitions can occur)
duplicate of same version idempotent overwrite
  • Decide what a delete means for facts already enriched (nothing, they are emitted) and for those still buffered.
  • Deserialization must accept null values (tombstones); a deserializer that throws on null kills the job (Chapter 12).
  • Keep before/after images separate: use the "after" image for upserts, key from the "before" for deletes. Assumption: Debezium-style envelope. Envelope format is a connector concern, not covered by the fetched pages.
  • Ensure both streams use the same key serialization and the same key partitioning logic in keyBy, not Kafka's partitioner.

4.7 Bootstrapping reference data before the stream (cold start)

Problem: at start, the fact stream is hot and the reference topic is behind. Facts see an empty table.

Strategy How Trade-off
Buffer + timeout 4.3 pending list with timer memory; need a "give up" rule
Start reference earlier separate job/savepoint pre-loaded via State Processor API (Chapter 30) operational complexity
Per-source offsets read reference from earliest, facts from a later offset does not guarantee the reference is done
Gate the facts process facts only after reference watermark / "caught up" marker latency at start; stall risk
Async lookup (4.8) query the store of record, no bootstrap external dependency

Watermark stalls from a lagging side: with connect/interval joins the operator watermark is the minimum of its inputs. A slow or idle reference partition holds the watermark, so timers (4.3, 4.5) and window joins stop firing while records still flow. Mitigations: withIdleness on the reference source (Chapter 1.5), watermark alignment (Chapter 1.6, 10), and make the reference side not drive event time for the fact side if you only need "latest known" (use processing-time give-up timers or a broadcast pattern whose reference side does not delay facts). Compacted topics often carry old timestamps; a reference stream with timestamps far in the past will hold the minimum back at start, then jump. WatermarkStrategy.noWatermarks() exists (verified: javap), but do not use it on the reference side of an event-time connect as a way to ignore it: bytecode shows the no-op source emits no watermarks and does not mark itself idle, and input channels start ACTIVE at Long.MIN_VALUE (StatusWatermarkValve), so the connected operator's minimum watermark would never advance and event-time timers would never fire (derived from bytecode, not runtime-tested: [unverified] at runtime). For "latest known" semantics use processing-time give-up timers on the fact side, or a broadcast pattern.

Idle-then-wake: after a reference partition has been marked idle, a delayed update arrives with an old timestamp; for upserts that is fine if you apply version guards (4.6), not timestamps.

4.8 Async I/O lookup as the alternative

Instead of holding the reference in state, query the system of record (database, service, cache) from AsyncFunction.

Verified (docs 2.3 asyncio page; AsyncDataStream / AsyncFunction signatures checked with javap 2.2.1): - asyncInvoke(input, ResultFuture) dispatches the request and completes the ResultFuture via callback; timeout() can be overridden. - AsyncDataStream.unorderedWait / orderedWait (plus ...WithRetry variants with AsyncRetryStrategy). Parameters: timeout (including retries; long + TimeUnit in the 2.2.1 signatures), capacity (max concurrent requests per parallel instance; int). AsyncRetryStrategy is used by the ...WithRetry variants. - Unordered emits as results finish, ordered preserves input order (buffers). In event-time unordered mode, order is kept only between watermarks. - The function itself is not multi-threaded; asyncInvoke must return quickly and use a non-blocking client or callbacks. - ResultFuture completes only on its first call. In-flight requests are recovered through checkpoints (exactly-once handling inside Flink; your external call must be idempotent/safe to repeat).

State-based (4.3/4.6) Async lookup
Consistency with stream time can be as-of event time reads current external value; not replay-stable
Cold start needs bootstrap none
Extra dependency at runtime none store availability and rate limits
State size grows with reference none (add an LRU cache)
Throughput local lookup bounded by capacity/latency/timeout

Details on tuning, caching and backpressure belong to Chapter 11; ML scoring uses the same operator (Chapter 31).

4.9 State growth

Source of growth Control
Interval/window join buffers bounds and window size; events held until watermark passes (stalled watermark means unbounded growth)
Reference per key (4.6) deletes/tombstones, TTL (Chapter 5) for keys not seen
Pending lists (4.3) give-up timer, cap size, DLQ
Versions (4.5) prune below the oldest pending fact
Broadcast state memory-bound on every task; no RocksDB

A stuck watermark is the most common cause of runaway join state. Alert on state size and watermark lag together (Chapter 13).

4.10 Decision guide

  1. Two fast fact streams, correlate within +/- seconds: interval join.
  2. Reference is small, changes rarely, needed on all keys: broadcast state.
  3. Reference is large or keyed, comes as CDC: connect + keyed state with upsert/tombstone handling.
  4. Need "valid at event time": versioned state + timers (4.5).
  5. Reference lives elsewhere, size/freshness better there: async lookup with a cache.

Figure 4.2: Decision guide from section 4.10.

4.11 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Join state grows without bound because a partition is idle and the minimum watermark never moves.
  • Cold start enriches facts with nulls; downstream treats null as "legit".
  • Tombstone not handled: deserialization failure, or deleted reference keeps enriching forever.
  • Broadcast update order assumed: tasks diverge on race.
  • Out-of-order or replayed reference records overwrite newer state without a version guard.
  • Interval join assumed to do left join: unmatched records vanish silently (inner only).
  • Async lookup with low capacity or no timeout handling: backpressure and stuck pipelines; retries re-hit a degraded service.
  • "Latest known" enrichment used for audit data: replays change history.

4.12 What the article got wrong here

  • The CDC temporal join relied on SQL DDL, a watermark on the changelog, and an implicit bootstrap. It never explained the cold-start race, deletes, idleness of the versioned side, or state growth. Chapter 19 rebuilds the blueprint using 4.3, 4.6 and 4.7.
  • It treated connect as a join; see Chapter 22 for the anomaly blueprint.

4.13 Self-check

  1. Which semantics does FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF give that "latest known" state does not?
  2. Why can two parallel tasks of a broadcast-state function produce different outputs for the same input?
  3. A tombstone arrives for key K while 5 facts for K are buffered. What are your options?
  4. The reference topic has an idle partition. Which timers stop firing, and what are two fixes?
  5. When is async I/O strictly better than a CDC-fed state table, and when worse?

  • Exact lateness rule of the interval-join late side output (API verified, rule not read).
  • noWatermarks() on a connected reference side: bytecode-derived stall, not runtime-tested.

Chapter 5: State types and state TTL

Goal: after this chapter you can pick the right state primitive for a job, configure TTL so state does not grow forever, say precisely what TTL does and does not promise, size state roughly, and choose a state backend.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (time), Chapter 3 (KeyedProcessFunction, where most state is used). Checkpointing of this state is Chapter 6.

5.1 Mental model

 keyBy(userId)           each parallel subtask owns a range of keys (key groups)
 ┌──────────┐            ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ record   │──hash────► │ subtask 2:  state[key=u17] -> {...}    │
 └──────────┘            │             state[key=u93] -> {...}    │
                         └────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Keyed state is scoped to (operator, current key). Inside processElement you only ever see the state of the key of the current record. It needs a keyBy first. This is what you use 95% of the time.
  • Operator (non-keyed) state is scoped to one parallel operator instance (e.g. a source remembering its Kafka offsets).
  • Broadcast state is operator state that is identical on every subtask, fed by a separate broadcast stream (5.4).
  • State is local to the task and snapshotted by checkpoints (Chapter 6). It is not a database you query from outside.

Figure 5.1: Keyed, operator and broadcast state per subtask, held in a local backend and snapshotted to checkpoint storage.

5.2 Keyed state primitives (verified against the 2.3 docs and the state interfaces' method signatures)

Primitive Holds Main methods Typical use
ValueState<T> one value value(), update(T) last seen record, flag "already emitted"
ListState<T> a list add(T), addAll(List<T>), get(), update(List<T>) buffer events until a timer fires
MapState<UK, UV> key-value map put, putAll, get, entries(), keys(), values() per-key sub-index, e.g. counts per device
ReducingState<T> one value, folded add(T) applies a ReduceFunction running sum/max, same in/out type
AggregatingState<IN, OUT> accumulator, exposes OUT add(IN) applies an AggregateFunction running average, different in/out type

All of them have clear() for the current key. You must call it yourself (or use TTL); nothing else removes state of a dead key.

Registering state: create a descriptor (name + type) in open(), get the handle via getRuntimeContext().

// sketch, not compiled
public class FirstSeen extends KeyedProcessFunction<String, Event, Event> {
    private transient ValueState<Boolean> seen;

    @Override
    public void open(OpenContext ctx) {                       // 2.x signature (verified: RichFunction.open(OpenContext))
        ValueStateDescriptor<Boolean> d = new ValueStateDescriptor<>("seen", Boolean.class);
        d.enableTimeToLive(StateTtlConfig.newBuilder(Duration.ofHours(24)).build());
        seen = getRuntimeContext().getState(d);
    }

    @Override
    public void processElement(Event e, Context ctx, Collector<Event> out) throws Exception {
        if (seen.value() == null) { seen.update(true); out.collect(e); }
    }
}

Choosing: prefer MapState over ValueState<HashMap> and ListState over ValueState<List>. With RocksDB (5.7), MapState entries and ListState appends are individual operations; a big value inside ValueState is deserialized and rewritten whole on every access.

5.3 Operator state

Used mostly by connectors/sources and sinks (e.g. Kafka offsets), rarely by application code. Redistribution on rescale is by pattern: even-split list, union list, or broadcast. If you find yourself implementing CheckpointedFunction in business logic, ask first whether keyed state would do. The interface is org.apache.flink.streaming.api.checkpoint.CheckpointedFunction with snapshotState(FunctionSnapshotContext) and initializeState(FunctionInitializationContext). The OperatorStateStore offers getListState (even-split redistribution), getUnionListState (every subtask gets the full list) and getBroadcastState(MapStateDescriptor) (verified: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 CheckpointedFunction, flink-core 2.2.1 OperatorStateStore; the mapping of method name to redistribution mode is from the method names and the docs' wording, not from bytecode).

5.4 Broadcast state

Operator-level state for propagating config or reference data to all parallel tasks, requiring a separate non-keyed input stream (verified). It is the building block of the enrichment pattern in Chapter 4. Key points to remember here: - every subtask holds a full copy, so it must be small; - it is a MapState declared by a MapStateDescriptor; - ordering between the broadcast stream and the data stream is not guaranteed, so design for "rule arrives after the event".

5.5 State TTL

Purpose: stop unbounded growth (user IDs, dedup keys, sessions). Builder (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 StateTtlConfig and StateTtlConfig$Builder):

// sketch, not compiled
StateTtlConfig ttl = StateTtlConfig
    .newBuilder(Duration.ofHours(24))                         // time to live
    .setUpdateType(StateTtlConfig.UpdateType.OnCreateAndWrite)       // default
    .setStateVisibility(StateTtlConfig.StateVisibility.NeverReturnExpired) // default
    .cleanupFullSnapshot()
    .build();
descriptor.enableTimeToLive(ttl);

Names confirmed from the 2.2.1 jar: StateTtlConfig.newBuilder(Duration) (the only newBuilder overload), Builder.setUpdateType(StateTtlConfig.UpdateType), Builder.setStateVisibility(StateTtlConfig.StateVisibility), build(), and the enums StateTtlConfig.UpdateType {Disabled, OnCreateAndWrite, OnReadAndWrite} and StateTtlConfig.StateVisibility {ReturnExpiredIfNotCleanedUp, NeverReturnExpired}. Convenience methods also exist: updateTtlOnCreateAndWrite(), updateTtlOnReadAndWrite(), neverReturnExpired(), returnExpiredIfNotCleanedUp(), useProcessingTime(), and setTimeToLive(Duration). Builder defaults: OnCreateAndWrite, NeverReturnExpired, processing time, background cleanup on (verified: bytecode of the Builder constructor). The sketch compiles against the 2.2.1 jars (checked with javac, see the verification log).

Update type and visibility

Option Values Meaning
Update type OnCreateAndWrite (default) TTL clock resets on create and write
OnReadAndWrite also resets on read (read becomes a write: extra cost)
Visibility NeverReturnExpired (default) expired value never returned, even if not yet physically removed
ReturnExpiredIfNotCleanedUp may return an expired value if cleanup has not reached it

Cleanup strategies

Strategy Method Backend Notes
Full snapshot .cleanupFullSnapshot() all expired entries are dropped from the snapshot, not from the live local state; shrinks checkpoint/savepoint size, helps restore
Incremental .cleanupIncrementally(int entriesPerCheck, boolean onRecordProcessing) heap only (docs: setting it for RocksDB has no effect) checks a few entries per state access (and optionally per record); defaults 5 entries, not per record
RocksDB compaction filter .cleanupInRocksdbCompactFilter(long queryFrequency, Duration periodicCompactionTime) (a one-argument (long) overload also exists) RocksDB expired entries removed when RocksDB compacts SST files
Disable .disableCleanupInBackground() all turns off the default background cleanup

Compaction filter, plainly: RocksDB only deletes data when it rewrites files. The filter checks entry timestamps during compaction and drops expired ones. queryFrequency is how many processed entries pass before Flink refreshes the "current time" the filter uses; the second argument is the age after which files are compacted, so old, untouched files are eventually rewritten. Defaults: queryFrequency 1000 entries and periodicCompactionTime 30 days (verified: bytecode of StateTtlConfig$RocksdbCompactFilterCleanupStrategy static initializer; semantics: docs 2.3 state page). Background cleanup is on by default in the builder (isCleanupInBackground = true, verified: bytecode), and the docs say a RocksDB compaction filter is used for background cleanup. The name and default of the RocksDB-module option that gates the filter live in flink-statebackend-rocksdb, which is not among the inspected jars: [unverified] whether the filter is active with no explicit cleanupInRocksdbCompactFilter call.

Figure 5.2: TTL expires an entry logically; cleanup removes it physically later, depending on backend and strategy.

What TTL does and does NOT guarantee

Does: - With NeverReturnExpired, your code never reads a value older than the TTL (per the docs' visibility option). - State eventually shrinks through the cleanup strategy you configured.

Does not: - Not event time. The docs state: "Only TTLs in reference to processing time are currently supported." A replay or backfill (Chapter 24) of old events gets processing-time TTLs, so an "event from last week" is treated as brand new. Replays run faster than real time, so state can pile up. - Not an immediate delete. Expiry is logical; physical removal depends on cleanup. Disk usage can lag far behind. - Not a timer. TTL fires nothing: no callback, no "on expiry" event. If you need an action at expiry (emit a session, close a window), use timers (Chapter 3). - Restore compatibility of TTL changes. Docs (2.3 state page): starting from Flink 2.2.0, migration between state with and without TTL enabled is seamless and does not fail on restore. Releases before 2.2.0 and changes to the TTL duration are not covered by that sentence: test a restore (Chapter 9). (verified: docs 2.3 state page via WebFetch) - Cost. TTL stores the last-modification timestamp with each value: on heap one extra Java object plus a primitive long, on RocksDB 8 bytes per entry (verified: docs 2.3 state page). - Granularity. All state collection types support per-entry TTL: list elements and map entries expire independently (verified: docs 2.3 state page). - Only processing time. StateTtlConfig.TtlTimeCharacteristic has the single value ProcessingTime (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1).

5.6 State size estimation (rules of thumb, Assumption: my own arithmetic, not from the docs)

state bytes  ≈ live keys × (key bytes + value bytes + per-entry overhead)
checkpoint   ≈ state bytes (full) | only changed SST files (incremental RocksDB)
  1. Count live keys at steady state: distinct keys seen within the TTL window, not distinct keys ever.
  2. Measure serialized value size with your real serializer (Chapter 8), not sizeof.
  3. Heap objects are several times bigger than serialized bytes; RocksDB data on disk is serialized, and per the RocksDBConfigurableOptions source on the release-2.2 branch the default for state.backend.rocksdb.compression.per.level is Snappy (verified: GitHub source via WebFetch summary; the RocksDB module jar was not inspected). Separately, execution.checkpointing.snapshot-compression (default false) compresses snapshots (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 ExecutionOptions).
  4. Multiply by growth you expect and by safety margin; then confirm in the Web UI checkpoint "State size" and in production metrics (Chapter 13).
  5. Per-key limit: with RocksDB a single key or value is capped at 2^31 bytes (verified). A ListState that grows without bound per key hits this and gets slow long before.

Capacity planning proper is Chapter 17.

5.7 State backends overview

HashMapStateBackend EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend ForStStateBackend
Stored as Java objects on heap serialized bytes in RocksDB (local disk) LSM-tree, supports remote filesystems
Speed fastest slower (serialization on each access) experimental
Limit JVM heap local disk n/a
Incremental checkpoints no yes yes
Status default if nothing is configured production use "experimental ... not fully available for production"

Config keys (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 StateBackendOptions/CheckpointingOptions, plus the 2.3 state backends page): - state.backend.type: default hashmap; also rocksdb, forst, or a fully qualified class name (old key state.backend is a deprecated alias) - execution.checkpointing.dir: where checkpoints go (deprecated aliases state.checkpoints.dir, state.backend.fs.checkpointdir) - execution.checkpointing.incremental: primary key for incremental checkpoints, default false; state.backend.incremental is a deprecated alias (bytecode withDeprecatedKeys) - state.backend.rocksdb.memory.managed: default true (docs 2.3 state backends page)

Incremental checkpoints record only changes since the previous checkpoint, shortening checkpoint time for large state (Chapter 6). Pointers: RocksDB tuning is Chapter 11; ForSt and the asynchronous State V2 API are Chapter 28 (experimental, no canonical savepoints per README facts). Rule of thumb (Assumption): small state and enough heap, use HashMap; state beyond heap or growing, use RocksDB.

5.8 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • State that is never cleared: no clear(), no TTL. Slow memory/disk growth, then OOM or a checkpoint that takes longer each day. Add TTL on day one.
  • TTL assumed to be event time: backfill floods state (see 5.5).
  • Big ValueState<List>/ValueState<Map> instead of ListState/MapState: rewrites on RocksDB.
  • OnReadAndWrite on hot keys: every read becomes a write.
  • Relying on ReturnExpiredIfNotCleanedUp for correctness: results then depend on cleanup timing.
  • Key skew: one huge key owns one subtask (Chapter 10).
  • Incremental cleanup on RocksDB: it is heap-only; use the compaction filter there.
  • Multi-tenancy: key by (tenantId, key) so tenants never share a state entry; per-tenant TTL needs separate descriptors or logic, since one descriptor has one TTL.
  • No uid() on stateful operators: state cannot be mapped back after a change (Chapters 6 and 9).

5.9 What the article got wrong

  • The dedup blueprint kept keys with no TTL and claimed exactly-once. Unbounded dedup state is the 5.8 first pitfall; Chapter 18 rebuilds it with TTL and honest guarantees.
  • Rolling-feature and sessionization blueprints (Chapters 20, 21) need explicit state lifetime; the article never discussed it.

  1. Why must keyBy come before keyed state, and what does "current key" mean inside processElement?
  2. A 24 h TTL job replays last month of Kafka data in two hours. What happens to state size, and why?
  3. State is on RocksDB. Which cleanup strategy applies, and why does cleanupIncrementally not help?
  4. Does TTL expiry trigger any code? What do you use instead?
