Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/fault-tolerance/state/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/state/state_backends/

Chapter 6: Checkpoints, savepoints, recovery

Goal: after this chapter you can configure checkpointing for a production job, explain what a barrier is and when to go unaligned, choose between a checkpoint and a savepoint, configure restarts, and say exactly what "exactly-once state" does and does not mean.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state, backends). Related: Chapter 7 (end-to-end delivery with Kafka), Chapter 9 (upgrades).

6.1 The mechanism: barriers

A checkpoint is a consistent snapshot of all operator state plus the source positions (docs: it persists "state and corresponding stream positions").

 source ──r r r [B n] r r──► map ──r r [B n] r──► keyed op ──► sink
                    │                    │              │
          snapshot offsets      forward barrier    snapshot state when
          then emit barrier                        barrier n arrived on ALL inputs
  1. The JobManager triggers checkpoint n; sources record their position and inject barrier n into the stream.
  2. An operator with several inputs waits until barrier n has arrived on every input (alignment), buffering/blocking the faster inputs, then snapshots its state and forwards the barrier.
  3. When every task has acknowledged, checkpoint n is complete.

Barriers travel inside the data stream, so a slow or backpressured pipeline delays them (Chapter 11).

6.2 Aligned vs unaligned (verified, "checkpointing under backpressure" page)

Aligned Unaligned
Barrier waits behind buffered data overtakes buffers; in-flight data becomes part of the checkpoint
Duration under backpressure grows "independent of the current throughput"
Checkpoint size state only state plus in-flight buffers (bigger, more I/O)

Unaligned limitations listed in the docs: no concurrent unaligned checkpoints; watermarks are generated after in-flight data is restored (can break ordering assumptions, see Chapter 1); long-running record processing can delay barrier handling; pointwise and broadcast connections are listed as limitations (ordering and consistency problems with rescaling and uneven consumer rates; the page's exact wording on whether Flink disables them was not confirmed); savepoints are always aligned and cannot run concurrently with unaligned checkpoints. Also from the 2.2.1 runtime bytecode: unaligned checkpoints are rejected for iterative jobs and for custom partitioners unless forced with execution.checkpointing.unaligned.forced (verified: javap StreamingJobGraphGenerator message strings, CheckpointingOptions).

Middle path: start aligned, switch to unaligned when alignment takes too long (aligned-checkpoint-timeout, below).

Figure 6.1: Aligned barriers hold back data behind the first barrier; unaligned barriers overtake it and in-flight data joins the checkpoint.

6.3 Configuration (keys copied from the 2.3 checkpointing page)

Enable: env.enableCheckpointing(<interval ms>), or set execution.checkpointing.interval (no default; verified: javap CheckpointingOptions.CHECKPOINTING_INTERVAL). Note the 2.x naming: keys live under execution.checkpointing.*. The older names are still accepted as deprecated aliases in 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 (withDeprecatedKeys in CheckpointingOptions): state.checkpoints.dir and state.backend.fs.checkpointdir for execution.checkpointing.dir, state.backend.incremental for execution.checkpointing.incremental, state.savepoints.dir and savepoints.state.backend.fs.dir for execution.checkpointing.savepoint-dir. Prefer the new names.

Key Default Java method What it does
execution.checkpointing.mode EXACTLY_ONCE setCheckpointingConsistencyMode(org.apache.flink.core.execution.CheckpointingMode) (setCheckpointingMode(org.apache.flink.streaming.api.CheckpointingMode) still exists but is @Deprecated) EXACTLY_ONCE or AT_LEAST_ONCE
execution.checkpointing.timeout 10 min setCheckpointTimeout(long) checkpoint is discarded after this
execution.checkpointing.min-pause 0 ms setMinPauseBetweenCheckpoints(long) minimum gap between end of one and start of next
execution.checkpointing.max-concurrent-checkpoints 1 setMaxConcurrentCheckpoints(int) overlapping checkpoints allowed
execution.checkpointing.tolerable-failed-checkpoints 0 setTolerableCheckpointFailureNumber(int) consecutive failures before the job fails over
execution.checkpointing.unaligned.enabled false enableUnalignedCheckpoints() allow barriers to bypass buffers (primary key; execution.checkpointing.unaligned is a deprecated alias)
execution.checkpointing.aligned-checkpoint-timeout 0 ms setAlignedCheckpointTimeout(Duration) aligned-to-unaligned switch time (0 = start unaligned; only relevant if unaligned is enabled; old key execution.checkpointing.alignment-timeout deprecated)
execution.checkpointing.externalized-checkpoint-retention NO_EXTERNALIZED_CHECKPOINTS setExternalizedCheckpointRetention(...) retention on cancel
execution.checkpointing.dir none checkpoint storage location
execution.checkpointing.incremental false incremental checkpoints (RocksDB / ForSt); primary key, state.backend.incremental is the deprecated alias
execution.checkpointing.savepoint-dir none env.setDefaultSavepointDirectory(String/URI/Path) default savepoint location

Resolved: the checkpointing page lists execution.checkpointing.unaligned.enabled, while the "under backpressure" page shows execution.checkpointing.unaligned: true. In the CheckpointingOptions bytecode of both 2.2.1 and 2.3.0, ENABLE_UNALIGNED is defined with the key execution.checkpointing.unaligned.enabled and withDeprecatedKeys("execution.checkpointing.unaligned"). So .enabled is the primary key and the shorter one is a deprecated alias that still works; use execution.checkpointing.unaligned.enabled. The backpressure page is stale. (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 CheckpointingOptions, plus a reflection dump of ConfigOption.fallbackKeys())

Any sample interval below is an Assumption, not a doc recommendation.

Tuning intuition

  • Interval: how much you re-process after a failure, and how long Kafka transactions stay open (Chapter 7). Typical starting range 30 s to 5 min (Assumption).
  • Timeout: must exceed worst realistic checkpoint duration; the 10 min default is usually enough until state is huge.
  • Min pause: guarantees the job gets breathing room between checkpoints; set it at a meaningful fraction of the interval if checkpoints are slow.
  • Tolerable failures: default 0 means one failed checkpoint restarts the job. Docs: it covers checkpoint IOExceptions, failures in the asynchronous phase on TaskManagers and checkpoint timeouts; failures in the synchronous phase always trigger a task failover regardless (verified: docs 2.3 checkpointing page). Raising it (e.g. 3) avoids restart storms from transient storage errors, but widens the window with no good checkpoint. Alert on it (Chapter 13).
  • Max concurrent: leave at 1 unless you know why.
  • Retention: use RETAIN_ON_CANCELLATION if you want to restore after a cancel, then clean up by hand (docs: "requires manual cleanup"). DELETE_ON_CANCELLATION means state is available only on job failure.
// sketch, not compiled
env.enableCheckpointing(60_000);
CheckpointConfig cc = env.getCheckpointConfig();
cc.setCheckpointTimeout(10 * 60_000);
cc.setMinPauseBetweenCheckpoints(30_000);
cc.setTolerableCheckpointFailureNumber(3);
cc.setExternalizedCheckpointRetention(ExternalizedCheckpointRetention.RETAIN_ON_CANCELLATION);
// ExternalizedCheckpointRetention is org.apache.flink.configuration.ExternalizedCheckpointRetention
// values: DELETE_ON_CANCELLATION, RETAIN_ON_CANCELLATION, NO_EXTERNALIZED_CHECKPOINTS (default)

The method names in this sketch compile against the 2.2.1 jars (javac check, see the verification log).

Checkpoint directory layout (verified): /checkpoint-dir/{job-id}/ containing shared/ (state spanning checkpoints), taskowned/ (state the JobManager must preserve), and chk-{n}/ (state belonging to a single checkpoint). Never delete shared/ by hand.

6.4 Checkpoint vs savepoint

Checkpoint Savepoint
Triggered by Flink, periodically you (CLI/REST), or stop
Purpose automatic failure recovery planned stop, upgrade, relocation, rescale
Lifetime managed by Flink (retention policy) permanent until you delete it
Alignment aligned or unaligned always aligned
Format backend-native canonical (default) or native

Figure 6.2: Checkpoints are Flink-managed recovery points; savepoints are user-triggered, always aligned and permanent.

Formats (verified): - Canonical (default): unified across backends, so you can restore with a different backend; stable; slower. - Native: backend-specific (e.g. SST files for RocksDB); faster; "available since Flink 1.15"; incremental RocksDB savepoints are self-contained. - ForSt does not support canonical savepoints (README facts table; Chapter 28).

CLI (copied):

bin/flink savepoint --type [native|canonical] <jobId> [<targetDir>]
bin/flink stop --type [native|canonical] --savepointPath <targetDir> <jobId>
bin/flink run -s <savepointPath> [-n] [-claimMode <mode>] <args>

-n allows non-restored state (use deliberately: it silently drops state of removed operators). Restore claim modes: NO_CLAIM (default; Flink does not own the files; forces a full checkpoint after restore), CLAIM (Flink owns and may delete the snapshot), LEGACY (deprecated; the docs say it is being removed in 2.0, but the RecoveryClaimMode enum in the 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 jars still contains LEGACY, so it is not gone; do not use it). The config key is execution.state-recovery.claim-mode (default NO_CLAIM; old key execution.savepoint-restore-mode is a deprecated alias). (verified: javap flink-core RecoveryClaimMode, StateRecoveryOptions)

Operator uids: set .uid("...") on every stateful operator. Auto-generated IDs depend on program structure, so refactors can make a savepoint unrestorable. Parallelism can change on restore (key groups, Chapter 10). Full upgrade rules: Chapter 9.

6.5 Restart strategies and failover regions

restart-strategy.type:

Strategy Value Parameters (default)
Fixed delay fixed-delay restart-strategy.fixed-delay.attempts (1), ...delay (1s)
Exponential delay exponential-delay ...initial-backoff (1s), ...max-backoff (1 min), ...backoff-multiplier (1.5), ...jitter-factor (0.1), ...reset-backoff-threshold (1h), ...attempts-before-reset-backoff (infinite)
Failure rate failure-rate restart-strategy.failure-rate.max-failures-per-interval (1), ...failure-rate-interval (1 min), ...delay (1s)
None none job fails immediately

Default: none without checkpointing; exponential-delay with checkpointing (verified: docs 2.3 task failure recovery page; javap RestartBackoffTimeStrategyFactoryLoader). All keys and defaults in the table above verified by a reflection dump of RestartStrategyOptions (flink-core 2.2.1); attempts-before-reset-backoff default is Integer.MAX_VALUE (shown as infinite); the no-restart strategy accepts none, off and disable (main value disable, verified: RestartStrategyType bytecode). Pitfall: fixed-delay with the default 1 attempt turns one flaky Kafka broker into a dead job; for a streaming job you want effectively unlimited, backed-off retries and an alert, not a silent stop.

Failover strategy: jobmanager.execution.failover-strategy = full (restart everything) or region (restart only the affected pipelined region). A region is a set of tasks connected by pipelined exchanges; batch exchanges mark boundaries. A typical keyBy job is one big region, so region rarely saves you anything for streaming; do not count on it. The Adaptive Scheduler is not the default for streaming jobs: jobmanager.scheduler defaults to Default and the option description says streaming jobs use the Default scheduler unless set (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1/2.3.0 JobManagerOptions, flink-runtime DefaultSlotPoolServiceSchedulerFactory, docs 2.3 elastic scaling page). The Adaptive Scheduler is opt-in (jobmanager.scheduler: adaptive, or reactive mode) and has no partial failover: it restarts the whole job, so jobmanager.execution.failover-strategy (default region) matters only for the default scheduler. See Chapter 15.

6.6 Recovery steps (what actually happens)

  1. A task fails (exception, lost TaskManager, failed checkpoint beyond tolerance).
  2. The restart strategy decides whether and when to restart.
  3. The failover strategy decides which tasks are cancelled.
  4. Flink picks the latest completed checkpoint (or the savepoint you named), redeploys tasks, and each task loads its state (for incremental RocksDB, re-downloads the needed files; large state means long recovery).
  5. Sources rewind to the recorded offsets; processing resumes. Everything after the checkpoint is reprocessed.
  6. Sinks: output written after the checkpoint is either rolled back (transactional sink) or repeated (non-transactional). See Chapter 7.

Figure 6.3: Recovery restores state and offsets from the same checkpoint; everything after it is reprocessed.

Manual recovery after the job is gone: bin/flink run -s <chk-n path> using a retained checkpoint (6.3) with the same uids.

6.7 What "exactly-once state" means

  • Guarantee: after recovery, each record affects Flink's internal state exactly once, because state and source offsets are restored from the same consistent snapshot.
  • It does not mean each record is processed once: records after the last checkpoint are processed again.
  • It does not by itself mean external effects happen once. Writes to a database, HTTP calls, or a non-transactional Kafka sink can repeat. End-to-end exactly-once needs a transactional or idempotent sink (Chapters 7 and 26).
  • execution.checkpointing.mode = AT_LEAST_ONCE weakens even the state guarantee (no alignment; duplicates can reach state).
  • TTL (Chapter 5) and side effects inside user code are outside this guarantee.

6.8 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Checkpoints that never finish under backpressure; fix backpressure first, unaligned second (Chapter 11).
  • Timeout too tight, then tolerable-failed-checkpoints = 0 causes a restart loop that makes things worse (more state to reload).
  • Checkpoint storage not writable or an expired credential: checkpoints fail, job keeps running until the tolerance is exhausted. Alert on consecutive failures and on "time since last successful checkpoint".
  • No uid(): savepoint restore fails after a harmless refactor.
  • Restoring with -n by habit: silently loses state.
  • Cancelling with DELETE_ON_CANCELLATION then needing the state.
  • Never testing a restore: practice stop-with-savepoint and restore in a non-production environment before you need it.
  • Savepoint storage shared across tenants/environments without access separation: use per-environment locations and access controls (Chapter 16).
  • Changing the state backend with a native savepoint: not portable; use canonical.

6.9 What the article got wrong

  • Claimed exactly-once for blueprints without a transactional/idempotent sink and without discussing checkpoint interval or restarts (Chapters 7, 18, 26).
  • Backfill blueprint ignored that recovery and replay reprocess data and repeat side effects (Chapter 24).

6.10 Self-check

  1. Why must a two-input operator align barriers, and what does unaligned change about checkpoint contents?
  2. Your job restarts after one failed checkpoint. Which key controls this, and what is its default?
  3. When would you pick a native over a canonical savepoint, and what do you lose?
  4. A job crashes 40 s after its last checkpoint. What is reprocessed, and why is state still "exactly-once"?
  5. Why is the region failover strategy of little help for a keyed streaming job?

6.11 Open items / unverified

  • Resolved from bytecode: primary unaligned key (.enabled; the short key is a deprecated alias), deprecated aliases of the dir/incremental/savepoint-dir keys, LEGACY still present in 2.2.1 and 2.3.0, retention default NO_EXTERNALIZED_CHECKPOINTS, checkpoint interval key execution.checkpointing.interval, Adaptive Scheduler not default.
  • Bounded/finished sources: execution.checkpointing.checkpoints-after-tasks-finish (default true, deprecated alias ...checkpoints-after-tasks-finish.enabled) exists (verified: javap CheckpointingOptions); detailed behavior beyond the option name is [unverified].
  • Changelog state backend: option state.changelog.enabled, default false (verified: javap StateChangelogOptions); operational behavior not covered here.
  • Checkpointing during recovery: Flink 2.3.0 adds execution.checkpointing.during-recovery.enabled (default false); the key is absent from 2.2.1 (verified: reflection dump of CheckpointingOptions for both jars). Semantics: [unverified].
  • [unverified] Whether the docs' wording "disabled" for pointwise/broadcast connections under unaligned checkpoints matches the runtime (page summary only).
  • [unverified] ForSt canonical-savepoint limitation (taken from the README facts table; belongs to Chapter 28).

Chapter 7: End-to-end delivery guarantees with Kafka

Goal: after this chapter you can say precisely where "exactly-once" holds in a Kafka -> Flink -> Kafka pipeline, configure KafkaSink transactions safely (prefix, timeouts, read_committed), and name the places where it silently degrades to at-least-once.

Version pin: Flink 2.2.x + Kafka connector 5.0.0 (no Kafka connector exists yet for Flink 2.3, see README). Facts below were checked against the Flink 2.2 docs and, for API names and defaults, against the real flink-connector-kafka-5.0.0-2.2.jar (javap/bytecode); anything else is marked [unverified].

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state), Chapter 6 (checkpoints, recovery).

7.1 Three guarantees, two different scopes

Guarantee After a failure and restart Typical cause
At-most-once records may be lost, never repeated no checkpoint restore, or NONE sink with source that skips
At-least-once nothing lost, some records processed or written twice replay from last checkpoint, sink not transactional
Exactly-once effect appears once needs source replay + state snapshot + atomic sink

Two scopes are routinely confused: - Exactly-once state (inside Flink): your keyed state and counters reflect each record once. Needs only a replayable source and checkpoints (Chapter 6). The docs say this holds only when the source participates in snapshotting. - End-to-end exactly-once: the external effect (Kafka topic, database) also appears once. Needs a sink that is either transactional (two-phase commit, 7.4) or idempotent (7.7).

 Kafka in ──► KafkaSource ──► operators (state) ──► KafkaSink ──► Kafka out ──► consumer
   replay by      offsets stored in           transaction commits only        isolation.level
   offset         checkpoint                  when checkpoint completes       = read_committed

7.2 Source side: offsets live in the checkpoint

  • The Kafka source stores its read position in Flink checkpoint state and restores from it. Kafka's committed offsets are not used for recovery. Docs: the source "does NOT rely on committed offsets for fault tolerance"; committing is only to expose progress for monitoring.
  • Offsets are committed to Kafka when a checkpoint completes (source property commit.offsets.on.checkpoint, default true; verified: bytecode of KafkaSourceOptions in connector 5.0.0-2.2). So consumer-group lag in Kafka tooling moves in steps at checkpoint cadence, and no checkpoint means a frozen group offset (Chapter 13).
  • Consequence: a restart from a savepoint/checkpoint replays from the snapshot offsets; a restart with no state falls back to your configured starting-offsets initializer (KafkaSourceBuilder.setStartingOffsets(...) with OffsetsInitializer.committedOffsets(), earliest(), latest(), timestamp(long) or offsets(Map); verified: javap). Know which one you are using (Chapter 24 for backfills).

7.3 KafkaSink and DeliveryGuarantee

Builder requirements (docs): bootstrap servers, record serializer, and for EXACTLY_ONCE a transactional id prefix. Verified from the 5.0.0-2.2 bytecode: build() fails for EXACTLY_ONCE without a prefix ("EXACTLY_ONCE delivery guarantee requires a transactionalIdPrefix"), the builder's default guarantee is NONE, and the builder pre-sets the producer property transaction.timeout.ms to 1 hour (Duration.ofHours(1)). Connector 5.0.0 also adds setTransactionNamingStrategy(TransactionNamingStrategy) with values INCREMENTING (the DEFAULT) and POOLING.

DeliveryGuarantee Behavior (docs wording condensed) Needs
NONE no guarantees; records may be lost or duplicated nothing
AT_LEAST_ONCE no loss; duplicates possible on Flink restart. Flushes pending records on checkpoint checkpointing enabled
EXACTLY_ONCE all records written in a Kafka transaction committed on a checkpoint setTransactionalIdPrefix, checkpointing

Sketch (Flink 2.2.x, connector 5.0.0; the builder calls were compiled with javac against the 2.2.1 and connector 5.0.0-2.2 jars):

KafkaSink<String> sink = KafkaSink.<String>builder()
    .setBootstrapServers("<KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP>")
    .setRecordSerializer(KafkaRecordSerializationSchema.builder()
        .setTopic("<OUT_TOPIC>")
        .setValueSerializationSchema(new SimpleStringSchema())
        .build())
    .setDeliveryGuarantee(DeliveryGuarantee.EXACTLY_ONCE)
    .setTransactionalIdPrefix("<TENANT_OR_JOB>-<SINK_NAME>")   // unique per job + sink, see 7.5
    .setProperty("transaction.timeout.ms", "<see 7.5>")
    .build();
stream.sinkTo(sink);

The source side of the same job needs env.enableCheckpointing(...) for any guarantee better than NONE to mean anything.

7.4 Two-phase commit, in one picture

 checkpoint n starts
   writer: flush, "pre-commit" the open Kafka transaction  -> committable_n  (stored in checkpoint state)
   all operators ack  -> checkpoint n COMPLETE
   committer: commit transaction of committable_n          -> records become visible
 crash between "complete" and "commit": on restore the committable is recovered from state and the commit is retried
 crash before "complete": the transaction is aborted/expired, source replays from checkpoint n-1

Why it works: the commit decision is made by the checkpoint, and the commit is retriable and idempotent from Flink's side. Why it is fragile: the transaction must still exist on the broker when the retry happens (7.5).

Figure 7.1: The commit decision is made by the checkpoint; the transaction must still exist on the broker when a commit is retried.

7.5 Transactions: prefix and timeouts (the settings that cause data loss)

transactionalIdPrefix. Kafka identifies transactional producers by transactional.id. The sink derives ids from your prefix: in connector 5.0.0-2.2 the id is <prefix>-<subtaskId>-<checkpointId> (verified: bytecode of TransactionalIdFactory.buildTransactionalId, recipe \u0001-\u0001-\u0001, called by both naming strategies). The builder also checks for a prefix that is too long (constant MAXIMUM_PREFIX_BYTES = 64000; whether it throws or only warns was not checked). - Must be unique per job and per sink in the same cluster. Two jobs with the same prefix fence each other's producers (zombie fencing aborts the other job's transactions). Assumption: the id layout above is an implementation detail of 5.0.0 and may change; treat the prefix as a stable identity. (Docs: use a unique prefix across applications on the same cluster "such that multiple running jobs do not interfere in their transactions" (verified: docs 2.2 Kafka page). The word "fencing" is Kafka's transactional-id mechanism and is not used in the Flink docs.) - Keep it stable across restarts/upgrades of the same job so leftover transactions can be found and resolved. Changing it during an upgrade can orphan open transactions [unverified: mechanism]; plan this in Chapter 9. What the 5.0.0 bytecode does show: leftover transactions are cleaned up by an abort strategy tied to the naming strategy (INCREMENTING uses PROBING, POOLING uses LISTING; enum pairing verified), and the ids they look for are built from the configured prefix, so ids with an old prefix are not obviously found by name; the exact abort behavior is not verified here. - Multi-tenant note: never share one prefix across tenants' jobs; include tenant/job id in it.

Timeouts. Docs: set producer transaction.timeout.ms to "maximum checkpoint duration + maximum restart duration or data loss may happen when Kafka expires an uncommitted transaction".

Setting Where Rule
transaction.timeout.ms (producer) sink setProperty >= max checkpoint duration + max restart/recovery time, with margin. The connector's builder default is 1 hour (verified: bytecode), so check it against the broker limit before relying on it
transaction.max.timeout.ms (broker) broker config must be >= the producer value, else the producer is rejected at init. Broker default (15 min per my Kafka knowledge) is [unverified]: not in the Flink docs or the jars, and the Kafka docs page could not be retrieved
checkpoint interval Flink transactions stay open for one whole interval, so interval must be well below the timeout

Failure mode: timeout shorter than (interval + checkpoint duration + restart). Broker aborts the transaction; on recovery the commit fails or finds nothing; the records are lost (source already advanced past them in the checkpoint). Alert on long restart times and checkpoint durations (Chapter 13).

7.6 Latency and the downstream contract

  • Docs: EXACTLY_ONCE "delays record visibility effectively until a checkpoint is written". End-to-end latency is at least one checkpoint interval. A 60 s interval means consumers see data in 60 s bursts.
  • Downstream consumers must set isolation.level=read_committed. Docs: if consumers read only committed data, no duplicates appear after a Flink restart. With read_uncommitted they see aborted/duplicate attempts, so you paid the latency for nothing.
  • A hanging open transaction (stuck job) blocks read_committed consumers at the last stable offset for that partition: one stalled job can stall unrelated consumers of the topic [unverified in Flink docs; Kafka behavior].

7.7 The idempotent alternative

If the sink can deduplicate by key (database upsert, compacted topic keyed by entity+version), use AT_LEAST_ONCE and make replays harmless. Costs: no visibility delay, no transaction timeout risk. Requirements: deterministic key, monotonic version or full-state overwrite (a replay must not move data backward). Docs list Cassandra as "exactly once only for idempotent updates". Full treatment in Chapter 26.

7.8 Sink V2 interfaces (what you implement for a custom sink)

Verified from the 2.2 sink docs and by javap of flink-core / flink-runtime 2.2.1 (legacy SinkFunction is deprecated and moved to a ...legacy package, still present in 2.2.1/2.3.0; do not use it, see Chapter 9). Sink, SinkWriter, SupportsWriterState, SupportsCommitter, StatefulSinkWriter, Committer are in org.apache.flink.api.connector.sink2; the three Supports*Topology interfaces are in org.apache.flink.streaming.api.connector.sink2. KafkaSink itself implements SupportsPostCommitTopology and a connector-internal TwoPhaseCommittingStatefulSink (committable = KafkaCommittable, holding producerId, epoch and transactionalId).

Interface Role
Sink serializable factory for SinkWriter
SinkWriter write(element, context), flush(endOfInput), writeWatermark(...)
SupportsWriterState writer state for recovery (needs StatefulSinkWriter)
SupportsCommitter enables exactly-once via two-phase commit; writer emits committables, Committer commits them
SupportsPreWriteTopology / SupportsPreCommitTopology / SupportsPostCommitTopology custom operators before writer / between writer and committer (aggregation) / after committer (cleanup, compaction)

7.9 Where exactly-once holds and where it breaks

Scenario Holds? Why / what to do
Kafka -> keyed state in Flink Yes offsets in checkpoint, state restored together (Ch 6)
Kafka -> Flink -> Kafka, EXACTLY_ONCE, read_committed consumers, timeout set correctly Yes two-phase commit (7.4)
Same, but consumers use read_uncommitted No they read uncommitted/aborted data
Same, transaction.timeout.ms < interval + restart No (loss) broker expires transaction (7.5)
AT_LEAST_ONCE sink No duplicates after restart; fine only if downstream is idempotent
Non-transactional, non-idempotent sink (HTTP call, e-mail, counter increment) No side effect repeats on replay
Two jobs share a transactionalIdPrefix No producers fence each other
Restart with no state (job resubmitted, earliest/latest initializer) No state and offsets are gone; this is a new job, not a recovery
Savepoint restore after changing source offsets, topic, or operator uids Depends replay range changes; Ch 9
Dedup in Flink state with a TTL shorter than the replay/redelivery window No key expires, duplicate passes; see 7.10
Upstream producer retries without idempotence (duplicates before Flink) No Flink sees two distinct records; exactly-once only counts what it reads
Cross-cluster or multi-sink fan-out Per sink each sink commits independently; one can commit while another's transaction expires

Figure 7.2: Where exactly-once holds in the chain and the numbered places it silently degrades.

7.10 What the article got wrong here

  • The dedup blueprint implied exactly-once by deduplicating with state, but never configured a transactional (or idempotent) sink, and the dedup state had no TTL/size bound, so it either grows forever or, once TTL'd, re-admits old duplicates. Dedup in state only removes duplicates older than the state's lifetime and already seen by Flink; it does not make the sink exactly-once. Chapter 18 rebuilds it; Chapter 26 covers idempotent sinks.

7.11 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Enabling EXACTLY_ONCE without checkpointing, or with a very long interval: data never becomes visible, or visibility is very late.
  • Checkpoint timeouts/failures repeatedly: transactions pile up, eventually expire (loss).
  • Restart storms: restart duration counts toward the timeout budget.
  • Broker transaction.max.timeout.ms lower than your setting: job fails at startup (good), but is often "fixed" by lowering the producer value below the safe bound (bad).
  • Forgetting read_committed in ops tools (console consumers, mirror makers, other Flink jobs).
  • Stateless restart masquerading as recovery (see table).

7.12 Self-check

  1. Why does the Kafka source commit offsets to Kafka at all, if recovery does not use them?
  2. Checkpoint interval 5 min, p99 checkpoint 40 s, worst restart 8 min. What is the minimum safe transaction.timeout.ms, and what must the broker allow?
  3. A downstream team complains that your output arrives "in bursts every minute". What is the cause and what are the two ways out?
  4. Your dedup state TTL is 1 h; the producer can redeliver after 2 h. Does the pipeline remain exactly-once?
  5. Which Sink V2 interface makes a custom sink two-phase-commit capable?

7.13 Open items / unverified

  • Resolved: transactional.id layout <prefix>-<subtask>-<checkpointId> and commit.offsets.on.checkpoint default true (bytecode, connector 5.0.0-2.2).
  • Behavior when the prefix changes (which transactions get aborted) [unverified]; only the naming/abort-strategy classes were inspected.
  • Broker default for transaction.max.timeout.ms (Kafka knowledge, not in Flink docs or jars) [unverified].
  • Last-stable-offset blocking behavior of stuck transactions [unverified in Flink docs] (Kafka behavior).
  • Whether connector 5.0.0 changed transaction handling vs 4.x: the 5.0.0 jar has TransactionNamingStrategy (INCREMENTING/POOLING) and abort strategies; a diff against 4.x was not done [unverified].

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/connectors/datastream/kafka/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/connectors/datastream/guarantees/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/dev/datastream/sinks/

Chapter 8: Serialization and type information

Goal: after this chapter you can predict which serializer Flink picks for your type, make Kryo fallback visible and avoid it, choose a Kafka wire format (JSON/Avro/Protobuf), and explain why serializer choice decides whether you can ever upgrade your state.

Version pin: Flink 2.2.x docs (Kafka connector 5.0.0 for the Kafka parts).

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state). Forward pointer: Chapter 9 (state evolution and upgrades).

8.1 Why Flink has its own type system

Flink serializes records between operators (network), and keyed state to the backend and into checkpoints. It builds a TypeInformation per type, which creates a TypeSerializer. Knowing the type lets Flink use compact, schema-aware binary formats and (for POJOs) evolve them. Anything it does not understand falls back to Kryo.

 type known to Flink?  ── tuple / row / POJO / record / primitive / Avro ──► dedicated serializer (fast, evolvable)
          └── no (generic type) ───────────────────────────────────────────► Kryo (slower, not evolvable)

Figure 8.1: Which serializer Flink picks, and why Kryo fallback blocks state evolution.

8.2 POJO rules (verified, 2.2 docs)

A class is a POJO if: 1. it is public and standalone (no non-static inner class); 2. it has a public no-argument constructor; 3. every non-static, non-transient field is public, or has a public getter and setter (JavaBean naming).

Java records are recognized as POJO types (docs: "since Flink 1.19"); they use the canonical constructor, so rules 2 and 3 do not apply. Sketch, not compiled:

public record Reading(String deviceId, long tsMillis, double value) {}   // record: OK
public class Event { public String key; public long ts; public Event() {} }  // classic POJO: OK

Common ways to silently lose POJO status: a non-public field without getter/setter, a missing no-arg constructor, a non-static inner class, a field of an interface/abstract type (that field alone becomes generic/Kryo). Chapter 1's Event follows these rules.

8.3 Type erasure, TypeHint and returns()

Java erases generics, so for lambdas Flink cannot see Tuple2<String,Integer> at runtime. Fixes (verified): - .returns(new TypeHint<Tuple2<String, Integer>>(){}) (anonymous subclass keeps the generic info); - .returns(SomeType.class) for non-parameterized types; - or build a TypeInformation manually. Prefer named classes/records over generic tuples and lambdas: they avoid the problem and make state types readable (Chapter 9).

8.4 Kryo fallback: cost and risk

When Flink cannot analyze a type it "falls back to Kryo". Costs: - Performance: slower serialization and larger bytes per record, a cost paid on every network hop and every state access (heavy with RocksDB, Chapter 11). Magnitude depends on the type [unverified: no benchmark fetched]. - State compatibility: docs: "When Kryo is used, there is no possibility for the framework to verify if any incompatible changes have been made", and a type contained in a Kryo-serialized type cannot evolve. A generic-typed value in state is a trap at the next upgrade. - Flink 2.0 upgraded Kryo to 5.6 (release notes) and state compatibility between 1.x and 2.x is not guaranteed. Anything Kryo-serialized in 1.x state is therefore a double risk; see Chapter 9.

Make Kryo loud (config keys verified)

Key Effect
pipeline.generic-types: false throws UnsupportedOperationException for types that would need Kryo (default true). Use in tests and CI, ideally in production
pipeline.force-kryo: true forces Kryo for POJOs (rarely wanted)
pipeline.force-avro: true serializes POJOs with Avro; needs flink-avro
pipeline.serialization-config registers custom serializers per type; type is pojo, kryo or typeinfo (verified: javap PipelineOptions description)

Sketch, not compiled:

Configuration conf = new Configuration();
conf.set(PipelineOptions.GENERIC_TYPES, false);   // constant verified: key pipeline.generic-types, default true
StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment(conf);

Registering a Kryo serializer in 2.x uses the config, not ExecutionConfig methods (removed in 2.0, confirmed: no Kryo methods in the 2.2.1 ExecutionConfig jar signatures; release notes list registerTypeWithKryoSerializer, addDefaultKryoSerializer, registerKryoType, getDefaultKryoSerializerClasses, getRegisteredKryoTypes). kryo-type is default or registered and requires a class field (verified: PipelineOptions description in the jar, same example as the docs' third-party serializers page):

pipeline.serialization-config:
  - org.example.MyType: {type: kryo, kryo-type: registered, class: org.example.MySerializer}

Custom serializers must extend Kryo's Serializer. Flink 2.0 also added more efficient built-in serializers for Map/List/Set, on by default.

8.5 Wire formats for Kafka

Distinct from Flink's internal serialization: this is what sits in Kafka topics.

Format Flink side Pros Cons
JSON DeserializationSchema (custom or Jackson-based) readable, no schema service big, slow, schema drift undetected; null/typo handling is yours
Avro AvroDeserializationSchema.forSpecific(Class) / .forGeneric(Schema) (package org.apache.flink.formats.avro); ConfluentRegistryAvroDeserializationSchema.forSpecific(Class, url) / .forGeneric(Schema, url) (package org.apache.flink.formats.avro.registry.confluent); modules flink-avro and (registry) flink-avro-confluent-registry [module name for the registry class: inferred from its source path] compact, evolvable, registry-checked generic records are "data intensive and slow" (docs); prefer specific classes
Protobuf custom DeserializationSchema/Kafka Deserializer; for Flink-internal use the com.twitter.chill.protobuf.ProtobufSerializer Kryo serializer (chill-protobuf 0.7.6 plus protobuf-java 3.7.0+, docs third-party serializers page) compact, strong evolution rules no first-class DataStream Kafka helper found in the docs or the core/connector jars [unverified]

Kafka source hooks (verified: javap connector 5.0.0-2.2): KafkaSourceBuilder.setDeserializer(KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema) (whole ConsumerRecord<byte[], byte[]>: key, headers, timestamp, via deserialize(ConsumerRecord, Collector)) or setValueOnlyDeserializer(DeserializationSchema); KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema.valueOnly(Class<? extends Deserializer>) wraps Kafka's own Deserializer classes.

Rules of thumb: - Deserialization failures must not kill the job in a loop: return null / emit to a dead-letter path (Chapter 12). (verified: the default DeserializationSchema.deserialize(byte[], Collector) skips a null result, javap flink-core 2.2.1; that the Kafka source wrapper uses that default method was not checked.) - Deserialize into a POJO/record/Avro specific class, not Map<String,Object> or JsonNode (both become Kryo/generic in state). - Keep wire schema evolution (registry compatibility) separate from state evolution (Chapter 9); both must hold.

8.6 Schema evolution and why state cares (preview of Chapter 9)

Verified rules: evolution supported only for POJO and Avro types, and only when restoring from savepoints (Flink >= 1.8). - POJO: fields may be removed (dropped) or added (Java default value); field types cannot change; class name and namespace must stay. - Avro: any change that is compatible under Avro schema resolution; generated classes must not be relocated or change namespace. - Keys: evolution of key schemas is not supported. - Kryo: no evolution, no verification.

Implication: pick state value types now (POJO/record/Avro) because you cannot fix a Kryo-serialized state later without state migration tools (Chapter 30).

8.7 Performance notes

  • Avoid generic tuples and Object fields in hot paths; prefer flat POJOs/records with primitives.
  • Reuse objects only if you understand pipeline.object-reuse (default false). The option description in the jar: when enabled, objects Flink uses for deserialization and for passing data to user functions are reused, which can cause bugs if the function is not aware of it (verified: javap PipelineOptions).
  • Large nested collections in ValueState are rewritten whole on each update with RocksDB; use MapState/ListState (Chapter 5, 11).
  • Measure: serialization CPU shows up as busy time in operators (Chapter 1.7 metrics, Chapter 13).

8.8 Pitfalls

  • Lambda returning generics without returns(...): InvalidTypesException at job build.
  • A field typed as an interface makes that field Kryo-serialized even if the class looks like a POJO.
  • Adding transient/non-POJO fields during a "small refactor" changes the serializer and breaks restore.
  • Changing the package/class name of a state type breaks restore (docs: class identity required).
  • Enabling pipeline.generic-types: false late: expect failures that reveal existing Kryo usage, which is the point.

8.9 Self-check

  1. Name three ways a class that "looks like a POJO" is actually treated as a generic type.
  2. Why does .returns(new TypeHint<...>(){}) need the anonymous subclass?
  3. A state value contains a java.time wrapper type handled by Kryo; you add a field to the outer POJO. What can and cannot evolve?
  4. Why is turning off generic types a better review gate than reading code?
  5. Avro on Kafka evolves compatibly through the registry. Does that make your Flink state evolvable? Why not automatically?

8.10 Open items / unverified

  • Resolved: PipelineOptions.GENERIC_TYPES constant and default (javap flink-core 2.2.1); pipeline.object-reuse semantics (option description).
  • Performance magnitudes of Kryo vs POJO/Avro: no benchmark fetched [unverified].
  • Native Protobuf DataStream Kafka deserialization helpers in 2.2 [unverified] (none found in docs; the flink-protobuf format module was not inspected).
  • Whether Java 25 affects Kryo 5.6 reflection access: Java 25 support is undocumented (README) [unverified].
  • Serializer-snapshot/compatibility API details (TypeSerializerSnapshot) deferred to Chapter 9.

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/dev/datastream/fault-tolerance/serialization/types_serialization/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/dev/datastream/fault-tolerance/serialization/schema_evolution/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/dev/datastream/fault-tolerance/serialization/third_party_serializers/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/release-notes/flink-2.0/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/connectors/datastream/formats/avro/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/connectors/datastream/kafka/

Chapter 9: State schema evolution and upgrade safety (including 1.x to 2.x)

Goal: after this chapter you can upgrade a stateful job safely (UIDs, savepoint procedure, schema and parallelism changes), and you can state precisely what the official docs say about moving a Flink 1.20 job to 2.x, and what they do not say. This chapter gives a checklist. It does not make the upgrade decision.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state), Chapter 6 (savepoints), Chapter 8 (serialization and types).

9.1 Mental model: state is addressed, not discovered

A savepoint is a set of state blobs keyed by operator ID and, inside each operator, by state name and key group. On restore Flink walks your new job graph and asks "which blob belongs to this operator?". Three things must line up:

 savepoint blob  --(operator UID)-->  operator in new job
                 --(state name)--->   state descriptor in that operator
                 --(serializer)--->   bytes readable by the new type

If any link breaks you get one of: restore failure, silently empty state (new operator), or dropped state (flag, 9.5).

9.2 Operator UIDs: always set them

  • Without an explicit UID, Flink generates the ID from the job graph structure. The docs say default IDs "are likely to change if an application is modified" (upgrade guide), so a harmless refactor can orphan your state.
  • Docs: assign .uid(String) to operators; strictly required only for stateful ones, recommended for all.
  • Reordering or inserting operators is safe only with explicit UIDs.
  • Choose stable, human-meaningful names. Never reuse a UID for a different state shape.

Sketch (not compiled):

events
  .keyBy(e -> e.key)
  .process(new DedupFunction()).uid("dedup-v1").name("dedup")   // uid is the contract; name is cosmetic
  .sinkTo(sink).uid("sink-main");

Rules of thumb: set UIDs on sources and sinks too (they hold offsets and transaction state, Chapter 7); do this in the first release, because adding UIDs later changes the ID and breaks restore from the old savepoint (Assumption: standard behavior, implied by the generated-ID statement; test it on a copy). Data unavailable in the fetched pages for an official migration recipe for "retrofit UIDs onto a running job"; the State Processor API (Chapter 30) is the usual tool, [unverified] here (a jar check of flink-state-processor-api only shows the API exists; it does not establish that it can re-assign UIDs of a running job's state).

9.3 Savepoint-based upgrade procedure

Official three steps (upgrade guide): stop with savepoint on the old version, update the cluster, resume from the savepoint on the new version.

bin/flink stop [--savepointPath <path>] <jobId>        # old version: drains and takes savepoint
# ... deploy new jar / new Flink version ...
bin/flink run -s <savepointPath> [-n] <app args>       # -n = --allowNonRestoredState

Restore mode flag from the savepoints page: -claimMode with NO_CLAIM (default; Flink does not own the snapshot, first checkpoint after restore is full) or CLAIM (Flink owns it and may delete it per retention). (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 RecoveryClaimMode: values CLAIM, NO_CLAIM, deprecated LEGACY, DEFAULT = NO_CLAIM; config key execution.state-recovery.claim-mode, older key execution.savepoint-restore-mode; -n corresponds to execution.state-recovery.ignore-unclaimed-state, older key execution.savepoint.ignore-unclaimed-state; the CLI flags themselves are in flink-clients, not inspected.)

Checklist before cutover: 1. Take the savepoint from the job as it runs today (not an older one). Keep it; do not delete until the new job has a successful checkpoint. 2. Savepoint files must be reachable at the same absolute path from the new installation (upgrade guide). 3. Restore into a scratch environment first (separate topic/output, separate consumer group, no side effects). 4. Verify: restore succeeds, no "cannot map state" error, state sizes comparable, output matches expectations. 5. Keep a rollback: the old job version plus the same savepoint (valid only if you did not claim and delete it).

Formats: canonical (default, backend-independent, can switch backends) vs native (backend-specific, faster, since 1.15) (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 SavepointFormatType has CANONICAL and NATIVE; the "since 1.15" is from the docs). Intermediate savepoints (1.15+) do not guarantee recovery semantics identical to checkpoints (savepoints page). ForSt has no canonical savepoints (see README table, Chapter 28).

Kafka specifics (Chapter 7): the source stores offsets in Flink state, so restoring from a savepoint resumes from those offsets, not from the consumer group's committed offsets. Do not change the Kafka source UID unless you intend to reset offsets.

Figure 9.1: Savepoint-based upgrade procedure and rollback.

9.4 State schema evolution

Per the schema-evolution page of the docs:

Type serializer Evolution supported?
POJO yes
Avro (specific/generic) yes, per Avro schema-resolution rules
Kryo (fallback for generic types) no
Anything nested inside a Kryo-serialized structure no, even if the outer type is a POJO

POJO rules: fields may be removed (old values dropped at next snapshot); fields may be added (initialized to Java defaults); declared field types may not change; class name and namespace may not change. POJO evolution needs savepoints taken with 1.8.0 or newer. Avro: generated classes may not be moved to another namespace.

Keys cannot evolve. Docs: key structure cannot be migrated because it could lead to non-deterministic behavior (dropping a key field could merge distinct keys). Treat key types as frozen; changing them means a new operator UID and state rebuild (replay from Kafka or bootstrap with the State Processor API, Chapter 30).

Practical guidance: - Make every state type a real POJO (public no-arg constructor, getters/setters or public fields) or Avro. Check at startup that none of your state types falls back to Kryo (Chapter 8 shows how to disable generic types). - Do not put ListState<SomeThirdPartyClass> in state; wrap it. - To change a field type: add a new field, dual-read for one release, drop the old field in a later release. - Same-name state with a different serializer family (for example POJO to Avro) is a migration, not an evolution: use a new state name or the State Processor API.

9.5 Adding and removing operators, allowNonRestoredState

Change Behavior (savepoints page)
Add a stateful operator starts with empty state
Remove a stateful operator restore fails unless -n / --allowNonRestoredState
Reorder / insert operators correct only with explicit UIDs
Change chaining allowed (upgrade guide)
Change operator state data type not allowed (upgrade guide); schema evolution rules in 9.4 apply

-n is a footgun: it also hides a typo in a UID, so state silently vanishes and the job starts "clean". Use it only after you have listed which UIDs are expected to be dropped, and compare against the restore log. State of a removed operator is lost unless another operator takes it over (upgrade guide).

9.6 Parallelism and max parallelism (key groups)

  • Parallelism can be changed on restore from a savepoint with no special configuration (savepoints page).
  • Mechanism: state is split into key groups; the number of key groups equals max parallelism and is fixed for the life of the state. Each subtask owns a contiguous range of key groups. Changing parallelism redistributes ranges; changing max parallelism would change which key goes to which group.
  • Docs (parallel execution page): default max parallelism is "roughly" parallelism + parallelism/2, clamped to min 128 and max 32768. Exact rule (verified: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 KeyGroupRangeAssignment.computeDefaultMaxParallelism): min(max(roundUpToPowerOfTwo(p + p/2), 128), 32768), i.e. the sum is rounded up to a power of two. Explicitly changing max parallelism when restoring the original job causes state incompatibility.
  • Consequence: set setMaxParallelism(...) explicitly on day one, high enough for future scale-out, not extreme (state backends keep structures that scale with key groups). Parallelism can never usefully exceed max parallelism.
  • Trap: a job started with parallelism 100 got default max 256 (150 rounded up to a power of two); scaling beyond 256 later is impossible without state rebuild. A job started at parallelism 200 got 512 (300 rounded up). A job started at parallelism 4 got 128.
  • Default max parallelism of your current processor job: Data unavailable (check the job config and the savepoint metadata).

9.7 Flink 1.x to 2.x: what the official docs say

The key question: can a 1.20 savepoint be restored in 2.x?

Release notes for 2.0 (fetched, 2.3 stable docs site): "State Compatibility is not guaranteed between 1.x and 2.x." Users cannot expect to restore 1.x checkpoints or savepoints in 2.0.

What that sentence does and does not give you:

Question Answer from the docs
Is restore of 1.20 state in 2.x guaranteed? No (explicit statement)
Does it always fail? Data unavailable. "Not guaranteed" is not "impossible".
Which state types / serializers are affected? Data unavailable (release notes mention Kryo upgrade to 5.6 and new built-in collection serializers, see 9.8; the link to state compatibility is not stated)
Is there an official migration tool for 1.x state? Data unavailable in fetched pages
Does the upgrade guide's compatibility matrix include 2.x? The fetched summary covered 1.8.x to 1.20.x only; 2.x row [unverified] (not checkable from jars), re-read the live table

Where to ask or check (in order): 1. Re-read the live compatibility table on the "Upgrading Applications and Flink Versions" page of the 2.2 and 2.3 docs. 2. Release notes for 2.1, 2.2, 2.3: later releases may add statements. 3. Apache Flink user mailing list (user@flink.apache.org) and the dev list; Flink JIRA search for "state compatibility 2.0". 4. The FLIP that introduced the incompatibility (name [unverified]; search JIRA/FLIP wiki for "Flink 2.0 state compatibility" or "serializer"). 5. Empirical test (9.10): restore a copy of your real 1.20 savepoint on 2.2.x in a scratch environment. This is the only authoritative answer for your job's state types.

Safe working assumption (labeled): Assumption: plan as if state must be rebuilt, until the scratch restore proves otherwise. Rebuild options: replay from Kafka (needs retention covering the state window, Chapter 24), or bootstrap new state with the State Processor API (Chapter 30; operates on 2.x, but reading 1.x savepoints is itself [unverified]).

Figure 9.2: Evidence flow for 1.20 to 2.x; the purple box lists what the docs leave unverified or unavailable.

Removed or changed (from the 2.0 release notes)

DataSet API removed (use DataStream, or Table API)
Scala DataStream and DataSet API removed (use Java DataStream)

Jar check (CORRECTED): the public classes are gone, but org.apache.flink.streaming.api.functions.source.legacy.SourceFunction and ...sink.legacy.SinkFunction (plus RichSinkFunction, PrintSinkFunction) still exist in the flink-runtime 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 jars, annotated @Internal and @Deprecated, and StreamExecutionEnvironment.addSource(...) / DataStream.addSink(...) still accept them. The release notes list more removals than the summaries I fetched returned (the fetch is partial). For an exhaustive config-key rename list: Data unavailable; run the official config migration tool against your real flink-conf.yaml and diff. Renames that the jars do confirm (new key, with the old key kept as a deprecated key in bytecode, flink-core 2.2.1): state.backend.type (old state.backend); execution.checkpointing.incremental (old state.backend.incremental, default false); restart-strategy.type (old restart-strategy); execution.state-recovery.path / .claim-mode / .ignore-unclaimed-state (old execution.savepoint.path / execution.savepoint-restore-mode / execution.savepoint.ignore-unclaimed-state); taskmanager.memory.network.min / .max / .fraction (old taskmanager.network.memory.min / .max / .fraction). Deprecated keys are still accepted in 2.2.1, but may be removed later. 9.8 Related risks beyond "does it restore"

  • Release notes: Kryo upgraded to 5.6 and new built-in collection serializers enabled by default. Anything that was Kryo-serialized in your 1.20 state is the first suspect for incompatibility (Assumption, not stated by the docs as a cause).
  • Removal of registerKryoType() and friends changes how you declare types.
  • Config files must be migrated to config.yaml; the deployment (Kubernetes operator, Chapter 15) must support the target Flink version: Data unavailable here.
  • Metrics, REST and scheduler defaults may differ; re-validate dashboards (Chapter 13). CORRECTED: the README claims the Adaptive Scheduler is the streaming default, but the jobmanager.scheduler option description in flink-runtime/flink-core 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 says: batch jobs default to AdaptiveBatch, streaming jobs default to Default (verified: javap JobManagerOptions; see Cross-chapter log).

9.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • No UIDs: refactor, deploy, state gone or restore error.
  • -n used to "make restore pass": job runs, state silently empty, duplicates or wrong aggregates.
  • Max parallelism left at default and then capped; or changed and restore fails.
  • Kryo fallback types in state: no evolution path, first schema change forces a rebuild.
  • Changing a keyBy key type or key fields.
  • Savepoint path not reachable from new cluster; savepoint deleted by CLAIM retention before rollback.
  • Doing Java upgrade, Flink major upgrade and connector upgrade in one release: unattributable failures.
  • Testing restore only with a tiny synthetic savepoint instead of a copy of production state (size, Kryo types, timers).

9.10 Upgrade checklist (for a cautious production 1.20 job; decision is yours)

Preconditions - [ ] Every operator, source and sink has an explicit UID; max parallelism set explicitly. If not, fix in 1.20 first and run a release. - [ ] Inventory state types: which are POJO, Avro, Kryo? (Chapter 8) - [ ] Record current max parallelism and savepoint size. - [ ] Confirm Kafka retention covers the replay window if rebuild is the fallback.

Evidence gathering (answer the open question) - [ ] Read live docs: upgrading page compatibility table (2.x rows), 2.0 to 2.3 release notes. - [ ] Ask the user/dev mailing list and search JIRA (9.7). - [ ] Scratch restore: copy of production 1.20 savepoint onto 2.2.x with connector 5.0.0, isolated sinks and consumer group. Record success or exact error.

Code and config migration - [ ] No SourceFunction/SinkFunction, DataSet or Scala in code or dependencies. - [ ] Kafka connector 3.x to 5.0.0 on Flink 2.2.x; Source/Sink V2 only. - [ ] flink-conf.yaml to config.yaml; check removed keys (9.7). - [ ] Replace removed ExecutionConfig registrations. - [ ] Java: decide separately; 17 is documented default, 21 per current docs page, 25 undocumented.

Cutover (only if the scratch restore passed, otherwise use the rebuild path) - [ ] flink stop with savepoint on 1.20; verify files; keep them. - [ ] Deploy 2.x job, flink run -s <path> (no -n unless a named list of dropped UIDs exists). - [ ] Watch first checkpoint, state size, lag, late rate, output parity (Chapter 13). - [ ] Rollback plan tested: old image plus the same savepoint.

9.11 Self-check

  1. Why is .uid() on a stateless map optional but on a source still wise?
  2. A job started at parallelism 200 with default max parallelism. What is the ceiling, and what does raising it cost?
  3. You removed an operator and used -n. How do you prove you dropped only what you intended?
  4. Which state types in your job would block schema evolution, and how do you find them?
  5. The docs say state compatibility is "not guaranteed" between 1.x and 2.x. What experiment turns that into a fact for your job?
