Chapter 10: Parallelism, partitions, key skew, and watermark alignment

Goal: after this chapter you can size parallelism against Kafka partitions and max parallelism, explain slots and chaining, recognise a hot key, apply two-phase (salted) aggregation, and say precisely what watermark alignment does in 2.3.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, idleness), Chapter 5 (keyed state), Chapter 6 (savepoints).

10.1 Four numbers that are often confused

Number Set by Meaning Changeable later?
Parallelism operator / env / client / config how many parallel subtasks an operator runs now yes (restart from savepoint)
Max parallelism setMaxParallelism() (operator, env, or system level) number of key groups; upper bound for future parallelism not safely (see below)
Task slots taskmanager.numberOfTaskSlots (default 1, verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 TaskManagerOptions) resource slices offered per TaskManager yes
Kafka partitions Kafka topic upper bound of useful source parallelism Kafka-side decision

Verified facts (parallel execution docs, 2.3): - Default max parallelism is "roughly operatorParallelism + (operatorParallelism / 2)" with a lower bound of 128 and an upper bound of 32768. Exact rule (verified: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 KeyGroupRangeAssignment.computeDefaultMaxParallelism): min(max(roundUpToPowerOfTwo(p + p/2), 128), 32768), so parallelism 100 gives 256, not 150. - Max parallelism determines the number of key groups. Too large costs state-backend overhead (structures scale with key groups). - Changing max parallelism when recovering from a savepoint causes state incompatibility. Pick it up front with headroom (Chapter 9).

Rules of thumb: - Source parallelism > Kafka partitions gives idle source subtasks (and idle-watermark trouble, 10.6). Source parallelism < partitions is fine; a subtask reads several partitions. - Parallelism of keyed operators must be <= max parallelism. Parallelism that does not divide max parallelism evenly gives uneven key-group counts per subtask (some subtasks get one more group). (verified: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 KeyGroupRangeAssignment.computeKeyGroupRangeForOperatorIndex: subtask i owns key groups ceil(i*maxP/p) to floor(((i+1)*maxP-1)/p), contiguous ranges whose sizes differ by at most one; a key group g goes to subtask g*p/maxP; it throws if max parallelism is smaller than parallelism.)

10.2 Slots, slot sharing, chaining

 TaskManager = 1 JVM, N slots (managed memory split per slot; CPU is NOT isolated)
 slot 1: [Source->Map->Filter (chained)] [keyed Window] [Sink]   <- one pipeline slice, slot sharing
 slot 2: [Source->Map->Filter (chained)] [keyed Window] [Sink]
  • A slot is "a fixed subset of resources of the TaskManager"; currently slots separate managed memory only, not CPU.
  • Slot sharing (default): subtasks of different operators of one job may share a slot. Consequence: a cluster needs as many slots as the job's highest parallelism, not the sum.
  • Chaining: adjacent operators are fused into one task (one thread), cutting handover and serialization cost. Controls: startNewChain(), disableChaining(), slotSharingGroup("name").
  • When to break the defaults: isolate a heavy operator (for example a RocksDB-heavy window or Async I/O stage, Chapter 11) into its own slot sharing group; or break a chain so a slow operator shows up separately in backpressure metrics.

10.3 How records reach subtasks

Call Behaviour (verified, operators docs)
keyBy(...) hash partitioning; same key always to same subtask; keys must have proper hashCode() (no arrays, no POJOs without it)
rebalance() round-robin over all downstream subtasks (network shuffle) (verified: method DataStream#rebalance() exists, javap flink-runtime 2.2.1; the round-robin wording is from the operators docs and the 2.3 adaptive-partitioner option text, which names rebalance and rescale as the round-robin-style partitioners)
rescale() round-robin to a subset of downstream subtasks; local transfer where possible; with 2 upstream and 6 downstream, each upstream feeds 3
shuffle() uniform random
broadcast() every element to all subtasks (Chapter 4)
partitionCustom(...) your Partitioner

Use rebalance() after a source whose partitions are uneven (some Kafka partitions busier) when the next stage is not keyed. Use rescale() when you only need local smoothing between stages of different parallelism and want to avoid a full shuffle. Neither helps keyed stages: keyBy decides placement.

10.4 Key skew and hot keys

Mental model: keyBy maps key -> key group -> subtask. Distribution is by key, not by volume. One tenant or device producing 50% of traffic pins 50% of the load on one subtask while the rest idle (blue in the web UI, one red box).

Detect (metrics verified in Chapter 1 / 10.2 of Chapter 11): per-subtask busyTimeMsPerSecond very uneven; one subtask backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond high upstream of it; per-subtask records-in uneven (metric numRecordsIn and rate numRecordsInPerSecond, verified: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 MetricNames; metrics are reported per subtask); checkpoint state size very uneven across subtasks. The web UI "Subtasks" view per vertex shows the imbalance without any code.

Mitigations, in order of cost: 1. Check the key: tenant id alone is a poor key if tenants are wildly unequal; add a second dimension (device id, hour bucket) if semantics allow. 2. Raise max parallelism headroom so the hash spreads many more key groups (does not help a single hot key). 3. Two-phase aggregation with salt for associative aggregates (count, sum, min, max, HLL sketches):

// (sketch, not compiled) phase 1: spread hot key over S salts, partial-aggregate; phase 2: merge
int S = 8;
DataStream<Partial> p1 = events
    .map(e -> Tuple2.of(e.key + "#" + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(S), e))   // salted key
    .returns(Types.TUPLE(Types.STRING, Types.POJO(Event.class)))   // lambdas lose generics; give the type explicitly
    .keyBy(t -> t.f0)
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
    .aggregate(new PartialAgg());                          // emits (key, windowEnd, partial)

DataStream<Result> p2 = p1
    .keyBy(p -> p.key + "|" + p.windowEnd)                 // original key + window end
    .window(TumblingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(1)))   // or a timer on windowEnd (Chapter 3)
    .aggregate(new MergeAgg());

Caveats: only for mergeable aggregates; not for per-key ordered logic or dedup (Chapter 18) where all records of a key must meet in one place; random salt makes replays non-deterministic in partial grouping (the merged result is still correct if the aggregate is associative and commutative, but floating point may differ); phase 2 adds latency of one window. If the aggregate is not mergeable, the options are a bigger subtask for that key, a custom partitionCustom plus own state, or a pre-aggregate before the shuffle (local combine; [unverified] whether DataStream offers a built-in one in 2.3; the DataStream method list in flink-runtime 2.2.1 has no obviously named local-aggregation method, but absence by name is not proof).

Figure 10.1: Key skew and the two-phase (salted) aggregation fix.

10.5 Adaptive partition selection (Flink 2.3, opt-in)

Verified from the 2.3 release notes (FLINK-31655, FLIP-339): - Replaces round-robin with load-aware routing to the least-loaded downstream channel, for non-keyed redistribution. - Release notes cite roughly 3x throughput improvement in benchmarks under skewed processing (slow downstream subtask), not skewed keys. - Config: taskmanager.network.adaptive-partitioner.enabled (default false), taskmanager.network.adaptive-partitioner.max-traverse-size (default 4).

Applies to rebalance and rescale partitioners (verified: option description in javap flink-core 2.3.0 NettyShuffleEnvironmentOptions: "adaptive partitioner feature for rescale and rebalance partitioners based on the load of the downstream tasks"; defaults false and 4 confirmed in bytecode; the keys are absent from 2.2.1). max-traverse-size is the maximum number of channels traversed when looking for the most idle channel. Not verified: interaction with ordering, maturity. Does not fix hot keys (keyed routing is deterministic). Test before enabling; it is off by default.

10.6 Idle partitions revisited

Chapter 1.5 covered the mechanism: watermark = min over inputs, so an empty partition stalls event time. Production checklist: - Source parallelism greater than partitions creates permanently idle subtasks. Match them, or set withIdleness. - withIdleness(Duration) is the lever (docs: marks unproductive inputs as idle, so watermarks continue). Cost: a waking partition may carry data older than the watermark, so it arrives late. - Idleness and alignment are separate features (both are set on WatermarkStrategy: withIdleness(Duration) and withWatermarkAlignment(String, Duration[, Duration]), verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1). An idle split should not hold back alignment groups; exact interplay [unverified] (not determinable from signatures). - Quiet tenants/topics at night are the typical trigger. Alert on watermark lag (Chapter 13), not only on consumer lag.

10.7 Watermark alignment

WatermarkStrategy.<Event>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(20))
    .withWatermarkAlignment("alignment-group-1", Duration.ofSeconds(20), Duration.ofSeconds(1));

Verified (2.3 docs; signatures verified by javap flink-core 2.2.1): group label binds sources that share alignment; max drift is the allowed watermark distance between sources in the group; update interval is how often watermarks are exchanged between TaskManagers and JobManager. Sources ahead are paused while lagging ones are read. Requirements: FLIP-27 sources only; not available when assigning watermarks after the source with DataStream#assignTimestampsAndWatermarks. Split-level alignment (since 1.17) needs source support for pause/resume; for upgrades from 1.15.x-1.16.x the docs mention pipeline.watermark-alignment.allow-unaligned-source-splits (verified: key exists in javap flink-core 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 PipelineOptions, default false).

Why: reading a topic with a backlog, partitions race at different speeds; the fast ones fill window state with far-future data while slow ones hold the watermark. Alignment bounds that state growth. Tradeoff: throttled sources, so total backlog drain can be slower or limited by the slowest partition.

What changed in 2.3 (verified from release notes, FLINK-37399)

  • Problem stated: announcement delays "inadvertently limiting how quickly a job could process a backlog".
  • Fix: a watermark alignment buffer (default size 3) delays applying the alignment algorithm.
  • Config: pipeline.watermark-alignment.buffer-size; setting it to 0 restores Flink 2.2 behaviour. (verified: javap flink-core 2.3.0 PipelineOptions.WATERMARK_ALIGNMENT_BUFFER_SIZE: int, default 3; the key is absent from 2.2.1.)
  • Mechanism (from the option's own description in the 2.3.0 jar): a ring buffer of watermark samples, updated at every updateInterval. When pausing consumption, the max allowed watermark is compared against the oldest sample in the ring buffer instead of the latest. So the unit of "size 3" is update intervals: with the default, splits may produce an arbitrary number of records for about 3 * updateInterval before alignment can pause them. The description says 3 was chosen to cover a round trip of 2 update intervals plus one more for network/GC hiccups, and that buffer size 1 can under-utilise resources when processing a backlog.
  • Not verified: tuning advice beyond that. Treat the default as a behaviour change when upgrading; if drift suddenly exceeds your maxDrift after 2.3, test buffer-size: 0.

10.8 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Parallelism changes after the first savepoint are fine; max parallelism changes are not.
  • keyBy on a low-cardinality key (country, tenant tier): at most as many busy subtasks as keys.
  • Salting a dedup or ordered-per-key job silently breaks correctness.
  • Alignment on a source with idle partitions plus no idleness: group minimum stalls, whole group pauses. Combine deliberately.
  • Source parallelism = partitions but partitions uneven: add rebalance() before CPU-heavy non-keyed work.
  • Slot sharing hides the real bottleneck: one fat operator slows every co-located subtask in the slot (CPU is not isolated).

10.9 Self-check

  1. Job has 12 Kafka partitions, max parallelism 128, source parallelism 24. What is idle, and what watermark symptom appears?
  2. Why does rescale() not fix a hot key?
  3. Which aggregates can use two-phase salting, and which cannot?
  4. After upgrading to 2.3 alignment seems looser. Which key do you test and what value restores 2.2 behaviour?
  5. Why can you raise parallelism but not max parallelism on a running stateful job?

10.10 Open items / unverified

  • Idle-vs-alignment interplay; built-in local pre-aggregation in DataStream.
  • Adaptive partition selection: ordering interaction and maturity.
  • Resolved by jar inspection (see VERIFICATION-LOG-09-12.md): alignment buffer mechanism, covered partitioners, key-group formula, records-in metric names.

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/release-notes/flink-2.3/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/event-time/generating_watermarks/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/execution/parallel/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/operators/overview/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/flink-architecture/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/deployment/config/ (partial)

Chapter 11: Backpressure, memory, RocksDB tuning, and Async I/O

Goal: after this chapter you can read backpressure to find the real bottleneck, reason about the TaskManager memory model, apply first-pass RocksDB and incremental-checkpoint settings, and call an external service with Async I/O without blocking the pipeline.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state), Chapter 6 (checkpoints), Chapter 10 (parallelism, skew).

11.1 Reading backpressure

Mental model: buffers between subtasks are bounded. When a downstream subtask is slow, its input buffers fill, the upstream cannot write, and it becomes "back pressured". Pressure propagates backwards; the culprit is the first busy task after the pressured ones, not the pressured ones.

Verified metrics (back pressure docs, 2.3; names confirmed by javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 MetricNames), per subtask, per second, summing to about 1000 ms: - busyTimeMsPerSecond: doing work. - idleTimeMsPerSecond: waiting for input. - backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond: unable to output because downstream buffers are full.

Web UI (verified): job graph colours: blue = idle, red = fully busy, black = fully back pressured, shades in between. Back Pressure tab status: OK (0-10% back pressured), LOW (>10-50%), HIGH (>50-100%). Values are averages over a few seconds, so bursty load can hide.

 Source --(black: pressured)--> Map --(black)--> Window(red: busy 100%) --> Sink(blue: idle)
                                                   ^ bottleneck: first red after black

Figure 11.1: Backpressure propagates backwards; the bottleneck is the first busy task.

Decision table:

Observation Likely cause See
One subtask red, siblings blue hot key / skew Chapter 10.4
All subtasks of an operator red operator too expensive or too little parallelism scale out, profile
Sink red or sink pressured external system slow batching, Async I/O, Chapter 26
Async operator pressured with capacity exhausted slow service or capacity too low 11.5
Checkpoint times grow with backpressure barriers queue behind in-flight data 11.2

11.2 Buffer debloating

Feature (verified, network buffer tuning docs): automatically adjusts in-flight data so consumption time matches a target; shorter queues mean faster checkpoint barriers under backpressure.

Keys and defaults (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 TaskManagerOptions): - taskmanager.network.memory.buffer-debloat.enabled (default false) - taskmanager.network.memory.buffer-debloat.target (default 1 s) - taskmanager.network.memory.buffer-debloat.period (default 200 ms) - taskmanager.network.memory.buffer-debloat.samples (default 20) - taskmanager.network.memory.buffer-debloat.threshold-percentages (default 25)

Limitations from the docs: works at subtask level, so inputs with different throughput may be buffered unevenly; it does not reduce total memory use (only caps used size); may underperform above roughly 200 parallel tasks without extra configuration. Related keys: taskmanager.network.memory.buffers-per-channel (default 2), taskmanager.network.memory.floating-buffers-per-gate (default 8), taskmanager.network.memory.max-overdraft-buffers-per-gate (default 5), taskmanager.network.memory.max-buffers-per-channel: these four are stated on the 2.3 network-buffer tuning docs page, but [unverified in jars]: the key strings were not found in the flink-core / flink-runtime 2.2.1 or 2.3.0 jars (a string search of every class), so the options may be defined in a module that was not inspected; check them against your pinned version's config reference before relying on them. taskmanager.memory.segment-size (default 32kb) is verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 TaskManagerOptions. Sizing formula from the docs: buffers = throughput x buffer round-trip / buffer size.

11.3 Memory model

 Total Process Memory = Total Flink Memory + JVM Metaspace + JVM Overhead      (container limit)
 Total Flink Memory   = Framework Heap + Task Heap + Managed + Network + Framework Off-heap + Task Off-heap

Figure 11.2: TaskManager memory model.

Component Key Notes
Task heap taskmanager.memory.task.heap.size operators and user code
Managed memory taskmanager.memory.managed.size or taskmanager.memory.managed.fraction (default 0.4) native; RocksDB, sorting, hashing, Python (consumer kinds OPERATOR, STATE_BACKEND, PYTHON)
Network taskmanager.memory.network.min (64m) / .max (unbounded) / .fraction (0.1) exchange buffers
Framework heap / off-heap taskmanager.memory.framework.heap.size, taskmanager.memory.framework.off-heap.size (128m each) do not touch without reason
Task off-heap taskmanager.memory.task.off-heap.size (0) direct/native memory in user code
Metaspace taskmanager.memory.jvm-metaspace.size (256m)
JVM overhead taskmanager.memory.jvm-overhead.min (192m) / .max (1g) / .fraction (0.1) thread stacks, code cache, GC

All keys and defaults in this table verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 TaskManagerOptions. The network keys taskmanager.memory.network.* have the older names taskmanager.network.memory.min/.max/.fraction as deprecated keys in bytecode. .fraction for network and overhead apply to total Flink / total process memory respectively.

Docs recommendation: set total process memory (or task heap) and let Flink derive the rest; do not set total memory plus its parts in conflicting ways. Slots split managed memory (Chapter 10.2), so more slots per TaskManager means less managed memory per slot. Container OOM-kills with a healthy heap usually mean native memory (RocksDB beyond budget, direct buffers); see 11.4. Total process memory key taskmanager.memory.process.size (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 TaskManagerOptions.TOTAL_PROCESS_MEMORY; its description says on containerized setups it should be the container memory); total Flink memory is taskmanager.memory.flink.size.

11.4 RocksDB basics and incremental checkpoints

Verified keys (large state tuning docs): - state.backend.type: rocksdb (the docs also mention forst, experimental, Chapter 28). - execution.checkpointing.incremental: true makes checkpoints upload only changes since the last completed checkpoint; big win for large state. (Savepoints stay full/canonical.) Default is false (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 CheckpointingOptions.INCREMENTAL_CHECKPOINTS; deprecated old key state.backend.incremental). state.backend.type verified in the same jar (StateBackendOptions, shortcuts hashmap, rocksdb, forst). The state.backend.rocksdb.* keys and the 0.4 managed fraction (0.4 verified in the jar) come from the large-state tuning page; the RocksDB state backend jar was not available, so those two state.backend.rocksdb.* keys are docs-verified only. - state.backend.rocksdb.memory.managed (default true): RocksDB uses Flink managed memory for buffers and caches. - state.backend.rocksdb.memory.write-buffer-ratio: raise when memtable flushes are frequent. - Docs: default managed fraction is 0.4, conservative; often increase on multi-GB TaskManagers. - Timers live in RocksDB by default; heap timers are faster for few timers but are memory-bound and affect checkpoint time (Chapter 3).

Tuning order: (1) measure with checkpoint metrics in the UI, (2) give RocksDB more managed memory, (3) adjust write-buffer ratio if flushes are frequent, (4) only then touch advanced RocksDB options. Local SSD, not network disks. Change one setting at a time. RocksDB state access serialises keys and values on every read: avoid large values per key (Chapter 5, 8). Incremental checkpoint retention and cleanup semantics: Chapter 6.

11.5 Async I/O for external lookups

Why: a blocking call per record caps throughput at 1/latency per subtask. Async I/O keeps many requests in flight per subtask. (For ML scoring on this path see Chapter 31.)

Verified API (async I/O docs, 2.3): - AsyncDataStream.unorderedWait(...) / orderedWait(...); with retries unorderedWaitWithRetry(...) / orderedWaitWithRetry(...). (verified: javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1 AsyncDataStream: unorderedWait(DataStream, AsyncFunction, long timeout, TimeUnit, int capacity) and an overload without capacity; the *WithRetry variants take (stream, func, long timeout, TimeUnit, [int capacity,] AsyncRetryStrategy).) - Implement AsyncFunction with asyncInvoke(input, ResultFuture<...>) and optionally timeout(input, ResultFuture<...>) (verified: asyncInvoke abstract, timeout a default method, both throws Exception; ResultFuture has complete(Collection), completeExceptionally(Throwable), complete(CollectionSupplier)). - asyncInvoke must return fast and complete the ResultFuture from a callback; the function is not called multi-threaded; blocking inside it defeats the purpose. - Capacity: how many async requests may be in progress per parallel subtask. When exhausted, the operator applies backpressure. - Timeout: maximum time from first invocation to final completion. Default on timeout: the default timeout() calls resultFuture.completeExceptionally(new TimeoutException("Async function call has timed out.")) (verified: javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1 AsyncFunction), which fails the task and, per the docs, restarts the job. Override timeout() to emit a fallback or empty result. - Ordering: unordered = lowest latency, results emitted as completed; with event time, watermarks do not overtake records and vice versa, so unordered only between watermarks. Ordered = preserves input order, more buffering and latency. - Retries (verified: javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1, package org.apache.flink.streaming.util.retryable): AsyncRetryStrategies.FixedDelayRetryStrategyBuilder(int maxAttempts, long backoffTimeMillis) and AsyncRetryStrategies.ExponentialBackoffDelayRetryStrategyBuilder(int maxAttempts, long initialDelay, long maxRetryDelay, double multiplier); both have ifResult(Predicate<Collection<OUT>>), ifException(Predicate<Throwable>) and build(). Ready-made predicates: RetryPredicates.EMPTY_RESULT_PREDICATE, RetryPredicates.HAS_EXCEPTION_PREDICATE, RetryPredicates.createExceptionTypePredicate(Class); AsyncRetryStrategies.NO_RETRY_STRATEGY exists. The millisecond unit of the delay arguments is inferred from the field names (backoffTimeMillis; initialDelay/maxRetryDelay unit not stated in bytecode).

Figure 11.3: Async I/O request flow within one subtask.

// (sketch, not compiled) enrich events from a lookup service; client is async, created in open()
public class Lookup extends RichAsyncFunction<Event, Enriched> {
    private transient MyAsyncClient client;                      // placeholder client type
    @Override public void open(OpenContext ctx) { client = MyAsyncClient.create("<LOOKUP_ENDPOINT>"); }
    @Override public void asyncInvoke(Event e, ResultFuture<Enriched> out) {
        client.get(e.key).whenComplete((v, err) -> {
            if (err != null) out.completeExceptionally(err);
            else out.complete(List.of(new Enriched(e, v)));
        });
    }
    @Override public void timeout(Event e, ResultFuture<Enriched> out) {
        out.complete(List.of(new Enriched(e, null)));           // degrade, do not restart the job
    }
}
DataStream<Enriched> out = AsyncDataStream.unorderedWait(events, new Lookup(), 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS, 100);

(open(OpenContext) is the 2.x signature: verified, javap flink-core 2.2.1 RichFunction.open(OpenContext) throws Exception; RichAsyncFunction inherits it from AbstractRichFunction. Argument order timeout (long), TimeUnit, capacity (int) verified against AsyncDataStream. This sketch compiled against the 2.2.1 jars.)

Sizing: capacity ~ target throughput per subtask x service latency (Little's law). Capacity above what the service tolerates just moves the queue. Idempotency: retries and job restarts repeat lookups; lookups must be side-effect free. For writes to an external system see Chapter 26.

11.6 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Blocking client inside asyncInvoke (JDBC): looks asynchronous, runs serially.
  • Default timeout behaviour restarts the job; one slow dependency becomes a restart loop. Always implement timeout().
  • Capacity too high overloads the dependency; too low shows as backpressure on the async operator.
  • Ordered mode with one slow request holds back all later results.
  • Debloating enabled but expecting lower memory: it does not lower reserved memory.
  • Managed memory fraction raised while the job has no RocksDB: wasted memory. RocksDB beyond budget: container kill.
  • Reading the first pressured operator as the culprit instead of the first busy one after it.

11.7 Self-check

  1. The sink is blue (idle) and the source is black. Where do you look next?
  2. What does execution.checkpointing.incremental change for checkpoints, and what does it not change?
  3. Which keys would you check when a container is OOM-killed but the heap is fine?
  4. Why must timeout() be overridden in production? What is the default?
  5. Capacity 100, service p99 2 s, 4 subtasks: what throughput ceiling does Little's law give?

11.8 Open items / unverified

  • buffers-per-channel, floating-buffers-per-gate, max-overdraft-buffers-per-gate, max-buffers-per-channel: documented but not found in the inspected jars.
  • RocksDB options beyond the two memory keys; predefined options names (not fetched; RocksDB jar not available).
  • Unit of the exponential-backoff builder's delay arguments.
  • No 2.3-specific changes to debloating, async I/O or RocksDB appear in the 2.3 release-note extract (extract may be partial).
  • Config table page fetch was truncated, so no key was cross-checked there.

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/monitoring/back_pressure/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/deployment/memory/mem_setup_tm/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/deployment/memory/network_mem_tuning/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/state/large_state_tuning/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/operators/asyncio/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/release-notes/flink-2.3/

Chapter 12: Poison pills and dead-letter handling

Goal: after this chapter you can keep one malformed record from stalling a job, route it to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) with enough context to diagnose and replay it, alert on the DLQ rate, and explain the restart loop that happens when you do not.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (side outputs, late data), Chapter 6 (restart strategies, recovery), Chapter 7 (Kafka delivery), Chapter 8 (serialization).

12.1 The failure mode: a poison pill

A poison pill is a record that deterministically makes processing fail. Replaying it after recovery fails again.

 Kafka offset 1041 (bad bytes)
      |
  source -> deserialize -> map/process -> sink
                 X exception escapes the operator
      |
  task fails -> job restarts from last checkpoint (offset < 1041)
      |
  reads 1041 again -> fails again -> ... (restart loop)

Why it is nasty: recovery is correct behavior. Flink restores state and re-reads from the checkpointed offset, so the same bad record comes back. Lag grows, checkpoints stop completing, and the job never makes progress. Assumption: the exception is not transient. Transient failures (a down dependency) are a different problem; restarting is the right answer there.

Figure 12.1: Poison-pill restart loop and DLQ routing with a side output.

12.2 Restart strategies: what they do and do not do (pointer to Chapter 6)

Verified against the 2.3 docs (task failure recovery page) and by javap of flink-core 2.2.1 RestartStrategyOptions (all keys, defaults and value aliases below match the bytecode, including disable/off/none):

Item Value
Config key restart-strategy.type
Values fixed-delay, exponential-delay, failure-rate, disable (aliases off, none)
Default, checkpointing disabled disable
Default, checkpointing enabled exponential-delay
Exponential-delay keys restart-strategy.exponential-delay.initial-backoff (1s), .max-backoff (1 min), .backoff-multiplier (1.5), .jitter-factor (0.1), .reset-backoff-threshold (1h), .attempts-before-reset-backoff (infinite)
Fixed-delay keys restart-strategy.fixed-delay.attempts (1), restart-strategy.fixed-delay.delay (1s)
Failure-rate keys restart-strategy.failure-rate.max-failures-per-interval (1), .failure-rate-interval (1 min), .delay (1s)

Interplay with poison pills: - With the default exponential delay and an infinite attempt limit, a poison pill gives you an endless loop with growing back-off (up to the max back-off), not a clean failure. The job looks "RUNNING" in between. - With fixed-delay and a small attempts, or failure-rate, the job eventually goes to FAILED. That is louder, but it still does not make progress; a restart strategy is a circuit breaker, not a fix. - The fix is to make the bad record a normal data-path event (sections 12.3 to 12.5). Keep restarts for transient faults.

12.3 Deserialization failures

Two Kafka-source hooks (verified on the connector page, release-2.2): KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema (whole ConsumerRecord: key, value, headers, offset) and a value-only DeserializationSchema via setValueOnlyDeserializer.

What the DeserializationSchema Javadoc says (verified): deserialize(byte[]) returns the object, "null if the message cannot be deserialized", and declares IOException. A second overload deserialize(byte[], Collector) can emit several records.

What the connector page does not say: what the Kafka source does when you return null or throw. The page has no section on ignore-failures or dead letters (verified absence). The connector 5.0.0-2.2 jar answers it (verified: javap flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2 and flink-core 2.2.1): - setValueOnlyDeserializer(DeserializationSchema) wraps your schema in KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema.valueOnly(...), which calls DeserializationSchema.deserialize(byte[], Collector). The default implementation of that overload calls deserialize(byte[]) and emits only if the result is non-null. So a null return silently drops the record: nothing is emitted, and KafkaRecordEmitter.emitRecord still advances the split's current offset to offset + 1 after the call. No log, no metric, no DLQ. (If you override the two-argument deserialize(byte[], Collector) yourself, you control emission.) - Any Exception thrown from the deserialization schema is caught in KafkaRecordEmitter.emitRecord and rethrown as IOException("Failed to deserialize consumer record due to", cause), which fails the task and triggers 12.1. - The other value-only path, KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema.valueOnly(Class<? extends org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.Deserializer>), passes the deserialized value to Collector.collect without a null check; what downstream does with a null element was not determined ([unverified]). Do not return null there. - Returning null silently loses the record with no trace. For a DLQ you need the bytes, so null is the wrong tool.

Recommended pattern: parse late, keep the bytes

Make the source deliver raw bytes plus metadata, and parse inside a process function where you can use a side output.

KafkaSource<byte[]>  (value-only deserializer returning the bytes unchanged)
      |
  ParseOrDlq (ProcessFunction)  --main--> typed Event stream
      |
      +--side output DLQ--> DlqRecord --> Kafka DLQ topic

Cost: you lose the record's partition/offset unless you use KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema to wrap them into a small carrier object. Do that; the offset is the single most useful DLQ field.

12.4 try/catch plus side output

Side outputs (verified): OutputTag is created as an anonymous inner class so type information survives erasure; ctx.output(tag, value) emits; stream.getSideOutput(tag) retrieves. Supported in ProcessFunction, KeyedProcessFunction, CoProcessFunction, KeyedCoProcessFunction, ProcessWindowFunction, ProcessAllWindowFunction.

Sketch, not compiled:

public class RawIn {                      // carrier produced by a KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema
    public String topic; public int partition; public long offset;
    public long kafkaTs; public byte[] value;
    public RawIn() {}
}

public class ParseOrDlq extends ProcessFunction<RawIn, Event> {
    public static final OutputTag<DlqRecord> DLQ = new OutputTag<>("dlq") {};
    private transient Counter dlqCount;                  // custom metric, see Chapter 13

    @Override public void open(OpenContext ctx) {
        dlqCount = getRuntimeContext().getMetricGroup().counter("dlqRecords");
    }

    @Override
    public void processElement(RawIn in, Context ctx, Collector<Event> out) {
        try {
            Event e = Parser.parse(in.value);            // may throw
            Validator.check(e);                          // business rules also throw
            out.collect(e);
        } catch (Exception ex) {                         // narrow this in real code
            dlqCount.inc();
            ctx.output(DLQ, DlqRecord.of(in, ex));
        }
    }
}

Rules: 1. Catch narrowly. Catch parse/validation exceptions, not everything. A catch (Exception) around a call to an external system turns an outage into a flood of DLQ records (every record "fails"). Transient errors should propagate (restart) or be retried; only deterministic data errors go to the DLQ. 2. Never throw from the DLQ path. Build the envelope defensively (truncate, hash, no parsing of the bad payload). 3. Put the same guard around downstream operators that can fail on data (maps, key selectors, window functions). A keyBy selector that throws on a null field is a poison-pill source too; guard before the keyBy. 4. open(OpenContext) is the 2.x form (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 RichFunction.open(OpenContext) throws Exception, inherited by ProcessFunction; this sketch's OpenContext, getRuntimeContext().getMetricGroup(), OutputTag, ctx.output calls compile against the 2.2.1 jars, with the metrics-core Counter taken from a 1.20.5 jar because 2.x metrics-core was not available).

12.5 DLQ record envelope design

The envelope is a contract with whoever debugs and replays. Suggested fields:

Field Purpose Note
reasonCode stable enum (PARSE_ERROR, SCHEMA_MISMATCH, VALIDATION_FAILED) alert/group on this
reasonDetail exception class plus short message truncate; messages can echo payload fragments
sourceTopic, partition, offset exact origin, enables replay from the carrier object
kafkaTimestamp ingestion time for ordering and age
failedAt processing wall time not event time
jobId/jobVersion, operator which code rejected it for regression tracking
tenantId isolation (see below) key the DLQ by it
payloadRef or payloadRedacted the evidence see PII caution
payloadSha256 match records without storing content cheap, safe

PII and tenant caution

  • Assumption: payloads may contain personal data or secrets. A DLQ is a second copy of the data, often with weaker access control and longer retention than the source. Treat it as in scope for the same classification.
  • Options, safest first: store only topic/partition/offset + hash and re-read the original from the source topic (works only while source retention covers it); store the payload encrypted with a key per tenant; store a redacted/truncated form. Redact at write time, in the job, never "later".
  • Never log the payload in task logs or put it in exception messages. Exception text often echoes input.
  • Multi-tenant: partition or prefix DLQ topics by tenant (or key by tenant and enforce ACLs per topic), and never let one tenant's consumers read another's rejects. Retention should be short and explicit.
  • Do not put secrets in reasonDetail. Sanitize before emitting.
  • Legal retention questions: Draft only. Review required by Legal, Compliance, or relevant Omnissa control owner.

12.6 Writing the DLQ

Route the side output to a Kafka sink (Chapter 7 for delivery semantics; the 2.x sink supports NONE, AT_LEAST_ONCE, EXACTLY_ONCE, verified: javap flink-connector-base 2.2.1 DeliveryGuarantee). For a DLQ, AT_LEAST_ONCE is normally enough: duplicates in the DLQ are harmless if replay is idempotent (use sourceTopic+partition+offset as the identity). Pin examples to Flink 2.2.x with Kafka connector 5.0.0 (no connector for 2.3 yet, README verified facts).

Isolation consideration: a failing DLQ sink must not stop the main sink. Within one job they share a failure domain; if the DLQ topic is unavailable the job restarts. Mitigations: the DLQ topic has the same availability as the main topic; or write DLQ records to a different, simpler sink. Open item: a non-blocking DLQ sink design.

12.7 Alerting on DLQ rate

  • Count rejects with a custom counter (dlqRecords above) and compare to numRecordsIn of the same operator (verified name: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 MetricNames.IO_NUM_RECORDS_IN = "numRecordsIn"). Alert on ratio and trend, not on a single record: one reject per hour may be normal, 2% for 10 minutes is not.
  • Alert separately on the DLQ topic's produce rate from outside Flink (broker metrics): a stalled job cannot tell you it stopped writing. Chapter 13 covers monitoring from outside the data path.
  • Group by reasonCode: a new code appearing is more interesting than a count going up.
  • Two classic signals: a step change right after a deploy (schema/parser regression), and a slow ramp (a producer fleet upgrade).
  • Also alert on restart count growth (numRestarts, verified job metric: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 MetricNames.NUM_RESTARTS); it catches the escaped-exception case where the DLQ stays empty because the bad record is not handled.

12.8 Replay from the DLQ

DLQ topic --(fix deployed)--> replay job --> original sink path
  1. Fix the cause first (parser, schema, producer). Replaying into a still-broken job just reproduces the loop.
  2. Replay with a separate job reading the DLQ with a bounded or explicit offset range, not by mixing it into the live topic. Re-run the same parse logic, so a still-bad record goes back to a new DLQ (tag the retry count; stop after N).
  3. Idempotent sinks (Chapter 26): the record may already have been processed after a partial success. Use sourceTopic+partition+offset as dedup identity.
  4. Event-time effects: replayed records are old. Late-data rules (Chapter 1) and window closing behave per the watermark of the replay job, not the original. Decide whether replayed events may update closed windows (Chapter 2, allowed lateness) or should go to a correction path.
  5. Ordering across the live stream is lost. Do not replay if downstream needs strict order per key [assumption].
  6. Record the replay (who, when, range) for audit.

12.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Returning null from the deserializer to "skip" bad data: silent loss (verified for the DeserializationSchema path, see 12.3).
  • Catch-all catch (Exception): turns outages into DLQ floods and hides real bugs.
  • DLQ without a consumer: grows until retention deletes the evidence. Someone owns triage.
  • DLQ envelope too rich: the payload copy becomes a PII liability (12.5).
  • Poison pill inside a checkpointed state function (for example a state update that throws) loops the same way as deserialization failures. Guard state mutations on data-dependent paths.
  • Exceptions in the sink serializer (a field that cannot be encoded) escape the same way; validate before the sink.
  • Restart storm masks the cause: exponential back-off makes the job look alive. Alert on numRestarts slope.
  • Unbounded retries on the DLQ itself (replay of a replay).
  • Schema evolution looks like a mass poison pill: sudden 100% DLQ rate. A circuit breaker (stop the job if the reject ratio exceeds a threshold) can be better than draining the topic into the DLQ. Open item: design the breaker.

12.10 Self-check

  1. Why does restoring from a checkpoint not make a poison pill go away?
  2. What is the trade-off between returning null from a DeserializationSchema and emitting the bytes to a DLQ?
  3. Name two reasons not to wrap a call to an external service in a catch-all that sends to the DLQ.
  4. Which envelope fields let you replay safely and which one is a PII risk?
  5. Why alert on the DLQ topic from outside the job as well as on the in-job counter?

  • Resolved by jar inspection: null return from a DeserializationSchema drops the record silently (12.3); open(OpenContext) signature (12.4).
  • [unverified] What downstream does with a null element emitted by the Deserializer-class value-only path (no null check in the wrapper).

Chapter 13: Observability and alerting

Goal: after this chapter you can list the Flink metrics you may trust by name, say which lag metrics are confirmed and which are not, build a dashboard for ingestion, consumer and watermark lag, and design alerts that fire on trends and still fire when the job is stalled.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (the three lags), Chapter 6 (checkpoints), Chapter 11 (backpressure), Chapter 12 (DLQ rate).

13.1 The metrics system and reporters

Flink exposes metrics (counters, gauges, histograms, meters) through scoped metric groups; user code registers its own via getRuntimeContext().getMetricGroup() (Chapter 12 sketch). Reporters ship them out.

Reporters documented on the 2.3 metric-reporters page (verified: WebFetch re-read; classes live in separate flink-metrics-* jars that were not in the jar set, so factory class names are docs-only):

Reporter Mode Notes
JMX pull
Prometheus pull counters map to gauges, histograms to summaries (per docs)
PrometheusPushGateway push supports HTTP Basic Auth (per docs)
Graphite push
InfluxDB push
StatsD push
Datadog push
OpenTelemetry push
Slf4j push logs metrics

Configuration is by name: metrics.reporter.<name>.factory.class (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 MetricOptions, prefix metrics.reporter.<name>, options factory.class, interval (push only), filter.includes and filter.excludes apply to every reporter). Per-reporter options (ports, hosts, intervals) are on the same page; copy them from there, not from this book. Pull reporters need a scrape target per JobManager/TaskManager pod (Chapter 15). Credentials for push reporters belong in secrets, never in the Flink config checked into git (Chapter 16).

13.2 Confirmed metric names (jar bytecode, Flink 2.2.1 and 2.3.0; 2.3 metrics page)

Metric Scope Meaning
numRecordsIn, numRecordsOut task/operator totals; use rate()
numLateRecordsDropped operator records dropped as late; registered only by window operators, and not incremented for events you route with sideOutputLateData, so count the side output yourself (Chapter 1.4) (verified: string constant only in WindowOperator, EvictingWindowOperator, AsyncWindowOperator, AsyncEvictingWindowOperator, flink-runtime 2.2.1; see Chapter 1)
currentInputWatermark task/operator last watermark received, ms
currentOutputWatermark operator last watermark emitted, ms
idleTimeMsPerSecond task ms per second idle
backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond task ms per second back pressured
busyTimeMsPerSecond task ms per second busy
lastCheckpointDuration job ms for the last checkpoint
numberOfFailedCheckpoints job count
numRestarts job restarts since submission
checkpointAlignmentTime task barrier alignment time (name verified: MetricNames.CHECKPOINT_ALIGNMENT_TIME; unit not verified here, check one scrape)
lastCheckpointSize, numberOfCompletedCheckpoints, numberOfInProgressCheckpoints job listed in the checkpointing section (verified: string constants in DefaultCheckpointStatsTracker, flink-runtime 2.2.1, which also registers lastCheckpointDuration, numberOfFailedCheckpoints, totalNumberOfCheckpoints)

Also on the page: an "End-to-End latency tracking" section (latency markers). Treat it as a debugging tool, not an SLA metric (Chapter 25). Config key: metrics.latency.interval, default 0 = disabled; "Enabling this feature can significantly impact the performance of the cluster"; companion keys metrics.latency.granularity (single/operator/subtask) and metrics.latency.history-size (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 MetricOptions).

Job-level availability metrics (verified: SchedulerBase.registerJobMetrics, flink-runtime 2.2.1 and 2.3.0, registers gauges named downtime, uptime and numRestarts; JobStatusMetrics adds per-status metrics selected by the list option metrics.job.status.enable, values STATE, CURRENT_TIME, TOTAL_TIME, default CURRENT_TIME; exact metric names not read). Correction: an earlier draft said uptime was absent in 2.3. It is registered in the jars. fullRestarts has no string constant in flink-runtime, flink-core or flink-streaming (2.2.1): treat it as removed and do not alert on it.

13.3 Source and Kafka lag metrics: the Chapter 1 question, settled from the jars

Chapter 1 flagged five names. They were resolved by reading string constants and bytecode of MetricNames, InternalSourceReaderMetricGroup (flink-runtime 2.2.1/2.3.0) and KafkaSourceReaderMetrics (flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2). All of this is registered by code, so it exists at runtime regardless of which docs page lists it.

Name What the jar shows Status
currentEmitEventTimeLag Gauge registered in the source operator's metric group by InternalSourceReaderMetricGroup. Value = (emit time) - (timestamp of last emitted event); emit time is "now", or the moment the source went idle if idle; -1 until an event with a timestamp was emitted verified (javap: getEmitTimeLag)
watermarkLag Gauge registered when the first watermark is seen. Value = (now, or idle-start if idle) - (last watermark). So it is wall clock minus watermark verified (javap: getWatermarkLag)
sourceIdleTime Gauge: 0 unless the source reader called idlingStarted; then now - idle-start in ms (time since the source went idle, not "time since last record" while records are flowing) verified (javap: getIdleTime). Corrects the earlier wording
pendingRecords Gauge via setPendingRecordsGauge; the Kafka source fills it from the consumer's per-partition records-lag metric (aggregation across partitions not read in detail) verified (name and source); aggregation semantics: unverified
currentFetchEventTimeLag Constant MetricNames.CURRENT_FETCH_EVENT_TIME_LAG exists, but no registration was found in flink-runtime, flink-connector-base, flink-streaming-java or flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2 (string appears only in MetricNames) name defined, not emitted by these jars: do not build dashboards on it for the Kafka source
records-lag-max Not a Flink-defined name. It is a Kafka consumer metric (consumer-fetch-manager-metrics, from Kafka's documentation; kafka-clients jar not in the jar set). Flink registers every metric from KafkaConsumer.metrics() as a gauge under KafkaSourceReader.KafkaConsumer using MetricName.name(), unfiltered (verified: registerKafkaConsumerMetrics), when register.consumer.metrics is true passes through; name confirmed only from Kafka knowledge, check one scrape

Other Kafka-source metrics (verified: KafkaSourceReaderMetrics constants, 5.0.0-2.2): group KafkaSourceReader with counters commitsSucceeded and commitsFailed, and per topic/partition gauges currentOffset and committedOffset (singular; earlier drafts wrote currentOffsets/committedOffsets, which is wrong). Consumer metrics sit under KafkaSourceReader.KafkaConsumer (docs example: <parent_groups>.operator.KafkaSourceReader.KafkaConsumer.records-consumed-total). Option register.consumer.metrics: boolean, default true (verified: KafkaSourceOptions, javap). numBytesIn is also derived from the consumer's bytes-consumed-total. Other source metrics present in MetricNames: pendingBytes, watermarkAlignmentDrift, numRecordsInErrors.

Practical reading: - Backlog size: pendingRecords (records not yet fetched), or lag computed outside Flink from broker end offsets minus committed offsets (see 13.6; committed offsets advance on checkpoint completion, so they lag the real position by up to a checkpoint interval (verified: commit.offsets.on.checkpoint option, default true, KafkaSourceOptions; the committedOffset gauge is separate)). - Time lag: currentEmitEventTimeLag is event-time based (wall clock at emit minus event timestamp); the old events being replayed make it large even when the job is healthy. Compare against Chapter 1 ingestion lag before concluding "Flink is slow". - watermarkLag is wall clock minus last watermark, so it depends on watermark strategy and idleness (Chapter 1.5): one idle partition holds the watermark and inflates it; while the source reader itself is idle the clock stops at the idle-start moment (verified: getLastEmitTime). - Exact metric scope and label names after export differ per reporter; check one real scrape.

Figure 13.1: Which lag is it? Metric names grouped by the question they answer and by how well the jars confirm them.

13.4 Dashboard design

One row per question, in this order (a reader should find the cause by reading top to bottom):

Row 1  Is data arriving?         Kafka produce rate (outside), numRecordsIn rate (source operator)
Row 2  Are we keeping up?        consumer lag (outside), pendingRecords, currentEmitEventTimeLag
Row 3  Is time moving?           now - currentInputWatermark per operator, watermarkLag, sourceIdleTime
Row 4  Who is the bottleneck?    busyTimeMsPerSecond / backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond / idleTimeMsPerSecond per task
Row 5  Is it correct?            late rate (numLateRecordsDropped + side-output counter), DLQ ratio (Chapter 12)
Row 6  Is it durable?            lastCheckpointDuration, numberOfFailedCheckpoints, lastCheckpointSize, numRestarts

Rules: - Plot per-subtask series (or max over subtasks) for busy/backpressure; averages hide key skew (Chapter 10). - Compute now - watermark in the monitoring system for non-source operators. The watermark is an epoch-ms gauge. For source operators watermarkLag is that subtraction already (13.3, verified in bytecode). - Never mix tenants in one unlabeled series if tenant data is exposed; keep tenant labels out of high-cardinality metrics and out of metric names (cardinality and isolation). - Sum of busy + idle + backpressured per second is about 1000 ms; a task at ~1000 busy is saturated [assumption: standard reading of these metrics, confirm in Chapter 11].

13.5 Alert design

Principles: 1. Alert on trends, not spikes. Use a sustained condition (for 10 minutes) or a slope (lag growing over 15 minutes), not a single sample. A post-restart catch-up spike is normal. 2. Alert on symptoms users feel first (freshness, completeness), then on causes (backpressure, checkpoint). 3. One page per problem. Group and inhibit: if the job is down, suppress the lag, late and DLQ alerts. 4. Every alert links to a runbook step: what to check next, which chapter explains it.

Alert Condition (sketch, tune on your data) Likely cause
Consumer lag growing lag slope > 0 for 15 min and lag above floor under-provisioned, skew, sink slow
Watermark stuck now - currentInputWatermark increasing while input rate > 0 idle partition, Chapter 1.5
Late rate late records / records in > x% for 10 min delay too tight, wake-up of idle source
Backpressure sustained backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond high for 10 min slow sink, skew, state backend
Checkpoint failing numberOfFailedCheckpoints increasing, or lastCheckpointDuration trend up state growth, backpressure, storage
Restart loop numRestarts increase repeated in an hour poison pill (Chapter 12), dependency
DLQ ratio rejects / numRecordsIn above threshold schema or parser regression

Thresholds here are placeholders: Data unavailable for your baseline. Derive them from a week of normal operation (the same method as the watermark delay in Chapter 1).

13.6 Monitor from outside the data path

A stalled job emits no records, so anything computed in-job (a lag measured on the last event, a counter that only increments on events) goes silent exactly when you need it. Silence must be an alert condition.

Three independent signals: 1. Broker side: consumer-group lag per partition (end offset minus committed offset) from a Kafka exporter or admin API, plus produce rate of input and output topics. Works when Flink is dead. 2. Flink side, metric freshness: alert on absence of the metric series (job's metrics not scraped for N minutes), e.g. Prometheus "absent" style rules. Pair with the Flink REST API job state, from a probe outside the cluster (REST: /jobs/:jobid/... routes exist, for example /jobs/:jobid/resource-requirements verified in flink-runtime; job-state probe route not checked here). 3. Synthetic end-to-end probe: a small producer writes a marker record with a known timestamp every minute to the input topic (per tenant if needed, with synthetic data only); a checker reads the marker from the output topic and alerts if it does not arrive within the SLA. This measures real freshness, including stalls and partition-specific problems. Use all partitions or key the markers so each partition is covered [assumption].

The article's SLA metric computed inside a SQL aggregate fails this test (Chapter 25).

Also alert on the monitoring itself: scrape failures, reporter push failures, dashboard data age.

Figure 13.2: Monitoring placed outside the data path so a stalled job still raises an alert.

13.7 Minimal custom metrics

Register your own counters/gauges for things Flink cannot know: dlqRecords (Chapter 12), lateEventsSideOutput (Chapter 1), parseErrors. Keep names stable, avoid per-key labels (unbounded cardinality), avoid PII in names or labels. Sketch, not compiled:

Counter late = getRuntimeContext().getMetricGroup().counter("lateEventsSideOutput");
// in processElement: late.inc();

13.8 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Alerting on numLateRecordsDropped alone misses lateness in custom process functions (Chapter 1.4).
  • Relying on currentFetchEventTimeLag (defined but not emitted by the Kafka source jars checked) or on records-lag-max (Kafka client name) without confirming them in your output.
  • Using committed-offset lag as a real-time position: offsets are committed on checkpoint completion, so lag looks flat/saw-toothed and a failing checkpoint makes it look like a stall (option commit.offsets.on.checkpoint, default true, verified in KafkaSourceOptions; stall inference is reasoning, see Chapter 7).
  • High-cardinality labels (per key, per tenant id) crashing the metrics backend.
  • Averages across subtasks; one saturated subtask is invisible.
  • Replays make event-time lag large by design; mute or separate during backfill (Chapter 24).
  • Alert fatigue from spike alerts; no alert on absence.

13.9 Self-check

  1. Which lag metrics are confirmed in the jars, and which would you verify against live output first?
  2. Why is now - currentInputWatermark not a lag you can read directly from Flink?
  3. Design an alert that fires when the whole job is hung.
  4. Why does committed-offset lag look wrong during a checkpoint failure?
  5. Why compare numRestarts growth with the DLQ rate?
