Chapter 14: Testing DataStream jobs

Goal: after this chapter you can test a Flink function at three levels (plain unit, operator harness, MiniCluster), drive watermarks and processing time by hand, prove timers and late-data logic, and test checkpoint/restore without a cluster.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, late data), Chapter 3 (timers, KeyedProcessFunction), Chapter 6 (checkpoints).

14.1 The test pyramid for Flink

Level Tool Tests Speed Time control
1. Plain unit JUnit, call method directly pure logic inside a function (mock Collector) ms n/a
2. Operator harness ProcessFunctionTestHarnesses, KeyedOneInputStreamOperatorTestHarness state, timers, watermarks, snapshot/restore of one operator ms full (you push watermarks and processing time)
3. MiniCluster MiniClusterWithClientResource whole job graph, partitioning, serialization, multi-operator seconds only via your data (bounded sources)
4. External systems Kafka in a container connector config, offsets, serdes, end-to-end tens of seconds none; avoid asserting on time

Rule: put 80% of your tests at levels 1-2. Level 3 proves wiring; level 4 proves the connector, not your logic.

Dependency (verified, 2.3 testing page): org.apache.flink:flink-test-utils, scope test. Docs also state the harness classes are not part of the public API and may change between versions. Pin your Flink version. Where the classes physically are (verified: jfind over the downloaded 2.2.1 jars): ProcessFunctionTestHarnesses, OneInputStreamOperatorTestHarness, KeyedOneInputStreamOperatorTestHarness and AbstractStreamOperatorTestHarness (package org.apache.flink.streaming.util) and MiniClusterResource/ MiniClusterResourceConfiguration (package org.apache.flink.runtime.testutils) are in flink-runtime-2.2.1-tests.jar (same layout in 2.3.0). MiniClusterWithClientResource is not in any downloaded jar: it belongs to flink-test-utils, which was not downloaded, so its package and members are unverified here (the docs page names it). Which artifact pulls the runtime test-jar transitively: unverified.

Figure 14.1: The four test levels and how the level 2 operator harness drives one operator.

14.2 Level 1: unit-testing a function

Design for it: keep business logic in plain methods or small FlatMapFunction/MapFunction classes with no static state. Stateless functions can be called directly with a list-backed Collector (the docs use a mock Collector for this). (Sketch, not compiled):

@Test void splitsTokens() throws Exception {
    List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
    new Tokenizer().flatMap("a b", new ListCollector<>(out));   // org.apache.flink.api.common.functions.util.ListCollector (verified: flink-core 2.2.1; constructor takes a List)
    assertEquals(List.of("a", "b"), out);
}

Anything touching RuntimeContext, keyed state, or timers cannot be tested this way. Go to level 2.

14.3 Level 2: operator test harnesses

A harness wraps one operator, gives it a fake runtime (state backend, timer service, output list) and lets you push records, watermarks and processing time. Class names verified on the 2.3 testing page:

Class Use for
ProcessFunctionTestHarnesses factory (verified: javap 2.2.1): forProcessFunction(ProcessFunction), forKeyedProcessFunction(KeyedProcessFunction, KeySelector, TypeInformation<K>), forCoProcessFunction, forKeyedCoProcessFunction, forBroadcastProcessFunction, forKeyedBroadcastProcessFunction, plus ...WithStateV2 variants for KeyedProcessFunction and KeyedCoProcessFunction (State V2, Chapter 28). All throws Exception
OneInputStreamOperatorTestHarness<IN, OUT> non-keyed operators
KeyedOneInputStreamOperatorTestHarness<K, IN, OUT> keyed operators; constructor (OneInputStreamOperator<IN,OUT>, KeySelector<IN,K>, TypeInformation<K>) (verified: javap 2.2.1; other overloads add max parallelism, parallelism, subtask index, or a serializer)

Verified harness methods (javap AbstractStreamOperatorTestHarness / OneInputStreamOperatorTestHarness, 2.2.1): open(), processElement(IN, long), processElement(StreamRecord<IN>), processWatermark(long), processWatermark(Watermark), setProcessingTime(long), advanceTime(long), extractOutputValues() (returns List<OUT>), getOutput() (returns ConcurrentLinkedQueue<Object>, includes watermarks), getSideOutput(OutputTag<X>), snapshot(long, long), initializeState(OperatorSubtaskState), setStateTtlProcessingTime(long), numEventTimeTimers(), numProcessingTimeTimers(), close(). The harness implements AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources works (verified). Call open() before use; it runs the function's open() and, if you did not call initializeState, initializes empty state first (verified: bytecode of open() calls initializeEmptyState when state was not initialized). Flink's own KeyedProcessOperatorTest (in the 2.2.1 tests jar) calls setup() on a hand-built harness before open()/initializeState(...); the ProcessFunctionTestHarnesses factories are the simpler route.

Mental model:

 test ──processElement(v, ts)────┐
 test ──processWatermark(w)──────┼─► [ operator + fake state + fake timer service ] ──► output list ──► assertions
 test ──setProcessingTime(p)─────┘                       ▲
                                                         └── side outputs, snapshots

14.3.1 Keyed function sketch (sketch, not compiled)

// Function under test: per key, emits a "timeout" if no event arrives within 10 s of event time.
@Test void timesOutAfterTenSeconds() throws Exception {
    try (var h = ProcessFunctionTestHarnesses.forKeyedProcessFunction(
            new TimeoutFn(), (Event e) -> e.key, Types.STRING)) {        // TimeoutFn extends KeyedProcessFunction<String, Event, String>
        h.open();
        h.processElement(new Event("k1", 1_000L), 1_000L);               // registers timer at 11_000
        h.processWatermark(10_999L);
        assertTrue(h.extractOutputValues().isEmpty());                   // timer not due
        h.processWatermark(11_000L);                                     // timer time <= watermark => fires
        assertEquals(List.of("timeout:k1"), h.extractOutputValues());
    }
}

Class Types is org.apache.flink.api.common.typeinfo.Types. The manual route is new KeyedOneInputStreamOperatorTestHarness<>(new KeyedProcessOperator<>(fn), keySelector, Types.STRING); KeyedProcessOperator is org.apache.flink.streaming.api.operators.KeyedProcessOperator (verified: flink-runtime 2.2.1, constructor takes a KeyedProcessFunction). Compile check: the imports and signatures above resolved with javac against the 2.2.1 jar set except for classes in jars that were not downloaded (flink-core-api, flink-metrics); the whole snippet is therefore only partly compile-checked.

14.4 Controlling time

Two independent clocks, two methods:

Clock You advance with Fires
Event time processWatermark(t) event-time timers with timestamp <= t, window closes
Processing time setProcessingTime(t) processing-time timers, processing-time windows

Principles: - Never Thread.sleep in a harness test. Time only moves when you say so, so tests are deterministic. - Watermark(t) covers timestamps <= t (Chapter 1), so test the boundary: watermark T-1 must not fire a timer at T; watermark T must. - Watermarks must be monotonic. Pushing a lower one is a bug in the test. - Harness processElement timestamps stand in for the timestamp assigner. Your WatermarkStrategy is not applied by the harness: test the strategy separately (14.4.1) or in a MiniCluster test.

14.4.1 Testing a WatermarkGenerator in isolation

A WatermarkGenerator is a plain object: call onEvent(event, ts, output) then onPeriodicEmit(output) with a capturing WatermarkOutput. Assert the Chapter 1 worked example (delay 5 s: max 9 s gives watermark 3.999 s). This is the cheapest "deterministic watermark demo". Alternatively write a punctuated generator that emits a watermark after every event, so a bounded fromData source yields fixed output (verified: StreamExecutionEnvironment.fromData(Collection<OUT>), fromData(OUT...) and fromData(Collection, TypeInformation) exist in 2.2.1; the generator interface is WatermarkGenerator<T> with onEvent(T, long, WatermarkOutput) and onPeriodicEmit(WatermarkOutput), verified).

14.4.2 Testing late data and side outputs

Sketch (not compiled), using the LateSplitter from Chapter 1:

h.processWatermark(15_000L);
h.processElement(new Event("k", 12_000L), 12_000L);       // <= watermark: late
h.processElement(new Event("k", 16_000L), 16_000L);       // on time
assertEquals(1, h.extractOutputValues().size());          // main output
assertEquals(1, h.getSideOutput(LateSplitter.LATE).size()); // getSideOutput(OutputTag<X>) returns a queue of StreamRecord<X> (verified: javap 2.2.1)

Also test: exactly-at-watermark event (late, by the <= rule), and window allowedLateness re-fire (Chapter 2) by pushing a watermark past window end, then a late element within lateness, then one beyond lateness.

14.5 Testing state and checkpoint/restore with harness snapshots

What to prove: after a snapshot and restore into a new operator instance, behavior continues correctly (Chapter 6, 9). Pattern, verified against the harness API and against Flink's own KeyedProcessOperatorTest (2.2.1 tests jar, bytecode: first harness open, processElement, snapshot(1, 1), close; second harness setup, initializeState(snapshot), open, setProcessingTime, processWatermark). snapshot(long checkpointId, long timestamp) returns OperatorSubtaskState; initializeState(OperatorSubtaskState) goes on a fresh harness before open():

OperatorSubtaskState snap;
try (var h1 = newHarness()) {
    h1.open();
    h1.processElement(new Event("k", 1_000L), 1_000L);     // builds state, registers timer
    snap = h1.snapshot(1L, 1_000L);
}
try (var h2 = newHarness()) {                               // brand-new instance, same function class
    h2.initializeState(snap);
    h2.open();
    h2.processWatermark(20_000L);                           // restored timer must still fire
    assertEquals(List.of("timeout:k"), h2.extractOutputValues());
}

Uses: - Prove timers and keyed state survive restore. - Prove a refactor stays compatible: keep a snapshot produced by the previous release as a test resource and restore it (golden-snapshot test). Fails when someone renames a ValueStateDescriptor or changes a serializer (Chapter 9). - Caveat: a harness snapshot is not a real savepoint through the cluster; it does not exercise the full path. For that use a MiniCluster/real savepoint test (14.6) or Chapter 30.

14.6 Level 3: MiniCluster integration tests

MiniClusterWithClientResource (name verified on the 2.3 testing page; it is a JUnit rule used with @ClassRule; its class is in flink-test-utils, not in the downloaded jars, so package and constructor are unverified) starts an embedded cluster. It is configured through MiniClusterResourceConfiguration.Builder (verified, javap 2.2.1, package org.apache.flink.runtime.testutils): setNumberTaskManagers(int), setNumberSlotsPerTaskManager(int), setConfiguration(Configuration), setShutdownTimeout(Duration), setRpcServiceSharing(RpcServiceSharing), withHaLeadershipControl(), build(). In the downloaded tests jar the JUnit 4 rule is org.apache.flink.runtime.testutils.MiniClusterResource and the JUnit 5 one is named InternalMiniClusterExtension (internal). A public JUnit 5 MiniClusterExtension is [unverified]: it would be in flink-test-utils.

Pattern (sketch, not compiled):

@ClassRule public static final MiniClusterWithClientResource CLUSTER =       // JUnit 4 rule; JUnit 5 equivalent: [unverified]
    new MiniClusterWithClientResource(new MiniClusterResourceConfiguration.Builder()
        .setNumberSlotsPerTaskManager(2).setNumberTaskManagers(1).build());

static final List<Out> SINK = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());   // static: tasks run in the same JVM

@Test void pipelineProducesExpected() throws Exception {
    SINK.clear();
    StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment();
    env.setParallelism(2);
    env.fromData(events).assignTimestampsAndWatermarks(strategy).keyBy(e -> e.key)
       .process(new MyFn()).sinkTo(new CollectSink());     // a tiny Sink V2 that appends to SINK
    env.execute();
    assertThat(SINK).containsExactlyInAnyOrder(...);
}

Rules: - Use a Sink V2 implementation (org.apache.flink.api.connector.sink2.Sink, verified: createWriter(WriterInitContext)), not the legacy SinkFunction. Correction: the legacy interface is not gone in 2.2.1/2.3.0: it was moved to org.apache.flink.streaming.api.functions.sink.legacy.SinkFunction (and ...source.legacy.SourceFunction), marked @Deprecated, and DataStream.addSink / StreamExecutionEnvironment.addSource still take them (verified: javap). Do not use them in new code. To just read results in a test, DataStream.executeAndCollect() (verified: overloads returning CloseableIterator<T> or List<T>) needs no custom sink. - Assert with containsExactlyInAnyOrder: parallelism makes order non-deterministic across keys. Only per-key order is stable. - Use parallelism > 1 and keyBy so serialization and partitioning are really exercised (a parallelism-1 test hides key-group bugs). - The static-list sink works only because MiniCluster runs in one JVM. It will not work on a real cluster. - Bounded input finishes the job and flushes event-time timers/windows with a final MAX watermark (SourceOperator references Watermark.MAX_WATERMARK, javap; the exact end-of-input path was not traced). This makes final-window logic testable but can hide missing-idleness bugs (Chapter 1.5): add a harness test for those.

14.7 Level 4: Kafka tests (Testcontainers-style)

Version note: the Kafka connector for Flink 2.3 does not exist yet; 5.0.0 targets 2.1.x/2.2.x. Pin the test project to Flink 2.2.x when Kafka is involved (README, verified).

Pattern: 1. Start a throwaway Kafka container per test class (Testcontainers KafkaContainer; the library is not in the jar set, so its API is unverified here; which image tag your org allows is [unverified]; use an internal registry mirror). 2. Create topics with the partition count you use in production (partition count affects watermarks and idleness). 3. Produce test records with explicit timestamps; run the job on a MiniCluster with a bounded Kafka source (KafkaSourceBuilder.setBounded(OffsetsInitializer) verified in connector 5.0.0-2.2 via javap; OffsetsInitializer.latest() not re-checked) so it terminates. 4. Consume from the sink topic and assert.

Placeholders only: <KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP> comes from the container, never a real broker. Keep these tests few; they are slow and flaky if they assert on timing.

14.8 What to test, checklist

Concern Level
Parsing, enrichment logic, null handling 1
Timer fires at T, not T-1; timer re-registered 2
Late event goes to side output; counter increments 2
State TTL expiry (Chapter 5) 2 (advance the TTL clock with setStateTtlProcessingTime(long): the harness wires a separate MockTtlTimeProvider, verified in bytecode, so setProcessingTime alone does not expire state)
Snapshot/restore, state compatibility 2
Key partitioning, serializers, multi-operator wiring 3
Idle partition holds watermark 2 or 4 (with an empty partition)
Connector config, offsets, exactly-once end to end 4

14.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Testing with parallelism 1 only: passes, then breaks at production parallelism (keys, ordering, skew).
  • Using the wall clock (System.currentTimeMillis) inside functions: untestable. Read time from ctx.timestamp() / timerService() or inject a clock.
  • Static state in functions leaks between tests; reset in @BeforeEach.
  • Harness does not run your WatermarkStrategy, so a wrong timestamp field passes harness tests and fails in the job.
  • Bounded MiniCluster tests flush with a final watermark and mask lateness and idleness bugs.
  • Pinning to non-public harness APIs: every Flink upgrade can break compile. Isolate harness creation in one helper class.
  • Asserting on global output order across keys: flaky.

14.10 Self-check

  1. Which harness method fires an event-time timer, and which fires a processing-time timer?
  2. Why does a harness test not catch a wrong timestamp assigner?
  3. Design a test that proves a timer survives restore. What do you keep as a golden resource across releases?
  4. Why can a bounded MiniCluster test pass while production windows never close?
  5. Why must the sink in a MiniCluster test be Sink V2 and thread-safe?

14.11 Open items / unverified

  • MiniClusterWithClientResource package, constructor and members, and a public JUnit 5 MiniClusterExtension: flink-test-utils was not downloaded.
  • Which published artifact brings the runtime tests jar (harness classes) transitively.
  • Testcontainers Kafka image/version; OffsetsInitializer.latest() for connector 5.0.0.
  • Resolved from jars (2.2.1): ProcessFunctionTestHarnesses factories, harness method names, KeyedProcessOperator, ListCollector, MiniClusterResourceConfiguration.Builder setters, fromData.
  • Whether the testing page covers TestHarness use for async state (State V2) operators: Data unavailable.

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/testing/

Chapter 15: Kubernetes deployment, HA, and autoscaling

Goal: after this chapter you can deploy a DataStream job in Application mode with the Flink Kubernetes Operator, configure HA and durable checkpoint/savepoint storage, choose an upgrade mode, and decide between the adaptive scheduler, Reactive Mode and the operator autoscaler.

Prerequisites: Chapter 6 (checkpoints, savepoints), Chapter 9 (upgrades), Chapter 10 (parallelism), Chapter 13 (metrics).

15.1 Mental model: two versioned things

The operator has its own version, independent of Flink. The stable operator docs show v1.16.0 (re-fetched: the release-1.16 compatibility page is labelled v1.16.0; the main docs are labelled v1.17-SNAPSHOT). Do not mix up "operator 1.16" with "Flink 1.16".

Supported Flink versions per the operator compatibility page (release-1.16 docs, re-fetched; the main page lists the same rows):

Flink Operator status
1.19, 1.20, 2.0, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4 Supported, "recommended for new deployments"
1.15, 1.16, 1.17, 1.18 Deprecated (still accepted so existing jobs keep running)
1.13, 1.14 No longer supported: rejected at validation, with an UnsupportedFlinkVersion warning event

The row "2.4" was double-checked because no Flink 2.4 release was known to me. It is not an artifact of one page: three independent operator sources list it (the compatibility page, the CRD reference's FlinkVersion allowed values v1_19..v2_4, and the FlinkVersion enum in the operator source on main, constants v1_13..v2_4). So the operator accepts flinkVersion: v2_4. Whether Flink 2.4 itself is released: [unverified] (no jars for it were available; the operator may list versions ahead of release). The operator is therefore documented to support Flink 2.3, even though the Kafka connector for 2.3 does not exist yet (README). For Kafka jobs stay on Flink 2.2.x. The operator project is not in the downloaded jars: everything about it here comes from its docs and GitHub source via the fetch tool (summaries; sub-pages under stable/ and main/ often return empty, release-1.16/ paths worked). Backward-compat policy: since operator 1.0.0, already-deployed resources survive operator and CRD upgrades; new resources are not guaranteed to deploy on old API versions. (From an earlier fetch of the compatibility page; the upgrade page re-fetched only confirms the normal upgrade process applies to operator 1.0.0 or later. Not re-verified in full.)

 kubectl apply FlinkDeployment (spec.job set => Application mode)
        │
 ┌──────▼───────┐  reconcile   ┌──────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
 │ Flink        │─────────────►│ JobManager   │──►│ TaskManagers   │
 │ Operator     │ upgrades,    │ (+ standby)  │   │ (autoscaled)   │
 │ (leader-     │ autoscaling  └──────┬───────┘   └───────┬────────┘
 │  elected)    │                     │ HA metadata       │ checkpoints
 └──────────────┘                     ▼                   ▼
                          high-availability.storageDir / execution.checkpointing.dir (object store, durable)

Figure 15.1: Operator, JobManager, TaskManagers, HA metadata and durable storage.

15.2 Application mode via the operator

The operator decides mode from the spec: "Whether it is Application or Session is decided by whether spec.job is set" (verified). It runs native or standalone deployment mode. Application mode = one cluster per job, job main() runs in the JobManager, good isolation (Chapter 16 tenant separation is easier: one namespace/cluster per tenant group).

Minimal FlinkDeployment (sketch, not applied; field names checked against the operator's examples/basic.yaml on main and the 1.16 CRD reference, both fetched; flinkVersion values v2_2 etc. verified from the FlinkVersion enum; the flinkConfiguration keys are Flink keys verified in the jars below):

apiVersion: flink.apache.org/v1beta1
kind: FlinkDeployment
metadata: { name: my-job }
spec:
  image: <REGISTRY>/my-job:<TAG>
  flinkVersion: v2_2                     # enum constant v2_2 (verified: operator FlinkVersion source)
  serviceAccount: flink
  flinkConfiguration:
    high-availability.type: kubernetes
    high-availability.storageDir: s3://<BUCKET>/ha
    execution.checkpointing.interval: 60s
    job.autoscaler.enabled: "true"
  jobManager:  { resources: { requests: { cpu: "1", memory: "2048m" } } }
  taskManager: { resources: { requests: { cpu: "2", memory: "4096m" } } }
  job:
    jarURI: local:///opt/flink/usrlib/my-job.jar
    parallelism: 4
    upgradeMode: last-state
    state: running

Notes on the sketch: in the 1.16 CRD reference jobManager/taskManager have both resource (cpu, memory, ephemeralStorage; deprecated) and resources (Kubernetes ResourceRequirements); the older release-1.14 example used resource:, the main example uses resources: requests:. serviceAccount: flink, image: and jarURI: local:///... follow the operator example. execution.checkpointing.interval is verified in flink-core 2.2.1 (CheckpointingOptions). Whether resources.limits is honoured the same way: unverified.

Credentials: use Kubernetes Secrets or workload identity; never inline keys (Chapter 16).

15.3 High availability (Kubernetes HA services)

Verified keys (2.3 docs re-fetched; high-availability.type and high-availability.storageDir also verified in flink-core 2.2.1 HighAvailabilityOptions):

Key Meaning
high-availability.type: kubernetes enable Kubernetes HA
high-availability.storageDir durable path (HDFS, S3, other filesystem) for JobManager metadata; Kubernetes stores only a pointer
kubernetes.cluster-id unique id per Flink cluster

RBAC: the service account must create, edit and delete ConfigMaps (verified, re-fetched). The page states Kubernetes 1.9 or later as a prerequisite. kubernetes.* keys live in flink-kubernetes, which was not downloaded: they are docs-verified only. Flink-core 2.2.1 also has high-availability.cluster-id; which of the two the Kubernetes HA services read is [unverified] (the HA page names kubernetes.cluster-id). Deleting the Flink deployment removes cluster resources but keeps the HA ConfigMaps, so a restarted cluster can recover jobs from the latest checkpoint (HA page). HA metadata (job graph, checkpoint pointers) lives in ConfigMaps + storageDir; losing storageDir means last-state recovery fails. The operator itself also has HA: "Flink's Kubernetes HA services with standby JobManagers for the jobs, and leader election for the operator itself" (overview page, re-fetched; detail page deployment/leader-election not fetched). Assumption: an operator-managed deployment sets kubernetes.cluster-id for you; the overview page does not say. [unverified]

15.4 Checkpoint and savepoint storage

  • Use an object store or shared filesystem reachable by all pods, with lifecycle rules that never delete retained checkpoints you may restore from.
  • The savepoint upgrade mode requires a checkpoint or savepoint directory to be defined (verified, job-management page re-fetched). Flink 2.2.1 key names (verified: javap CheckpointingOptions): execution.checkpointing.dir, execution.checkpointing.savepoint-dir, execution.checkpointing.num-retained (default 1), execution.checkpointing.externalized-checkpoint-retention (DELETE_ON_CANCELLATION, RETAIN_ON_CANCELLATION, NO_EXTERNALIZED_CHECKPOINTS). The older state.checkpoints.dir, state.savepoints.dir and state.checkpoints.num-retained are still present in the class as keys (deprecated names); new configs should use the execution.checkpointing.* keys.
  • Separate prefixes per job and per tenant (isolation, Chapter 16). Retain externalized checkpoints on cancel if you rely on last-state.

15.5 Upgrade modes (verified, operator job-management page, release-1.16 path re-fetched)

upgradeMode Requirement Stop Restore
stateless none cancel/delete empty state
last-state checkpointing enabled cancel, keep HA metadata HA metadata or latest snapshot
savepoint checkpoint or savepoint dir defined cancel with savepoint from that savepoint

job.state: running (default) or suspended (state preserved).

Caveats (verified): - savepoint needs a running job; for unhealthy jobs it falls back to the latest checkpoint only if HA is enabled and fallback is not disabled. - With last-state, you cannot change spec.flinkVersion while suspended; restore with the current version, then upgrade. - last-state depends on accessible HA metadata; manual recovery may be needed if lost. - The operator reacts only to spec changes. Edits to referenced ConfigMaps/Secrets are invisible; roll out with restartNonce. - Manual recovery: spec.job.initialSavepointPath; spec.job.savepointRedeployNonce triggers redeploy from the given path. - Triggering ad-hoc savepoints: spec.job.savepointTriggerNonce is listed in the 1.16 CRD reference ("manually trigger savepoints by changing value"); spec.restartNonce triggers a restart following the upgrade mode (job-management page).

Choosing: savepoint mode for planned code/state-schema changes (Chapter 9, canonical format, portable); last-state for fast restarts and parallelism changes with unchanged state schema; stateless only for stateless or disposable jobs. Whether a 1.20 to 2.x upgrade can restore state is Chapter 9's question: Data unavailable here.

15.6 Scheduling: adaptive scheduler, Reactive Mode (verified, elastic scaling page)

Feature Key / fact
Adaptive scheduler jobmanager.scheduler: adaptive (verified: enum SchedulerType = Default, Adaptive, AdaptiveBatch); adjusts parallelism to available slots, scales up again to configured parallelism; streaming only. Default: the option's default is Default; its description says "batch jobs will use the 'AdaptiveBatch' scheduler as the default, while streaming jobs will default to the 'Default' scheduler" (javap, 2.2.1 and 2.3.0). So the Adaptive Scheduler is not the streaming default in these jars: set it explicitly (see Cross-chapter log, README says otherwise)
Limits no partial failover; batch jobs use the Adaptive Batch Scheduler
Reactive Mode key scheduler-mode, value reactive (verified: JobManagerOptions, enum SchedulerExecutionMode.REACTIVE); uses all available slots
Reactive limits standalone Application mode only; "not by active resource managers (YARN, Kubernetes) or session clusters" (verified: option description in JobManagerOptions)
Tuning keys (defaults verified: javap JobManagerOptions, same in 2.2.1 and 2.3.0) jobmanager.adaptive-scheduler.resource-wait-timeout (5 min, negative = wait indefinitely; an earlier draft said -1), ...resource-stabilization-timeout (10 s; defaults to 0 when scheduler-mode is reactive; earlier draft said 0), ...executing.cooldown-after-rescaling (30 s; ...scaling-interval.min appears to be its deprecated key, also 30 s), ...scaling-interval.max (disabled by default), ...rescale-trigger.max-checkpoint-failures (2), ...rescale-trigger.max-delay, ...prefer-minimal-taskmanagers. ...min-parallelism-increase (1) is "not used anymore" per its description, so do not tune it

Consequence for Kubernetes: Reactive Mode works with standalone-mode deployments (where you scale TaskManagers, e.g. by replica count), not with native Kubernetes resource management. The operator autoscaler (15.7) is the managed alternative.

Rescale history (new in 2.3)

web.adaptive-scheduler.rescale-history.size: <positive int> (verified: present in flink-core 2.3.0 WebOptions, absent in 2.2.1; default 0, disabled when 0 or negative; description: maximum number of rescale records per job whose scheduler is Adaptive). When on, the UI/API shows per-rescale: id, trigger cause, terminal state, duration, per-vertex parallelism changes, scheduler state transitions. Enable it while tuning autoscaling to see why jobs rescale.

Resource declaration REST

PUT /jobs/<job-id>/resource-requirements re-declares per-vertex parallelism bounds (lowerBound/upperBound) on a running job (page says 1.18+). Route verified: JobResourceRequirementsHeaders in flink-runtime 2.2.1 has URL /jobs/:jobid/resource-requirements (the PUT method and lowerBound/upperBound names are from the docs page; the request-body class is JobResourceRequirements, body schema not read: [unverified]). Intended for the adaptive scheduler; this is the mechanism external autoscalers use.

15.7 Operator autoscaler (operator v1.16 docs)

Enable: job.autoscaler.enabled: "true" in flinkConfiguration (key and default false verified: operator AutoScalerOptions). Settings at resource or operator level and "changes apply without restarting the job": from an earlier fetch, [unverified] this session.

Requirements (verified, autoscaler page re-fetched): streaming jobs only; FLIP-27 sources for busy-time metrics; standardized connector metrics (FLIP-33) for backlog (Chapter 13 shows which of those the Kafka source actually emits); in-place rescaling needs jobmanager.scheduler: adaptive, otherwise each scaling is a full job upgrade (restart).

Key Default Meaning
job.autoscaler.metrics.window 15 min averaging window
job.autoscaler.stabilization.interval 5 min settle time after start/rescale
job.autoscaler.utilization.target 0.7 target utilization
job.autoscaler.utilization.max / .min unset by default; the autoscaler docs say target + 0.3 / target - 0.3 scale-up/down thresholds (dead band). The 0.3 comes from job.autoscaler.target.utilization.boundary (default 0.3, verified in AutoScalerOptions); exact precedence between boundary and max/min: [unverified]
job.autoscaler.catch-up.duration 30 min time to clear backlog
job.autoscaler.restart.time 5 min expected rescale downtime
job.autoscaler.vertex.min-parallelism / .max-parallelism 1 / 200 per-vertex bounds; the max is ignored if higher than the Flink max parallelism configured in the Flink config or on the operator (source description)

Loop: collect (once per reconciliation pass, default every minute; verified on the autoscaler page) -> evaluate per vertex -> execute. No action while utilization stays in the band. Safe start: job.autoscaler.scaling.enabled: "false" (default true) evaluates but does not apply (metrics-only; verified, option description). Other defaults in the table verified in AutoScalerOptions (main) and the generated config table.

15.8 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • HA storageDir on a non-durable or per-pod volume: failover loses the job graph.
  • last-state with HA metadata deleted (namespace cleanup, ConfigMap TTL jobs): job restarts empty or stuck.
  • Missing ConfigMap RBAC: JobManager cannot elect a leader; crash loop.
  • Autoscaler without adaptive scheduler: every decision restarts the job; flapping parallelism causes repeated downtime and Kafka lag spikes.
  • Autoscaling is bounded by Kafka partitions and key-group count (maxParallelism, Chapter 10): scaling past partitions adds idle subtasks (and idle watermarks, Chapter 1.5).
  • Autoscaling a skewed job scales the hot subtask's vertex but does not fix skew (Chapter 10).
  • Config changes in a Secret/ConfigMap do not trigger a rollout; use restartNonce.
  • Reactive Mode assumed to work on native Kubernetes: it does not.
  • Changing parallelism changes keyed-state distribution; maxParallelism must be set from day one (cannot be raised without state migration).

15.9 Self-check

  1. Operator is "1.16" and Flink is "2.2". Which one does flinkVersion refer to?
  2. Why does last-state need HA, and what happens if the storageDir is wiped?
  3. Why can't you use Reactive Mode with the native Kubernetes resource provider?
  4. The autoscaler keeps restarting your job on every rescale. What is the first config to check?
  5. A job has 12 Kafka partitions and the autoscaler wants parallelism 40. What happens?

  • Whether Flink 2.4 exists/is released (the operator lists it); resources.limits handling.
  • Operator leader-election detail page and whether it sets kubernetes.cluster-id automatically; high-availability.cluster-id vs kubernetes.cluster-id roles.
  • Request body schema of resource-requirements REST; which scheduler modes the operator uses for it.
  • Precedence of utilization.boundary vs utilization.max/min; autoscaler "changes apply without restart" claim.
  • kubernetes.* keys: flink-kubernetes jar not downloaded (docs only).
  • Operator-docs "stable" and main URL paths often return empty from the fetch tool (summaries, sometimes wrong language path); content was read from release-1.16 paths plus GitHub main. The stable alias may point to a different version later. The fetch tool summarizes; field spellings were cross-checked on two sources each.

  • Autoscaler behavior on Flink 2.3 specifically (FLIP-27 sources only, Kafka connector 5.0.0 on 2.2.x): not tested.

Chapter 16: Security

Goal: after this chapter you can turn on TLS for Flink's internal and REST traffic, decide who may reach the REST API, keep secrets out of code, config files, savepoints and logs, configure Kafka client security and ACLs for a Flink job, list every place personal data can land, and describe tenant isolation you can actually enforce.

Prerequisites: Chapter 6 (checkpoints/savepoints), Chapter 7 (Kafka delivery guarantees), Chapter 12 (DLQ), Chapter 15 (Kubernetes). Kafka examples assume Flink 2.2.x with Kafka connector 5.0.0 (no connector for 2.3 yet, see README). This chapter is engineering guidance, not legal advice. Draft only. Review required by Legal, Compliance, or the relevant control owner.

16.1 Where the attack surface is

 client/CLI/UI --REST--> JobManager <--internal RPC/data/blob--> TaskManagers
                              |                                      |
                         checkpoint storage  <-----------------------+
                         (object store / DFS)
 Kafka brokers <--- Kafka client (SASL/SSL) --- sources/sinks inside TaskManagers
 DLQ topic, logs, metrics, heap dumps, savepoints  = places data and secrets can leak

Three separate trust boundaries: (1) who can call the REST API (which can submit jars and trigger savepoints), (2) who can talk to the cluster's internal ports, (3) who can read what the job writes out (state, topics, logs).

Figure 16.1: The three trust boundaries around a Flink cluster.

16.2 SSL/TLS: internal vs REST (verified: 2.3 docs re-fetched, and key names/defaults by javap of flink-core 2.2.1 SecurityOptions)

Scope Enable key Other keys (all verified names)
Internal (RPC, data exchange, blob) security.ssl.internal.enabled (default false) security.ssl.internal.keystore, .keystore-password, .key-password, .truststore, .truststore-password
REST / external security.ssl.rest.enabled (default false) same suffixes under security.ssl.rest.*, plus security.ssl.rest.authentication-enabled (default false)
Shared security.ssl.algorithms, security.ssl.protocol (default TLSv1.2, verified in bytecode; value is a single protocol, "it doesn't support comma separated list"). Also exist (verified): security.ssl.verify-hostname, security.ssl.internal.cert.fingerprint, security.ssl.rest.cert.fingerprint, *.keystore-type, *.truststore-type

Mental model: - Internal connections use mutual TLS: both sides present a certificate. The docs note a self-signed certificate can act as a shared secret inside one deployment. Anything that holds the keystore can join the cluster, so protect it like a password. - REST does not authenticate clients by default. Enabling security.ssl.rest.authentication-enabled makes REST use mutual TLS. The docs recommend instead putting a sidecar proxy (Envoy or NGINX are named) in front, bound to loopback, which then owns authentication and authorization (re-fetched SSL page: "the REST endpoint does not authenticate the client" by default; Envoy and NGINX are named). Flink itself has no user/role model for REST [no user-level authn/authz found in the docs or option classes checked; absence is not proof]. Related keys verified in flink-core 2.2.1: rest.bind-address, rest.bind-port, rest.address, and the UI switches web.submit.enable (jar upload via UI) and web.cancel.enable; their defaults were not read. - On Kubernetes, keystores/truststores go into the image or a mounted directory (docs). Prefer a mounted Secret (16.5).

Sketch of config with placeholders only (sketch, not compiled; paths are examples):

security.ssl.internal.enabled: true
security.ssl.internal.keystore: /opt/flink/tls/internal.keystore
security.ssl.internal.truststore: /opt/flink/tls/internal.truststore
# passwords: do NOT write them here, see 16.5. Inject via env/secret mechanism.
security.ssl.rest.enabled: true
security.ssl.rest.keystore: /opt/flink/tls/rest.keystore

Heuristic (not a Flink fact): use a separate keystore for REST and internal, so rotating the public-facing certificate does not rotate the cluster-internal trust.

16.3 REST authentication in practice

Option Strength Note
Nothing (default) none anyone reaching the port can submit jars: effectively code execution in your cluster
security.ssl.rest.authentication-enabled (mTLS) client cert required cert distribution to every operator and CI job
Sidecar/ingress proxy with SSO per-user identity, audit recommended by the docs pattern; the proxy is your responsibility
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy network-level complements, does not replace, authentication

Rule: the REST port is an admin interface. Never expose it to a general network. Restrict who can submit jars; a submitted job runs with the cluster's credentials (Kafka, checkpoint storage).

16.4 Kerberos (brief)

Verified keys (javap SecurityOptions, flink-core 2.2.1): security.kerberos.login.keytab, security.kerberos.login.principal, security.kerberos.login.use-ticket-cache, security.kerberos.krb5-conf.path, security.kerberos.login.contexts. Deprecated-looking short names security.keytab and security.principal also exist. The JAAS security module makes the configured credential available to Kafka, ZooKeeper and other JAAS-based components. A static JAAS file overrides the dynamic entries (docs). Flink also has a pluggable DelegationTokenProvider API (verified: org.apache.flink.core.security.token.DelegationTokenProvider in flink-core; providers found in flink-runtime 2.2.1: HadoopFSDelegationTokenProvider, HBaseDelegationTokenProvider; none in flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2). Option keys security.delegation.tokens.enabled etc. exist. Details of Kafka-with-Kerberos (SASL_GSSAPI) are [unverified] here; most teams use SASL/SCRAM or mTLS with Kafka and skip Kerberos. A keytab is a long-lived credential: treat it like a password.

16.5 Secrets handling

Where secrets must never appear:

Place Why it is dangerous
Source code and git permanent, copied everywhere
Job arguments / ParameterTool shown in UI the job configuration (global job parameters) is visible in the Web UI and REST responses. Flink masks values whose key contains one of: password, secret, fs.azure.account.key, apikey, api-key, auth-params, basic-auth, service-key, token, jaas.config, http-headers; the mask is ****** (verified: GlobalConfiguration.SENSITIVE_KEYS/HIDDEN_CONTENT, and ConfigurationUtils.hideSensitiveValues used by the REST classes ConfigurationInfo and JobConfigInfo$ExecutionConfigInfo, 2.2.1). A secret under any other key name, or inside a value, is shown in clear
Flink config file in the image image layers are readable by anyone with pull access
Operator or function fields if a field is serialized into a closure it travels in the job graph; if it lands in state it lands in checkpoints/savepoints
Logs and exception messages printing the Kafka Properties object prints sasl.jaas.config
Savepoints state is copied out of the cluster; a secret in state leaves with it

Kubernetes (verified keys, native deployment): kubernetes.secrets (secretName:/mount/path, mounts files) and kubernetes.env.secretKeyRef (env:ENV_VAR_NAME,secret:secretName,key:keyName, ;-separated). Prefer mounted files over env vars (env vars leak into process listings, crash dumps and some debug endpoints; heuristic). kubernetes.service-account sets the JobManager's service account; keep its RBAC to what pod management needs. Using an operator or a secret manager (external secrets, CSI driver): [unverified] here, see Chapter 15.

Pattern: keep the secret value out of anything serialized with the job. Warning, corrected: KafkaSource stores its client Properties in a field (private final Properties props, verified: javap flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2) and the source is serialized with the job graph, so any value you pass to setProperty(...) in main() travels to the TaskManagers, including a sasl.jaas.config read from a file in main(). Earlier draft claimed otherwise. Two ways to avoid it, both [unverified] because they rely on Kafka client behaviour and the kafka-clients jar was not in the jar set: (a) a Kafka config provider: config.providers=file, config.providers.file.class=org.apache.kafka.common.config.provider.FileConfigProvider, and a property value of the form ${file:<path>:<key>}, resolved by the client on the TaskManager; (b) a JAAS file mounted from a Secret and selected with the JVM option -Djava.security.auth.login.config=<path> via env.java.opts.taskmanager / env.java.opts.jobmanager (option keys verified in CoreOptions), with no sasl.jaas.config property at all. Sketch with (a) (sketch, not compiled; placeholders only):

// Sketch, not compiled. Only a file path and a key name are serialized with the job; the secret value is read by the Kafka client on the TaskManager.
KafkaSource<String> src = KafkaSource.<String>builder()
    .setBootstrapServers(System.getenv("KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP"))        // <KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP>
    .setTopics("<TOPIC_IN>")
    .setGroupId("<GROUP_ID>")
    .setProperty("security.protocol", "SASL_SSL")
    .setProperty("sasl.mechanism", "SCRAM-SHA-512")
    .setProperty("config.providers", "file")
    .setProperty("config.providers.file.class", "org.apache.kafka.common.config.provider.FileConfigProvider")
    .setProperty("sasl.jaas.config", "${file:/var/run/secrets/kafka/client.properties:sasl.jaas.config}")  // only the placeholder is serialized [unverified, Kafka knowledge]
    .setProperty("ssl.truststore.location", "/var/run/secrets/kafka/truststore")
    .setValueOnlyDeserializer(new SimpleStringSchema())
    .build();

Hygiene: if a secret ever reached a log, a savepoint or a repo, rotate it; deleting the artifact is not enough. Do not log Properties; log a redacted key list instead.

16.6 Kafka client security

The connector forwards properties to the Kafka client. Builder methods (verified: javap connector 5.0.0-2.2): KafkaSourceBuilder.setProperty(String,String) and setProperties(Properties); KafkaSinkBuilder.setProperty(String,String) and setKafkaProducerConfig(Properties) (the sink builder has no setProperties; an earlier draft claimed both builders had it). The docs show SASL_PLAINTEXT and a SASL_SSL example with SCRAM-SHA-256 plus truststore and keystore. The source builder's string constants show it sets or checks bootstrap.servers, group.id, key.deserializer, value.deserializer, auto.offset.reset and enable.auto.commit; the sink builder handles bootstrap.servers, key.serializer, value.serializer and transaction.timeout.ms (constants only: override-versus-default behaviour per key was not traced). security.*, sasl.* and ssl.* keys are not among them, so they pass through. Use TLS (SASL_SSL or SSL), not PLAINTEXT.

Source and sink need the same security properties, separately configured. Keep them in one shared builder helper (see Chapter 23 for tenants).

ACLs the job needs (checklist checked against Kafka's "Authorization and ACLs" page, kafka.apache.org/41, fetched; ACL syntax is Kafka's, not Flink's; the Flink docs do not discuss ACLs)

Role Kafka resource Operation
Source Topic (input) Read, Describe
Source Group (consumer group id) Read
Sink, at-least-once Topic (output) Write, Describe
Sink, exactly-once TransactionalId (prefix) Write, Describe (Kafka requires these for transactional producers)
Sink, exactly-once Cluster IdempotentWrite: Kafka docs say it is required for idempotent produce and "automatically enabled when producer has TransactionalId authorization (KIP-679, Kafka 3.0+)"; grant it explicitly only on older brokers
DLQ topic Topic Write (job), Read (the replay tool only)

Verified against the Kafka page: PRODUCE needs Write on Topic (plus Write on TransactionalId if transactional); FETCH Read on Topic; OFFSET_COMMIT/JOIN_GROUP Read on Group; METADATA and LIST_OFFSETS Describe on Topic; INIT_PRODUCER_ID, ADD_PARTITIONS_TO_TXN, ADD_OFFSETS_TO_TXN, END_TXN Write on TransactionalId; FIND_COORDINATOR Describe on Group (consumer) or Describe on TransactionalId (transactional producer); TXN_OFFSET_COMMIT Write TransactionalId, Read Group, Read Topic. Operation names on that page: Read, Write, Create, Delete, Alter, Describe, ClusterAction, DescribeConfigs, AlterConfigs, IdempotentWrite, CreateTokens, DescribeTokens, All; resources Topic, Group, Cluster, TransactionalId, DelegationToken, User. That Read implies Describe and that ACLs may use a PREFIXED pattern type are Kafka knowledge not quoted by the fetched summary: [unverified], check on your Kafka version.

Notes: - Use a prefixed ACL on TransactionalId matching setTransactionalIdPrefix(...). The docs require setTransactionalIdPrefix for DeliveryGuarantee.EXACTLY_ONCE and say to use a unique prefix per application on the same cluster. Unique prefixes also give you one ACL per job (Chapter 7). - Separate principals per job; never reuse an admin principal. A job must not be able to create or delete topics. - Backfill jobs (Chapter 24) get a different group id and a read-only principal.

16.7 Where PII lands (and how to contain it)

Place What lands there Containment
Keyed and operator state whole records, keys, buffered window contents store minimal fields or hashes; state TTL (Chapter 5)
Checkpoints a copy of all state, in checkpoint storage encrypt at rest at the storage layer; short retention; restrict bucket/path IAM
Savepoints full, portable state copy, kept indefinitely same as above, plus an explicit expiry owner; do not copy to laptops
Logs (JM/TM, exceptions) records in exception messages, toString(), debug logging never log payloads; log ids/hashes; ship logs to a store with access control
DLQ topic the raw failing record (Chapter 12) same classification as the source topic, short retention, own ACL
Heap/thread dumps all live objects incl. secrets disable automatic dumps in prod or write to a restricted volume. JVM flags are set through Flink options verified in CoreOptions: env.java.opts.all, env.java.opts.jobmanager, env.java.opts.taskmanager (and env.java.default-opts.*); the flags themselves (e.g. -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:HeapDumpPath) are JVM facts, not checked here; whether Flink's defaults enable dumps was not read
Metrics/labels keys used as metric labels (user id, tenant) never label metrics with user ids; bounded labels only
Side outputs, test fixtures copies in other topics and in the repo scrub data before using it in tests (Chapter 14)

Figure 16.2: Where personal data can land and how to contain it.

Encryption at rest: the checkpoint docs I fetched do not describe built-in encryption of checkpoint or savepoint files (Data unavailable). Assume Flink writes plaintext state files and rely on storage-layer encryption (server-side encryption, volume encryption) and access policies. This is an Assumption; test it by reading a checkpoint file with a plain viewer.

Retention: ExternalizedCheckpointRetention (RETAIN_ON_CANCELLATION, DELETE_ON_CANCELLATION, also NO_EXTERNALIZED_CHECKPOINTS) decides whether cancelled-job checkpoints stay behind (verified: enum in flink-core 2.2.1, config key execution.checkpointing.externalized-checkpoint-retention, setter CheckpointConfig.setExternalizedCheckpointRetention). Prefer DELETE_ON_CANCELLATION when you do not need to resume from them, and use a storage lifecycle rule as a backstop. Number of retained checkpoints: execution.checkpointing.num-retained, default 1 (verified: javap CheckpointingOptions; old name state.checkpoints.num-retained still present).

Deleting a person's data (erasure requests) is hard in Flink: it is in state, in old checkpoints and in savepoints. Design for it: key state by a pseudonymous id, keep PII outside Flink and join late, short TTL. Chapter 27 builds this.

16.8 Multi-tenant isolation notes

Isolation must be enforced by the platform, not by a field in the record.

Level Strength Mechanism
One tenant field, shared job weakest (convention) filter in code; one bug leaks everything
Separate topics per tenant, shared job medium per-topic ACLs on the job principal still allow the one job to read all
Separate jobs and principals per tenant strong each job has its own Kafka principal, ACLs, checkpoint path, secrets
Separate clusters or namespaces strongest NetworkPolicy, namespace RBAC, separate keystores

Rules (heuristics): one checkpoint prefix per job and tenant, IAM-scoped; never share a consumer group or transactional-id prefix across tenants; tenant id is part of every log line and metric dimension (bounded set); keys include tenant id so state cannot collide. Dynamic fan-out and topic-pattern limits are in Chapter 23.

Pitfalls / failure modes

  • REST port reachable on a pod network with no auth: anyone can upload a jar.
  • Enabling internal SSL on only the JobManager config: connections fail; all processes need matching keystores and truststores.
  • Certificate expiry: a cluster that restarts after a cert expires cannot form. Alert on expiry dates.
  • Passwords in flink-conf baked into the image, or printed with a Properties.toString().
  • Exactly-once sink without a TransactionalId ACL: the job fails on producer init, or worse, someone grants a wildcard * ACL to "fix it".
  • Savepoints stored in a world-readable bucket "for convenience".
  • A DLQ topic with no retention holds PII for years.
  • Dev heap dumps committed to tickets.

What the article got wrong

Its PII "view" was a convention, not a control: any consumer of the base topic or of Flink state still sees raw data. Enforcement needs ACLs, separate topics and storage-level policies (Chapter 27).

Self-check

  1. Which two SSL scopes does Flink distinguish, and which one is mutual TLS by default?
  2. Why is a self-signed internal keystore effectively a shared secret?
  3. List four places a Kafka password can leak from a Flink job, and one control for each.
  4. What ACL resources does an exactly-once sink need beyond Write on the topic?
  5. A user asks for erasure. Name three stores where their data may still exist after you delete the topic record.

Open items / unverified

  • Redaction: resolved (key-name based masking, see 16.5); not covered: values under non-sensitive keys, logs of user code.
  • Built-in encryption of checkpoints/savepoints: Data unavailable (no statement found, no option found by name search in the config classes read). Assumed none.
  • Kerberos-with-Kafka (SASL_GSSAPI) specifics. [unverified]
  • Secret managers (CSI, external secrets) with Flink on Kubernetes. [unverified]
  • Kafka config providers (FileConfigProvider) and -Djava.security.auth.login.config as ways to keep the JAAS secret out of the job graph: Kafka/JVM knowledge, [unverified] (kafka-clients not in the jar set).
  • Kafka ACL "Read implies Describe" and PREFIXED pattern: Kafka knowledge, [unverified]; the operations/resources table itself matches the Kafka authorization page.
  • Heap-dump flag defaults in Flink: not read. [unverified]
  • DelegationTokenProvider for Kafka: no provider found in flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2 or flink-runtime; stated as not found, not as impossible.
  • kubernetes.* keys (docs-only; flink-kubernetes jar not downloaded).
