Chapter 17: Capacity planning

Goal: after this chapter you can estimate slots, state size, checkpoint cost and Kafka partition needs for a job, add headroom for catch-up, fill in a worked template, and validate the numbers with a load test.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state, TTL), Chapter 6 (checkpoints), Chapter 10 (parallelism, skew), Chapter 11 (memory, RocksDB), Chapter 13 (metrics).

Read this first. Flink publishes no sizing formula. Everything below labeled Heuristic is a rule of thumb from practice, not a Flink fact. All numbers in the worked example are ASSUMED and must be replaced with your measurements. Metric names below were confirmed as string constants in the Flink 2.2.1 jars (flink-runtime MetricNames, DefaultCheckpointStatsTracker, MetricsTrackingValueState); they were not re-checked against 2.3.0 jars.

17.1 The sizing loop

 measure per-slot throughput --> estimate state --> estimate checkpoint cost
        ^                                                    |
        |                                                    v
   load test & adjust  <-- add headroom <-- pick parallelism & partitions

Figure 17.1: The sizing loop with the ASSUMED worked-example numbers of 17.8; replace every number with a measurement.

Capacity is set by the first resource to saturate: CPU (serialization, user code), state backend I/O, network, sink or external service, or checkpoint duration. Find which one before adding slots.

17.2 Throughput per slot: measurement method

Heuristic procedure (a slot is one task slot; with default slot sharing one slot can run a whole pipeline slice): 1. Deploy the real job (real serializers, real state, real sink) with parallelism P0 on a dedicated test cluster. 2. Feed it a backlog from Kafka (replay a representative day) so the source is never starved. 3. Let it warm up (caches, RocksDB compaction) for a fixed period; discard it. 4. Over a steady window read per-task numRecordsInPerSecond (verified) and busyTimeMsPerSecond, backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond (verified: flink-runtime 2.2.1 MetricNames). 5. Compute max sustainable rate per slot = records/s per task divided by (busyTimeMsPerSecond / 1000). This normalizes for idle time: a task 40% busy doing 2,000 rec/s can do about 5,000 rec/s at 100% busy. Heuristic; do not plan above about 70% busy. 6. Find the bottleneck operator: the first one with high busy time while downstream is idle. Backpressure appears upstream of the bottleneck (Chapter 11). 7. Repeat at 2 or 3 parallelism values. If throughput does not scale about linearly, suspect key skew (Chapter 10), a hot partition, or an external sink limit.

Use a mixed payload size and key distribution that matches production; uniform synthetic keys hide skew.

17.3 State size estimation

Formula (Heuristic):

state_bytes = live_keys x bytes_per_key_entry x versions x overhead
  • live_keys: distinct keys alive at once. With TTL (Chapter 5): keys active within the TTL window, plus not-yet-cleaned entries. TTL expiry is lazy-ish by backend; treat real size as larger than the minimum. Cleanup specifics: Chapter 5.
  • bytes_per_key_entry: serialized key + value. Measure it, do not guess: write 1 million sample entries and compare checkpoint size before and after. The state-size histograms (for example valueStateGetValueSize) exist in the metrics page but are off by default: enable with state.size-track.keyed-state-enabled: true (sampled every state.size-track.sample-interval, default 100 accesses; verified: flink-core 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 StateSizeTrackOptions). With TTL on, the tracked value size includes the TTL timestamp (same option description).
  • versions: copies held at once. Window state holds one entry per open window per key; sliding windows multiply by size/slide. Interval joins and timers hold buffered records for the join range.
  • overhead: serializer framing, RocksDB write amplification and compaction slack. Heuristic: 1.5x to 3x on disk for RocksDB; JVM heap objects on the heap backend cost more than serialized bytes. Verify by measurement.

TTL effect: state size trends to (arrival rate of new keys x TTL), not unbounded. Without TTL, "keys x bytes" grows with the key universe forever. Dedup and per-user state must have TTL or an explicit cleanup timer (Chapters 3, 5, 18).

17.4 Checkpoint size, duration, cost

Verified metrics (string constants in flink-runtime 2.2.1 DefaultCheckpointStatsTracker): lastCheckpointSize, lastCheckpointFullSize, lastCheckpointDuration, numberOfCompletedCheckpoints, numberOfFailedCheckpoints.

Heuristics: - Full checkpoint size is about state size (plus in-flight data if unaligned, Chapter 6). Incremental checkpoints (RocksDB) upload only changes, so lastCheckpointSize can be far below lastCheckpointFullSize. - Duration is roughly (data to upload per checkpoint) / (aggregate upload bandwidth), plus alignment time under backpressure. - Set the interval so duration is well under the interval (target below about 50% of it) and leave a minimum pause so checkpointing does not run back-to-back. - Storage cost = retained checkpoints x average stored size, plus request cost. Incremental checkpoints share files, so stored size is not simply N x size. Savepoints are full and kept until you delete them. - Restore time matters for recovery SLO: it scales with state size and download bandwidth. Test it.

17.5 Kafka partitions vs parallelism

Rule Basis
A source subtask reads whole partitions; parallelism above partition count leaves subtasks idle consequence of the split model; confirm in Chapter 10
Idle subtasks hold back watermarks unless idleness is set verified: Kafka 2.2 docs say the source does not go idle automatically if parallelism exceeds partitions; lower parallelism or add an idle timeout
Pick partitions = a multiple of expected max parallelism (for example 48 for up to 48 slots) Heuristic; even assignment
Raising partitions later changes key-to-partition mapping for keyed producers and breaks per-key ordering in the cutover Kafka behavior, state it to the team
Partition count is a ceiling on source parallelism only; downstream keyed operators can have higher parallelism after a shuffle Heuristic, verify with your topology

Also consider max parallelism (key groups) fixed per job: it caps how far you can later rescale a keyed job from state (Chapter 9, Chapter 10). Choose it generously at first deploy.

17.6 Headroom for catch-up and backfill

Steady-state sizing is not enough: after an outage or a deploy the job must drain a backlog while new data keeps arriving.

 drain_time = backlog / (capacity - incoming_rate)
 required capacity = incoming_rate + backlog / target_drain_time

Heuristic: plan capacity at 2x peak steady rate if you need to catch up within hours; 1.3x if a day is acceptable. Capacity during catch-up must also cover bigger checkpoints, and the sink and downstream systems must withstand 2x rates (Chapter 24 for backfill). Alternatively run the backfill as a separate job and temporary slots (Chapter 15).

17.7 Memory configuration pointers

Do not size memory here; use Chapter 11 for: heap vs managed memory vs network buffers, RocksDB managed memory, and async I/O. Capacity inputs you must hand to that chapter: state bytes per slot, number of slots per TaskManager, and buffer needs. Heuristic: fewer, larger TaskManagers share JVM overhead better; more, smaller ones limit blast radius. Network-buffer needs grow with the upstream parallelism (verified: the description of taskmanager.network.memory.read-buffer.required-per-gate.max in flink-core 2.2.1 says an input gate's buffer need is computed at runtime from factors such as upstream parallelism); see Chapter 11.

17.8 Worked estimation template

All numbers are ASSUMED. Replace each with a measurement.

Input Symbol ASSUMED value
Peak incoming rate R 60,000 rec/s
Average record size S 1 KB
Max sustainable rate per slot at 100% busy (measured in 17.2) C 8,000 rec/s
Target max busy B 70%
Live keys (active users in TTL window) K 20,000,000
Bytes per key entry (measured) E 200 B
Versions per key V 1
Overhead factor O 2
Stored checkpoints retained N 3
Incremental change ratio per interval D 5%
Checkpoint interval I 60 s
Upload bandwidth, aggregate W 200 MB/s
Catch-up target T 2 h after a 1 h outage

Calculation: - Slots for steady load = R / (C x B) = 60,000 / (8,000 x 0.7) = 10.7, round up to 11 slots. - Catch-up: backlog = 1 h x 60,000 = 216,000,000 rec. Required capacity = R + backlog / T = 60,000 + 216,000,000 / 7,200 = 90,000 rec/s. Slots = 90,000 / (8,000 x 0.7) = 16.1, so 17 slots. Plan 17 (or scale up temporarily, Chapter 15). - Parallelism choice: 24 gives headroom and divides 48 partitions evenly. Partitions: 48 (multiple of the plan). - State = K x E x V x O = 20,000,000 x 200 x 1 x 2 = 8 GB total; per slot at 24 = about 333 MB. - Full checkpoint about 8 GB (if stored uncompressed); incremental delta = 8 GB x 5% = 400 MB per interval, upload time = 400 / 200 = 2 s. First full checkpoint = 8 GB / 200 MB/s = 40 s: fits under the 60 s interval but only barely; revisit. - Storage = roughly base 8 GB + deltas retained; order of 8 to 12 GB for N=3 (shared files). Assumption; measure. - Input bandwidth to Kafka: R x S = 60 MB/s (before replication on the broker side).

Sanity checks: Is R x S within broker and network limits? Does the sink handle 90,000 rec/s? Does a restore of 8 GB meet your recovery target?

17.9 Load-test procedure

  1. Define goals: steady rate, peak rate, catch-up time, recovery time, checkpoint duration limit.
  2. Build a data generator (or replay) with production-like key distribution, payload size, out-of-order and late ratios.
  3. Isolated environment: same Flink version, Java, state backend and TLS/security settings as production (TLS costs CPU).
  4. Warm up, then run ramp steps (50%, 100%, 150%, 200% of peak), 20 to 30 minutes each (heuristic).
  5. Record per step: rate in/out, busy and backpressure per operator, checkpoint size and duration, failures, GC time, Kafka consumer lag, sink latency.
  6. Chaos checks: kill a TaskManager mid-run; measure restore time and lag recovery. Run an outage backlog test (pause the job 1 h, resume).
  7. Run a long soak (many hours to a day) to expose state growth, TTL behavior and leaks.
  8. Decide: capacity = highest step that holds busy below the target, with checkpoints healthy and lag draining. Write down the result and the date.

Use production data only if allowed by policy; otherwise synthetic data with the same shape (Chapter 16).

Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Averages hide skew: one hot key pins one slot at 100% while the rest idle (Chapter 10).
  • Planning from a quiet day; no headroom for a deploy-time backlog.
  • Estimating state from record count, not distinct keys, or ignoring TTL.
  • Ignoring the sink: Flink scales, the database does not.
  • Changing max parallelism later: cannot be done from state without care (Chapter 9).
  • Checkpoint interval shorter than checkpoint duration: permanent checkpointing, no progress.
  • Test cluster with a different serializer (Kryo fallback) from production (Chapter 8).

Self-check

  1. Why divide observed rate by busy fraction, and why not plan to 100% busy?
  2. State grows linearly for a week. Name two causes and one fix for each.
  3. 48 partitions, you want 96 slots. What happens at the source, and what does it do to watermarks?
  4. How much capacity do you need to drain a 2-hour backlog in 4 hours at 20,000 rec/s incoming? (Show the formula.)
  5. Which numbers in your sizing are measured and which are assumed?

Open items / unverified

  • Per-state size histograms exist (state.size-track.keyed-state-enabled, default false; sampled, 17.3). A total per-operator state size metric available by default: not found in the jars checked. [unverified]
  • Network-buffer sizing numbers (see Chapter 11) and slot-sharing effects on per-slot throughput: no source found. [unverified]
  • Kafka source metric names pendingRecords, currentOffset, committedOffset, records-lag exist as constants in connector 5.0.0 KafkaSourceReaderMetrics (verified: javap/jkeys on flink-connector-kafka-5.0.0-2.2); split-assignment details remain in Chapter 13/10.
  • Compression: execution.checkpointing.snapshot-compression exists, default false, description "use compression for the state snapshot data" (verified: flink-core 2.2.1 ExecutionOptions). Its effect on size for your data and interaction with incremental RocksDB checkpoints: not checked, measure. [unverified]
  • The coefficients in 17.3 to 17.8 (overhead 1.5x to 3x, 70% busy, 2x headroom, 50% interval) are heuristics, not Flink facts.

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/metrics/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/state/checkpoints/ - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/connectors/datastream/kafka/

Chapter 18: Blueprint 1, deduplication by idempotency key

Goal: after this chapter you can build a keyed dedup operator whose state is bounded, size its retention from a measured retry window, choose between "first arrival wins" and "earliest event time wins", and state precisely what dedup does and does not guarantee when the output goes to a KafkaSink.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, late data), Chapter 3 (timers, cleanup timers), Chapter 5 (state, TTL, sizing), Chapter 6 (recovery), Chapter 7 (delivery guarantees). Kafka parts pin to Flink 2.2.x + connector 5.0.0 (Chapter 7).

18.1 What the article got wrong

The article's faults are taken as described in the task brief (no TTL, exactly-once claim, minute bucketing); the finer points below (for example "never sized retention") are this book's reading of the blueprint and were not re-checked against the article text.

  • No state bound. Dedup keys were kept with no TTL and no cleanup (Chapter 5.9). Either state grows with every key ever seen, or, once someone adds a bound, nobody can say which duplicates are still caught.
  • Claimed exactly-once. Deduplicating by state is not an exactly-once sink (Chapter 7.10). It removes duplicates that Flink sees within the state lifetime; it says nothing about how the result is written to Kafka.
  • Minute bucketing as the dedup window (as described for the blueprint): a duplicate is caught only if original and retry land in the same bucket. A retry 2 s later straddling a minute boundary is not caught (18.4). Effective window is anywhere from 0 to the bucket size, depending on where the original falls.
  • It never sized retention from data, never defined which copy wins, and never said what happens to late events.

18.2 Design in one picture

 Kafka in ─► assign event time ─► keyBy(tenantId + idempotencyKey) ─► Dedup (KeyedProcessFunction)
                                                                         │ state: first-seen marker (+ts)
                                                                         │ timer: cleanup at eventTs + retention
                                                                         ├─► unique events ─► KafkaSink
                                                                         └─► side outputs: too-old, duplicate counter

Design decisions, each explained below: 1. Key = (tenantId, idempotencyKey) composite, so tenants never share state (Chapter 5.8). Assumption: the producer supplies a stable idempotency key and the same logical event always carries the same key. 2. State = a ValueState<Long> holding the earliest event timestamp seen (not a bare Boolean: the timestamp lets you compute the deadline, detect "too old", and support 18.6). ValueState<Boolean> is fine if you only need first-arrival semantics. 3. Cleanup = an event-time cleanup timer (Chapter 3.6) as the primary bound, plus state TTL as a backstop (18.3). 4. Retention = measured retry window plus watermark delay plus margin (18.5).

Figure 18.1: The dedup operator decision path with its event-time cleanup timer and TTL backstop.

18.3 Timer, TTL, or both

Mechanism Clock Strength Weakness
Cleanup timer (Chapter 3.6) event time replay-stable: a backfill treats old data consistently; can emit a side effect stalls if the watermark stalls (Chapter 1.5); one timer per live key (checkpointed, Chapter 3.4)
StateTtlConfig processing time only (verified: 2.3 state docs, "Only TTLs in reference to processing time are currently supported"; jar: StateTtlConfig.TtlTimeCharacteristic has the single constant ProcessingTime, flink-core 2.2.1) no timers; RocksDB compaction filter removes data (Chapter 5.5) not replay-stable; a replay at 100x speed keeps keys 100x longer in data time and floods state

Recommendation: use the timer for correctness (retention is defined in data time, so a replay behaves like live), and put a TTL larger than the timer's wall-clock equivalent as a backstop for the case where the watermark stalls and timers never fire. The backstop must not be shorter than the retention, or it silently shortens your dedup window.

Verified TTL builder (2.3 state page; method and enum names also checked with javap on flink-core 2.2.1 StateTtlConfig and StateTtlConfig.Builder; the two enum values shown are the builder defaults, confirmed in the Builder constructor bytecode):

StateTtlConfig ttl = StateTtlConfig
    .newBuilder(Duration.ofHours(6))                                   // backstop, > retention
    .setUpdateType(StateTtlConfig.UpdateType.OnCreateAndWrite)         // default
    .setStateVisibility(StateTtlConfig.StateVisibility.NeverReturnExpired) // default
    .build();

Cleanup strategy for TTL on RocksDB is the compaction filter, not cleanupIncrementally (Chapter 5.5). Verified (2.3 state docs): "The RocksDB state backend adds 8 bytes per stored value, list entry or map entry" for the TTL timestamp, and "The TTL configuration is not part of check- or savepoints", so the TTL must be set in code every time the descriptor is created. Verified (docs and jar): background cleanup is on by default (Builder.isCleanupInBackground is initialised to true in the bytecode) and the docs describe the RocksDB default as a compaction filter that queries the current timestamp every 1000 processed entries; the RocksDB backend itself is not in the jars checked, so that default rests on the docs.

18.4 Minute buckets versus a sliding retention

If the key is (idempotencyKey, minute(eventTs)), or dedup runs in a 1-minute tumbling window:

 bucket 12:00:00-12:00:59 | bucket 12:01:00-12:01:59
              original 12:00:59.8 ─┐   retry 12:01:00.6
                                   └── different bucket: NOT deduplicated

Figure 18.2: Article design (minute bucket, boundary leak) versus the corrected sliding retention per key.

Scheme Guaranteed dedup window Cost
Per-minute bucket in key 0 s (worst case) to 60 s state = keys per bucket; boundary leaks
Bucket plus lookup of previous bucket at least 60 s 2 lookups per event
Sliding retention per key (this chapter) exactly retention after the first copy one entry per live key + one timer

Buckets are cheap to expire (drop a whole bucket) but the guarantee is statistical. The sliding design gives a clean statement: "any duplicate whose event timestamp is within retention of the first accepted copy is dropped". Prefer it unless timer count is the bottleneck (then coalesce timers to minute granularity as in Chapter 3.4, which only extends retention by up to a minute and does not reintroduce a boundary leak).

18.5 Sizing retention from the measured retry window

  1. From a representative period (include an incident day), compute for every idempotency key with more than one copy: delta = arrival_time(copy_n) - arrival_time(copy_1) (Kafka append time, or your own ingest time). You get the retry-delay distribution.
  2. Take a high percentile (p99.9 or the SLA you owe) of delta, not the mean. Producer retry policies often have a long tail (exponential backoff, offline mobile devices, DLQ replays; Chapter 12).
  3. retention >= p99.9(delta) + watermark delay (Chapter 1.7) + margin. The watermark term is needed because the cleanup timer runs on event time: a timer registered at eventTs + retention only fires when the watermark passes it.
  4. Re-measure when producers change (new SDK, new retry policy). Alert on the admitted-duplicate suspects: events whose key was seen before the retention but was already cleaned (you can only see this by comparing with a long-horizon batch check; Data unavailable inside the job).

Anything outside the retention is re-admitted as new (Chapter 7.9, row "dedup TTL shorter than redelivery window"). State this limit in the SLA.

State size estimation (Assumption: my own arithmetic, Chapter 5.6)

live keys   ≈ unique keys per second × retention seconds         (NOT total ever seen)
bytes/key   ≈ key bytes + 8 (Long value) + 8 (TTL, RocksDB) + timer entry + LSM/heap overhead

Illustrative numbers, replace with yours: 5,000 unique events/s, 1 h retention gives 18,000,000 live keys. At 100 bytes per key all-in (composite string key ~48 B, value 8 B, TTL 8 B, timer ~16 B, overhead) that is about 1.8 GB total, spread over subtasks. Heap objects are several times larger (Chapter 5.6), so this size points to RocksDB. Duplicates do not add keys, but a duplicate storm still adds reads. Confirm with the checkpoint "State size" in the Web UI (Chapter 13) and plan capacity in Chapter 17.

18.6 First-seen versus earliest-event-time with out-of-order data

Two different questions are hiding in "which copy do I keep":

Semantics Emits When Output is
First arrival wins the copy Flink processes first immediately depends on arrival order; replay across partitions may pick a different copy
Earliest event time wins the copy with the smallest eventTs after a hold period (event-time timer at firstTs + hold) deterministic given the data, at the cost of hold latency

Out-of-order example (same key, two copies with different event timestamps, e.g. a re-stamped retry):

 arrival 1: copy B, eventTs = 10:00:05     -> first-arrival emits B
 arrival 2: copy A, eventTs = 10:00:03     -> dropped; but A is the "earlier" event

Earliest-event-time mode needs an extra buffered event per key during the hold: ValueState<Event> best, replaced when a smaller eventTs arrives, emitted from onTimer once the watermark passes bestTs + hold, after which only the marker stays until the cleanup deadline. It doubles timers (hold + cleanup) or chains them (one timer, state machine). Use it when downstream logic depends on the earliest timestamp (billing, session starts). If copies are byte-identical (plain producer retry), first-arrival is enough and cheaper. Assumption: most idempotency-key retries re-send the identical payload.

18.7 Late events and the watermark

Dedup works at arrival time, not at window close, so a late event (eventTs <= watermark, Chapter 1.4) still finds its key if the key is alive. Rules:

  1. Cleanup deadline is max(eventTs, currentWatermark) + retention. If you use eventTs alone for an event already behind the watermark, the deadline may be in the past: the timer fires at the next watermark and the key vanishes immediately, so the next copy slips through.
  2. If eventTs < currentWatermark - retention, the key could already have been cleaned. You cannot tell "first copy" from "copy of something cleaned". Decision (pick one explicitly): admit and flag, drop and count, or side-output to a "too old to dedup" stream for a batch reconciliation. This sketch side-outputs.
  3. A stalled watermark (idle partition, Chapter 1.5) means timers do not fire and state grows; the TTL backstop (18.3) and an alert on watermark lag (Chapter 13) catch this.

18.8 Sketch (not compiled)

API names in this sketch were compile-checked with javac against the Flink 2.2.1 jars (small stubs stood in for the flink-core-api interfaces ValueState, MapState, ListState, AggregateFunction, KeySelector, which were not among the jars; the surrounding classes are placeholders). Behavior is not tested.

// (sketch, not compiled) first-arrival dedup with event-time cleanup and TTL backstop
public class Dedup extends KeyedProcessFunction<String, Event, Event> {
    public static final OutputTag<Event> TOO_OLD = new OutputTag<>("dedup-too-old") {};
    private final long retentionMs;                        // from 18.5
    private transient ValueState<Long> deadline;           // cleanup deadline of the live key

    public Dedup(long retentionMs) { this.retentionMs = retentionMs; }

    @Override
    public void open(OpenContext ctx) {                    // 2.x signature (verified: RichFunction.open(OpenContext), flink-core 2.2.1)
        ValueStateDescriptor<Long> d = new ValueStateDescriptor<>("dedup-deadline", Long.class);
        d.enableTimeToLive(StateTtlConfig.newBuilder(Duration.ofHours(6)).build());   // backstop
        deadline = getRuntimeContext().getState(d);
    }

    @Override
    public void processElement(Event e, Context ctx, Collector<Event> out) throws Exception {
        long wm = ctx.timerService().currentWatermark();
        if (deadline.value() != null) { return; }                         // duplicate: drop (count it, Chapter 13)
        if (e.eventTsMillis < wm - retentionMs) { ctx.output(TOO_OLD, e); return; }   // 18.7 rule 2
        long due = Math.max(e.eventTsMillis, wm) + retentionMs;          // 18.7 rule 1
        due = ((due / 60_000) + 1) * 60_000;                              // coalesce to the minute (Chapter 3.4)
        deadline.update(due);
        ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(due);
        out.collect(e);                                                   // first copy wins
    }

    @Override
    public void onTimer(long ts, OnTimerContext ctx, Collector<Event> out) throws Exception {   // ValueState.value() throws
        Long d = deadline.value();
        if (d != null && d == ts) { deadline.clear(); }                   // stale-timer guard, Chapter 3.5
    }
}

Wiring: stream.keyBy(e -> e.tenantId + "|" + e.idempotencyKey).process(new Dedup(retentionMs)) with a uid("dedup") (Chapter 6.8), then sinkTo(kafkaSink). Note Math.max(eventTs, wm) and the TOO_OLD check use the operator's watermark at arrival. That watermark depends on how records and watermarks interleave across input partitions, so a replay after recovery can in principle decide differently for events near the retention edge (the same cross-partition caveat as 18.6). Not verified beyond reasoning.

18.9 What dedup guarantees, and what it does not (versus Chapter 7)

Claim True? Why
Duplicates within retention of the first accepted copy are dropped Yes state lookup, restored consistently with offsets on recovery (Chapter 6.7)
Output has no duplicates ever No duplicates after retention, or "too old", pass
Pipeline is exactly-once end to end Only if the sink is transactional KafkaSink with DeliveryGuarantee.EXACTLY_ONCE plus read_committed consumers (Chapter 7.3 to 7.6)
Restart does not create duplicates in state Yes state and source offsets from the same snapshot
Restart does not create duplicates in output Only with the 2PC sink otherwise records written after the last checkpoint are repeated; dedup state was rolled back, so they are accepted again
Upstream producer duplicates (before Kafka) Handled by dedup, within retention exactly-once in Flink counts what it reads, not what producers sent twice (Chapter 7.9)

Key subtlety: after a restore, Flink replays from the checkpoint offsets with the dedup state of the same checkpoint, so the replay re-derives the same decisions (modulo cross-partition arrival order, 18.6). Combined with a transactional sink, the aborted transaction's records are discarded and replayed output is committed once. With an AT_LEAST_ONCE sink, the replayed records are re-emitted, and dedup in Flink cannot see them because they are already past it; make the consumer idempotent (Chapter 26).

Sink choice (sketch of the wiring is in Chapter 7.3): EXACTLY_ONCE needs transaction.timeout.ms >= max checkpoint duration + max restart time, a unique transactionalIdPrefix per tenant/job/sink, and visibility is delayed by up to one checkpoint interval (Chapter 7.5, 7.6).

18.10 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • No retention at all or TTL only: unbounded state, or replay-unsafe retention (18.3).
  • Retention shorter than the real retry tail: duplicates leak at the worst time (incidents, when retries peak).
  • TTL backstop shorter than the timer retention: silently shortens the window.
  • Retention measured in arrival time, enforced in event time (or reverse) without adding watermark delay: effective window is smaller than the number you wrote.
  • Idempotency key not unique across tenants/event types: legitimate events dropped as "duplicates" (data loss, silent). Include tenant and event type in the key.
  • Hot key: one key with millions of copies is cheap in state but concentrates load on one subtask (Chapter 10).
  • Timer count: millions of live keys means millions of timers; coalesce (Chapter 3.4) and watch checkpoint duration.
  • Dedup placed after a sink-side retry layer: Flink cannot dedup what the sink repeats.
  • Changing retention or key composition on a running job: key or state layout change is a state change (Chapter 9); changing only the constant is safe, changing the key is not.
  • Logging idempotency keys: may contain PII; redact (Chapter 16, 27).

18.11 Self-check

  1. A retry arrives 3 s after the original but the original sat 70 s behind the watermark. Is it deduplicated, and which rule (18.7) decides?
  2. State TTL is 1 h (processing time). You replay a day of data in 30 minutes. What happens to dedup state versus an event-time timer design?
  3. 5,000 unique keys/s, retention 2 h, 100 bytes per key. Estimate live state, and explain why duplicates do not change it.
  4. Your sink is AT_LEAST_ONCE. After a restart the topic contains two copies of some record that dedup "accepted once". Why?
  5. When would you pay for the earliest-event-time mode instead of first-arrival?

18.12 Open items / unverified

  • RESOLVED (verified): open(OpenContext) throws Exception on RichFunction, inherited by KeyedProcessFunction via AbstractRichFunction (javap flink-core/flink-streaming-java 2.2.1; 2.3.0 jars not diffed for this).
  • [unverified] whether timer firing order versus records at equal timestamps could let a copy slip through exactly at the deadline (Chapter 3.5 left this open).
  • Per-timer memory/byte cost in the size estimate: not measured; the 100-byte figure is an Assumption (measure per Chapter 17).
  • Measured retry-window distribution for your producers: Data unavailable (must be produced from your own Kafka data).
  • RocksDB compaction-filter TTL cleanup default: background cleanup is on by default per the docs and the builder bytecode (18.3); the RocksDB backend's own handling was not inspected (backend jar not available here).

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/fault-tolerance/state/ - (Kafka, transaction and checkpoint facts are inherited from Chapters 5 to 7 and their sources.)

Chapter 19: Blueprint 2, CDC enrichment with a hand-built temporal join

Goal: after this chapter you can enrich a fact stream from a CDC (Debezium-style) reference topic using DataStream state, handle deletes and tombstones, order cold start safely, choose between "latest known" and "as-of event time", and bound the wait so a stalled reference side cannot freeze or silently corrupt the output.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, idleness), Chapter 3 (timers), Chapter 4 (4.3, 4.5 to 4.7 are the building blocks; this chapter assembles them and does not repeat them), Chapter 5 (state, TTL), Chapter 12 (poison pills). Kafka facts pin to Flink 2.2.x + connector 5.0.0 (Chapter 7).

19.1 What the article got wrong

The article's faults are taken as described in the task brief (CDC join as DDL, watermark declared on the changelog, bootstrap); the finer points below are this book's reading and were not re-checked against the article text.

  • SQL DDL as the design. The join was a SQL temporal join over a CDC-format table. This book does not use SQL; the DDL hid every decision below (Chapter 4.1).
  • Watermark declared on the changelog. A watermark on the CDC side is a promise that no older version will arrive. CDC topics are compacted, replayed from snapshots and have idle partitions; the declared watermark was neither derived nor monitored. One idle reference partition holds the whole join (19.7).
  • Bootstrap was implicit. Nothing said what a fact sees before the reference is loaded: silent nulls or silent drops (19.5).
  • Deletes and tombstones were never discussed, nor late reference updates, nor state growth (19.6, 19.8, 19.9).
  • It never stated whether the result should be as-of event time (replay-stable) or latest known (not replay-stable). Pick explicitly (19.2).

19.2 Decide the semantics first (Chapter 4.1)

Latest known As-of event time
Reads the reference value in state when the fact is processed version with greatest validFrom <= fact.ts
Replay/backfill (Chapter 24) enriches history with today's reference same output as live, given complete reference history
State one row per key versions per key (bounded), plus buffered facts
Latency none once reference exists fact waits until reference watermark >= fact.ts
Needs reference watermark no yes, honest and not stalled
Use for operational labels, routing billing, audit, ML features (Chapter 21)

This chapter builds as-of with an explicit, bounded fallback to latest-known. Latest-known is the degenerate case (skip the wait).

19.3 Topology

 reference topic (compacted, key = business key) ─► deserialize envelope ─► RefEvent{key, op, version, validFrom, row}
                                                                              │ keyBy(key)
 fact topic ─────────────────────────────────────► Fact{refKey, ts, ...}      ▼ keyBy(refKey)
                                                         └──────► KeyedCoProcessFunction ─► Enriched ─► KafkaSink
                                                              state per key: versions, pending facts, timers
                                                              side outputs: unmatched/fallback/late-ref

Both inputs are keyed by the same key with identical key serialization (Chapter 4.6). The operator's watermark is the minimum of both inputs (Chapter 4.5), so the reference watermark gates fact timers: that is the semantics we want for as-of and the failure mode we must bound (19.7). Verified (javap CombinedWatermarkStatus.updateCombinedWatermark, flink-core 2.2.1, used by AbstractStreamOperator.processWatermark1/2): each input starts at Long.MIN_VALUE, the combined value is the minimum over inputs that are not idle (the maximum if all are idle) and never moves backwards.

Figure 19.1: Topology of the hand-built as-of join; the Debezium envelope facts are checked against the Debezium docs (19.4).

19.4 Consuming the changelog (builds on Chapter 4.6)

Consumption rules, in the order the data hits you:

Record Meaning (Debezium convention; verified against the Debezium docs, see below) Action
create/update with after new version of the row versions.put(validFrom, row) if version is newer than what you hold
snapshot read (initial table scan) existing row at connector start same as create; validFrom may be the snapshot time, not the real change time
delete (before set, after null) row removed (which columns before carries depends on the source database setup, for example Postgres REPLICA IDENTITY) put a tombstone version (deleted=true) at validFrom; do not just clear() in as-of mode (19.6)
Kafka null value (tombstone for log compaction) follows a delete event so compaction can drop the key (configurable in Debezium: tombstones.on.delete) usually ignore (the delete event already acted); must not crash the deserializer
  • Debezium facts (verified against debezium.io stable docs, PostgreSQL and MySQL connector pages): op is c create, u update, d delete, r read (snapshot), plus t truncate and m message; a delete event has before and a null after; the envelope carries source metadata (position) and ts_ms; the source.snapshot field distinguishes snapshot from streaming events (values seen in the docs: "true", "false", "incremental"); "after a delete event is emitted, the connector emits a tombstone event that has the same key as the delete event but a null value" (MySQL page), controlled by tombstones.on.delete. Connector-specific: check the page for your connector and version. Not verified here: exact source position field names per connector and whether ts_ms of snapshot records is the snapshot time (the docs call ts_ms the time the connector processed the event).
  • Flink-side verified facts: KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema (with valueOnly() and setValueOnlyDeserializer(DeserializationSchema)) is the DataStream hook; OffsetsInitializer offers earliest(), latest(), committedOffsets(), timestamp(ms); default is earliest() if unset (2.2 Kafka page). Null/tombstone behavior: the Kafka docs do not say, but the connector bytecode does (verified: javap flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0): the wrapper behind KafkaRecordDeserializationSchema.valueOnly(DeserializationSchema) (KafkaValueOnlyDeserializationSchemaWrapper) passes record.value() to your schema without a null check, so a tombstone arrives as null bytes; SimpleStringSchema.deserialize(byte[]) does new String(bytes, charset) and therefore throws on null; and the default DeserializationSchema.deserialize(byte[], Collector) silently drops a record when your deserialize(byte[]) returns null (flink-core 2.2.1). So: write your own deserialization that returns a typed RefEvent (op = TOMBSTONE_NULL) or skips, and route unparseable bytes to the DLQ (Chapter 12), never throw.
  • We deliberately do not use the SQL CDC formats; you parse the envelope yourself (Chapter 8 for POJO/serializer choices).
  • Version guard: use the source's monotone position (log sequence/offset) or its change timestamp as version; drop a record whose version <= the stored one for that validFrom slot. Kafka partition reordering after restarts or producer retries can deliver out of order (Chapter 4.6). Never guard with Kafka record timestamp.

19.5 Bootstrap and cold start ordering (builds on Chapter 4.7)

At a fresh start both topics are read at once: facts are hot, the reference reads from earliest() and is hours behind. Without a rule, facts see no reference.

Recommended ordering rule: facts wait, bounded, until the reference watermark passes them or the bound expires, then fall back. Concretely:

  1. Reference source starts from earliest() (compacted topic holds the latest row per key, snapshot included). Fact source starts wherever the business requires.
  2. Facts buffer in pending (19.7 sketch). Event-time timer at fact.ts fires when both inputs' watermarks have passed it: reference caught up to that time.
  3. A processing-time give-up timer (now + maxWait) guarantees an answer when the reference watermark cannot advance (idle, stalled, empty compacted partition).
  4. On give-up, emit with enrichment=FALLBACK_LATEST (use the newest known version) or enrichment=MISSING if none exists, and count both. Downstream must treat missing as "unknown", never as a legitimate null (Chapter 4.11).

Alternatives (Chapter 4.7): pre-load state with a savepoint built by the State Processor API (Chapter 30), or read facts only after a "caught up" signal. Per-source offsets alone do not prove the reference is complete.

Restart is not cold start: after a checkpoint restore, reference state and pending facts are restored together with offsets (Chapter 6.6), so no new bootstrap is needed. A resubmit without state is a cold start (Chapter 7.9).

Figure 19.2: Cold start ordering with a bounded wait; as-of results are replay-stable, fallback results are not.

19.6 Deletes, tombstones and versioned semantics

  • Latest-known mode: delete = clear() the row. Facts after that see "no reference". Facts already emitted stay as emitted (Chapter 4.13 question 3).
  • As-of mode: a delete is a version too. versions.put(deleteTs, TOMBSTONE); a fact with ts after it sees "deleted at that time"; a fact with ts before it sees the earlier row. Do not drop the history on delete, or a late fact (19.9) enriches wrongly.
  • Pending facts at the moment of delete: if their ts is before the delete, they still resolve to the earlier version once the watermark allows; if after, emit enrichment=DELETED. Decide per business rule and document it.
  • Physical removal: a deleted key still holds its tombstone version until the cleanup timer (19.8) clears it. This is the only way old keys leave state.
  • Re-creation after delete: a later create has a newer version; it wins by the version guard (19.4).

19.7 Sketch: bounded as-of join (sketch, not compiled)

public class AsOfEnrich extends KeyedCoProcessFunction<String, Fact, RefEvent, Enriched> {
    private final long maxWaitMs;            // processing-time give-up bound
    private final long keepVersionsMs;       // retain history at least this long behind the watermark
    private transient MapState<Long, RefEvent> versions;    // validFrom -> row or tombstone
    private transient ListState<Fact> pending;               // facts waiting for the reference watermark
    private transient ValueState<Long> giveUpAt;             // processing-time deadline of the oldest pending fact

    @Override
    public void open(OpenContext ctx) { /* descriptors: versions, pending, giveUpAt; TTL backstop on versions (Chapter 5) */ }

    @Override
    public void processElement1(Fact f, Context ctx, Collector<Enriched> out) throws Exception {
        pending.add(f);
        ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(f.ts);                         // fires when BOTH watermarks passed f.ts
        if (giveUpAt.value() == null) {
            long due = ctx.timerService().currentProcessingTime() + maxWaitMs;
            ctx.timerService().registerProcessingTimeTimer(due);
            giveUpAt.update(due);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void processElement2(RefEvent r, Context ctx, Collector<Enriched> out) throws Exception {
        RefEvent old = versions.get(r.validFrom);
        if (old != null && old.version >= r.version) return;                    // version guard (19.4)
        if (r.validFrom < ctx.timerService().currentWatermark()) {
            ctx.output(LATE_REF, r);                                             // 19.9: still stored, but flag it
        }
        versions.put(r.validFrom, r);                                            // delete = tombstone version (19.6)
        ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(r.validFrom + keepVersionsMs); // prune/cleanup point (19.8)
    }

    @Override
    public void onTimer(long ts, OnTimerContext ctx, Collector<Enriched> out) throws Exception {
        boolean processing = ctx.timeDomain() == TimeDomain.PROCESSING_TIME;
        List<Fact> keep = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Fact f : pending.get()) {
            boolean ready = processing || f.ts <= ts;                           // event-time: reference watermark reached f.ts
            if (!ready) { keep.add(f); continue; }
            RefEvent v = asOf(f.ts);                                            // greatest validFrom <= f.ts, scanning versions
            out.collect(Enriched.of(f, v, processing ? Mode.FALLBACK : Mode.AS_OF));
        }
        pending.update(keep);
        giveUpAt.clear();
        // if keep is non-empty, re-register the give-up timer; prune versions older than the oldest pending ts and keepVersionsMs
        // cleanup: if versions empty and pending empty, clear everything for the key
    }
}

Notes on the sketch: - ctx.timeDomain() (on KeyedCoProcessFunction.OnTimerContext) and TimeDomain.EVENT_TIME / PROCESSING_TIME (package org.apache.flink.streaming.api) verified with javap (flink-runtime / flink-streaming-java 2.2.1). The sketch was compile-checked with javac against the 2.2.1 jars (stubs for the flink-core-api state interfaces); behavior is not tested. - The give-up path uses the processing-time timer, which fires even when the watermark is stuck (Chapter 3.2). It is the bounded wait. - The event-time timer has a single delivery rule: the operator watermark is the minimum over the non-idle inputs (verified, 19.3), so it fires only after the reference side has advanced or been marked idle. - pending is a ListState; scanning is O(n) per fire. Fine for small n per key; cap it (19.10) otherwise.

19.8 State growth and cleanup (builds on Chapter 4.9)

State Grows with Bound
versions reference changes per key over history kept prune versions older than min(oldest pending fact ts, watermark - keepVersionsMs), always keeping the newest version at or before that point
reference keys never touched again number of distinct keys ever seen cleanup timer when the key's last activity is older than the retention; TTL backstop (processing-time, Chapter 5.5)
pending stall duration x fact rate give-up timer (19.7), per-key cap with overflow to DLQ/side output
timers one per pending fact and per version coalesce timestamps (Chapter 3.4)

Keep the reference key's history longer than the maximum expected fact lateness (Chapter 1.7) plus maxWait; otherwise a late fact finds no matching version. Estimate: keys x (versions kept per key x row bytes) + buffered facts; with 10 M reference keys, 2 versions of 300 bytes, that is about 6 GB (Assumption, my arithmetic; use Chapter 5.6 to refine). Alert on state size together with watermark lag (Chapter 4.9, 13).

19.9 Reference-side watermarks, idle partitions, late reference updates

Idle reference partitions stall everything (Chapter 1.5, 4.7). A compacted reference topic is typically quiet; some partitions have no records for days. With connect, the operator watermark is the minimum over both inputs, so one silent reference partition freezes event-time timers: facts keep arriving, pending grows, nothing is emitted until the processing-time give-up fires. Controls:

Control Effect Cost
WatermarkStrategy.withIdleness(Duration) on the reference source (Chapter 1.5) idle partitions stop holding the minimum a reference change arriving after the partition was marked idle with an old timestamp becomes late (below)
Parallelism <= partitions on reference no empty subtasks (docs: not automatically idle) scaling limit
Watermark alignment (Chapter 1.6, 10) stops a hot side racing ahead cannot fix a silent side
Bounded wait + fallback (19.5, 19.7) guarantees progress without the reference watermark fallback results are latest-known, not as-of
Reference source with WatermarkStrategy.noWatermarks() (factory exists, verified) does not make facts stop waiting: the reference input then stays at Long.MIN_VALUE, so the operator watermark never advances unless that input is marked idle (verified from the combine logic, 19.3); for "latest known" mode do not register event-time timers for facts, emit in processElement1 immediately an operator whose watermark is stuck also stalls every event-time operator downstream; whether noWatermarks().withIdleness(...) marks the input idle was only compile-checked, not run [unverified]

Honest reference watermarks. Use the CDC change timestamp as the event time for the reference side with a small bounded out-of-orderness, not the Kafka append time: after a connector restart or snapshot, append times jump while change times stay put. Records replayed from a compacted topic carry old change timestamps (and snapshot records may carry the snapshot time, 19.4); at start the reference watermark is far in the past and jumps forward as it catches up (Chapter 4.7). This is acceptable for as-of mode because facts wait; it is why the give-up bound is mandatory.

Late reference updates (a version with validFrom older than the current watermark; delayed connector, replay of a topic, an idle partition waking up): options. 1. Store it in versions anyway (history is corrected) and count it. Facts already emitted are not re-emitted; future facts get the corrected value. This is the default in the 19.7 sketch. 2. Re-emit a correction for facts already emitted: requires keeping emitted facts (state explodes) and a downstream that accepts updates (Chapter 26). Usually not worth it. 3. Drop and DLQ if validFrom is older than keepVersionsMs behind the watermark (history already pruned). Whichever you pick, publish the lateness count (Chapter 13) because it measures the quality of the as-of promise.

19.10 Output and delivery

Emit Enriched with an explicit enrichment field (AS_OF, FALLBACK_LATEST, MISSING, DELETED) so consumers can filter fallbacks and a later batch correction can find them. Write to KafkaSink per Chapter 7.3 to 7.6 (EXACTLY_ONCE needs a transactional prefix, timeout >= checkpoint + restart, read_committed consumers). Note that fallback results depend on the wall clock (processing-time timer), so a replay of the same input may emit a different mode than the original run: as-of results are replay-stable, fallback ones are not. If you need full determinism for audit, set maxWait high and route to a DLQ rather than fall back (Chapter 12).

19.11 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Silent nulls at cold start treated downstream as "no customer" (19.5).
  • Idle reference partition: pending grows, latency rises to maxWait for every fact, fallback rate near 100% (19.9). Alert on fallback rate and pending size.
  • Reference watermark from Kafka append time: restarts and snapshots break the as-of ordering (19.9).
  • Version guard missing: an old CDC record overwrites a newer row after a reorder (19.4).
  • Delete implemented as clear() in as-of mode: late facts enrich with the wrong or no row (19.6).
  • Deserializer throws on null/tombstone or envelope surprise: the job restarts forever (Chapter 12).
  • Unbounded pending from one hot key or a long stall: OOM or huge checkpoints; cap and spill to a side output.
  • Pruning versions below the oldest pending fact only: forget a late fact still inside the lateness window.
  • Different key serialization (trim/case/tenant prefix) between fact and reference: join never matches. Normalize once; include tenant in the key (Chapter 5.8).
  • Schema change in the source table: new columns break the POJO/serializer; plan evolution (Chapter 9).
  • Reference change timestamps from many tables/partitions with skew: one slow table makes the join wait; consider one operator per reference table.

19.12 Self-check

  1. Name the three things the SQL temporal join did implicitly that you now write by hand, and which one this chapter bounds with a processing-time timer.
  2. The reference topic has 12 partitions; 3 are silent for a week. Which timers stop, what do facts experience, and what are two fixes with their costs?
  3. A delete for key K arrives, then a fact with ts before the delete. In as-of mode, what do you emit and why is clear() wrong?
  4. Why is the fallback result not replay-stable, and how do you make the audit path deterministic?
  5. A late reference version arrives with validFrom before the watermark. What are your three options and what does each cost?

19.13 Open items / unverified

  • RESOLVED (verified): Debezium op codes, delete shape and tombstone-after-delete (19.4). Still open: per-connector source position field names and the meaning of ts_ms for snapshot records.
  • RESOLVED (verified in bytecode): the stock valueOnly wrapper does not guard null values; SimpleStringSchema throws on null (19.4).
  • RESOLVED (verified): TimeDomain, ctx.timeDomain() and open(OpenContext) in the 2.2.1 jars (2.3.0 jars not diffed for these).
  • WatermarkStrategy.noWatermarks() on a connected side: stalls the combined watermark unless idle (19.9, verified from the combine logic); whether idleness rescues it was not run [unverified].
  • RESOLVED (verified): two-input operator watermark is the minimum over non-idle inputs (19.3); this holds for any pair of strategies since it is computed from received watermarks.
  • Kafka connector for Flink 2.3: none yet; examples pin to 2.2.x + connector 5.0.0.
  • Measured reference lag, fallback rate and key churn for your tables: Data unavailable.
