Chapter 20: Blueprint 3, sessionization

Goal: after this chapter you can build per-key sessions in the DataStream API, say exactly when a session may be emitted, handle late events that merge or extend sessions, emit provisional updates plus one final close, compute first/last event and duration without Oracle KEEP DENSE_RANK, choose the gap from data, and estimate open-session state.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, late data), Chapter 2 (session windows, triggers, allowed lateness), Chapter 3 (timers), Chapter 5 (state, TTL). Output idempotency is Chapter 26.

20.1 What the article got wrong

The article's faults are taken as described in the task brief (Oracle syntax, late emission); the state-lifetime point (3) is this book's addition.

  1. Oracle syntax in a Flink job. It computed first/last values with Oracle's KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST/LAST ...). That is not Flink syntax, and this book does not use SQL at all. In the DataStream API you keep firstEvent and lastEvent (by event time) in the accumulator. See 20.5.
  2. Late emission was ignored. An event-time session is only known to be finished when the watermark passes lastEventTs + gap (see 20.2). The article presented sessions as "what just happened". They are not: a session is emitted at least gap + watermark delay after its last event, and a late event can extend or merge sessions that were already emitted. It never said what happens then.
  3. No state-lifetime story (Chapter 5.9): open sessions are state, and key cardinality is unbounded.

20.2 Mental model: sessions are emitted late by construction

A session for a key is a maximal run of events where consecutive event timestamps are no more than gap apart. Flink's session assigner creates one window [ts, ts + gap) per event and merges windows that intersect (Chapter 2.2). The merged window ends at lastEventTs + gap. Verified (javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1): EventTimeSessionWindows.assignWindows returns new TimeWindow(ts, ts + sessionTimeout), and TimeWindow.intersects is start <= other.end && end >= other.start, so two events exactly gap apart touch and are merged; maxTimestamp() is end - 1.

events (key K, gap = 30 min):  10:00   10:10   10:25 ........................ 11:30
windows:       [10:00,10:30) [10:10,10:40) [10:25,10:55)          [11:30,12:00)
merged:        [10:00 ............................ 10:55)          [11:30,12:00)
fires when watermark >= 10:54:59.999  (window max timestamp, see Chapter 2.3)

Earliest emission time (event time) of a closed session: lastEventTs + gap, then plus the watermark delay (Chapter 1.2), and only if new data advances the watermark on every input (idleness, Chapter 1.5). Example: gap 30 min, delay 10 s: the session whose last event is 10:25 is emitted when events stamped about 10:55:10 arrive. So the "current open sessions" view is always at least gap behind. If a consumer needs "is this user active right now" that is a different question, answered by provisional updates (20.4), not by the closed session.

Figure 20.1: Session windows merge per-event windows; a late event can bridge two sessions, and earlier results are not retracted.

20.3 Option A: built-in session windows

Verified (2.3 docs, and javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1): EventTimeSessionWindows.withGap(Duration) for a static gap, and EventTimeSessionWindows.withDynamicGap(SessionWindowTimeGapExtractor<T>) for a per-element gap (the extractor interface is long extract(T), in org.apache.flink.streaming.api.windowing.assigners; ProcessingTimeSessionWindows has the same two factories). The docs state a session window operator requires a merging trigger and a merging window function (ReduceFunction, AggregateFunction, ProcessWindowFunction); Chapter 2.7 notes AggregateFunction.merge is mandatory here. The trigger requirement is enforced at graph-build time (verified: WindowOperatorBuilder.trigger throws "A merging window assigner cannot be used with a trigger that does not support merging." when Trigger.canMerge() is false, which is its default). The sketch below was compile-checked with javac against the 2.2.1 jars (stubs for flink-core-api interfaces).

// (sketch, not compiled)
public class SessionAcc {                      // POJO accumulator
    public long firstTs = Long.MAX_VALUE; public String firstEvent;   // e.g. first page / event type
    public long lastTs  = Long.MIN_VALUE; public String lastEvent;
    public long count;
    public SessionAcc() {}
}

public class SessionAgg implements AggregateFunction<Event, SessionAcc, SessionAcc> {
    public SessionAcc createAccumulator() { return new SessionAcc(); }
    public SessionAcc add(Event e, SessionAcc a) { return fold(a, e.eventTsMillis, e.type, 1); }
    public SessionAcc getResult(SessionAcc a)    { return a; }
    public SessionAcc merge(SessionAcc a, SessionAcc b) {            // called when sessions merge
        if (b.count == 0) return a;
        SessionAcc r = fold(a, b.firstTs, b.firstEvent, 0);
        r = fold(r, b.lastTs, b.lastEvent, 0);
        r.count = a.count + b.count;
        return r;
    }
    private SessionAcc fold(SessionAcc a, long ts, String ev, long n) {
        if (ts < a.firstTs) { a.firstTs = ts; a.firstEvent = ev; }   // replaces KEEP DENSE_RANK FIRST
        if (ts > a.lastTs)  { a.lastTs  = ts; a.lastEvent  = ev; }   // replaces KEEP DENSE_RANK LAST
        a.count += n;
        return a;
    }
}

OutputTag<Event> lateTag = new OutputTag<>("late-session-events") {};
var sessions = events
    .keyBy(e -> e.userKey)
    .window(EventTimeSessionWindows.withGap(Duration.ofMinutes(30)))
    .allowedLateness(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
    .sideOutputLateData(lateTag)
    .aggregate(new SessionAgg(), new AddKeyAndWindow());   // ProcessWindowFunction adds key, window start/end
// duration = lastTs - firstTs (event-time span of activity); window end - window start = duration + gap.

Ties on equal timestamps: fold keeps the first one seen; if equal-timestamp order matters, add a tie-breaker (sequence number). Report duration = lastTs - firstTs, not window length, or every session is inflated by the gap.

Late events and merging (verified behavior, plus what follows from it)

  • allowedLateness default is 0 (Chapter 2.4): a late event is dropped (to the side output if you attached one).
  • With lateness L, a late event that is assigned a window is added or merged, and the session fires again (docs: "late firings", updated results, possible duplicates the application must handle).
  • A late event can bridge two sessions: an event at 10:40 between a session whose last event is 10:25 and one starting 11:00 (gap 30 min; windows [10:25,10:55), [10:40,11:10), [11:00,11:30) chain together) merges both. Note the sessions must be more than gap apart to be separate: 10:25 and 10:55 would already be one session, see 20.2. State of both is merged via merge; downstream gets a new result with an earlier start and a later end. The earlier emitted results are now wrong; they are not retracted by Flink. Consequence: the session identity must be stable enough to upsert. Key the output by (key, sessionStart) and treat a merged session with a new earlier sessionStart as superseding the old ids; emit a tombstone/"superseded by" record for the absorbed ids if consumers must delete them. Assumption: this is a design choice of this book; Flink gives no built-in retraction in DataStream.
  • Window state is deleted at window.maxTimestamp() + L, i.e. window end - 1 ms + L (Chapter 2.4). A long gap plus lateness means long-lived state (20.7).
  • Exact behavior of whether a late event that only extends an already-fired session counts as a "late firing" for merged windows in edge cases: [unverified] (not tested; the docs describe late firings generally).

20.4 Early firing: provisional updates and a final close

The default trigger is EventTimeTrigger: nothing until the session is closed (20.2). To show a live session:

Option B1: custom Trigger on the session window. Return FIRE (keeps contents, Chapter 2.5) on selected elements and let the default end-of-window timer produce the final result. A trigger on session windows must return true from canMerge() and implement onMerge(window, OnMergeContext) (default onMerge throws UnsupportedOperationException, default canMerge is false; verified, javap Trigger), re-registering its timers (Chapter 2.5). Verified: trigger(...) overrides the default trigger (EventTimeSessionWindows.getDefaultTrigger() returns EventTimeTrigger.create()), so you must re-implement the end-of-session firing too. Built-in triggers present in flink-streaming-java 2.2.1 (verified): EventTimeTrigger, ProcessingTimeTrigger, CountTrigger, PurgingTrigger, ContinuousEventTimeTrigger.of(Duration), ContinuousProcessingTimeTrigger, DeltaTrigger, ProcessingTimeoutTrigger.of(Trigger, Duration). ContinuousEventTimeTrigger, CountTrigger and PurgingTrigger declare canMerge(), so they pass the merge check; ProcessingTimeoutTrigger does not override canMerge() and would be rejected on session windows. How ContinuousEventTimeTrigger fires on merged sessions (it fires on interval boundaries and on the window's max timestamp) was not tested [unverified]. Pitfall: a trigger that returns FIRE but forgets to fire at maxTimestamp() never closes sessions.

Option B2: KeyedProcessFunction that owns sessions (recommended when you need provisional output, custom close rules, or per-session metadata). Chapter 2.8 and 3.7 already give the rationale. The design:

state per key:  MapState<Long sessionStart, Session>      (usually 1-2 entries; see below)
processElement(e):
   find sessions with  start - gap <= e.ts <= lastTs + gap   -> candidates   (inclusive, like TimeWindow.intersects)
   if none: create Session(start=e.ts)
   else: merge e and all candidates into one Session (new start = min, lastTs = max)
         delete the event-time timers of absorbed sessions, remove their map entries
   register event-time timer at session.lastTs + gap  (delete the previous one first)
   emit PROVISIONAL(session) if it is new, or enough event time passed since the last provisional
onTimer(ts):
   session whose (lastTs + gap) == ts  ->  emit FINAL(session); clear it from the map
   (ignore stale timers: compare ts with the stored deadline, Chapter 3.3)

Figure 20.2: Early-firing design with a KeyedProcessFunction: provisional updates, one final close.

// (sketch, not compiled)
public class Session { public long start, lastTs, count, lastProvisionalTs;
                       public String firstEvent, lastEvent; public Session() {} }

public class Sessionizer extends KeyedProcessFunction<String, Event, SessionOut> {
    static final long GAP = 30 * 60_000L, PROVISIONAL_EVERY = 60_000L;
    private transient MapState<Long, Session> open;          // key: session start

    @Override public void open(OpenContext c) {
        open = getRuntimeContext().getMapState(new MapStateDescriptor<>("open", Long.class, Session.class));
    }

    @Override public void processElement(Event e, Context ctx, Collector<SessionOut> out) throws Exception {
        long ts = e.eventTsMillis;
        if (ts + GAP <= ctx.timerService().currentWatermark()) {      // would close at once: session already
            ctx.output(Late.TAG, e); return;                          // finalised past our lateness budget
        }
        Session s = new Session(); s.start = ts; s.lastTs = ts; s.count = 1;
        s.firstEvent = s.lastEvent = e.type;
        List<Long> absorbed = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Map.Entry<Long, Session> en : open.entries()) {          // few entries per key
            Session o = en.getValue();
            if (ts >= o.start - GAP && ts <= o.lastTs + GAP) {        // within gap; inclusive, matches TimeWindow.intersects
                absorbed.add(en.getKey());
                s = merge(s, o);                                      // min start/first, max last/last, sum count
            }
        }
        for (Long k : absorbed) {
            ctx.timerService().deleteEventTimeTimer(open.get(k).lastTs + GAP);
            open.remove(k);
        }
        open.put(s.start, s);
        ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(s.lastTs + GAP);
        if (!absorbed.isEmpty() || ts - s.lastProvisionalTs >= PROVISIONAL_EVERY) {
            s.lastProvisionalTs = ts;
            out.collect(SessionOut.provisional(ctx.getCurrentKey(), s));   // plus tombstones for absorbed ids
        }
    }

    @Override public void onTimer(long ts, OnTimerContext ctx, Collector<SessionOut> out) throws Exception {
        for (Map.Entry<Long, Session> en : open.entries()) {
            if (en.getValue().lastTs + GAP == ts) {
                out.collect(SessionOut.fin(ctx.getCurrentKey(), en.getValue()));
                open.remove(en.getKey()); return;
            }
        }
    }
}

Notes on the sketch: - Timer deletion on absorbed sessions matters: deleteEventTimeTimer is verified API (Chapter 3.1). Timers are per (key, timestamp); two sessions of one key never share a deadline unless identical lastTs, which onTimer handles by the scan. - The late check above is a design choice, not Flink's allowedLateness: a session is final once the watermark passes lastTs + GAP. To keep late events able to reopen finals, delay the timer by an extra L (final at lastTs + GAP + L) and tag emissions with a version. - Timing difference to the built-in window: the window fires when the watermark reaches maxTimestamp() = end - 1 = lastTs + gap - 1 (verified, 20.2), while this timer at lastTs + GAP fires when the watermark reaches lastTs + GAP, one millisecond later. Use lastTs + GAP - 1 if you need identical results. - onTimer modifying MapState while iterating is only safe because we return right after remove; keep it that way. - Provisional cadence uses event time here for determinism (Chapter 1.1, 24). It also only advances when data flows; if a quiet user must show "last seen", add a processing-time timer for that single purpose and accept non-determinism (Chapter 3.2). - Whether to ship firstEvent/lastEvent as strings or a compact POJO: serialization choices are Chapter 8.

Choosing between A and B

Need Built-in session window KeyedProcessFunction
Final sessions only, static or dynamic gap yes overkill
Provisional updates every N seconds custom trigger (onMerge required) natural
Close rule other than a gap (logout event, max duration cap) no yes
Cap session length (bot with an event every second) awkward add if lastTs - start > MAX then close and start a new one
Backfill with the same results yes (event time) yes (event time only)

Cap the maximum session length in production. A single bot key that never idles for 30 min yields an unbounded session and an unbounded count; emit a forced close at, say, 24 h of event time.

20.5 First event, last event, duration without KEEP DENSE_RANK

KEEP (DENSE_RANK FIRST ORDER BY ts) means "the value from the row with the smallest ts". Equivalent here: keep the (ts, value) pair with the smallest ts (first) and the largest (last) in the accumulator and update both on each event and each merge (sketch in 20.3). It is O(1) state per session, order-independent (works for out-of-order and late events), and needs no buffering of events. A plain ProcessWindowFunction with the full event Iterable would work but buffers every event of the session (Chapter 2.7): do not. Distinct counts or percentiles over a session need a sketch accumulator (Chapter 8 on serialization).

20.6 Choosing the gap from data

  1. For each key, compute inter-event gaps (event time of consecutive events). Plot or bucket the distribution (log scale).
  2. Real behavior is bimodal: short in-session gaps and a long tail of between-session idle times. Pick the gap in the valley between modes (often a knee in the CDF), not a round number such as 30 min by habit.
  3. Check sensitivity: compute session counts and average length at gap = 10, 20, 30, 60 min. If counts change sharply near your gap, the result is fragile.
  4. Per-segment gaps (mobile vs web) via withDynamicGap (verified) or a KeyedProcessFunction; the extractor must be deterministic and cheap. Changing the gap changes state semantics (Chapter 9).
  5. The gap also sets latency (20.2) and state lifetime (20.7): doubling the gap doubles the minimum emission delay and open-session time.
  6. Out-of-order tolerance and gap interact: delay (Chapter 1.7) and allowed lateness extend the time a session stays in flux. Choose delay from the arrival-lag p99.

No numbers are given for your fleet. Data unavailable: derive them from a week of real data per 1.7.

20.7 State size per open session

open sessions per key  ~ 1 (sometimes 2 with out-of-order)         live keys = keys active within gap (+ lateness L)
state bytes  ~ live keys x (key + sessions x (Session POJO + per-entry overhead))   + timers (1 per session)
  • Window-based: per (key, window) the accumulator, plus window metadata for merging, plus a cleanup timer at maxTimestamp + L (window end - 1 ms + L). Until the merge completes, each event briefly is its own window (docs: window per record then merge, Chapter 2.2).
  • With AggregateFunction the accumulator is constant size: SessionAcc above is three longs (firstTs, lastTs, count) and two small strings. Strings (first/last event type) dominate; use an enum or small int.
  • Assumption: per-entry overhead and timer overhead are not measured here. Chapter 17 measures with real serializers; Chapter 5.6 gives the formula.
  • Peak live keys = peak distinct active users in gap + L + watermark delay, not daily distinct users. Estimate it from the data in 20.6.
  • A KeyedProcessFunction needs a state-lifetime guarantee: the closing timer is the cleanup (Chapter 3.6). Do not also rely on TTL for sessions: TTL is processing-time based and fires no callback (Chapter 5.5), so a TTL-expired session would vanish without a final emission.
  • Hot keys (bots, shared accounts) create long sessions on one subtask: Chapter 10.

20.8 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • "Sessions never appear": watermark stalled by an idle partition (Chapter 1.5); with a 30 min gap the symptom is easy to misread as "just slow".
  • Output is always at least gap behind: a product requirement mismatch, not a bug. Use provisional updates for "now".
  • Merging window function missing (AggregateFunction.merge returns wrong data): merged sessions silently lose first/last or counts. Unit-test merge with out-of-order input (Chapter 14).
  • Duplicates after allowedLateness: each late firing re-emits; the sink must upsert by (key, sessionStart) and handle sessionStart changing on merge (20.3, Chapter 26).
  • Unbounded sessions from always-active keys: cap length (20.4).
  • Replay or backfill with processing-time session windows gives nonsense (Chapter 2.9); use event time.
  • Provisional and final confusion downstream: carry an explicit status (PROVISIONAL/FINAL) and a monotonic version; consumers keep the highest version per session id.
  • Key choice: key by (tenantId, userId) so tenants never share a session (Chapter 5.8).
  • Too-large gap + allowedLateness on millions of keys: state and checkpoint size grow with it (Chapter 6, 17).

20.9 Self-check

  1. Gap 30 min, watermark delay 10 s, last event of a session at 10:25. At what event time is the session emitted, and what if no later events arrive?
  2. A late event arrives between two already-final sessions. Describe what each design (window with allowedLateness, KeyedProcessFunction with extra L) emits, and what the sink needs.
  3. Why is duration = windowEnd - windowStart wrong for a session window?
  4. Why not use state TTL to clean abandoned sessions in the KeyedProcessFunction design?
  5. How would you pick the gap, and what happens to state if you double it?

20.10 Open items / unverified

  • RESOLVED (verified): built-in ContinuousEventTimeTrigger exists in 2.2.1 (and declares canMerge); its firing behavior on merged sessions is untested here. The 2.3.0 jars were not diffed for the trigger package.
  • Exact onMerge contract (what a custom trigger must do with timers) beyond the signatures above: docs summary only; test with the harness (Chapter 14).
  • Precise "late firing" semantics for merged windows in edge cases (20.3).
  • RESOLVED (verified): getRuntimeContext().getMapState(MapStateDescriptor) (returns org.apache.flink.api.common.state.MapState; a v2 overload also exists) and open(OpenContext) in the 2.2.1 jars.
  • Per-session and per-timer state overhead: Data unavailable (measure in Chapter 17).
  • Session behavior under State V2 / ForSt (Chapter 28): data unavailable.

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/operators/windows/

Chapter 21: Blueprint 4, rolling feature table and add_to_cart_15m

Goal: after this chapter you can build a true "events in the last 15 minutes per user" feature in the DataStream API, compare a sliding window with per-key bucketed counters, make the counter shrink as time passes, expire dead keys, decide event-time versus processing-time freshness, handle late events, and publish the result as upserts to a compacted Kafka topic that a serving layer reads by key.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (time), Chapter 2 (sliding windows, state cost), Chapter 3 (timers, cleanup), Chapter 5 (MapState, TTL). Kafka sink semantics are Chapter 7; idempotent writes are Chapter 26. Kafka usage assumes Flink 2.2.x with Kafka connector 5.0.0 (README verified facts; no connector for 2.3 yet).

21.1 What the article got wrong

The "hello feature" was a rolling add_to_cart_15m counter built with a CURRENT_TIMESTAMP filter on a running aggregate. That is not a sliding window:

  1. CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is evaluated per row at processing time. A predicate such as "event time > now - 15 min" is applied when the row arrives, to that row. It filters old events on entry, but nothing ever re-evaluates it later. The counter for a key therefore only goes up; an event that was inside the 15 minutes at arrival is never subtracted when it ages out. The "15m" in the name is a lie: the value is "adds that arrived recently, accumulated since the job began".
  2. Counter never expires. With no input for a user, the state keeps its last count forever. The feature served is stale, and the state is never freed (Chapter 5.8, first pitfall).
  3. Non-deterministic. Replays and backfills (Chapter 24) give different results because "now" differs per run (Chapter 1.1).
  4. No late-data, TTL, serving or schema story.

The correct statement: a rolling count at time T is count of events with ts in (T - 15 min, T]. Something must remove events as T advances. That is what the two designs below do.

Figure 21.1: The article's counter only goes up and never expires; bucketed counters sum to 7 at T = 10:12 and a timer evicts the oldest bucket.

21.2 Mental model: feature = (key, as-of time) -> value

events (add_to_cart, user u1)  ──► keyed state ──► feature value as of time T ──► upsert key=(tenant,u1,add_to_cart_15m)
                                      ▲                    ▲
                           must evict ageing events   must re-emit when value DECREASES too

Two requirements people forget: (a) the value must decrease when events age out, and (b) that decrease must be emitted, otherwise the serving layer keeps the old high value until the next event for that key.

21.3 Design A: sliding window

SlidingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(15), Duration.ofMinutes(1)) (verified: javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1 SlidingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration, Duration); also the docs; allowedLateness(Duration) and sideOutputLateData compile-checked against 2.2.1 jars).

// (sketch, not compiled)
cartEvents
  .keyBy(e -> e.tenantId + "|" + e.userId)
  .window(SlidingEventTimeWindows.of(Duration.ofMinutes(15), Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
  .allowedLateness(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
  .sideOutputLateData(lateTag)
  .aggregate(new CountAgg(), new AddKeyAndWindowEnd());   // emits (key, windowEnd, count) every minute per active key
Aspect Cost / behavior
Copies per event size/slide = 15 windows (Chapter 2.2); with AggregateFunction, one long per (key, window)
State per active key 15 accumulators + metadata + about 15 trigger timers, plus 15 more cleanup timers when allowedLateness > 0 (verified: javap WindowOperator.cleanupTime = maxTimestamp + allowedLateness, EventTimeTrigger registers at maxTimestamp; the two coincide, and are deduplicated, only when lateness is 0). Assumption: byte overhead per window not measured
Slide 1 s instead of 1 min 900 copies; usually the wrong trade (Chapter 2.9)
Output one record per key per slide for every window that has data; no output for a window with zero events, so a user whose count falls to 0 never gets a "0" emitted (the last window containing events is the last output)
Freshness at least slide + watermark delay behind (Chapter 2.3); window fires on watermark only
Exactness exact at slide granularity: windows end on minute boundaries

Weakness to design around: no empty-window output. If the feature must reach 0, either have the serving layer treat a missing/old as_of as 0 (21.8), or use Design B. Verified fact used here: sliding windows create several of each element, the docs warn about it, and aggregating functions store one value per window.

Use A when: the slide can be coarse (1 to 5 min), the feature count is small, and a window-aligned result is fine.

21.4 Design B: per-key bucketed counters in MapState, eviction by timers

Idea: store counts in fixed buckets (say 1 minute) in MapState<Long bucketStart, Integer count>. The rolling count at time T is the sum of buckets whose start is in the retained range. State per key is at most window/bucket entries (15), independent of event rate; each event is O(1) update plus an O(buckets) sum. Eviction removes buckets that fell out of the window, one timer per key.

bucket = floor(ts / 60_000) * 60_000        retained range for as-of T:  bucket(T) - 14 min .. bucket(T)
state:  { 10:00 -> 2,  10:03 -> 1,  10:09 -> 4 }          T = 10:12  -> sum = 7
timer:  at oldest bucket start + 15 min (first bucket to expire)

Figure 21.2: Design B update and expiry cycle; Design A emits nothing for an empty window.

// (sketch; compiles against Flink 2.2.1 jars, semantics checked by simulation, not run on a cluster)
public class RollingCount extends KeyedProcessFunction<String, Cart, FeatureRow> {
    static final long BUCKET = 60_000L, WINDOW = 15 * BUCKET;
    private transient MapState<Long, Integer> buckets;
    private transient ValueState<Long> nextTimer;          // the single timer we own

    @Override public void open(OpenContext c) {
        buckets   = getRuntimeContext().getMapState(new MapStateDescriptor<>("buckets", Long.class, Integer.class));
        nextTimer = getRuntimeContext().getState(new ValueStateDescriptor<>("nextTimer", Long.class));
    }

    @Override public void processElement(Cart e, Context ctx, Collector<FeatureRow> out) throws Exception {
        long wm = ctx.timerService().currentWatermark();
        long b  = (e.eventTsMillis / BUCKET) * BUCKET;
        if (b + WINDOW <= wm) { ctx.output(Late.TAG, e); return; }      // bucket already expired: too late (21.7)
        buckets.put(b, buckets.contains(b) ? buckets.get(b) + 1 : 1);
        evict(wm);                                                      // evict by the WATERMARK only, never by a time ahead of it
        long asOf = Math.max(wm, e.eventTsMillis);                      // evaluate at the freshest event time we know
        out.collect(row(ctx.getCurrentKey(), sum(asOf), asOf));
        rearm(ctx, asOf);
    }

    @Override public void onTimer(long ts, OnTimerContext ctx, Collector<FeatureRow> out) throws Exception {
        Long expected = nextTimer.value();
        if (expected == null || expected != ts) return;                 // stale timer (Chapter 3.3)
        evict(ctx.timerService().currentWatermark());
        out.collect(row(ctx.getCurrentKey(), sum(ts), ts));             // the DECREASE is emitted
        rearm(ctx, ts);
    }

    private void evict(long wm) throws Exception {                      // drop buckets whose window has fully passed the watermark
        List<Long> dead = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Long k : buckets.keys()) if (k + WINDOW <= wm) dead.add(k);
        for (Long k : dead) buckets.remove(k);
    }

    private long sum(long asOf) throws Exception {                      // read-only: buckets still inside (asOf-15m, asOf]
        long lo = ((asOf - WINDOW) / BUCKET + 1) * BUCKET;              // first bucket start strictly after asOf-15m
        long total = 0;
        for (Map.Entry<Long, Integer> en : buckets.entries()) if (en.getKey() >= lo) total += en.getValue();
        return total;
    }

    private void rearm(Context ctx, long now) throws Exception {        // next expiry of the oldest live bucket
        Long old = nextTimer.value();
        if (old != null) ctx.timerService().deleteEventTimeTimer(old);
        Long oldest = null;
        for (Long k : buckets.keys()) if (oldest == null || k < oldest) oldest = k;
        if (oldest == null) { nextTimer.clear(); return; }               // no buckets: key is dead, state is empty
        long t = oldest + WINDOW;                                        // when that bucket leaves the window
        ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(t);
        nextTimer.update(t);
    }
}
// (compile-checked against the 2.2.1 jars; `OnTimerContext` extends `Context`, so `rearm` accepts both. State interfaces were checked with flink-core-api 1.20.5, see the verification log.)

Why `evict` is separate from `sum`: a first version evicted inside `sum(asOf)` with `asOf = max(watermark, event time)`. When an event ahead of the watermark\narrives, that evicts buckets the watermark still allows; a later out-of-order event then sees a count with those buckets missing. A plain-Python simulation (300 random out-of-order events, 5 seeds) gave 4 to 12 wrong counts per run for the combined version and 0 for the split version, compared with a brute-force count.

Properties: - Exact rolling count at bucket granularity. Events are counted from the start of their bucket: the window edge is quantised to 1 minute (a 15-minute feature really covers 14 to 15 minutes of events depending on position). Smaller buckets cost more entries; 15 buckets is a sensible start. Assumption: this error is acceptable for the feature; verify with the feature owner. - Self-cleaning. When the last bucket expires, rearm clears nextTimer and the key holds no state; no TTL needed for live keys. - One timer per key, so timers = active keys, not events (Chapter 3.4 cost model). Timers fall on bucket boundaries plus 15 minutes, so they are naturally coalesced across events of the same bucket. - Output is emitted on each event (can be coalesced, 21.9) and on each expiry. The expiry emission is what Design A lacks. - Out-of-order inside the bucket range is free: addition is commutative, no ordering needed (Chapter 1). - Event-time timers fire only when the watermark moves (Chapter 3.2). If the whole input stops, counts never decay; see 21.6.

A versus B

A: sliding window B: bucketed MapState + timer
State per active key ~15 window accumulators + metadata + timers up to 15 map entries + 1 timer
Output on decay to 0 none yes (timer)
Output cadence every slide, fixed on event and on expiry, you control it
Late events allowedLateness + re-fire (Chapter 2.4) accepted while bucket is live; you decide the rest
Multiple features / windows one operator per window size one state, several window lengths from the same buckets
Code to own little you own correctness (Chapter 3.7 warning)

Several lengths (5 m, 15 m, 1 h) from one bucket map: keep buckets for the longest length and sum different suffixes. 1 h of 1-minute buckets is 60 entries per key.

21.5 TTL for dead keys

  • Design B cleans itself when the buckets expire (21.4), as long as the timer fires.
  • If you also keep other per-key state (last value emitted, version), clear it in the same rearm branch where no buckets remain, or it leaks (Chapter 3.6).
  • State TTL (Chapter 5.5) is processing time, fires no callback, and is logical not physical deletion. As a safety net for keys whose timer never fires (stuck watermark) TTL can bound state, but it will also delete live buckets of slow keys, so set it well above the window (e.g. several times 15 min), Assumption: value to be chosen by measuring.
  • Replay danger (Chapter 5.5): replaying a month of events at high speed under processing-time TTL treats everything as fresh; with event-time timers B is replay-safe, TTL is not.
  • Cardinality: live keys = keys with an event in the last 15 min (plus watermark delay), not total users. Estimate from data (Chapter 17).

21.6 Event-time versus processing-time freshness

Question Event-time design (A, or B with event-time timers) Processing-time timers in B
Replay/backfill gives the same answer yes no
Counts decay when input stops no (watermark stalls, Chapter 3.2) yes (wall clock)
Value reflects "events in the 15 minutes before wall-clock now" only while watermark is near now yes
Late events defined by watermark counted by arrival time; late events count as fresh

Recommendation: compute with event time (deterministic, replayable, Chapter 1.1) and make freshness visible to the consumer by writing as_of_event_ts and a computed_at wall-clock stamp on every row. The serving layer then decides: "if now - as_of_event_ts > X, treat the value as stale". A hybrid (processing-time heartbeat timer that emits as_of = now for quiet keys) fits live serving, but breaks replays; if you do it, gate it with a flag and never use it in backfill. Idle sources: withIdleness (Chapter 1.5) so the watermark can advance.

21.7 Late events

  • Window route: allowedLateness re-fires the window (Chapter 2.4). Beyond that, side output.
  • Bucket route: a late event is accepted if its bucket is still live (bucket start within the window relative to the watermark); the counter is corrected and a corrected row is emitted. If bucket + 15 min <= watermark it is already outside the window as of now: it cannot change the current value, so route it to the late side output for accounting only (Chapter 1.4).
  • Event time before the watermark but within the window still affects the "now" value, which means rows can be revised downwards or upwards: consumers must treat the key as upsert and keep the latest.
  • Watermark delay (Chapter 1.7) sets the trade-off: more delay, fresher-correct but slower features. For features, a short delay (seconds) plus correction-by-late-update is usually the right default. Assumption: pick from measured p99.
  • Counting late events matters for model/feature drift; keep the side-output counter (Chapter 13).

21.8 Emitting to an upsert-style compacted topic, and serving by key

Pattern: one Kafka topic per feature set, record key = serving key, value = latest feature row, topic with log compaction so Kafka keeps the latest value per key.

Flink ──(key=tenant|user, value=row)──► topic (cleanup.policy=compact) ──► serving cache / KV store
                                                      └─► tombstone (null value) when the key goes dead
  • Choose the Kafka record key deterministically (tenantId|userId): the same key must always hit the same partition so compaction and ordering per key hold (Chapter 7, 10).
  • Always include the tenant in the key (multi-tenant isolation, Chapter 5.8, 27).
  • Compaction is a Kafka feature: cleanup.policy=compact. Assumption: standard Kafka behavior; confirm retention/compaction settings with the Kafka operators. Compaction is not instantaneous, so a reader of the whole topic sees old versions until compaction runs.
  • Order and idempotency: a retry or a recovery replays rows; an older row must never overwrite a newer one. Put a monotonic version (e.g. as_of_event_ts, tie-broken by sequence) in the value and let the consumer apply "write only if version is newer" (Chapter 26 develops this).
  • Delivery: with Kafka sink AT_LEAST_ONCE duplicates are harmless for upserts of the same key/version; exactly-once transactional mode has latency and settings implications (Chapter 7). Key serialization on the sink (verified: javap flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2 KafkaRecordSerializationSchemaBuilder): setKeySerializationSchema(SerializationSchema<? super T>), or setKafkaKeySerializer(Class<? extends Serializer>) / setKafkaKeySerializer(Class, Map<String,String>); the value uses setValueSerializationSchema(...) or setKafkaValueSerializer(...); a key serializer set twice is rejected (checkKeySerializerNotSet). A tombstone needs a SerializationSchema that returns null for the value: [unverified] (not run).
  • Dead keys: when design B clears a key (no buckets), emit a final row with value = 0 and as_of, optionally followed by a tombstone after a grace period so the topic does not hold dead keys forever. Whether to tombstone at all depends on the serving layer; both are valid. Without either, the stale last value stays in the cache: that is the article's "never expires" bug moved downstream.
  • Serving by key: the consumer materialises the topic into a KV cache (point lookup by tenant|user|feature). Flink Queryable State is an alternative that exposes keyed state directly; in 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 the runtime jars still contain QueryableStateStream and KeyedStream.asQueryableState, but QueryableStateStream is annotated @Deprecated (verified: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1, class present in 2.3.0), and the 2.0 release notes page did not mention it, so this book does not rely on it. State inside Flink is not a database for outside readers (Chapter 5.1).
  • Coalesce output: for high-rate keys emit at most once per N seconds (a timer or per-key lastEmitTs), otherwise the topic carries one row per event. Cadence is a product choice, Assumption: 1 to 5 s is typical, not measured.

21.9 Schema of the feature row

Keep the value small, versioned, self-describing, and free of PII (Chapter 27: use a surrogate id, never raw email or name).

Field Type Meaning
tenant_id string isolation scope, part of the Kafka key
entity_id string the keyed entity (surrogate user id)
feature string e.g. add_to_cart_15m; one topic can hold several features, or one topic per feature
value long the count (0 allowed)
window_ms long 900000; makes the row self-describing
as_of_event_ts long event time the value was computed for; freshness input for the reader
computed_at long wall-clock emit time, diagnostics only, never used in logic
version long monotonic per key (e.g. as_of_event_ts, then a counter); last-writer-wins guard
schema_ver int evolution (Chapter 8, 9)
status enum LIVE, DEAD (zero and key retired)

Serialization with Avro/Protobuf or a Flink POJO: Chapter 8. Adding a window length means a new feature name, not a changed meaning of an existing one.

21.10 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Copying the article's counter: no eviction, no decay, no expiry (21.1).
  • Decay never emitted (Design A has no empty windows; Design B without the expiry timer): feature stays high after activity stops.
  • Event-time timers with a stalled watermark never evict (idle partition, Chapter 1.5); the feature freezes silently. Alert on watermark lag (Chapter 13).
  • A timer per event instead of one per key: timer storm (Chapter 3.8). Keep a single nextTimer.
  • Sliding window with 1 s slide: 900 copies per event and a huge checkpoint (Chapter 2.9).
  • Reading a whole MapState per event on a hot key: 15 entries is fine; 1 h at 1 s buckets (3600) per hot key is not. Pick bucket size from window/buckets (about 15 to 60).
  • Wrong-key aggregation: key by (tenant, entity); a global key is one subtask (Chapter 10).
  • Processing-time TTL in replay wipes or floods state (21.5).
  • Out-of-order rows overwrite newer values downstream: no version guard (21.8).
  • Hot users/bots: one key dominates a subtask; cap or sample (Chapter 10).
  • Changing bucket size/window on a running job changes state meaning; plan as a state migration (Chapter 9).

21.11 Self-check

  1. Explain in two sentences why CURRENT_TIMESTAMP in a filter does not make a counter rolling.
  2. A user adds to cart at 10:00 and never again. What does Design A serve at 10:30, what does Design B serve, and what must the serving layer do in each case?
  3. State size: 20 M active users, 15 one-minute buckets, 12 bytes per entry plus overhead. Roughly how large is Design B's state compared with Design A, and which number is an Assumption?
  4. The watermark stalls for 20 minutes. What happens to B's output and what do you add so readers know?
  5. Why must the Kafka record key include the tenant, and why does the row need a version?

21.12 Open items / unverified

  • StateTtlConfig: only TtlTimeCharacteristic.ProcessingTime exists (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1), so event-time TTL is not available; setters seen: setTimeToLive(Duration), updateTtlOnCreateAndWrite(), cleanupFullSnapshot() etc.
  • Exactly-once transactional settings for connector 5.0.0 (Chapter 7). Key-serializer calls are verified (21.8).
  • Queryable State: present but @Deprecated in 2.2.1 runtime (verified); whether the separate queryable-state client artifact is published for 2.x: Data unavailable.
  • Behavior of MapState iteration cost under RocksDB for small maps vs ListState: Data unavailable (measure, Chapter 11).
  • Measured per-window and per-entry overhead for A and B: Data unavailable (Chapter 17).
  • Whether the exact bucket math matches an off-by-one convention your consumers expect (window edge inclusivity, Chapter 2.3 boundary is also [unverified]). Verified in this chapter: a bucket b is dropped when b + 15 min <= watermark and the timer fires when the watermark reaches oldest + 15 min (simulation).
  • open(OpenContext) is verified (javap AbstractRichFunction.open(OpenContext) throws Exception); getRuntimeContext().getMapState/getState compile against the jars (state interfaces checked with 1.20.5 core-api).

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/dev/datastream/operators/windows/

Chapter 22: Blueprint 5, anomaly scoring with hysteresis

Goal: after this chapter you can build per-key anomaly detection as one KeyedProcessFunction: a rolling baseline that never contains the point being scored, a cold-start rule, a zero-variance guard, a hysteresis state machine that opens an alert at z >= T_open and closes it only after N minutes below T_close, deduplicated alerts, late-event handling, and state cleanup.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, late side output), Chapter 3 (timers, stale-timer rule, cleanup timers), Chapter 5 (state, TTL), Chapter 10 (key skew). Delivery of the alert topic: Chapter 7 and Chapter 26.

22.1 What the article got wrong

Article Problem Fix here
Called .connect(keyed) on the same stream (a stream connected to a keyed view of itself) connect joins two different inputs that need different handling (map1/map2, Chapter 4 patterns: events + rules). Connecting a stream to itself gives every record to both inputs, so you process each record twice with two code paths and no shared per-key state unless both sides are keyed identically. The docs describe connect as keeping two stream types and sharing state between them; they do not describe a self-connect use case One input, one keyBy, one KeyedProcessFunction (22.2). Use connect only when a genuine second stream exists (rule/threshold updates via broadcast, Chapter 4)
Scala-style snippet (Scala API) Flink 2.0 release notes: "Scala DataStream and DataSet API - Please migrate to the Java DataStream API." Scala code cannot be a Flink 2.x blueprint Java only (this book). Scala language use via the Java API is a separate question: Data unavailable
Baseline included the scored point A spike inflates its own mean/std, so z shrinks and large anomalies self-mask Score first, then update (22.3)
Threshold crossing = alert Flapping around the threshold produces alert storms Hysteresis state machine (22.5)
No cold start, no zero-variance rule, no late-event or cleanup story std = 0 gives infinity/NaN; new keys alert on 2 samples; state grows forever 22.4, 22.7, 22.8

We also deliberately do not use SQL for this blueprint (book rule).

22.2 Topology: one keyed operator

 Kafka metric events
   │  WatermarkStrategy (Ch 1), uid("src")
   ▼
 keyBy(tenantId + "|" + entityId + "|" + metric)        <- ONE keyBy, key includes tenant (Ch 23.6)
   ▼
 AnomalyFn (KeyedProcessFunction)                       <- baseline + z + state machine + timers
   ├── main output : AlertEvent {OPEN | CLOSE}  ──► sink (Ch 7 / Ch 26)
   └── side output : late / invalid points      ──► counter, DLQ (Ch 12)

Why one function: the baseline, the z-score, the open/closed state and the close timer are all per-key state that must be read and written atomically for each record. processElement and onTimer are serialized per operator instance (Chapter 3.4), so no locks are needed. Splitting this over two operators (score, then a second keyed stage for hysteresis) is legal but doubles shuffles and makes ordering between them your problem.

If thresholds must change at runtime, add a second different stream (broadcast thresholds, Chapter 4) and use keyBy(...).connect(broadcast) via the broadcast-state pattern. That is the legitimate use of connecting.

Figure 22.1: The article's self-connect versus the single keyed operator.

22.3 Baseline: rolling mean and standard deviation

Two options. Pick on whether you need a true sliding window.

Welford online (whole history or exponentially decayed) Bucketed window stats
State 3 numbers per key: n, mean, M2 MapState<bucketStart, (n, sum, sumSq or mean/M2)>, e.g. 1-minute buckets x 60
Window none: all history (or decayed, see below) exact sliding window of W minutes, bucket granularity
Removal of old data impossible for plain Welford evict whole buckets by timer
Seasonality, drift poor better; you can also keep same-hour-of-week baselines (Assumption: your choice)
Cost tiny W / bucket entries per key

Welford update (numerically stable, for a new value x): n += 1; d = x - mean; mean += d / n; M2 += d * (x - mean); var = M2 / (n - 1) (sample variance, needs n >= 2). Merging two partial stats (bucketed option, Chan et al.): n = na + nb; d = mb - ma; mean = ma + d*nb/n; M2 = M2a + M2b + d*d*na*nb/n. Do not use E[x^2] - E[x]^2 on large-magnitude values: catastrophic cancellation.

Exclude the current point from its own baseline. Order inside processElement: 1. compute z from the baseline as it stands before this record; 2. run the state machine (22.5); 3. only then fold x into the baseline.

Poisoning: should points scored as anomalous enter the baseline? Policy choice, state it explicitly. Common rule (Assumption): while the alert is OPEN, do not update the baseline, otherwise a long incident becomes the new normal and the alert closes by itself. Counter-risk: a genuine level shift never re-baselines. Add a maximum open duration that forces a re-baseline and a human-visible alert.

Exponential decay variant (cheap, no buckets): mean += a*d; var = (1-a)*(var + a*d*d); the effective window is roughly 1/a samples. Assumption: formula from standard EWMA variance literature, not from Flink docs.

22.4 Cold start, min samples, zero variance

Situation Rule
n < MIN_SAMPLES (say 30; Assumption, tune per metric) no score, no alert; just learn. Emit nothing, optionally count "warming" keys
std == 0 or std < EPS (constant metric) do not divide. Options: skip scoring; or use a floor std_eff = max(std, EPS_ABS, REL * abs(mean)). The floor turns "went 0 to 5 on a flat series" into a large z, which is usually what you want, so choose it deliberately
NaN / infinite / null value reject to a side output (Chapter 12); never feed it to Welford, one NaN poisons the key forever
Gap longer than the window baseline is stale; treat as cold start again (reset or decay)
New key after a restart without state cold start for every key at once; expect a quiet period. Chapter 9 on keeping state across upgrades

Cold start is also a multi-tenant fairness matter: a new tenant must not generate alerts on day one.

22.5 Hysteresis state machine

          z >= T_open                                    below = (z < T_close)
 CLOSED ───────────────────► OPEN ──┬── point with z >= T_close: belowSince = null, delete close timer
   ▲   emit OPEN(alertId)           └── point with z <  T_close: if belowSince == null: belowSince = ts,
   │                                      register event-time timer at ts + N minutes
   └─── onTimer(ts + N min) and still below: emit CLOSE(alertId), CLOSED

Requires T_open > T_close (for example 4.0 and 2.0; Assumption, tune on your data). The band between them keeps the state unchanged: OPEN stays OPEN, CLOSED stays CLOSED. That band is the hysteresis.

Figure 22.2: Hysteresis state machine; OPEN closes only after N minutes of event time below T_close.

State per key (all cleared on cleanup, 22.8):

State Type Meaning
stats POJO (n, mean, m2, or buckets) baseline
phase ValueState<Integer> (0 CLOSED, 1 OPEN) state machine
openedAt ValueState<Long> event ts of OPEN; part of the alert id
belowSince ValueState<Long> start of the current below-T_close run, or null
closeTimer ValueState<Long> the one pending timer timestamp (stale-timer guard, Chapter 3.3)

Close condition is "below for N minutes of event time" measured from the first below point, reset by any point at or above T_close. Alternative definition: N consecutive points below. Pick one; they differ for irregular sampling.

22.6 Alert dedup

  • Emit only on transitions (CLOSED to OPEN, OPEN to CLOSED). While OPEN, further z >= T_open points emit nothing (optionally a bounded "still open" heartbeat every X minutes, via a second timer).
  • Give each alert a deterministic id, alertId = key + "|" + openedAt. After a crash and replay the same OPEN is regenerated with the same id, so a downstream upsert/idempotent consumer drops the duplicate (Chapter 26). Without a transactional or idempotent sink, replays duplicate alerts; Kafka exactly-once covers the topic only for read_committed consumers (Chapter 7.9).
  • Do not use a TTL to expire the OPEN flag (Chapter 5.5: TTL is processing time and silent). Close it with logic.

22.7 Late events and out-of-order data

  • A point with ts <= currentWatermark is late (Chapter 1.4). Route it to a side output and do not touch the baseline or the state machine: updating after the fact reorders history that earlier decisions were based on.
  • If lateness is common, raise the watermark delay (costs alert latency, Chapter 1.2) rather than reprocessing.
  • Within the allowed out-of-orderness, points arrive out of order. Welford is order-independent in result (up to floating-point); the hysteresis belowSince logic is order-sensitive. Choose: buffer points per key in ListState until the watermark passes them and process sorted (cost: state and latency), or accept order sensitivity inside the watermark delay. Assumption: most monitoring use cases accept the latter; document it.
  • Event-time timers fire only when the watermark advances. If a key (or the whole input) goes silent, an OPEN alert does not close by timer until a later watermark passes belowSince + N. Per-partition idleness (Chapter 1.5) and a stalled job (Chapter 25) both hold alerts OPEN. If "close when the metric disappeared" is a requirement, add a separate processing-time heartbeat decision (Chapter 3.2) and state which clock you mean.

22.8 State cleanup

Per Chapter 3.6: every key that can go quiet needs a cleanup deadline. - Keep one cleanup timer at lastEventTs + RETENTION, replacing it on each record (or compare a stored deadline in onTimer). It clears stats, phase, openedAt, belowSince, closeTimer. - If the key is OPEN at cleanup time, emit a final CLOSE (reason expired) first, otherwise the alert hangs forever downstream. - For bucketed stats, evict buckets older than W at each record or in the same timer. - Timers per key: at most two (close, cleanup). Event-time timers are deduplicated per (key, timestamp) (Chapter 3.4); coalesce timestamps to whole minutes to bound them. - Key cardinality is tenants x entities x metrics: estimate with Chapter 5.6 and Chapter 17.

22.9 Sketch

// (sketch; compiles against Flink 2.2.1 jars with stub Stats/Alert/Metric classes; semantics not run on a cluster)
// Names of Stats/Alert helpers are illustrative.
public class AnomalyFn extends KeyedProcessFunction<String, Metric, Alert> {
    static final double T_OPEN = 4.0, T_CLOSE = 2.0, EPS = 1e-9;
    static final long   N_MS = 5 * 60_000L, RETENTION_MS = 24 * 3_600_000L;
    static final int    MIN_SAMPLES = 30;
    public static final OutputTag<Metric> REJECT = new OutputTag<>("reject") {};

    private transient ValueState<Stats> stats;      // n, mean, m2
    private transient ValueState<Integer> phase;    // null/0 closed, 1 open
    private transient ValueState<Long> openedAt, belowSince, closeTimer, cleanupAt;

    @Override public void open(OpenContext c) { /* getRuntimeContext().getState(new ValueStateDescriptor<>(...)) x6 */ }

    @Override
    public void processElement(Metric m, Context ctx, Collector<Alert> out) throws Exception {
        long wm = ctx.timerService().currentWatermark();
        if (m.ts <= wm || !Double.isFinite(m.value)) { ctx.output(REJECT, m); return; }   // 22.7

        Stats s = stats.value() == null ? new Stats() : stats.value();
        boolean open = phase.value() != null && phase.value() == 1;

        // 1. score against the baseline WITHOUT this point (22.3)
        Double z = null;
        if (s.n >= MIN_SAMPLES) {
            double std = Math.sqrt(s.m2 / (s.n - 1));
            z = Math.abs(m.value - s.mean) / Math.max(std, EPS);        // zero-variance guard (22.4)
        }

        // 2. state machine (22.5)
        if (z != null) {
            if (!open && z >= T_OPEN) {
                phase.update(1); openedAt.update(m.ts); clearBelow(ctx);
                out.collect(Alert.open(ctx.getCurrentKey(), m.ts, z));
                open = true;
            } else if (open && z >= T_CLOSE) {
                clearBelow(ctx);                                          // back above T_close: restart the count
            } else if (open && belowSince.value() == null) {              // z < T_CLOSE
                long due = ((m.ts + N_MS + 59_999L) / 60_000L) * 60_000L; // coalesce UP to the minute (rounding down would close early)
                belowSince.update(m.ts); closeTimer.update(due);
                ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(due);
            }
        }

        // 3. fold into baseline only now, and not while OPEN (22.3 policy)
        if (!open) { s.add(m.value); stats.update(s); }

        // cleanup deadline (22.8)
        Long old = cleanupAt.value(); if (old != null) ctx.timerService().deleteEventTimeTimer(old);
        long c = m.ts + RETENTION_MS; ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(c); cleanupAt.update(c);
    }

    @Override
    public void onTimer(long ts, OnTimerContext ctx, Collector<Alert> out) throws Exception {
        Long ct = closeTimer.value();
        if (ct != null && ct == ts) {                                     // stale-timer guard (Chapter 3.3)
            out.collect(Alert.close(ctx.getCurrentKey(), openedAt.value(), ts));
            phase.update(0); openedAt.clear(); belowSince.clear(); closeTimer.clear();
        }
        Long cu = cleanupAt.value();
        if (cu != null && cu == ts) {
            if (phase.value() != null && phase.value() == 1)
                out.collect(Alert.closeExpired(ctx.getCurrentKey(), openedAt.value(), ts));
            stats.clear(); phase.clear(); openedAt.clear(); belowSince.clear(); closeTimer.clear(); cleanupAt.clear();
        }
    }
    private void clearBelow(Context ctx) throws Exception {
        Long t = closeTimer.value(); if (t != null) ctx.timerService().deleteEventTimeTimer(t);
        belowSince.clear(); closeTimer.clear();
    }
}
// wiring: events.keyBy(m -> m.tenantId + "|" + m.entityId + "|" + m.metric).process(new AnomalyFn()).uid("anomaly")

Timer rounding: the timer is rounded up to a whole minute. A simulation of the first version (rounding down) closed an alert 30 s early (belowSince = 30.001 s, due = 5:00.000 instead of at least 5:30.001), violating "N minutes below T_close"; rounding up can only delay.

Note a subtle point the sketch glosses over: when the same millisecond equals both the close and cleanup timestamps, both branches run in one onTimer call; they are written to tolerate that. Also two-sided abs(z) is an Assumption; many metrics only matter in one direction.

22.10 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Self-masking spikes: scoring after updating the baseline (22.3).
  • Baseline poisoning by long incidents: updates continue while OPEN, the incident becomes normal and closes itself.
  • Alert flapping: T_open == T_close, or N too short for the sampling interval.
  • Close never fires: stalled watermark (idle partition, silent job) keeps OPEN forever (22.7, Chapter 1.5).
  • Stale close timer acting after a re-open: always compare ts with closeTimer (Chapter 3.3).
  • Division by zero / NaN: constant metrics, or one NaN in Welford.
  • Alert storm on restart without state: all keys cold, then all start alerting together when MIN_SAMPLES is reached on a shared incident. Warm up from history (Chapter 24, Chapter 30).
  • Hot key: one huge tenant pins one subtask (Chapter 10.4). Salting does not apply, scoring is order and state dependent.
  • State growth without cleanup timers; processing-time TTL misused for the OPEN flag.
  • Duplicate alerts after replay with a non-idempotent sink (Chapters 7, 26).

22.11 Self-check

  1. Why can a single huge spike fail to alert if the baseline is updated before scoring?
  2. A metric is constant for a day, then moves by 1 unit. What does your design emit, and why is a std floor a decision, not a detail?
  3. Draw the transitions for T_open = 4, T_close = 2, N = 5 min over z = 5, 1.5 (t=0), 3 (t=2), 1.5 (t=3), then silence. When does CLOSE fire, and what must be true of the watermark?
  4. Why is stream.connect(stream.keyBy(...)) not an anomaly pattern, and when is connect right?
  5. Why must the close timer be compared against stored state in onTimer?

22.12 Open items / unverified

  • KeyedProcessFunction#open(OpenContext) and getRuntimeContext().getState(...): verified (javap flink-streaming-java/flink-core 2.2.1 AbstractRichFunction.open(OpenContext) throws Exception; sketch compiles; state interfaces checked with flink-core-api 1.20.5 because 2.x core-api was not available). Unchecked: 2.3.0 differences.
  • Whether the docs rule out or discuss self-connect: the operators page does not address it [unverified]; the argument in 22.1 is design reasoning, not a quoted prohibition. API facts verified (javap 2.2.1): DataStream.connect(DataStream<R>) and connect(BroadcastStream<R>) exist, CoMapFunction has map1/map2.
  • Whether Scala-language wrappers of the Java API are usable on 2.x: Data unavailable. Scala DataStream/DataSet API removal: verified (2.0 release notes quote in 22.1; also no org/apache/flink/api/scala or streaming/api/scala classes in the 2.2.1 core/runtime/streaming-java jars).
  • Welford, Chan merge and EWMA variance formulas are standard statistics, not Flink facts. Checked numerically in this review (1000 samples near 1e9: Welford and Chan merge match statistics.variance within 1e-6 relative; the EWMA recursion converges to about the true variance); still add tests (Chapter 14).
  • Timer ordering within a key and exact watermark/timer boundary: [unverified] (Chapter 3.5).
  • Statistical choice of T_open, T_close, N, MIN_SAMPLES, window: Assumption, to be tuned on your data.
