Chapter 23: Blueprint 6, multi-tenant fan-out

Goal: after this chapter you can route one input stream to per-tenant Kafka topics with a topic selector, explain why topic-pattern cannot do this, estimate what many topics cost (transactions, partitions, producers), handle unknown tenants, and choose between one shared job and separate jobs per tenant with an explicit cost-versus-isolation decision.

Version pin: Flink 2.2.x + Kafka connector 5.0.0 (no connector exists for Flink 2.3 yet, README). Kafka facts below were read from the Flink 2.2 connector docs and the connector 5.0.0-2.2 jar; anything else is marked [unverified].

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state keys, TTL), Chapter 7 (KafkaSink, transactions), Chapter 10 (skew), Chapter 12 (DLQ). Chapters 11, 16, 17 for backpressure, security, capacity.

23.1 What the article got wrong

Article Problem Fix here
Used topic-pattern to fan out to tenant_<id> topics In the Flink Kafka connector, topic patterns are a source subscription feature (setTopicPattern(Pattern) on the KafkaSource builder, taking a java.util.regex.Pattern, e.g. Pattern.compile("topic.*"); there is no String overload: verified by javap flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2 KafkaSourceBuilder). The sink has fixed topics or per-record selection, nothing pattern-based. A pattern cannot say "write to the topic named after this record's tenant" Sink-side KafkaRecordSerializationSchema with a topic selector (23.2)
Implied fan-out is free Each topic adds partitions, producer transactions, ACLs and monitoring; failures couple all tenants in one job 23.4, 23.5, 23.8
No unknown-tenant story Typos or new tenants either create topics by accident or crash the job 23.7
No isolation discussion Shared state keys, shared quotas, shared failure domain 23.6

23.2 Dynamic topic routing on the sink

Verified (2.2 Kafka connector docs and javap of flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2): KafkaRecordSerializationSchema.builder() returns a KafkaRecordSerializationSchemaBuilder<T> (package org.apache.flink.connector.kafka.sink). It needs a value serializer and a topic: either setTopic(String) or setTopicSelector(TopicSelector<? super T>), where TopicSelector<IN> is an interface extending java.util.function.Function<IN, String> and Serializable, so a lambda e -> "events." + e.tenantId() works (the sketch below compiles against the jars). Other builder methods: setKeySerializationSchema, setKafkaKeySerializer, setValueSerializationSchema, setKafkaValueSerializer, setPartitioner(KafkaPartitioner), setHeaderProvider(HeaderProvider), build(). The selector must be serializable: do not capture non-serializable objects.

// (sketch; compiles against Flink 2.2.1 + connector 5.0.0-2.2 jars; not run) RoutedEvent is a record with tenantId()
KafkaSink<RoutedEvent> sink = KafkaSink.<RoutedEvent>builder()
    .setBootstrapServers("<KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP>")
    .setRecordSerializer(KafkaRecordSerializationSchema.<RoutedEvent>builder()
        .setTopicSelector(e -> "events." + e.tenantId())            // tenantId already validated (23.7)
        .setValueSerializationSchema(new RoutedEventSchema())
        .build())
    .setDeliveryGuarantee(DeliveryGuarantee.EXACTLY_ONCE)
    .setTransactionalIdPrefix("fanout-<JOB_ID>")                    // unique per job (Chapter 7.5)
    .setProperty("transaction.timeout.ms", "<see Chapter 7.5>")
    .build();
routed.sinkTo(sink).uid("fanout-sink");

Rules for the selector (design, Assumption): - Pure function of the record: no I/O, no state, no clock. It runs on the hot path of every record. - Output must come from an allowlist, never raw input text. Otherwise a record can steer data to any topic the producer is allowed to write (23.6). - Topic names are a contract: <env>.<domain>.<tenantId>.<version>; tenant ids restricted to a safe charset and length. Kafka topic naming constraints (allowed characters, length): [unverified] here, check Kafka docs.

Alternative with the same effect: a single shared topic keyed by tenant (consumers filter). Cheaper, weaker isolation (23.8).

23.3 Why topic-pattern is source-only

 SOURCE:  KafkaSource.builder().setTopicPattern(Pattern.compile("events\\..*"))   discovers existing topics matching a regex   (read side)
 SINK:    selector(record) -> exactly one topic name              decides a destination per record            (write side)

A subscription pattern answers "which topics exist that I should read". A sink must answer "where does this record go". Verified: the sink builder (javap) has only setTopic and setTopicSelector; setTopicPattern exists only on KafkaSourceBuilder. Do not search for a sink-side pattern, and do not model it in a table definition either (no SQL in this book).

Figure 23.1: Pattern subscribes on the source side; the sink uses a selector, fed only validated tenants.

Related source-side point: reading many tenant topics with a pattern means new topics appear at runtime. Partition discovery interval key partition.discovery.interval.ms (verified: javap KafkaSourceOptions: "A non-positive value disables the partition discovery. The default value is 5 minutes"). Per-partition watermarks, idle topics at night and per-tenant skew all apply (Chapters 1.5, 10).

23.4 Topic count, partitions and limits

Flink docs do not publish a maximum topic count for KafkaSink; cluster limits belong to Kafka and your broker sizing.

Cost driver Why it grows with tenants Status
Partitions tenants x partitions per topic partitions on the cluster. Brokers and controllers have practical ceilings broker limits [unverified], size with your Kafka team
Transactions every open transaction covers all partitions written in that checkpoint (23.5) mechanism [unverified] in detail
Producer resources each additional topic/partition touched adds metadata and batching buffers on the writer one current producer per writer subtask (verified); pooling across checkpoints [unverified]
Small batches traffic spread thinly across topics means tiny batches, lower throughput, higher request rate general Kafka behavior, Assumption
Ops ACLs, quotas, retention, monitoring, lag alerts per topic grows linearly

Practical limit planning: pick a ceiling on tenants-per-job (for example a few hundred; Assumption, measure) and shard by tenant group when it is exceeded (23.8). Add Data unavailable where you cannot get a broker-side number.

23.5 Exactly-once with many topics

Chapter 7 applies unchanged, scaled up: - EXACTLY_ONCE writes records in Kafka transactions committed when the checkpoint completes (verified). With a selector, one checkpoint's transaction(s) can touch many topics; the commit makes all of them visible together or none (per the docs' model of commit on checkpoint; each KafkaWriter subtask holds a single currentProducer (verified: javap KafkaWriter field FlinkKafkaInternalProducer currentProducer), so one open transaction per writer subtask at a time, whatever topics it writes to; that a Kafka transaction can span topics is Kafka behavior, Assumption, not run here). - Visibility is delayed to checkpoint cadence for every tenant (Chapter 7.6). Consumers need isolation.level=read_committed. - Timeout rule unchanged: producer transaction.timeout.ms >= max checkpoint duration + max restart duration, below the broker's transaction.max.timeout.ms (Chapter 7.5). More topics and bigger flushes lengthen the pre-commit phase, so checkpoint duration grows with tenant count; re-measure. - One stuck transaction can hold back read_committed readers at the last stable offset on each partition it touched. In a shared sink that means one job's stall delays all tenants' consumers ([unverified] in Flink docs, Kafka behavior, Chapter 7.6). - transactionalIdPrefix must be unique per job and per sink. Do not reuse it across per-tenant jobs or tenant shards; include the shard/tenant in it (Chapter 7.5, 23.8). - If many tenants make transactions too heavy, AT_LEAST_ONCE plus idempotent keys on the consumer side is the alternative (Chapter 26).

23.6 Tenant isolation: what you must enforce yourself

Flink gives no tenant isolation. Everything below is your design.

Layer Risk Control
State keys keyBy(deviceId) while two tenants reuse the same id: tenants share one state entry, data leaks across them key by tenant + entity: keyBy(e -> e.tenantId() + "|" + e.entityId()); assert tenant id is never null; never use a global MapState entry without a tenant dimension (Chapter 5.8)
Broadcast/config state one tenant's rule applied to another key rule maps by tenant id
Routing record steered to another tenant's topic selector from allowlist (23.2); route on the authenticated tenant id, not a free-text payload field
Kafka ACLs one shared principal can write every tenant topic, so a bug leaks everywhere per-tenant principals only if jobs are per tenant. In one shared job the job principal needs write to all tenant topics; accept and compensate with the allowlist and tests. Details Chapter 16
Quotas a noisy tenant consumes broker bandwidth Kafka client quotas per principal are only effective if principals differ [unverified], Assumption
Logs and metrics tenant data in logs, cross-tenant metric labels redact payloads in logs; use tenant id as a label only if cardinality is bounded (Chapter 13)
TTL one TTL descriptor per state, cannot differ per tenant separate descriptors or logic (Chapter 5.8)
Key skew big tenant pins one subtask Chapter 10.4; consider isolating the big tenant (23.8)
Test data cross-tenant leakage only shows with colliding ids property test: same entity id in two tenants must never meet (Chapter 14)

23.7 Unknown tenants and the DLQ

The selector must never turn unknown input into a topic.

 events ─► validate(tenantId in registry?) ─┬─ known   ─► routed stream ─► KafkaSink (selector)
                                            ├─ unknown ─► side output ─► DLQ topic (Chapter 12), with reason + raw bytes hash
                                            └─ invalid ─► side output ─► DLQ
  • Registry source: a broadcast stream of tenant config (Chapter 4), or a static allowlist loaded at start (needs restart to add tenants). Broadcast ordering is not guaranteed (Chapter 5.4): a new tenant's first events can arrive before the registry entry. Decide: park them in a bounded buffer/DLQ for replay, not drop.
  • Never rely on Kafka's topic auto-creation (broker setting auto.create.topics.enable): a typo creates a topic silently. Disable it and provision tenants by process. Assumption: auto-create default and semantics from Kafka knowledge, [unverified] here.
  • A write to a missing topic with auto-create off fails; in a shared job that failure can restart the whole job for all tenants (23.8). The registry check is how you avoid it.
  • DLQ record: tenant (if any), reason, source topic/partition/offset, timestamp. Do not copy PII payloads into a wider-access DLQ (Chapter 27).

23.8 One shared job versus job per tenant

Blast radius: a shared job is one failure domain. A poison record, a state bug, a stuck transaction, a slow tenant topic, or a checkpoint failure affects all tenants. Backpressure is shared too: the sink is one operator, so a slow or unavailable partition for tenant A back-pressures the whole pipeline and delays tenant B (Chapter 11; whether sink-level per-topic isolation exists: [unverified], assume none).

Dimension One shared job Job per tenant Job per tenant group (shard)
Blast radius all tenants one tenant one group
Backpressure coupling yes no within group
Resource cost lowest (shared slots, one JobManager) highest: JobManager, slots, checkpoints per tenant medium
Ops (deploy, upgrade, savepoints) one N (needs automation) N/group
State isolation by key discipline only (23.6) physical by key + physical across groups
Kafka ACL/quota isolation weak (one principal) strong (principal per job) medium
Onboarding a tenant registry entry new deployment registry or new shard
Noisy neighbour likely none within group
Transactions / topic count per job high small bounded
Tail latency (checkpoint size) worst best middle
Fits many small, similar tenants, same SLA few large tenants, strict contracts, regulated data the common middle: tiers by size/SLA

Decision rules (Assumption, tune to your contracts): 1. Regulated or contractually isolated tenant: own job, own principal, own topics. 2. Top few tenants by volume: own jobs (also fixes skew, Chapter 10.4). 3. Long tail of small tenants: shared job(s), capped at a tenant-count ceiling from 23.4, sharded by hash of tenant id or by tier. 4. Review when one tenant's incident has hurt another: that is evidence to split.

Cost check: model per-job fixed overhead (JobManager, minimum TaskManager, checkpoint storage) times tenants against the shared job's amortized cost. Numbers are Data unavailable here; Chapter 17 shows how to estimate.

Figure 23.2: Blast radius and cost trade-off of the three job layouts.

23.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Searching for or documenting a sink topic pattern: it does not exist (23.3).
  • Selector builds names from unvalidated payload fields: leakage or accidental topic creation.
  • keyBy(entityId) without tenant: cross-tenant state sharing.
  • Same transactionalIdPrefix for several tenant jobs: producers fence each other (Chapter 7.5).
  • Topic auto-creation left on.
  • One tenant's partition outage back-pressures all tenants; checkpoints start failing; transactions expire (Chapter 7.11).
  • Visibility latency of exactly-once surprises low-latency tenants (Chapter 7.6).
  • Partition count explosion on the cluster.
  • Hot tenant on one subtask (Chapter 10).
  • Replaying a backfill for one tenant through the shared job reprocesses others (Chapter 24).
  • Tenant offboarding leaves state and topics behind: add cleanup timers and a topic retirement process.

23.10 Self-check

  1. Which builder call selects the topic per record, and why can't setTopicPattern replace it?
  2. Two tenants both have device id 42. What breaks if you keyBy(deviceId), and what is the fix?
  3. A tenant record arrives with a tenant id not in the registry. List three possible outcomes and pick one.
  4. In a shared job with EXACTLY_ONCE, which settings determine whether tenant A's slow topic can cost tenant B data (loss, delay)?
  5. You have 3 huge tenants and 500 small ones. Propose a job layout and defend it with the table in 23.8.

23.11 Open items / unverified

  • setTopicSelector argument type (TopicSelector<? super T>, extends Function<IN,String>, package org.apache.flink.connector.kafka.sink): verified (javap 5.0.0-2.2).
  • One writer subtask has one current producer (verified); how producers are pooled/reused across checkpoints in 5.0.0 (TransactionNamingStrategy exists on KafkaSinkBuilder) [unverified].
  • Published or practical limits on topic and partition counts per broker/cluster [unverified] / Data unavailable.
  • Kafka topic naming rules, quota behavior per principal, auto.create.topics.enable default [unverified] (Kafka docs not fetched).
  • Source-side discovery key verified (partition.discovery.interval.ms, default 5 min per the option description); whether new topics matching a pattern are found by the same interval: assumed, not run.
  • Whether sink-level backpressure is per partition or global [unverified].
  • Cost numbers per job vs shared job: Data unavailable (Chapter 17).

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-2.2/docs/connectors/datastream/kafka/ - Chapters 5, 7, 10 of this book (sources listed there)

Chapter 24: Blueprint 7, backfills and replays

Goal: after this chapter you can design a backfill that reads bounded history and then live data, choose BATCH or STREAMING execution deliberately, keep side effects out of the replay, run a shadow-topic cutover that can be rolled back, and compare production against the shadow output without fooling yourself.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks), Chapter 6 (savepoints), Chapter 7 (offsets live in the checkpoint), Chapter 9 (savepoint upgrades, uids), Chapter 10 (watermark alignment), Chapter 13 (lag metrics muted during replay). Version note: Kafka examples are pinned to Flink 2.2.x with Kafka connector 5.0.0 (no connector exists for 2.3 yet, README). No SQL: everything here is DataStream API.

24.1 What the article got wrong

Faults in the backfill blueprint (design-level; offsets and side effects): - Offsets treated as portable. A shadow topic (copy of the input) has different offsets from the original. Offsets, and committed consumer-group positions, cannot be carried across; only timestamps are comparable (24.5). - Side effects ignored. A replay re-executes every sink. A sink to an OLTP database, a notification ("nudge"), an HTTP call or an e-mail repeats its effect for history (Chapter 7, table 7.9, "non-transactional, non-idempotent sink"). 24.4. - Replay speed treated as free. Replaying fast changes watermark behaviour (state growth, mass late events). 24.3. - Cutover with no rollback. Once the new job has committed output and consumers moved, going back is not possible unless you planned for it. 24.5. - Retention assumed. If the topic retention is shorter than the history you want, the backfill silently reads less. 24.5. - No kill switch. Nothing stopped a runaway replay. 24.7.

24.2 Reading history, then live: two building blocks

Bounded Kafka read (verified, Kafka connector page, release-2.2)

KafkaSource.builder().setBounded(OffsetsInitializer) reads until all partitions reach the stopping offsets, then the source finishes (the job can finish too). setUnbounded(OffsetsInitializer) keeps streaming mode (Boundedness.CONTINUOUS_UNBOUNDED) but still stops at the given offsets. (verified: javap flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2 KafkaSourceBuilder: setBounded sets Boundedness.BOUNDED, setUnbounded sets CONTINUOUS_UNBOUNDED; both set the stopping initializer.) Verified OffsetsInitializer factories (javap OffsetsInitializer): earliest(), latest(), committedOffsets(), committedOffsets(OffsetResetStrategy), timestamp(long), offsets(Map<TopicPartition, Long>) and offsets(Map<TopicPartition, Long>, OffsetResetStrategy). timestamp(long) resolves via Kafka offsetsForTimes (first offset whose timestamp is >= the value), and falls back to the end offset when none exists (bytecode: TimestampOffsetsInitializer calls endOffsets and offsetsForTimes). Verified: partition.discovery.interval.ms is overridden to -1 only when the source is BOUNDED (bytecode KafkaSourceBuilder.parseAndSetRequiredProperties, i.e. setBounded), so new partitions are not discovered during a bounded read; with setUnbounded the configured interval (default 5 minutes) stays.

The stopping offset is exclusive (verified: bytecode of KafkaPartitionSplitReader: a split is empty/finished when position >= stoppingOffset, and KafkaPartitionSplitRecords emits a record only if offset < stoppingOffset). So setBounded(timestamp(c)) reads the records before the first record with timestamp >= c, and a live source starting at timestamp(c) continues with exactly that record: no gap, no overlap per partition (when timestamps are monotone within a partition).

Choosing stopping offsets: OffsetsInitializer.latest() evaluated when the job starts is the simplest "up to now". For a reproducible backfill, prefer timestamp(cutoffMillis) so the same range is read again on a re-run [assumption: record timestamps are broker/producer timestamps and monotone enough per partition; check the topic's timestamp type].

Hybrid Source (verified, release-2.2 docs)

  • Class org.apache.flink.connector.base.source.hybrid.HybridSource<T> (verified: jar listing of flink-connector-base 2.2.1; an earlier draft had the wrong package ...connector.base.HybridSource), Maven artifact flink-connector-base.
  • Builder (javap): static HybridSource.builder(Source) returns HybridSource.HybridSourceBuilder<T, EnumT>; addSource(Source); addSource(SourceFactory, Boundedness); build(). SourceFactory.create(SourceSwitchContext) and SourceSwitchContext.getPreviousEnumerator() are nested interfaces of HybridSource. Usage: HybridSource.builder(firstSource).addSource(secondSource).build(). It "sequentially reads from heterogeneous sources": history first, then the next source.
  • Fixed switch position (docs example): first FileSource, second KafkaSource with OffsetsInitializer.timestamp(switchTimestamp + 1). The + 1 is right there because the file data is read up to and including switchTimestamp; for a bounded Kafka first source the stopping offset is exclusive (see above), so the live source must start at timestamp(cutoff), not cutoff + 1.
  • Dynamic switch position: addSource(switchContext -> {...}, Boundedness.CONTINUOUS_UNBOUNDED) where switchContext.getPreviousEnumerator() gives the end position of the previous source (the docs example derives a Kafka timestamp(...) start from it).
  • The docs' only worked example is file history to Kafka live. A Kafka history (bounded) to Kafka live chain uses the same mechanism with two KafkaSources. What is verified: HybridSourceBuilder.addSource(factory, boundedness) enforces Preconditions.checkArgument(previous entry is BOUNDED, "All sources except the final source need to be bounded.") (bytecode, flink-connector-base 2.2.1); addSource(Source) takes source.getBoundedness(); a KafkaSource built with setBounded reports BOUNDED; the final source may be CONTINUOUS_UNBOUNDED, and HybridSource.getBoundedness() returns the last entry's. So a bounded Kafka source may be a non-final source and an unbounded Kafka source is allowed only as the last one. [unverified] only the end-to-end run (two KafkaSources switching, checkpoint/restore across the switch): nothing was executed. Test it in a harness (Chapter 14) before relying on it.
  • Earlier sources must be Boundedness.BOUNDED: verified (message above); the check fails at build time with IllegalArgumentException.
  • The switch is by timestamp (history stops before timestamp(cutoff), live starts at timestamp(cutoff), both exclusive/inclusive as above). It is only as exact as your timestamps. Duplicates or gaps at the boundary are possible if the history source and live source disagree on the cutoff; design the downstream to tolerate a small overlap (Chapter 26) rather than assume zero.

When not to use it: if history lives in the same topic you will keep reading, a single KafkaSource started from timestamp(t0) (or earliest()) already gives "history then live" with no switch. Use Hybrid Source when the history is in a different system (files, object store) or a different topic.

Figure 24.1: History then live with Hybrid Source (the boundedness rule is verified; a Kafka-to-Kafka end-to-end run is not); BATCH cannot host the live half.

24.3 BATCH vs STREAMING execution mode, and fast replays

Verified (execution-mode page, stable docs): env.setRuntimeMode(RuntimeExecutionMode.BATCH) or -Dexecution.runtime-mode=BATCH; values STREAMING (default), BATCH, AUTOMATIC (chosen from source boundedness).

STREAMING BATCH
Sources bounded or unbounded bounded only (so no live tail; AUTOMATIC picks it from boundedness)
Watermarks your heuristic generator runs only MAX_WATERMARK at end of input; custom assigners ignored
Timers fire as watermark advances all fire at "end of time"
Checkpointing yes not supported; CheckpointListener incompatible
Kafka EXACTLY_ONCE sink yes unavailable
State backend configured backend ignored; input grouped by key, state for one key at a time
Rolling reduce/sum incremental updates only final result
Processing time advances jumps to the "end of time" once the input is fully processed (docs), so results are deterministic

Consequences: - BATCH is the efficient choice for pure bounded history (no live tail), and what the State Processor API uses (Chapter 30). It gives deterministic event-time results because timestamps are sorted per key. - BATCH cannot be Hybrid-Source "then live": the live source is unbounded. For history-then-live use STREAMING. - BATCH output differs by design: no intermediate rolling updates, only finals. Do not compare it row-for-row against a streaming job's output (24.6). - A BATCH job has no checkpoints: a failure restarts the stage, not "from the last checkpoint". Plan for a rerun.

Fast replay in STREAMING mode (read from earliest() at full speed): - Event time races ahead of wall clock. Windows fire early relative to wall time, which is fine, but... - Partitions drain at different speeds. The fastest advance their own watermark; the operator watermark is the minimum (Chapter 1), so fast partitions buffer window state for data far ahead of the slowest. State and memory blow up. - Fix: watermark alignment (Chapter 10.7): withWatermarkAlignment(group, maxDrift, updateInterval) throttles sources ahead of the group. Verified in Chapter 10 and by javap (WatermarkStrategy.withWatermarkAlignment(String, Duration, Duration) exists in 2.2.1); 2.3 changed its algorithm (pipeline.watermark-alignment.buffer-size, default 3, ring buffer of announced watermarks; 0 restores the pre-2.3 behaviour; verified: 2.3.0 flink-core option text, absent in 2.2.1), but there is no 2.3 Kafka connector, so test the behaviour you actually pin. - A partition that is empty or ends early (bounded) holds back or releases the minimum: set idleness deliberately (Chapter 1.5). A partition that ended must not freeze alignment; the interplay is [unverified] (Chapter 10.10). - Backpressure from the sink is more likely at replay speed (Chapter 11); throttle the source or scale the sink side. - Lag and late-event alerts fire spuriously during replay: separate the backfill job's metrics or mute them (Chapter 13.8).

24.4 Side-effect safety

A replay re-runs everything downstream of the source. Classify every sink before the first run:

Sink Replay-safe? Action
Kafka EXACTLY_ONCE to a shadow topic yes (isolated) default for the shadow job (Chapter 7)
Kafka to the production output topic no never point a backfill at it
Upsert/OLTP with deterministic key + version yes if idempotent Chapter 26; guard against overwriting newer data with older
OLTP insert/increment, counters no disable or write to a shadow table
Notifications, e-mail, webhooks ("nudges") no disable in backfill mode
Third-party API call no disable, or call a stub

Pattern: make the sink selectable by a mode flag so the same pipeline runs in LIVE, SHADOW or BACKFILL mode, where non-idempotent sinks are replaced by a no-op or a "log and count" sink. Do not rely on someone remembering to comment code out. In BACKFILL mode, also give the job a different transactionalIdPrefix and consumer group than production (Chapter 7.5, two jobs sharing a prefix fence each other).

24.5 Shadow topic cutover

 prod input  --> prod job  --> prod output ---> consumers
      |
      +-- mirror/copy --> shadow input --> backfill job --> shadow output   (compare, 24.6)

Figure 24.2: Shadow path, cutover problems and the cutover order.

Problems, and the design response:

Problem Why Response
Offsets differ a copy has its own offsets; the prod job's checkpointed offsets mean nothing on the shadow topic map by timestamp (OffsetsInitializer.timestamp), not offset
Consumer group mapping prod group's committed offsets are on the prod topic; commits only expose progress anyway (Chapter 7.2) use a distinct group for the shadow job; never reuse the prod group
Retention must cover history brokers delete segments older than retention; earliest() is only the earliest retained check retention before planning; if history is gone, you need an archive source (Hybrid Source with files)
Partition counts or key hashing differ per-key order and key groups change keep partition count and partitioner identical, or accept per-key re-ordering
No rollback after freeze once consumers are moved and the old job and its savepoint/data are discarded, you cannot go back keep the old job's last savepoint and the old output topic until the new path has run for an agreed period (Chapter 6, 9)
Output overlap/gap at switch both jobs emit around the cutoff, or neither choose a cutoff timestamp, make downstream idempotent (Chapter 26), verify counts either side

Cutover sequence (sketch of the order, not an automation): 1. Freeze the old job with a savepoint (stop with savepoint, Chapter 6.4). Record the timestamp. 2. Start the new job from the shadow path at timestamp(cutoff), or from the savepoint if state is unchanged (Chapter 9). 3. Compare (24.6). Only then repoint consumers. 4. Keep the old output topic and savepoint for the rollback window. Decision on its length: yours.

State bootstrap. If the new logic needs state that history would take too long to rebuild (long windows, large dedup state), build it from history in a BATCH job and start live from that savepoint. Mechanism, limits and uid matching: Chapter 30 (State Processor API) and Chapter 9. Not repeated here.

24.6 Comparing prod and shadow correctly

Naive row-for-row diffs mislead. Rules: 1. Compare on event time, in closed windows only. Exclude the most recent windows (not yet final) and the cutoff region. 2. Compare aggregates by key and window, not by arrival order or output offset. Outputs differ in order and in intermediate emissions (early or late firings, Chapter 2). 3. Expect legitimate differences: late events (prod's watermark delay at the time vs the replay's deterministic one), allowed-lateness refires, idle-partition effects (Chapter 1.5), changed logic. Count them, do not just diff. 4. Never compare BATCH output against STREAMING output without accounting for finals-only emission (24.3). 5. Report match rate, missing keys, extra keys, value deltas with a tolerance; a pass criterion agreed before the run. 6. Tenant data: compare per tenant inside the tenant's boundary, do not mix tenants in a shared diff output (Chapter 23). 7. Use synthetic or hashed identifiers in any shared comparison report; no raw PII.

24.7 Global kill switch in config

A backfill is a long, expensive, side-effecting job. Give it an off switch that works without a redeploy: - A config flag (e.g. an environment variable or a control topic) read in the sink-gating operator, with states ENABLED, DRY_RUN (count, do not write), PAUSED. Default is the safe state (DRY_RUN) so a misconfigured job does nothing. - Reading a control topic through broadcast state (Chapter 4) lets operators flip it at runtime without restart. A static config requires a restart from a savepoint (Chapter 9). - The kill switch gates sinks, not sources: stopping the read while a sink still flushes buffered data is not "off". - Also keep an operational stop: flink stop with savepoint (Chapter 6.4) so the replay can be resumed. - Log every flip with who/when; do not log payloads.

24.8 Sketch (not compiled)

History from a bounded Kafka range, then live, with a mode flag. Flink 2.2.x, Kafka connector 5.0.0.

// (sketch; compiles against Flink 2.2.1 + connector 5.0.0-2.2 jars, not run)
// imports: org.apache.flink.connector.base.source.hybrid.HybridSource, org.apache.flink.connector.kafka.source.KafkaSource,
//          org.apache.flink.connector.kafka.source.enumerator.initializer.OffsetsInitializer
KafkaSource<Event> history = KafkaSource.<Event>builder()
    .setBootstrapServers("<KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP>")
    .setTopics("events-shadow")
    .setGroupId("backfill-history")                       // distinct from prod group
    .setStartingOffsets(OffsetsInitializer.timestamp(startTs))
    .setBounded(OffsetsInitializer.timestamp(cutoffTs))   // stop at cutoff
    .setValueOnlyDeserializer(new EventDeserializer())
    .build();

KafkaSource<Event> live = KafkaSource.<Event>builder()
    .setBootstrapServers("<KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP>")
    .setTopics("events")
    .setGroupId("backfill-live")
    .setStartingOffsets(OffsetsInitializer.timestamp(cutoffTs))   // stopping offset above is exclusive: no +1 for Kafka-to-Kafka
    .setValueOnlyDeserializer(new EventDeserializer())
    .build();

HybridSource<Event> hybrid = HybridSource.builder(history).addSource(live).build();   // boundedness rule verified; end-to-end run: [unverified]

WatermarkStrategy<Event> wm = WatermarkStrategy
    .<Event>forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
    .withTimestampAssigner((e, ts) -> e.eventTsMillis)
    .withIdleness(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
    .withWatermarkAlignment("replay", Duration.ofMinutes(5), Duration.ofSeconds(1));  // Chapter 10

DataStream<Event> in = env.fromSource(hybrid, wm, "hybrid").uid("src");
DataStream<Result> out = in.keyBy(e -> e.key).process(new MyLogic()).uid("logic");

switch (mode) {                                   // LIVE | SHADOW | BACKFILL
    case LIVE     -> out.sinkTo(prodSink).uid("sink");
    case SHADOW   -> out.sinkTo(shadowKafkaSink).uid("sink");        // different topic and txn prefix
    case BACKFILL -> out.sinkTo(new CountingNoopSink<>()).uid("sink"); // side effects off
}

Pure bounded history instead: set RuntimeExecutionMode.BATCH, drop the live source, drop alignment and idleness (no effect in BATCH, 24.3), use a non-transactional or idempotent sink.

24.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Replay with production sinks enabled: duplicate notifications or OLTP writes.
  • Reusing the production consumer group or transactionalIdPrefix (fencing, offset confusion).
  • Assuming earliest() means "all history": it means earliest retained.
  • Starting from the old savepoint on a changed topic: offsets from a different topic are restored (Chapter 7.9, 9).
  • Fast replay without alignment: state explosion, then OOM (Chapter 11).
  • BATCH mode with an EXACTLY_ONCE Kafka sink (unavailable) or with expectations of checkpoints.
  • Boundary off-by-one at the Hybrid switch: duplicates or a gap.
  • Dedup state TTL shorter than the replayed span (Chapter 7.9; Chapter 18).
  • Comparing outputs without excluding open windows.
  • No kill switch, or a switch that gates only the source.

24.10 Self-check

  1. Why can you not reuse the production job's checkpointed offsets on a shadow topic, and what do you use instead?
  2. Why can a BATCH job not be the "then live" half of a backfill, and what does it do with your watermark strategy?
  3. Name three sinks that make a replay unsafe and how you neutralise each.
  4. Fast replay: which mechanism stops fast partitions from filling state, and what is its cost?
  5. What must still exist after cutover so you can roll back?

  • Kafka-to-Kafka Hybrid Source: boundedness restriction verified (non-final sources must be BOUNDED, message in bytecode); the end-to-end run is [unverified].
  • OffsetsInitializer.offsets(Map): verified (javap), with an OffsetResetStrategy overload.
  • Whether withWatermarkAlignment works through HybridSourceReader: the reader delegates pauseOrResumeSplits to the current reader (bytecode) but alignment with HybridSource was not run: [unverified].
  • [unverified] Exact interplay of alignment, idleness and finished (bounded) partitions; 2.3 buffering algorithm (Chapter 10.10).
  • Record timestamp semantics for the cutoff (create time vs log-append time): Assumption, check topic config.
  • No 2.3 Kafka connector; examples target Flink 2.2.x / connector 5.0.0.
  • Retention values and comparison tolerances: Data unavailable.
  • Code is a sketch, not compiled.

Chapter 25: Blueprint 8, SLA metrics

Goal: after this chapter you can define three lag SLAs (event lag, watermark lag, consumer lag), say which metrics back each one and how sure we are of them, add custom metrics from a RichFunction, run an external prober that catches stalls, write alerts that fire on sustained trends, and map a symptom to a lag type to an action.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (three lags), Chapter 10 (skew, alignment), Chapter 11 (backpressure), Chapter 13 (metric names and their verified/unverified status), Chapter 24 (mute during backfills).

25.1 What the article got wrong

  • Lag computed with CURRENT_TIMESTAMP / CURRENT_WATERMARK inside a SQL aggregate. Wrong for three reasons: 1. CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is wall-clock at evaluation, non-deterministic, and changes on replay and restart; the number depends on when the row happened to be processed, not on the data (Chapter 1.1). 2. It sits in the data path. A stalled job, a stuck partition or a dead TaskManager emits no rows, so the "lag metric" stops updating and the dashboard shows the last good value or nothing: blind to stalls, which is the exact case an SLA exists for (Chapter 13.6). 3. Aggregating it (max or avg over a window) mixes event-time and wall-clock semantics, and the window only closes if the watermark advances, which is the thing that is broken when lag is bad.
  • It conflated three different lags into one number (Chapter 1.7), so an alert could not say what to do.
  • No baseline, spike-based thresholds, no alert on absence.

We deliberately do not use SQL; the DataStream design below needs no SQL equivalent.

Figure 25.1: In-job lag is blind to stalls; an external marker prober alerts on absence.

25.2 Define the SLAs: three lags, one question each

SLA Definition Measure from Blind to stall?
Event (freshness) lag wall clock minus event time of the newest record delivered to the output external prober or the output topic's newest event time, read outside Flink no, if measured outside
Watermark lag wall clock minus the current watermark of an operator currentInputWatermark / currentOutputWatermark (verified, Ch 13.2; verified: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 MetricNames); watermarkLag (verified: MetricNames.WATERMARK_LAG in flink-runtime 2.2.1; a generic source metric, exposed by sources that implement it); subtraction done in monitoring no, a stuck watermark makes it grow
Consumer lag backlog between broker head and Flink's position outside: end offset minus committed offset; inside: pendingRecords (verified: MetricNames.PENDING_RECORDS in flink-runtime 2.2.1, and KafkaSourceReaderMetrics in flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2 derives it from the consumer's per-partition records-lag) no for the outside measure

Rules: - State each SLA as percentile over a window, per pipeline (e.g. "p95 event lag below X for 99% of 5-minute windows"). The target X: Data unavailable; derive from a week of baseline (Chapter 1.7 method). - Event lag is what users feel; watermark lag is how far your windows are behind; consumer lag is how far behind the topic Flink is. A job can have healthy consumer lag and bad watermark lag (stuck/idle partition, Chapter 1.5). - Subtract in the monitoring system. The watermark metric is an epoch-ms gauge, Flink does not give the difference unless watermarkLag is exported (Chapter 13.4).

25.3 Metric status (carried over from Chapter 13, not re-verified here)

Verified on the 2.3 metrics page and in org.apache.flink.runtime.metrics.MetricNames (javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 jars): currentInputWatermark, currentOutputWatermark, numRecordsIn, numRecordsOut, busyTimeMsPerSecond, backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond, idleTimeMsPerSecond, numRestarts. numLateRecordsDropped is on the 2.3 metrics page and is a string constant in WindowOperator / AsyncWindowOperator (flink-runtime 2.2.1). Checkpoint metrics: as Chapter 13. Verified as registered in flink-runtime 2.2.1 bytecode (Chapter 13): currentEmitEventTimeLag, watermarkLag, sourceIdleTime, pendingRecords (generic source-reader metrics, so they appear only for sources that implement them; see Chapter 13 for the Kafka source). currentFetchEventTimeLag exists only as a constant: no registration was found in the checked jars, so do not alert on it (Chapter 13). Kafka-specific names, corrected here (verified: javap KafkaSourceReaderMetrics, flink-connector-kafka 5.0.0-2.2): the per-partition gauges are currentOffset and committedOffset (singular), registered under the group KafkaSourceReader with sub-groups topic and partition; the earlier text KafkaSourceReader.currentOffsets / committedOffsets (plural) was wrong. The connector also registers the Kafka consumer's own metrics under a KafkaConsumer group when register.consumer.metrics is on (option key verified in KafkaSourceOptions). [unverified] by name in these jars: records-lag-max (a Kafka-consumer metric name, not defined in Flink code; the connector code only references records-lag in the consumer-fetch-manager-metrics group). Do not build an SLA on it until you see it in your reporter output. Exported label names differ per reporter: check one real scrape. Caveats that change interpretation: - currentEmitEventTimeLag is large during replays by design (Chapter 13.3, 24). - watermarkLag is inflated by one idle partition unless idleness is set. - Committed-offset lag is saw-toothed at checkpoint cadence (Chapter 7.2; verified: Kafka source option commit.offsets.on.checkpoint, "Whether to commit consuming offset on checkpoint", KafkaSourceOptions).

25.4 Custom metrics via the metric group

Verified (2.3 metrics page; javap flink-core 2.2.1/2.3.0 RichFunction): register in a RichFunction open(); in 2.x the signature is open(OpenContext) (OpenContext is an empty marker interface). RuntimeContext#getMetricGroup() returns org.apache.flink.metrics.groups.OperatorMetricGroup (javap), a MetricGroup. MetricGroup signatures (verified: source of flink-metrics-core, GitHub release-2.2, because that jar was not downloaded): Counter counter(String), <T, G extends Gauge<T>> G gauge(String, G), <H extends Histogram> H histogram(String, H), <M extends Meter> M meter(String, M). - Counter: getRuntimeContext().getMetricGroup().counter("name"), org.apache.flink.metrics.Counter. - Gauge: ...gauge("name", new Gauge<T>() { public T getValue() {...} }), org.apache.flink.metrics.Gauge (verified: Gauge<T> has the single abstract method T getValue(); getMetricType() is a default method). - Histogram: Dropwizard wrapper org.apache.flink.dropwizard.metrics.DropwizardHistogramWrapper around com.codahale.metrics.Histogram(new SlidingWindowReservoir(500)); needs artifact flink-metrics-dropwizard (docs show 2.3.0; Maven Central metadata lists 2.3.0 as latest; DropwizardHistogramWrapper(com.codahale.metrics.Histogram) verified in source). The Prometheus reporter maps histograms to summaries (Chapter 13.1). - Meter: org.apache.flink.dropwizard.metrics.DropwizardMeterWrapper(com.codahale.metrics.Meter) or Flink's own org.apache.flink.metrics.MeterView (constructors MeterView(int timeSpanInSeconds), MeterView(Counter), MeterView(Counter, int), MeterView(Gauge<? extends Number>); markEvent(), markEvent(long)) (verified: flink-metrics source, GitHub release-2.2).

What to measure that Flink cannot know: - Per-record event lag at the sink (now - eventTs) as a Histogram: tells you p95/p99, but remember it goes silent when the job stalls. Use it for distribution on a healthy job, never as the only SLA signal (25.5). - Gauge of the last event timestamp seen (epoch ms): monitoring computes now - gauge, so a stall shows up as a growing number as long as the gauge series is still scraped. It does not help if the whole TaskManager is gone: then alert on series absence (25.5). - Counters: late events routed to the side output (Chapter 1.4), DLQ records (Chapter 12), parse errors. - Cardinality: no per-key or per-tenant-id labels (Chapter 13.7). Tenant isolation: tenant-level SLAs belong in a bounded label set, or a separate job per tier, never raw ids in names.

public class LagProbe extends RichMapFunction<Result, Result> {          // sketch, not compiled
    private transient Histogram eventLagMs;
    private transient volatile long lastEventTs;

    @Override public void open(OpenContext ctx) {
        MetricGroup g = getRuntimeContext().getMetricGroup();
        eventLagMs = g.histogram("eventLagMs",
            new DropwizardHistogramWrapper(new com.codahale.metrics.Histogram(
                new com.codahale.metrics.SlidingWindowReservoir(500))));
        g.gauge("lastEventTsMs", (Gauge<Long>) () -> lastEventTs);
    }
    @Override public Result map(Result r) {
        lastEventTs = Math.max(lastEventTs, r.eventTsMillis);
        eventLagMs.update(System.currentTimeMillis() - r.eventTsMillis); // wall clock in a metric, not in the data
        return r;
    }
}

Wall-clock use here is acceptable because it feeds a metric, not the business result, so replays do not change outputs. A lambda for Gauge works because it has one abstract method (verified from source, see above); the cast (Gauge<Long>) is needed because gauge(String, G extends Gauge<T>) is generic and a bare lambda gives the compiler no target type. The docs use an anonymous class. Compile status: signatures were checked against the sources; the sketch itself was not compiled, because flink-metrics-core and flink-core-api jars were not available offline.

25.5 External prober and synthetic heartbeat

The only signal immune to the job's own failure (Chapter 13.6):

 prober ----marker(eventTs=now, id)----> input topic ---> Flink ---> output topic ---> checker
   |                                                                                        |
   +--- records send time ---------------------------------- alerts if no marker within SLA +

Design: - A small producer outside the Flink cluster writes a marker record per minute with a known event timestamp and a unique id, one per input partition (or keyed to cover each partition, assumption) so a stuck partition is caught. - The pipeline passes markers through the normal path (marker field recognised by your logic, never a fake tenant's data). Markers must be synthetic: no real customer data, no PII, flagged so downstream consumers can filter them. - A checker reads the output topic and computes arrival_wall_clock - marker_send_time = true end-to-end latency, per partition. No marker for N minutes = alert, regardless of what Flink reports. - Markers do not exercise every key or every window type; they prove path liveness, not correctness (Chapter 14 for that). - Alert on the prober itself (if the prober stops, that is also an incident). - Windowed jobs: a marker passes through a window only when the watermark advances. That is useful: it tests the stall you care about. Document which latency a window job should show (window size plus delay).

25.6 Alert rules

Principles (Chapter 13.5): trends not spikes, symptoms before causes, one page per problem, every alert links a runbook row.

Alert Rule sketch (tune on baseline; thresholds Data unavailable) Type
Event lag SLA p95 of prober latency above target for 10 min sustained symptom, page
No marker no marker arrived within SLA window per partition symptom, page (works on stalls)
Watermark stuck now - currentInputWatermark rising for 15 min while numRecordsIn rate > 0 cause: idle/stuck partition
Watermark lag high now - watermark above target for 10 min cause
Consumer lag growing outside lag slope > 0 over 15 min and above floor cause: capacity or skew
Metrics missing series for the job absent for N min, or REST job state not RUNNING (verified: 2.3 REST docs, GET /jobs/overview and GET /jobs/:jobid return a state field with values incl. RUNNING, FAILING, RESTARTING) dead job or scrape
Backpressure backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond high for 10 min per subtask (max, not avg) cause: sink or skew
Late rate late/records-in above x% for 10 min delay too tight

Rules of thumb: - Use p95 over a sustained window for latency, and slope for lag; avoid single-sample and max thresholds, which fire on restart catch-up. - Use for:-style durations; add inhibition so "job down" suppresses lag/late/DLQ alerts. - Mute or split alerts for backfill and replay jobs (Chapter 24). - Burn-rate style alerting on the SLA (error budget) is common practice but not covered by Flink docs: [assumption].

25.7 Dashboard

Same row order as Chapter 13.4, with this chapter's additions at the top: Row 0: SLA panel = prober latency p50/p95/p99 per partition, marker arrival count, error budget remaining. Then: produce rate, consumer lag (outside), pendingRecords, now - watermark per operator, busy/backpressure per subtask (max), late rate, DLQ ratio, checkpoint health. Annotate deploys, savepoints and backfills so humans can explain steps.

25.8 Runbook table: symptom to lag type to action

Symptom Which lag is high Likely cause First action Chapter
Output stale, markers missing, metrics still flowing event lag, watermark lag stuck/idle partition holds minimum check per-partition watermarks; set/tune withIdleness 1.5, 10.6
Output stale, no metrics at all event lag (blind in-job) job/TM down, crash loop check job state and numRestarts; poison pill? 12, 15
Consumer lag growing, backpressure high consumer lag slow sink or skew find saturated subtask; fix sink/skew 10, 11
Consumer lag growing, busy low everywhere consumer lag source starved/few partitions or checkpoint stalls check partitions vs parallelism, checkpoint health 10.1, 6
Consumer lag flat but non-zero, sawtooth none (artifact) commits on checkpoint do not page; check checkpoint failures 7.2
Event lag high, consumer lag ~0 ingestion lag upstream producers late escalate upstream 1.7
Watermark lag high, records flow watermark lag idle partition or large delay config idleness, delay review 1.5
Late rate rising, lags fine none delay too tight or idle wake-up review p99 arrival delay 1.7
Lags large after replay started all (by design) backfill confirm it is the backfill; mute 24
Lag after redeploy decays all, transient catch-up watch the slope, do not page 6.6

Figure 25.2: Symptom to lag type to first action (the 25.8 runbook).

25.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Only in-job metrics: silent on stalls (25.1).
  • Alerting on averages or on records-lag-max before confirming it in your output (Chapter 13.10).
  • Treating committed-offset lag as live position.
  • One idle partition inflating watermarkLag and causing false pages.
  • Wall clock and event time mixed in the business output instead of only in metrics.
  • Per-key labels crashing the metrics backend; cross-tenant leakage via labels.
  • Prober markers leaking into real consumers or counting toward business totals.
  • Clock skew between prober, broker and Flink hosts: lag error of the skew size (assumption: NTP-synced hosts).

25.10 Self-check

  1. List the three ways CURRENT_TIMESTAMP in a SQL aggregate breaks an SLA, including why a stalled job hides it.
  2. Which of your three lag SLAs still reports during a total job outage, and why?
  3. Why is a Histogram of per-record event lag insufficient alone? Which companion signal fixes that?
  4. Write the rule for "watermark stuck" so it does not fire on an idle topic.
  5. Consumer lag is sawtoothed but flat. Page or not, and what do you check?

Chapter 26: Blueprint 9, idempotent writes

Goal: after this chapter you can build an at-least-once pipeline whose sink is idempotent and order-safe (effectively-once), choose between that and a two-phase-commit sink, and spot the key/version mistakes in the article's design.

Prerequisites: Chapter 6 (checkpoints, replay), Chapter 7 (delivery guarantees, Sink V2), Chapter 12 (poison pills), Chapter 14 (testing).

26.1 What the article got wrong

  • It used MD5(order_id + update_ts) as the primary key. The key then identifies a version, not the entity. Every update inserts a new row, so the table is an append-only history that looks like an upsert target. "Latest state per order" now needs a second query or dedup, and nothing prevents two versions coexisting.
  • It wrapped the timestamp in COALESCE(update_ts, '0'). All records with a null update_ts for the same order hash to the same key, so distinct updates collapse into one row, and which one survives depends on arrival order. A null version is a data-quality failure to reject or route to the DLQ (Chapter 12), not a value to default.
  • It had no ordering guard: a replayed or out-of-order older update can overwrite a newer one.
  • The hash adds nothing: you can already key by order_id. (A hash of version fields is fine as a dedup token, never as the row identity.)
  • It wrote this as SQL DDL. This book does not use SQL; the DataStream design is below.

26.2 Mental model: effectively-once

 Kafka --(at-least-once replay after failure)--> Flink --> sink
                                                          |
   exactly-once effect = at-least-once delivery + a write that is
        (a) idempotent: same record twice == once
        (b) monotonic: older version never replaces newer

Flink guarantees state consistency (Chapter 6); after a restart it re-sends records written after the last checkpoint. Duplicates at the sink are normal, not a bug. Make the sink tolerate them (Chapter 7.7).

Requirements: 1. Deterministic key = entity id (order_id, plus tenantId if multi-tenant: the key is (tenant_id, order_id), never order_id alone). 2. A version that totally orders updates per key: source-assigned sequence number, row version, or update_ts. Event time from a producer clock can tie or skew. Assumption: the upstream gives a per-entity monotonic version; if only timestamps exist, add a tiebreaker (e.g. Kafka offset within a single-partition-per-key topic). 3. Conditional upsert: apply only if incoming.version > stored.version. 4. Keep ordering by routing all updates of one key through one partition (Chapter 10) so Flink itself rarely reorders; the guard covers the rest.

26.3 Conditional upsert

Generic shape (the condition is the point; dialect syntax varies and is not verified here):

Store Idempotent + guarded write
PostgreSQL-style insert with ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET ... WHERE excluded.version > target.version (verified: PostgreSQL INSERT docs: optional WHERE condition on DO UPDATE, EXCLUDED is the proposed row; rows failing the condition are locked but not updated). Other PostgreSQL-compatible databases: check
MySQL-style ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE has no WHERE clause (verified: MySQL 8.4 docs), so the guard goes into each assignment, e.g. c = IF(new.version > version, new.c, c) with new the row alias from the docs (the docs example uses IF() in an assignment); every column needs it, and the order in which assignments see already-updated columns matters (put the version assignment last; MySQL's left-to-right evaluation is [unverified] here). Awkward and error-prone (see partial-column guards in 26.8)
Key-value / document store compare-and-set or conditional put on version attribute
Compacted Kafka topic key = entity id; compaction keeps the last written, not the highest version (Kafka log-compaction semantics, not re-fetched here), so guard in Flink state or upstream (a stale replay still wins)

Behavior table for one key, stored version 7:

Incoming Result Why
v8 applied newer
v8 again (replay) no-op not greater than stored
v6 (late/out-of-order) ignored older never overwrites newer
v7 with different payload ignored; count it a conflict: same version, different data means an upstream bug
no version (null) reject to DLQ cannot order it

Deletes: model as a tombstone with a version, or a deleted flag row with a version. A hard delete lets a replayed older upsert resurrect the row. Keep tombstones at least as long as the maximum replay window.

Figure 26.1: The article's per-version key versus an entity key with a version guard, showing an out-of-order update being rejected.

26.4 Design in DataStream

Kafka -> parse (keep bytes, Ch.12) -> validate (version != null, tenant, id) -> keyBy(tenant,id)
      -> [optional] KeyedProcessFunction: drop versions <= last seen (state, with TTL, Ch.5)
      -> batching JDBC sink with conditional upsert

The in-Flink "last seen version" filter is an optimization (fewer DB writes), not a correctness mechanism: its TTL can expire (Chapter 7.9, last-but-one row). The database guard is the source of truth.

26.5 JDBC sink in the DataStream API

Availability (verified: flink.apache.org/downloads; Maven Central maven-metadata.xml; 2.3 JDBC docs page): the downloads page lists JDBC connector 4.0.0 for Flink 2.0.x and 4.1.0 for Flink 2.1.x and 2.2.x (3.4.0 is for 1.20.x). The 2.3 docs page states "There is no connector (yet) available for Flink version 2.3"; Maven Central has no 2.3 build either (latest 4.1.0-2.2). Same pinning rule as Kafka: use Flink 2.2.x with 4.1.0.

Maven coordinates (CORRECTED; verified: Maven Central metadata and poms). From 4.0 the connector is split. The old aggregate artifact org.apache.flink:flink-connector-jdbc stops at 3.4.0-1.20 (so looking only at it suggests nothing exists for 2.x). The 2.x code is in flink-connector-jdbc-core (versions 4.0.0-2.0, 4.1.0-2.1, 4.1.0-2.2), plus one module per database (flink-connector-jdbc-postgres, -mysql, -oracle, -sqlserver, -db2, -oceanbase, -cratedb, -trino, same versions; the postgres pom depends on -core). The DataStream JdbcSink class lives in -core (org.apache.flink.connector.jdbc.core.datastream.sink.JdbcSink, GitHub tag v4.1.0). Whether a DataStream job needs the per-database module as well as -core and the driver: [unverified] (the database modules hold dialects, which are mainly used by the Table side). The connector is not in the Flink binary; bundle it and the JDBC driver.

API (CORRECTED; verified: GitHub apache/flink-connector-jdbc tag v4.1.0 sources). The chapter earlier showed JdbcSink.sink(sql, builder, options, connection). That static factory returned a SinkFunction and is used with addSink; it exists in 3.3.x but not in the 4.x sources (the tag's only JdbcSink is the Sink V2 class below), and Flink 2.0 removed SinkFunction. The 2.3 docs page and the connector's own docs at v4.1.0 still show the old addSink(JdbcSink.sink(...)) form: treat that page as stale for 2.x. The 4.1.0 API is a Sink V2 JdbcSink<IN> (implements Sink, SupportsWriterState, SupportsCommitter) with JdbcSink.builder() returning JdbcSinkBuilder<IN>: withQueryStatement(String, JdbcStatementBuilder<IN>), withExecutionOptions(JdbcExecutionOptions), buildAtLeastOnce(JdbcConnectionOptions | JdbcConnectionProvider), buildExactlyOnce(JdbcExactlyOnceOptions, SerializableSupplier<XADataSource> | XaConnectionProvider). JdbcStatementBuilder<T> is a serializable BiConsumerWithException<PreparedStatement, T, SQLException>. JdbcExecutionOptions.builder() has withBatchSize(int) (default 5000), withBatchIntervalMs(long) (default 0) and withMaxRetries(int) (default 3). JdbcConnectionOptions.JdbcConnectionOptionsBuilder has withUrl, withDriverName, withUsername, withPassword, withProperty, withConnectionCheckTimeoutSeconds.

Sketch (not compiled: the connector jars were not available offline, signatures copied from the v4.1.0 sources; SQL is a placeholder text in a Java string, not Flink SQL):

String upsert = "<UPSERT statement with conditional version guard, 4 params: tenant,id,version,payload>";

stream.sinkTo(
    JdbcSink.<Order>builder()
        .withQueryStatement(upsert, (ps, o) -> {
            ps.setString(1, o.tenantId); ps.setString(2, o.orderId);
            ps.setLong(3, o.version);    ps.setString(4, o.payload); })
        .withExecutionOptions(JdbcExecutionOptions.builder()
            .withBatchSize(1000)        // docs example values
            .withBatchIntervalMs(200)
            .withMaxRetries(5)
            .build())
        .buildAtLeastOnce(connectionOptions));   // URL/driver/user from secrets, see Ch.16.5; never hardcode

Batching and flush (verified: connector docs; v4.1.0 JdbcWriter/JdbcOutputFormat sources; javap flink-runtime 2.2.1 SinkWriterOperator): a batch executes when the interval elapses, the batch size is reached, or a checkpoint starts (SinkWriterOperator.prepareSnapshotPreBarrier calls SinkWriter.flush(false), and JdbcWriter.flush flushes the batch in at-least-once mode). So records buffered before the barrier are written before the checkpoint's barrier passes the sink; a flush failure surfaces as an exception that fails the task and the job replays from the last good checkpoint. Flush errors from the interval thread are stored and rethrown on the next write or flush.

Failure replay: after a restart, rows written since the last checkpoint arrive again. Idempotent key + version guard make that harmless. Retry (withMaxRetries) re-executes the batch after an SQLException from executeBatch (verified: JdbcOutputFormat.flush, v4.1.0: up to maxRetries further attempts, re-preparing the statement, reconnecting if the connection is invalid, sleeping 1000*i ms); again safe only because the write is idempotent.

Within one batch, the same key can appear twice (v8 then v9 in either order depending on your upsert dialect and batch semantics). Either collapse the batch to the max version per key before sending, or rely on a guard that is correct under any order [verify per DB; batched statements are executed in order, but confirm].

Throughput knobs: batch size, flush interval, sink parallelism, DB connection pool, and key-ordered partitioning (Chapter 11 for backpressure). A slow DB shows as backpressure at the sink; do not raise retries to hide it.

26.6 Idempotent versus two-phase commit

Question Idempotent upsert Sink V2 two-phase commit (SupportsCommitter, Ch.7.8; verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 org.apache.flink.api.connector.sink2.SupportsCommitter) JDBC XA exactly-once
Output visible when immediately (per flush) after checkpoint completes after checkpoint completes
Duplicates possible yes, harmless no no, and maxRetries must be 0 (docs warn of duplicates otherwise; verified: v4.1.0 JdbcWriter throws IllegalArgumentException for EXACTLY_ONCE with maxRetries != 0, citing FLINK-22311)
Needs a key + version yes no no
Store needs transactions no (conditional write) yes (or staged commit) XA support (XADataSource)
Failure mode missing guard overwrites newer data expired/hung transaction blocks readers or loses data (Ch.7.5) XA recovery complexity, driver/database XA support (the docs say the driver and database must support XA; per-driver status [unverified])
Append-only event log sink poor fit (no natural key) good possible
Entity-state table best fit overkill overkill
Readers see partial progress yes (per-key consistent, cross-key not atomic) no (atomic per checkpoint) no

Rule: state tables keyed by entity: idempotent. Atomic multi-row/multi-key visibility or append-only logs: two-phase commit. Cross-key atomicity is the real deciding question; idempotent upserts give per-row correctness only.

26.7 Iceberg and OLAP sinks (brief)

  • Iceberg: the page I fetched returned only navigation, so Data unavailable for class names, upsert/equality-field configuration and supported Flink versions. The ToC lists append, overwrite and upsert write modes for the DataStream API. Commits are checkpoint-driven in general design [unverified]; check connector compatibility with 2.2.x/2.3 before committing to it.
  • Upsert on lake tables needs an equality key (entity id) and still needs the version guard unless the table format resolves ordering for you [unverified].
  • OLAP stores (ClickHouse, Druid, Pinot, Doris and similar): connector availability for Flink 2.x and their upsert/version semantics (e.g. replacing engines that keep the highest version) are [unverified]; treat each as "must be verified" and keep the same contract: entity key + version + replay-tolerant.

26.8 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Row identity includes the version (the article's bug): table grows per update; "current row" is ambiguous.
  • Defaulting a missing version to 0/'0': collapses updates, and 0 loses to everything.
  • Guard compares timestamps from client clocks that can skew or tie; use a monotonic sequence where possible.
  • Unguarded INSERT ... ON CONFLICT UPDATE (or equivalent): replay of an old record overwrites newer data.
  • Partial-column guards: only some columns conditional; row ends up mixing versions.
  • Hard deletes with replay: deleted rows come back.
  • Key missing the tenant: cross-tenant overwrite (isolation breach, Chapter 16.8).
  • maxRetries > 0 on the XA sink: documented as duplicate-prone; in 4.1.0 the writer refuses to start with it (verified: source).
  • Treating the Flink-state dedup filter as the guarantee; its TTL expires.
  • Logging the failing row's payload on constraint errors (PII, Chapter 27).

26.9 Self-check

  1. Your key is (order_id) and the table has version. A replay sends v6 after v7 is stored. What does the DB do, and what must you assert in a test?
  2. Why does COALESCE(update_ts,'0') turn two distinct updates into one, and what should happen to null-version records?
  3. A checkpoint starts while a JDBC batch is half full. What happens?
  4. Pick idempotent upsert or two-phase commit: (a) latest-status table per device, (b) audit log, (c) two tables that must change together.
  5. Why is the in-Flink "last seen version" state not enough on its own?

26.10 Open items / unverified

  • Resolved: JDBC 4.x coordinates (split artifacts, 4.1.0-2.2) and the builder API (JdbcSink.builder()); see 26.5.
  • No JDBC connector release supports Flink 2.3 (verified: docs page and Maven Central latest 4.1.0-2.2).
  • Whether the DataStream sink needs a per-database module in addition to -core: unverified.
  • Conditional-upsert syntax per database and in-batch ordering semantics: unverified, depends on your DB (JDBC executeBatch ordering is driver behavior; not checked).
  • XA sink driver requirements per database: unverified.
  • Iceberg DataStream sink classes, upsert configuration, Flink 2.x compatibility: Data unavailable.
  • OLAP connectors for Flink 2.x: unverified.
  • Test ideas to add in Chapter 14 style: replay older version, duplicate delivery, null version, same-version conflict.
