Chapter 27: Blueprint 10, PII guardrails

Draft only. Review required by Legal, Compliance, or relevant Omnissa control owner.

Goal: after this chapter you can place PII controls where they are enforceable, build a redaction/tokenization first operator, list every place raw PII persists in a Flink job, and test that nothing sensitive leaves. This is engineering guidance, not legal advice.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state TTL), 6 (checkpoints/savepoints), 12 (DLQ), 14 (testing), 16 (security, esp. 16.7).

27.1 What the article got wrong

  • It "protected" PII with a masking view over a table that held the raw data. A view is a convention: anyone with table access, any other consumer of the topic, the checkpoints, the logs and the DLQ still see raw values. Access control that depends on everyone querying the right object is not a control.
  • It applied the protection at the last step. By then raw PII had already been written to the source topic, to Flink state, to checkpoints and to every intermediate topic.
  • It did not mention hashing pitfalls (unsalted hashes of low-entropy values are reversible by lookup), retention, or where else the data lands.
  • It was SQL; here the control is a DataStream operator plus producer/gateway enforcement.

27.2 Principle: enforce where data enters, minimize where it flows

 producer / API gateway          Kafka                Flink                         sinks
 [allow-list schema,   -->  [raw topic: restricted] --> [op 1: redact/tokenize] --> sanitized topics/tables
  reject unknown fields]      (own ACL, short TTL)       everything after op 1
                                                          sees no raw PII
  1. Producer/gateway (strongest): schema registry or contract with an allow-list of fields; unknown fields rejected, not passed through. Fields classified at the schema level (public / internal / PII). Best place: data never exists raw downstream.
  2. First Flink operator: if raw PII must enter Flink, the very first operator after the source redacts or tokenizes, before keyBy, state, windows, side outputs.
  3. Sinks: sanitized only. A masking view may remain as defense in depth, never as the control.
  4. Deny by default: new fields are dropped until someone classifies them.

27.3 First operator: allow-list, redact, tokenize

Design: - Parse into a minimal output type that contains only allowed fields (allow-list by construction: the output class cannot carry what it doesn't declare). Do not copy the input then delete fields (deny-list); a new field slips through. - Per field policy: DROP, KEEP, REDACT (replace with constant), TOKENIZE (stable pseudonym), GENERALIZE (e.g. truncate). - Free-text fields: assume PII; drop or run pattern redaction as a best-effort backstop, never as the only control (misses are certain). - Failures (cannot parse, unknown schema): send to the DLQ without the raw payload (Chapter 12.5: reference/hash/encrypted). - Keep the raw source object out of every later record, exception message and metric label.

Tokenization choices:

Technique Property Caveat
Plain hash (SHA-256 of email) deterministic reversible by dictionary/lookup for low-entropy values (emails, phones, IDs)
Salted hash, static salt deterministic across records salt must be secret and stored as a secret (Ch.16.5); effectively a weak keyed hash
Keyed HMAC (secret key, per tenant) deterministic, joinable within a tenant, not reversible without key key management and rotation; rotation changes all tokens (plan re-key window)
Random token via vault/lookup service not derivable needs a service call (Async I/O, Chapter 11), availability dependency
Encryption (reversible) recoverable by key holders key access control is the real control; ciphertext in state is still sensitive

Rule: per-tenant keys so tokens do not link people across tenants (Chapter 16.8). Compare HMAC outputs with constant-time comparison where it matters. Whether a token still counts as personal data is a Legal question.

Sketch (not compiled; allow-list by construction):

public class SanitizedEvent {            // only allowed fields exist here
    public String tenantId; public String subjectToken; public long eventTsMillis; public String action;
    public SanitizedEvent() {}
}

public class Sanitizer extends RichMapFunction<RawEvent, SanitizedEvent> {
    private transient Mac hmac;          // keys from secret mechanism, not literals (Ch.16.5)
    @Override public void open(OpenContext ctx) { /* load per-tenant key ids; init Mac */ } // 2.x form (verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1/2.3.0 `RichFunction#open(OpenContext)`)
    @Override public SanitizedEvent map(RawEvent r) {
        SanitizedEvent s = new SanitizedEvent();
        s.tenantId = r.tenantId;
        s.subjectToken = token(r.tenantId, r.subjectId);   // HMAC, never plain hash
        s.eventTsMillis = r.eventTsMillis;
        s.action = r.action;             // email, name, IP, free text: deliberately not copied
        return s;
    }
    private String token(String tenant, String id) { /* HMAC-SHA256 with tenant key, hex */ return null; }
}

27.4 Where raw PII persists, and containment

(Extends the table in Chapter 16.7; do not repeat its details.)

Location Raw PII present if... Containment
Raw (ingress) topic producers send it restricted ACL, short retention, separate from consumer-facing topics; or fix at producer
Operator/keyed state op 1 comes after state or a keyBy on raw ids sanitize first; key by token; state TTL (Ch.5)
Checkpoints state holds raw storage encryption, restricted IAM, retention; Flink file encryption not found in docs I read (Ch.16.7); also no encryption classes in the flink-core 2.2.1 jar, which is not proof for the whole distribution
Savepoints same, kept indefinitely (verified: savepoint docs, a savepoint holds each stateful operator's state, and Flink never deletes it in NO_CLAIM mode, the default) named owner and expiry; never copy to workstations
Task/JM logs exceptions echo input, toString() log ids/tokens only; see 27.7
DLQ payloads failing record kept verbatim reference + hash, or encrypted per tenant (Ch.12.5)
Heap dumps live objects hold raw no automatic dumps in prod, or restricted volume (JVM concern)
Metric labels, side outputs, test fixtures user ids as labels; copies in other topics/repo bounded labels; sanitize fixtures

Figure 27.1: Enforce at the producer or gateway and in operator 1; every place raw PII can still persist needs its own containment.

Containment order of value: stop it entering (gateway) > drop it in op 1 > shorten lifetimes > encrypt and restrict access to what remains.

Erasure/"forget" requests: state, old checkpoints and savepoints cannot be edited per person in practice. Design: keep PII outside Flink, key state by pseudonymous token, short TTL, and destroy the per-subject mapping or key (crypto-shredding) [design option; legal sufficiency is for Legal to confirm]. The State Processor API (Chapter 30) can rewrite state offline, but treat it as exceptional.

27.5 Lineage and classification tags

  • Tag every schema field with a classification and every topic/table with the highest classification it contains.
  • Carry a schemaVersion and sanitized=true marker (header or field) on op-1 output; sinks assert the marker and reject anything missing it.
  • Keep a registry of "which job reads which topic" so a new consumer of a raw topic is a reviewed event.
  • Lineage tooling integration with Flink 2.x: Data unavailable (not researched).

27.6 Retention

  • Set per-artifact retention: raw topic (shortest feasible), DLQ, checkpoints (ExternalizedCheckpointRetention, Ch.16.7; verified: enum in flink-core 2.2.1 with DELETE_ON_CANCELLATION, RETAIN_ON_CANCELLATION, NO_EXTERNALIZED_CHECKPOINTS), savepoints (explicit expiry), logs, sinks.
  • Back up policy with storage lifecycle rules; job config alone is not enough.
  • Retention periods are a policy decision.

27.7 Logging hygiene

  • Never log record bodies, request payloads or toString() of events. Log tenantId, token, topic/partition/offset.
  • Wrap or sanitize exceptions: parsers often echo the offending bytes; truncate and strip before logging or DLQ reasonDetail.
  • Disable DEBUG for operator packages in production; debug logs are the usual leak.
  • No keys, salts or tokens in logs or job args (Chapter 16.5); Flink's web UI/REST show configuration values: Flink hides values only for keys whose names contain password, secret, token, api-key, apikey, service-key, auth-params, basic-auth, http-headers, jaas.config or fs.azure.account.key (verified: javap GlobalConfiguration constants SENSITIVE_KEYS/HIDDEN_CONTENT, and ConfigurationUtils.hideSensitiveValues used by REST ConfigurationInfo and JobConfigInfo, flink-core/flink-runtime 2.2.1), so name your own secret keys accordingly or keep them out of the config.
  • Ship logs to a store with the same access discipline as data.

27.8 Testing that nothing leaks (Chapter 14)

  • Canary values: build test records containing recognizable fake PII (clearly synthetic, e.g. canary-email-001), run the pipeline with test harnesses/mini-cluster, and assert that no sink output, side output, DLQ record, log capture or state snapshot contains the canary strings.
  • Schema test: output type has no field outside the allow-list (reflection check against a checked-in list); adding a field fails the build until classified.
  • Property test: random strings in unknown fields never reach output.
  • Failure-path test: malformed record with PII goes to DLQ without payload text.
  • Log capture test: force an exception in op 1; assert the log appendix lacks the canary.
  • Contract test on sinks: rejects records lacking the sanitized marker.
  • Fixtures must be synthetic; never paste production samples into tests (Ch.16.7).

27.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Masking view only (the article's design).
  • Deny-list redaction: new field added upstream flows through unredacted.
  • Unsalted/unkeyed hash of email or phone used as "anonymous" id.
  • One global HMAC key for all tenants; or key in source code/config file.
  • Redaction placed after keyBy or after a join: raw ids already in state and checkpoints.
  • Redacting the main stream but writing the raw record to the DLQ, side output or exception.
  • Savepoints kept "just in case", copied to shared drives.
  • Token rotation without a re-key plan breaks joins and dedup.
  • Free-text regex redaction treated as complete.
  • High-cardinality metric labels containing user identifiers.

27.10 Self-check

  1. Why is a masking view not a control, and what would an actual control look like at the producer?
  2. Why is SHA-256(email) not anonymization, and what do you use instead?
  3. List five places in a Flink job that can hold raw PII even after your sink output is clean.
  4. Why allow-list by construction rather than delete fields from the incoming object?
  5. Write the assertion that proves a DLQ record contains no payload text.

27.11 Open items / unverified

  • Flink-native encryption of checkpoints/savepoints: not found in docs I read (Data unavailable); assume storage-layer encryption.
  • Lineage/catalog integration for Flink 2.x: Data unavailable.
  • Whether tokens/pseudonyms count as personal data and required retention/erasure timelines: out of scope; Legal/Compliance.
  • Secret-loading API for per-tenant keys in a Flink 2.x operator: see Chapter 16.5; open(OpenContext) signature verified (flink-core jar).
  • Cryptographic statements (unsalted hashes of low-entropy values are reversible by lookup, HMAC with a secret key, constant-time comparison, crypto-shredding) are general security practice, not Flink facts; they were not checked against a source here.
  • Verified this pass (Flink-specific): where PII persists (state, checkpoints, savepoints, DLQ/logs by design), checkpoint retention enum, config-value masking rules.
  • Flink facts were re-checked against the 2.2.1/2.3.0 jars and the savepoints page (see VERIFICATION-LOG-25-28.md); the rest still comes from Chapters 12 and 16.

Sources: - https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/ops/state/savepoints/ - flink-core / flink-runtime 2.2.1 jars (javap); Chapters 12 and 16

Chapter 28: ForSt and State V2 (async state) - awareness only

Goal: after this chapter you can explain what disaggregated state (ForSt) and the asynchronous State V2 API are, how the programming model differs from the blocking state calls of Chapter 5, when they could matter, and why they are not on the cautious production path today.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state, backends), Chapter 6 (checkpoints, savepoints), Chapter 11 (RocksDB, Async I/O).

28.1 Mental model: why this exists

With RocksDB (Chapter 11.4) state lives on the TaskManager's local disk. That couples three things: state size is bounded by local disk, checkpoints copy files out of the TaskManager (CPU/network bursts), and recovery must download state back.

 RocksDB today                              Disaggregated state (ForSt)
 TaskManager                                TaskManager
 ┌───────────────┐                          ┌───────────────┐
 │ operator      │  blocking get()          │ operator      │  async get() -> StateFuture
 │ local SST     │                          │ local cache   │         │
 └──────┬────────┘                          └──────┬────────┘         ▼
        │ checkpoint = upload files                │            remote filesystem (primary state)
        ▼                                          ▼
   remote checkpoint store                    checkpoint = mostly metadata / already-remote files

Remote reads are slower than local-disk reads (Assumption: milliseconds versus microseconds is general experience, not a number from the docs). A blocking read per record would stall the task thread, so the design pairs a remote-capable backend (ForSt) with an asynchronous state API (State V2) that lets the runtime keep many state reads in flight. ForSt provides the storage, State V2 hides the latency. They are separable in code, though: if the configured backend does not support async keyed state (the default StateBackend#supportsAsyncKeyedStateBackend() returns false, and ForStStateBackend overrides it to true), StreamTaskStateInitializerImpl wraps the synchronous keyed backend in an AsyncKeyedStateBackendAdaptor (verified: javap flink-runtime 2.2.1). So the V2 API can run over HashMap or RocksDB, but then the futures wrap synchronous local calls, so (inference) you get no remote-latency benefit; the docs recommend ForSt for the new API.

Figure 28.1: RocksDB local state versus ForSt disaggregated state (ForSt is EXPERIMENTAL).

28.2 What the 2.3 docs say (verified)

Disaggregated state management page (2.3): - Claimed benefits: state size limited by external storage (S3, HDFS) rather than local disk; lightweight checkpoints without periodic bursts; recovery that does not download state ("the recovery time is independent of the state size"); compute and storage scale independently. - Status: experimental; the page says "The disaggregated state management is still in experimental state." Code agrees: ForStStateBackend and ForStOptions carry @Experimental (verified: GitHub apache/flink release-2.3 sources), and KeyedStream#enableAsyncState() and org.apache.flink.api.common.state.v2.ValueStateDescriptor are annotated @Experimental (verified: javap flink-streaming-java / flink-core 2.2.1 and 2.3.0). - The docs enable it with state.backend.type: forst plus execution.checkpointing.incremental: true and execution.checkpointing.dir (verified: docs; forst is a recognized shortcut name and org.apache.flink.state.forst.ForStStateBackendFactory is the factory class, javap StateBackendLoader flink-runtime 2.2.1/2.3.0; the ForSt module flink-statebackend-forst is a separate artifact, not among the downloaded jars, on Maven Central up to 2.3.0). The 2.3 docs also say, for DataStream jobs, that it "Requires using new State V2 APIs". - The page lists supported operators only for SQL (rank, deduplicate, aggregate, join, window aggregates). We deliberately do not use SQL in this book, so that list does not tell us anything about DataStream operators; for those see 28.3 (verified from the runtime jar). - Synchronous state APIs: the option state.backend.forst.sync.enforce-local (default true) is described in the source as "Whether to enforce local state for operators in synchronous mode when enabling disaggregated state", for jobs that mix synchronous and asynchronous operators. So an operator that keeps using the Chapter 5 API gets local state, not the remote benefit. (This replaces an earlier quoted phrase "fall back to local-only management" that I could not confirm verbatim.) - The docs add: for SQL, unsupported operators fall back to the synchronous implementation; and ForSt is currently based on frocksdb, with a Rust-based version stated as targeted for August 2026 (a plan on the page, not something verified here; check the current docs).

State backends page (2.3): "Does not support canonical savepoint, full snapshot, changelog and file-merging checkpoints. Always perform incremental snapshots." and "still in the experimental stage and is not fully available for production". Source agrees on savepoints: ForStStateBackend.supportsSavepointFormat returns true only for SavepointFormatType.NATIVE, and supportsNoClaimRestoreMode() is true (release-2.3 source). So native-format savepoints are possible, canonical ones are not.

ForSt config keys (CORRECTED; verified: ForStOptions source, GitHub apache/flink release-2.2 and release-2.3, identical)

The ForSt module jar was not available offline, so these come from the source. The 2.3 docs page lists the same keys but shows different values for two defaults (see the note below the table).

Key Meaning (from source descriptions) Default in source
state.backend.type set to forst (shortcut verified in the jar) hashmap (verified, javap StateBackendOptions and config docs)
state.backend.forst.primary-dir where ForSt puts its SST files; shortcuts: share the checkpoint directory, or use the TaskManager's local dir the checkpoint directory (shortcut)
state.backend.forst.local-dir local directory on the TaskManager for metadata files none; <WORKING_DIR>/tmp
state.backend.forst.cache.dir where ForSt caches SST files; falls back to a /cache subdirectory of the local dir none
state.backend.forst.cache.size-based-limit upper bound of the cache size; at least one of the two cache limits must be set to enable the cache 0 (disabled)
state.backend.forst.cache.reserve-size disk space kept free; cache evicts oldest files when the disk is short 256mb; 0 disables this limit
state.backend.forst.sync.enforce-local keep synchronous-mode operators on local state when disaggregated state is enabled true
state.backend.forst.executor.read-io-parallelism read IO threads 3
state.backend.forst.executor.write-io-parallelism write IO threads, only valid when executor.inline-write is false 1
state.backend.forst.executor.inline-write run write requests in the coordinator thread true
state.backend.forst.executor.inline-coordinator task thread acts as coordinator false

Note: the 2.3 docs page (as summarised by the fetch tool) shows cache.size-based-limit 1GB and cache.reserve-size 10GB as defaults. The source says 0 and 256 MiB, and the cache is off until you set a limit. Trust the source; if you rely on the cache, set the limits explicitly. There are more keys (memory, LRU, timer-service, options-factory) that this chapter does not cover.

The page also shows table.exec.async-state.enabled: true; that is a Table/SQL option and is irrelevant here. Exact semantics of local-dir vs primary-dir vs cache.dir beyond the source descriptions above, and behavior when remote storage is slow or down: [unverified].

28.3 The programming model: blocking vs asynchronous (verified)

Today (Chapter 5): blocking calls

// sketch, not compiled
Long c = count.value();            // returns the value, thread waits
count.update(c == null ? 1 : c + 1);
out.collect(...);

State V2: you get a future and continue in a callback

Enable on the keyed stream:

KeyedStream<WordCount, String> keyed = words.keyBy(WordCount::getWord).enableAsyncState();
// verified: javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1/2.3.0: public KeyedStream<T, KEY> enableAsyncState(), annotated @Experimental.
// (The docs page shows the type as KeyedStream<WordCount>, which is missing the key type parameter.)

State types live in package org.apache.flink.api.common.state.v2 (not the Chapter 5 package): ValueState, ListState, MapState, ReducingState, AggregatingState, with descriptors of the same package (ValueStateDescriptor(String, Class<T> | TypeInformation<T> | TypeSerializer<T>) etc.). Verified: javap flink-core 2.2.1 (RuntimeContext has overloads such as getState(org.apache.flink.api.common.state.v2.ValueStateDescriptor<T>), getListState, getMapState, getReducingState, getAggregatingState for v2 beside the old ones) and the implementing classes in flink-runtime 2.2.1 (the v2 interfaces themselves are in a jar I did not have). Methods carry an async prefix: - ValueState: asyncValue() returns StateFuture<T>, asyncUpdate(T) returns StateFuture<Void>. - ListState: asyncGet() returns StateFuture<StateIterator<T>> (an iterator type, not a List), asyncAdd(T), asyncAddAll(List<T>), asyncUpdate(List<T>). - MapState: asyncGet(UK), asyncPut(UK, UV), asyncPutAll(Map), asyncRemove(UK), asyncContains(UK), asyncEntries(), asyncKeys(), asyncValues() (the last three return StateFuture<StateIterator<...>>), asyncIsEmpty(). - ReducingState / AggregatingState: asyncGet(), asyncAdd(...). All state types: asyncClear(). They return a StateFuture<T> (a Flink type, not CompletableFuture) with chainable methods. Verified signatures (javap AsyncFutureImpl, flink-core 2.2.1; the parameter types are Flink's own throwing functional interfaces, not java.util.function):

Method Purpose
thenAccept(ThrowingConsumer<? super T, ? extends Exception>) consume the result, returns StateFuture<Void>
thenApply(FunctionWithException<? super T, ? extends U, ...>) transform the result
thenCompose(FunctionWithException<..., ? extends StateFuture<U>, ...>) chain a dependent async access
thenCombine(StateFuture<? extends U>, BiFunctionWithException<...>) join two futures
thenConditionallyAccept/Apply/Compose(condition, ...) conditional variants (branch on a boolean computed from the result) 
// sketch, not compiled (the v2 interfaces and flink-core-api were not on the offline classpath; method names and
// return types were checked with javap on the implementing classes); shape follows the docs, types simplified
// state: org.apache.flink.api.common.state.v2.ValueState<Long> count, obtained in open(OpenContext) with
//   count = getRuntimeContext().getState(new org.apache.flink.api.common.state.v2.ValueStateDescriptor<>("c", Long.class));
public void flatMap(Word w, Collector<WordCount> out) {
    count.asyncValue()
         .thenApply(c -> c == null ? 1L : c + 1)
         .thenAccept(n -> count.asyncUpdate(n).thenAccept(v -> out.collect(new WordCount(w.word, n))));
}

Which DataStream operators use async state (verified: javap flink-streaming-java and flink-runtime 2.2.1, calls guarded by KeyedStream.isEnableAsyncState(); the 2.3 jar has the same enableAsyncState method): - keyed.flatMap(FlatMapFunction) becomes AsyncStreamFlatMap; the docs example uses a rich flat-map function. There is no async map operator in the runtime jar (jfind over asyncprocessing/operators), so the docs' mention of RichMapFunction is not backed by a dedicated operator I could find: [unverified], use flatMap. - keyed.process(KeyedProcessFunction) becomes AsyncKeyedProcessOperator, which implements Triggerable with onEventTime and onProcessingTime (so timers are wired in); DeclaringAsyncKeyedProcessFunction also exists in flink-runtime. Whether a given timer pattern is safe, and the restrictions on the callback style there, are [unverified] (Chapter 3 patterns are not re-validated for State V2). - keyed.reduce(ReduceFunction) sets enableAsyncState on its transformation. - Windows: keyed.window(...) propagates the flag to WindowedStream, which then builds AsyncWindowOperator / AsyncEvictingWindowOperator via WindowOperatorBuilder.asyncReduce, asyncAggregate, asyncApply, asyncProcess, and has trigger(AsyncTrigger) (async triggers such as AsyncEventTimeTrigger, AsyncCountTrigger exist). - keyed.connect(other).process(KeyedCoProcessFunction) becomes AsyncKeyedCoProcessOperator; KeyedStream.IntervalJoined references AsyncIntervalJoinOperator. Stability of these operators is not stated beyond the @Experimental markers above.

Ordering and safety rules (from the docs)

  • For elements of the same key, the user-code entry points are invoked strictly in order of arrival; callbacks of one element chain sequentially.
  • State operations of different elements may complete out of order (that is where the throughput comes from).
  • Do not mix synchronous and asynchronous state access in the same function (docs: "highly not recommended").
  • Stay in the callback style: the docs describe no blocking read of a StateFuture in user code (the StateFuture interface itself was not available to inspect; the internal AsyncFutureImpl has a get(), which is not user API).
  • Avoid reading/writing mutable member fields from callbacks; pass data through state results and closures.
  • TTL: docs say only processing-time TTL is supported; the docs example uses StateTtlConfig.newBuilder(Duration.ofSeconds(1))... with descriptor.enableTimeToLive(ttlConfig) on the v2 descriptor (the v2 runtime has a ttl package; exact v2 StateTtlConfig class not checked: [unverified]).

Mental model for the third rule: your code is cut into pieces at each state access; the runtime schedules the pieces, so anything outside the future chain (a field, a loop counter) may be read before or after another element touched it.

Figure 28.2: State V2 asynchronous call model and its ordering rules (State V2 API is @Experimental in the jars).

28.4 When it might matter

Situation Relevance
State fits on local SSD, RocksDB checkpoints are fine none; stay on RocksDB
State of many TB, local disk is the limit the use case ForSt targets
Recovery time dominated by downloading state (Chapter 6.6) docs claim state-size-independent recovery
Checkpoint bursts hurt latency docs claim lighter checkpoints
Compute and storage should be sized/costed separately (cloud) design goal
Latency to remote storage is high and the logic is read-heavy per record you pay it per access unless async overlap hides it

Real-world numbers (throughput vs RocksDB, cache hit effects, cost): Data unavailable from the docs I fetched. Do not assume parity; benchmark with your own keys and value sizes (Chapter 17).

28.5 Decision table: should we use it today?

Question Answer for the cautious production path
Is ForSt production-ready? No. Docs: experimental; Chapter 5.7 quotes "not fully available for production".
Is State V2 production-ready? Experimental by annotation: KeyedStream#enableAsyncState() and the v2 ValueStateDescriptor carry @Experimental (javap, 2.2.1 and 2.3.0). The State V2 docs page gives no stability statement I could see.
Can we take canonical savepoints? No canonical savepoints for ForSt (docs and supportsSavepointFormat accept only NATIVE; native savepoints are possible). This breaks the portable upgrade/backend-switch story of Chapters 6 and 9.
Full snapshots / changelog backend? No for ForSt.
Does it need code changes? Yes. Rewrite state access to futures; cannot mix with sync access (28.3).
Does Kafka-based dedup/sessionization of this book need it? No. State is TTL-bounded and moderate (Chapters 18, 20).
Is it compatible with our Java 17 / Flink 1.20-vs-2.x decisions? Irrelevant until the above change; Java 25 is undocumented anyway (README).
Recommended action Do not use in production. Use HashMapStateBackend or EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend. Revisit when docs drop the "experimental" label, savepoints are supported, and your own benchmark shows a need.
Safe experiment A non-production job in a sandbox, new keyed operator written against V2, measure; never as the only copy of important state.

28.6 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Choosing ForSt to "save disk cost" without measuring remote-read latency under your access pattern.
  • Switching backends with a canonical savepoint assumption: ForSt cannot produce one, so you may have no clean way back to RocksDB (Assumption on the exact restore paths; verify before any trial).
  • Keeping synchronous calls in a function after enableAsyncState(): the docs say it is "highly not recommended" to mix them; I could not confirm a hard prohibition.
  • Capturing mutable fields inside callbacks, causing cross-element interference.
  • Assuming the SQL-only operator list covers DataStream operators.
  • Configuring primary-dir on a bucket shared across environments or tenants without access separation (Chapter 16).
  • Expecting changing execution.checkpointing.incremental and checkpoint storage semantics to match RocksDB without re-reading the ForSt page. (Resolved: state.backend.incremental is a deprecated key of execution.checkpointing.incremental, verified: javap CheckpointingOptions withDeprecatedKeys, flink-core 2.2.1 and 2.3.0; use the execution. name. Chapters 6 and 11 should say the same.)

28.7 Self-check

  1. Why does a remote state backend need an asynchronous API to be useful?
  2. Two records with the same key arrive back to back under State V2. What ordering is guaranteed, and for what?
  3. Why should you not mix value() and asyncValue() in one function?
  4. Name two operational capabilities from Chapter 6 that ForSt does not offer.
  5. What evidence would you need before putting ForSt in production?

  • Resolved by the jars: State V2 API is @Experimental; KeyedProcessFunction, windows, keyed connect and interval join have async operators (28.3). Still [unverified]: the safety restrictions for timers and windows in async mode, and the missing async map operator vs the docs' RichMapFunction mention.
  • [unverified] FLIP numbers for State V2 / ForSt. The 2.3 release notes list FLIP-564, 550, 557, 559, 558, 565, 555, 339, 495, 487, 547, 549, 560, 553, 561, but the extract I got did not link any to ForSt or async state ("Not mentioned"). I will not guess which FLIP applies.
  • [unverified] local-dir, primary-dir, cache.dir interplay beyond the source descriptions in 28.2, and failure behavior when remote storage is slow or unavailable.
  • Resolved: KeyedStream<T, KEY> enableAsyncState(); V2 state is obtained with getRuntimeContext().getState(v2 descriptor) in open(OpenContext) (javap RuntimeContext, docs).
  • Performance, cost, and benchmark data: Data unavailable.
  • Restoring a ForSt checkpoint into a different backend: Data unavailable (source: only NATIVE savepoint format, so no canonical path).

Chapter 29: FlinkCEP - pattern matching on event sequences

Goal: after this chapter you can read and write a CEP pattern, choose contiguity and skip strategy, explain why CEP depends on watermarks, handle late and timed-out matches, estimate its state cost, and decide when a KeyedProcessFunction is the better tool.

Prerequisites: Chapter 1 (watermarks, late data), Chapter 3 (KeyedProcessFunction, timers), Chapter 5 (state), Chapter 6 (checkpoints). CEP is DataStream only (README facts); no SQL MATCH_RECOGNIZE here.

29.1 Mental model

You describe a sequence of named steps (a Pattern), Flink compiles it into a state machine (NFA) and runs it per key. Matches are delivered as Map<String, List<Event>>: step name to the events that matched it.

 events (per key, event-time order) ──► Pattern: "login_fail" ──► "login_fail" ──► "success"  within 5 min
                                                    NFA partial matches kept in state (SharedBuffer)
                                                        └─► match { login_fail:[e1,e2], success:[e3] }

Figure 29.1: A CEP pattern as a per-key state machine, with the within() window, timed-out partial matches and late events.

29.2 Pattern API (verified: 2.3 CEP page; javap flink-cep 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 Pattern, CEP)

Start with Pattern.begin("name"); apply with PatternStream<Event> ps = CEP.pattern(input, pattern);.

Concern Methods
Conditions where(...) (AND), or(...), until(...) (stop condition for looping steps), subtype(Class)
Strict contiguity next("n"), notNext("n") : the next event must match
Relaxed contiguity followedBy("n") : non-matching events in between are ignored
Non-deterministic relaxed followedByAny("n") : also continues matches that already consumed an event, producing more combinations
Negation notFollowedBy("n") (needs a within, see below)
Quantifiers oneOrMore(), times(n), times(min, max), timesOrMore(n), optional(), greedy()
Looping contiguity consecutive() (strict between repeats), allowCombinations() (non-deterministic relaxed between repeats)
Time bound within(Duration) on the sequence; also within(Duration, WithinType) (enum FIRST_AND_LAST, PREVIOUS_AND_CURRENT; semantics not documented in the sources I could check: [unverified], this chapter uses the one-argument form)

within: "maximum time interval" for a sequence to match; an incomplete sequence exceeding it is discarded. Only one temporal constraint applies to a sequence; if several are set, the smallest wins. A pattern ending in notFollowedBy() requires one. The parameter type is java.time.Duration (verified: javap flink-cep 2.2.1 and 2.3.0 Pattern.within(java.time.Duration); the docs example is within(Duration.ofSeconds(10))). Time is not used. Some quantifier methods also take a Duration (oneOrMore(Duration), times(int, Duration), timesOrMore(int, Duration); javap); their semantics are not covered here.

Choosing contiguity (rule of thumb, Assumption): fraud/security sequences usually want followedBy (other noise events are normal); use next only when adjacency is the business meaning; followedByAny multiplies matches and state, use sparingly.

29.3 Skip strategies (verified names, javap flink-cep)

After a match, which partial matches survive? Passed as Pattern.begin("start", AfterMatchSkipStrategy.skipPastLastEvent()). Verified (javap flink-cep 2.2.1/2.3.0): AfterMatchSkipStrategy is an abstract class with static factories noSkip(), skipToNext(), skipPastLastEvent(), skipToFirst(String), skipToLast(String), and Pattern.begin(String, AfterMatchSkipStrategy) exists. There is no public constructor form to use.

Strategy Effect
noSkip() default; emit all possible matches
skipToNext() discard partial matches that start with the same event as the emitted match
skipPastLastEvent() discard all partial matches that started before the match ended
skipToFirst(name) / skipToLast(name) discard partial matches that started before the first/last event of step name

For alerting ("one alert per incident") start with skipPastLastEvent(); it bounds both output volume and state. With noSkip() on looping patterns the number of matches can grow combinatorially.

29.4 Reading the result: PatternProcessFunction (verified: javap flink-cep 2.2.1/2.3.0)

// sketch, not compiled
public class FraudAlert extends PatternProcessFunction<Txn, Alert> {
    @Override
    public void processMatch(Map<String, List<Txn>> match, Context ctx, Collector<Alert> out) {
        Txn first = match.get("small").get(0);
        Txn big   = match.get("big").get(0);
        out.collect(new Alert(first.accountId, first.tsMillis, big.amountCents));
    }
}
  • Signature from docs: processMatch(Map<String, List<IN>> match, Context ctx, Collector<OUT> out); Context gives time info and side outputs.
  • Timed-out partial matches: also implement TimedOutPartialMatchHandler<IN> with processTimedOutMatch(Map<String, List<IN>> match, Context ctx). It has no main output, only side outputs via the context.
  • Legacy select() / flatSelect() still exist; write the new form (see the wiring bullet below).
  • Wire it: patternStream.process(new FraudAlert()) (verified: javap PatternStream.process(PatternProcessFunction<T,R>) returns SingleOutputStreamOperator<R>; an overload also takes a TypeInformation<R>). PatternProcessFunction is an abstract class (extends AbstractRichFunction); Context extends TimeContext and adds output(OutputTag<X>, X).
  • PatternStream.select(...) and flatSelect(...) are wrapped via PatternProcessFunctionBuilder (verified: javap PatternStream.select calls PatternProcessFunctionBuilder.fromSelect).

29.5 Keyed vs non-keyed

Keyed stream (keyBy) Non-keyed stream
Parallelism scales with key distribution parallelism 1 (docs)
Meaning pattern evaluated independently per key (per account, per device) one global sequence
State per key one subtask holds all of it

Always key by the entity whose sequence matters (and by tenant too, Chapter 5.8, so tenants never share a match). A non-keyed CEP job is a single-subtask bottleneck and a single point of skew; only acceptable for tiny, low-rate streams.

29.6 Time: the sorting buffer and why watermarks matter (verified: 2.3 CEP page; CepOperator bytecode shows a MapState element queue)

In event time the operator buffers incoming events and sorts them by timestamp; buffered events are processed when a watermark arrives, so order is guaranteed between watermarks. The docs state the library "assumes correctness of the watermark". Consequences:

  1. No watermark progress, no matches. An idle partition (Chapter 1.5) holds the minimum; sequences are never evaluated. withIdleness applies.
  2. Latency = watermark delay. A match is emitted only after the watermark passes the last event, so the bounded-out-of-orderness delay (Chapter 1.2) adds to alert latency.
  3. Buffer = memory. Events sit in state until the watermark releases them; a large delay or stalled watermark inflates state.
  4. Replays are deterministic in event time (Chapter 24); in processing time the timestamp is when the event entered the operator, so results vary.

Late events (behind the last watermark) are dropped unless you route them (verified: javap PatternStream.sideOutputLateData(OutputTag<T>); PatternStream.inEventTime()/inProcessingTime() also exist):

// sketch; API names checked against flink-cep 2.2.1 by javap
OutputTag<Txn> LATE = new OutputTag<>("late-txn") {};
SingleOutputStreamOperator<Alert> alerts = CEP.pattern(keyedTxns, pattern)
        .sideOutputLateData(LATE)
        .process(new FraudAlert());
DataStream<Txn> late = alerts.getSideOutput(LATE);      // count it (Chapter 1.4), alert on rate

A late event is not inserted into the sequence afterwards; it can only be counted or handled separately. Missing a step because of lateness means a missed detection, so size the delay with data (Chapter 1.7) and monitor the late rate.

Figure 29.2: Keyed versus non-keyed CEP parallelism, and the event-time sorting buffer that waits for the watermark.

29.7 State cost and the SharedBuffer cache

Partial matches live in a SharedBuffer inside Flink state (verified: javap SharedBuffer holds MapState fields eventsBuffer, entries, eventsCount), plus the sorting buffer from 29.6 (a MapState in CepOperator). Cost drivers (Assumption, my reasoning, not docs): - number of live keys times partial matches per key (loose patterns like oneOrMore + followedByAny are the worst); - the within window length (partial matches live up to that long); - noSkip() on looping patterns; - the watermark delay (events held before evaluation).

Always set within. A pattern without a time bound can keep partial matches indefinitely: unbounded state (Chapter 5.8). Add a stop condition until(...) to open-ended loops.

Optional SharedBuffer cache config (verified: keys, types and defaults from javap of CEPCacheOptions in flink-cep 2.2.1 and 2.3.0; the option description says the cache limit only has an effect for the RocksDB backend, where each state access is a serialized read):

Key Default
pipeline.cep.sharedbuffer.cache.entry-slots (int) 1024
pipeline.cep.sharedbuffer.cache.event-slots (int) 1024
pipeline.cep.sharedbuffer.cache.statistics-interval (Duration) 30 min

The keys are read through SharedBufferCacheConfig.of(ReadableConfig) (javap), so they are ordinary configuration options (cluster or job configuration). The jar's description of the two slot options mentions the legacy key name state.backend; in 2.x the backend key is state.backend.type (Chapter 28/15), so read that text as "RocksDB backend". Tuning guidance (when to raise, memory effect): [unverified]; measure checkpoint size and RocksDB read latency (Chapters 11, 13) before and after. These options are not new in 2.3: the same three keys and defaults exist in flink-cep 2.2.1 (verified: javap CEPCacheOptions in both jars).

29.8 Fraud-style example sketch

Pattern: "three small card-testing transactions followed by a large one on the same account within 10 minutes."

// sketch, not compiled
Pattern<Txn, ?> p = Pattern
    .<Txn>begin("small", AfterMatchSkipStrategy.skipPastLastEvent())     // verified: javap AfterMatchSkipStrategy
    .where(SimpleCondition.of(t -> t.amountCents < 500))
    .times(3).consecutive()
    .followedBy("big")
    .where(SimpleCondition.of(t -> t.amountCents > 50_000))
    .within(Duration.ofMinutes(10));                                      // verified: javap Pattern.within(Duration)

DataStream<Txn> txns = ...;   // watermarked (Chapter 1), keyed by (tenantId, accountId)
CEP.pattern(txns.keyBy(t -> t.tenantId + "|" + t.accountId), p)
   .sideOutputLateData(LATE)
   .process(new FraudAlert());

Notes: consecutive() here means the three small ones must be adjacent to each other; followedBy tolerates other transactions before the big one. SimpleCondition.of(FilterFunction<T>) exists (verified: javap flink-cep 2.2.1/2.3.0); the docs form is an anonymous SimpleCondition subclass overriding filter(T). The sketch's pattern and imports were checked name by name against the jar signatures; a full javac run was not possible because flink-core-api was not in the toolkit jars. Alerts reaching an external system need an idempotent sink (Chapters 7, 26): recovery can re-emit a match.

29.9 When to prefer a KeyedProcessFunction (Chapter 3)

Prefer CEP when Prefer KeyedProcessFunction when
the logic is a readable sequence of 2-5 steps with contiguity rules the logic is counting, thresholds, running aggregates, rate limits
order-sensitive and out-of-order data must be sorted for you you need a timer-driven action ("no event for 15 min")
you want skip strategies and combinations built in you need explicit control of state size, TTL, and cleanup
patterns change rarely rules are dynamic or per-tenant (config via broadcast, Chapter 4)
you need custom lateness handling (e.g. re-emit, update)

Practical rule (Assumption): if the pattern is "N events of kind A within T" or "A without B within T", a few lines of ValueState + a timer are cheaper, easier to test (Chapter 14), and easier to size than CEP. Reach for CEP when the contiguity and skip semantics are the hard part.

29.10 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Non-keyed CEP: parallelism 1 (29.5).
  • Watermark stalls (idle partition) silently suppress all matches (29.6).
  • No within or no until: unbounded partial-match state.
  • followedByAny / allowCombinations / noSkip producing alert storms and state blowup.
  • Late events dropped without a side-output counter: invisible missed detections.
  • Using processing time and expecting replay-reproducible alerts.
  • Timed-out matches ignored: if "step 1 without step 2" is the business signal, implement TimedOutPartialMatchHandler.
  • Pattern changes on a running job: treat as a state change (Chapter 9). The computation states and shared buffer live in Flink state (verified: bytecode above), but exact restore compatibility after editing a pattern is [unverified].
  • No uid() on the CEP operator (Chapters 6, 9).
  • Same-pattern duplicates after recovery sent to a non-idempotent sink.

29.11 Self-check

  1. Why does CEP stop producing matches when one Kafka partition goes idle?
  2. A pattern is begin("a").next("b"). Events arrive a, x, b. Is there a match? Change one method so there is.
  3. What happens to an event that arrives after the watermark has passed its timestamp? How do you observe it?
  4. Which state grows when you add oneOrMore().followedByAny without until or within?
  5. Your rule is "5 failed logins in 1 minute". CEP or KeyedProcessFunction, and why?

29.12 Open items / unverified

  • Resolved (verified by javap, flink-cep 2.2.1 and 2.3.0): within(Duration), skip-strategy factories, PatternStream.process, SimpleCondition.of, SharedBuffer cache keys and defaults; the cache options exist in 2.2.1 too, so they are not new in 2.3.
  • [unverified] Tuning guidance for the SharedBuffer cache keys; whether they have any effect with non-RocksDB backends (their description says only RocksDB); semantics of within(Duration, WithinType).
  • [unverified] Compatibility of restoring state after changing a pattern.
  • [unverified] Behavior of CEP with State V2 / ForSt (Chapter 28). Only fact found: CepOperator and SharedBuffer use the classic org.apache.flink.api.common.state ValueState/MapState API, not state.v2 (javap 2.3.0); whether that runs on ForSt is not confirmed.
  • Dynamic CEP patterns (changing rules without redeploy): no dynamic-pattern classes found in the flink-cep 2.3.0 jar (jar listing); treat as not available in core Flink 2.3.
  • State size per partial match: Data unavailable.

Chapter 30: The State Processor API

Goal: after this chapter you can read a savepoint as a dataset, bootstrap state from historical data, modify or repair an existing savepoint offline (rename UIDs, drop an operator, patch keys), and say when this tool is the wrong choice.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state types), Chapter 6 (savepoints), Chapter 9 (UIDs, evolution, 1.x to 2.x). Related: Chapter 24 (backfill).

30.1 Mental model: a savepoint is a database you can query and rewrite

A savepoint (Chapter 6) is a directory of state files plus metadata. Chapter 9 explained that state is addressed by operator UID and state name. The State Processor API lets a normal Flink program treat that directory as input and output:

 savepoint dir ──read──► DataStream (BATCH job) ──your logic──► new state ──write──► new savepoint dir
 (offline, no running streaming job involved)                                     (restore with: flink run -s)

It runs as a batch-style Flink job. It never touches a running job; you stop the job with a savepoint, transform, restore.

Figure 30.1: Read, modify and write a savepoint offline in a batch-style job.

30.2 Entry classes (verified: 2.3 State Processor API page and javap flink-state-processor-api 2.2.1/2.3.0)

All classes below are in package org.apache.flink.state.api (functions in org.apache.flink.state.api.functions); the signatures in the table were read from the 2.3.0 jar with javap.

Purpose Class / method (as printed in the docs)
Maven artifact flink-state-processor-api
Open a savepoint for reading SavepointReader.read(env, "<path>", new HashMapStateBackend()); a two-argument overload read(env, path) also exists
Read keyed state savepoint.readKeyedState(OperatorIdentifier.forUid("my-uid"), new ReaderFunction()) with a KeyedStateReaderFunction<K, OUT>
Read operator state readListState(OperatorIdentifier, String stateName, TypeInformation<T>), readUnionState(...) (same shape), readBroadcastState(OperatorIdentifier, String stateName, TypeInformation<K>, TypeInformation<V>) returning DataStream<Tuple2<K,V>>; each has an overload with custom TypeSerializer parameters
Read window state savepoint.window(WindowAssigner) returns a WindowSavepointReader with reduce, aggregate and process(String uid, WindowReaderFunction, keyType, stateType, outType); WindowReaderFunction.readWindow(key, context, elements, out); context has window(), windowState(), globalState(), triggerState(...), registeredEventTimeTimers(), registeredProcessingTimeTimers()
Create a brand new savepoint SavepointWriter.newSavepoint(env, backend, maxParallelism); overloads without backend and with a long checkpoint id exist
Modify an existing savepoint SavepointWriter.fromExistingSavepoint(env, oldPath, backend) (a variant without backend exists)
Add or replace an operator's state .withOperator(OperatorIdentifier.forUid("uid"), transformation)
Build the transformation OperatorTransformation.bootstrapWith(dataStream).keyBy(...).transform(new MyBootstrapper()); returns StateBootstrapTransformation<T>. OneInputStateTransformation also has setMaxParallelism(int) and transform(StateBootstrapFunction) / transform(BroadcastStateBootstrapFunction) for non-keyed state
Bootstrap functions StateBootstrapFunction (operator state), KeyedStateBootstrapFunction (keyed), BroadcastStateBootstrapFunction (broadcast)
Change an operator's identity changeOperatorIdentifier(OperatorIdentifier.forUid("old"), OperatorIdentifier.forUid("new")); OperatorIdentifier.forUidHash(...) also exists
Drop an operator's state removeOperator(...)
Write the result .write(newPath) (returns void; the job still has to be executed with env.execute(...))

The DataStream reader/writer take any StateBackend instance (javap), and the docs example uses HashMapStateBackend. For the SQL "state" connector the option state.backend.type accepts the shortcuts hashmap, rocksdb and forst (verified: javap SavepointConnectorOptions description, flink-state-processor-api 2.3.0 and a forst reference in 2.2.1). The shortcut rocksdb maps to org.apache.flink.state.rocksdb.EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackendFactory and forst to org.apache.flink.state.forst.ForStStateBackendFactory (verified: javap flink-runtime 2.3.0 StateBackendLoader), so "RocksDB" means EmbeddedRocksDBStateBackend. That ForSt state can be read or written through the DataStream SavepointReader/SavepointWriter end to end is [unverified] (see Chapter 28).

Execution mode: the docs say code using SavepointWriter must run under BATCH execution mode (env.setRuntimeMode(RuntimeExecutionMode.BATCH); the 2.3 docs page says "your application must be executed under BATCH execution"; the jar does not enforce it, no check found in SavepointWriter bytecode, so a missing setting is a silent misconfiguration). This is the 2.x DataStream-only route; the old DataSet API is removed (Chapter 9).

30.3 Reading state

You supply a reader that mirrors how the original operator declared state. Keyed state needs the same descriptors (name and serializer, Chapter 5/8) registered in open().

// (sketch, not compiled) dump per-key counters from the operator with uid "counter"
public class CounterReader extends KeyedStateReaderFunction<String, CounterRow> {
    private ValueState<Long> count;
    @Override public void open(OpenContext ctx) {          // verified: javap RichFunction.open(OpenContext) in flink-core 2.3.0
        count = getRuntimeContext().getState(new ValueStateDescriptor<>("count", Types.LONG));
    }
    @Override public void readKey(String key, Context ctx, Collector<CounterRow> out) throws Exception {
        out.collect(new CounterRow(key, count.value()));
    }
}

StreamExecutionEnvironment env = StreamExecutionEnvironment.getExecutionEnvironment();
env.setRuntimeMode(RuntimeExecutionMode.BATCH);
SavepointReader sp = SavepointReader.read(env, "<SAVEPOINT_PATH>", new HashMapStateBackend());
DataStream<CounterRow> rows = sp.readKeyedState(OperatorIdentifier.forUid("counter"), new CounterReader());
rows.sinkTo(...);   // any Sink V2, e.g. files: inspect, diff, audit

What each state kind needs:

State kind Reader Gotcha
Keyed (Value/List/Map) KeyedStateReaderFunction state name + serializer must match what the job wrote
Operator list readListState() one element stream across subtasks
Union list readUnionState() returns a single copy (as if parallelism 1)
Broadcast readBroadcastState() single copy; you pass the broadcast state name plus key and value TypeInformation (javap), result is Tuple2<K,V> records
Window WindowReaderFunction window assigner must match the job's (30.4)
Timers via reader Context (timer metadata) read-only metadata

Useful first step: the metadata function savepoint_metadata(path) (verified: the name is a constant in SavepointMetadataTableFunction, flink-state-processor-api 2.3.0) lists, per the jar's column names, checkpoint-id, operator-name, operator-uid, operator-uid-hash, operator-parallelism, operator-max-parallelism, operator-subtask-state-count, operator-total-size-in-bytes and operator-coordinator-state-size-in-bytes. It is a SQL-flavoured function; this book does not use SQL (Chapter 1 rule), so use it only as a quick inspection from the SQL client. The docs (2.3 page) also say the State Table API supports keyed state only (the connector's state-type is VALUE, LIST or MAP, javap), so for operator, broadcast or window state use the DataStream readers above.

30.4 Window state: the assigner must match

For window state, the docs say the window assigner configuration on the bootstrap transformation must match the one on the DataStream window (assigner type, size, slide, gap; and the state shape implied by your aggregate/process function, Chapter 2). Mismatch means the restored job cannot find or interpret the window contents. Treat window bootstrap as the hardest case: prefer rebuilding windows by replay (Chapter 24) unless the history window is long.

30.5 Bootstrapping state from historical data

Use case: a new job needs warm state on day one (rolling features, dedup keys, session tables) without replaying months of Kafka.

 historical files/tables ──► (BATCH) bootstrapWith ──keyBy──► KeyedStateBootstrapFunction ──► new savepoint
                                                                                               │
 new streaming job (same uid, same descriptors, same key type) ◄── flink run -s <new savepoint> ┘

Figure 30.2: Bootstrapping keyed state from history and handing off to Kafka at the cutoff.

// (sketch, not compiled)
public class FeatureBootstrapper extends KeyedStateBootstrapFunction<String, HistRow> {
    private ValueState<Long> count;
    @Override public void open(OpenContext ctx) {
        count = getRuntimeContext().getState(new ValueStateDescriptor<>("count", Types.LONG));
    }
    @Override public void processElement(HistRow r, Context ctx) throws Exception {
        count.update(r.total);
        // ctx.timerService().registerEventTimeTimer(...) possible, see timers below
    }
}

StateBootstrapTransformation<HistRow> t = OperatorTransformation
    .bootstrapWith(historicalStream)               // bounded DataStream built in BATCH mode
    .keyBy(r -> r.key)
    .transform(new FeatureBootstrapper());

SavepointWriter.newSavepoint(env, new HashMapStateBackend(), 128)   // 128 = max parallelism, choose per Chapter 9.6
    .withOperator(OperatorIdentifier.forUid("counter"), t)
    .write("<NEW_SAVEPOINT_PATH>");
env.execute("bootstrap");

Rules that bite: - Same UID, same state name, same type/serializer, same key type and keyBy logic as the streaming operator (Chapters 8, 9). - Max parallelism is fixed in the new savepoint (third argument of newSavepoint); it is the upper bound for rescaling later (Chapter 9.6). - Timers: bootstrap functions can register event-time and processing-time timers (verified: javap KeyedStateBootstrapFunction.Context.timerService()). The 2.3 docs say that if a bootstrap function creates timers, the state can only be restored by a process-type function (KeyedProcessFunction etc.), and that processing-time timers whose time has passed fire immediately on restore (docs; README verified fact), so a late restore can trigger a burst of callbacks (Chapter 3). Prefer event-time timers for bootstraps. - Handoff to the stream: the savepoint is a snapshot of history. The streaming job must start reading Kafka at an offset that continues from the history cutoff with neither a gap nor an overlap. Offsets are not part of the bootstrapped state unless you also bootstrap the Kafka source operator's state. I found no API for that in the State Processor API jar (no source-offset helper among the public classes, javap 2.3.0), but a Kafka-source-specific approach is [unverified]. Typical approach: choose the cutoff timestamp, start the job from timestamp-based offsets, and make the state logic idempotent (Chapters 18, 24, 26). - Side effects: a bootstrap run emits nothing downstream. Do not mix sinks into it except for audit outputs.

30.6 Modifying a savepoint

fromExistingSavepoint copies metadata and keeps the operators you do not touch.

Task How Notes
Rename an operator UID changeOperatorIdentifier(forUid("old"), forUid("new")) use when you must add a missing explicit UID: the old identity is a hash (forUidHash), the new one forUid (Chapter 9.2)
Remove dead state removeOperator(...) permanent in the new savepoint; safer than -n allowNonRestoredState on every restart (Chapter 6)
Replace or add an operator's state withOperator(id, transformation) replaces that operator's state wholesale
Change max parallelism rebuild the operator with newSavepoint(env, backend, maxParallelism); OneInputStateTransformation.setMaxParallelism(int) sets it per bootstrapped operator no in-place option among the public SavepointWriter methods (javap 2.3.0: fromExistingSavepoint, newSavepoint, removeOperator, withOperator, withConfiguration, changeOperatorIdentifier, write); effect on restored existing-operator state is [unverified]

Flow: stop with savepoint (Chapter 6) -> run the modification job -> flink run -s <new path> with the new jar -> validate -> keep the old savepoint until the new job passes (Chapter 9.10).

30.7 Repair use case: fixing corrupted state

Scenario: a bug wrote a wrong value for a subset of keys (for example a counter reset or a duplicated id in a dedup set).

  1. Stop with a savepoint; keep it immutable as the rollback point.
  2. Read the affected operator (30.3) into a DataStream; write it out and quantify the damage (count, key list).
  3. Define the repair as a pure function oldValue -> newValue or a join against corrected data.
  4. Run a read-then-bootstrap job: read keyed state, apply the fix, re-emit as a KeyedStateBootstrapFunction input via withOperator. The new transformation replaces the whole operator state, so you must re-emit unchanged keys too; forgetting them silently deletes them.
  5. Restore a scratch job from the repaired savepoint, compare sampled keys with the report from step 2, then promote.

Limits: this fixes state, not the outputs already emitted downstream; reconcile those with an idempotent sink (Chapter 26). Everything is tenant-scoped data: keep the audit dump access controlled and PII-redacted (Chapters 16, 27).

30.8 Risks and compatibility

  • Version coupling: savepoint formats and serializers move between Flink versions. The 2.0 release notes state state compatibility is not guaranteed between 1.x and 2.x (Chapter 9.7). Whether the 2.x State Processor API can read a 1.20 savepoint: STILL UNVERIFIED (not provable from a jar; no docs statement found). Test it on a copy.
  • Serializer drift: if your reader or bootstrapper uses a different serializer than the job (Kryo fallback vs POJO vs Avro, Chapter 8), the restore fails or, worse, state is silently mis-decoded.
  • Mismatched UID/state name produces "dropped" state without any error if you run with -n.
  • Not a live tool: it works on a stopped job's snapshot; changes since the savepoint are lost unless you stop-with-savepoint right before.
  • Size: bootstrapping terabytes through one batch job needs real resources; test on a sample first (Chapter 17).
  • Backend portability: canonical savepoints restore across backends; native ones do not (Chapter 6.4).

30.9 Pitfalls / failure modes

Symptom Likely cause
Restore fails with serializer/type error descriptor type differs from original (Chapters 5, 8)
Job restores but state is empty UID or state name mismatch, or -n hid it
Burst of timer callbacks after restore processing-time timers overdue (30.5)
Writer job runs streaming mode BATCH mode not set (30.2)
Repaired savepoint lost most keys modification replaced the operator state but only re-emitted a subset (30.7)
Windows empty after restore assigner/trigger mismatch (30.4)

  1. Why must a keyed reader register the same state descriptors as the original operator?
  2. Your bootstrap registers processing-time timers; the job is restored a day late. What happens?
  3. How do you safely add .uid("x") to an operator that never had one, while keeping its state?
  4. In a repair job, why is "only emit corrected keys" dangerous?
  5. Which state kinds can the State Table API read?

  • Whether the State Processor API can read 1.20 savepoints: [unverified].
  • Bootstrapping Kafka source offsets as state. [unverified]

Chapter 31: ML inference in a DataStream job via Async I/O

Goal: after this chapter you can score events against an external model server from a DataStream job, choose ordering, capacity, timeout and retries from a latency budget, degrade safely with fallback scores, cache with keyed state, and monitor it.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5 (state/TTL), Chapter 11.5 (Async I/O basics), Chapter 12 (DLQ), Chapter 13 (observability), Chapter 26 (idempotency).

31.1 What Flink provides, and what it does not

Question Answer Status
ML_PREDICT SQL (since 2.1) and Table API (new in 2.2) verified (2.2.0 release post)
VECTOR_SEARCH SQL feature (2.2 post says SQL-only; README says SQL/Table API) verified, wording differs
Model inference in the DataStream API Not mentioned in the 2.2 release post or the Async I/O page; no inference class exists in the async packages of flink-streaming-java 2.3.0 (jar listing for "Inference" / "Predict" / "Model" under functions/async) verified absent in jars (2.3.0); docs not mentioning it is consistent
Built-in model providers OpenAI built in plus a custom provider interface (ModelProviderFactory via Java SPI, per FLIP-525), for the SQL/Table feature partly verified: the 2.2.0 release post shows an OpenAI-provider model example; the "custom provider interface" detail is from FLIP-525 as returned by a web search, not from the stable docs (404 on the page paths I tried)
Async batching for DataStream Async I/O Not mentioned on the Async I/O page; no batching class in the async packages of flink-streaming-java 2.3.0 (the only "Batch" hits under async are AsyncSinkWriterConfiguration in flink-connector-base, which is a sink buffer setting, unrelated) verified absent in jars (2.3.0)

This book deliberately does not use SQL (Chapter 1 rule). So the DataStream route is: your own async client + AsyncDataStream.

Flink Agents (open-source sub-project)

Apache Flink Agents is a separate sub-project "for building event-driven AI agents directly on Flink's streaming runtime" (0.2.0 announcement, fetched). It reads and writes DataStream/Table API streams, supports chat and embedding models, has Java API parity as of 0.2, and is a preview: "APIs and configuration options are experimental and may undergo non-backward compatible changes." Maven Central metadata for org.apache.flink:flink-agents-api lists 0.3.1 as the latest release (versions 0.1.0 to 0.3.1; verified by fetch, metadata dated July 2026). The Flink Agents installation docs (0.3 and main) say it "requires a stable release of Flink version 1.20.3 or higher"; an upper bound (such as 2.3.x) was not stated in what I fetched: [unverified]. Its docs list Java 21+ as recommended, with Java 11-20 lacking async execution. It targets LLM agents (tools, memory), not a plain "score this row with my classifier" call. Use plain Async I/O for classic model scoring; evaluate Agents only for LLM-agent workloads. Whether the project is preview-only today: the 0.2.0 announcement calls it a preview; its 0.3.x docs/README I fetched do not state a status, so production readiness is Data unavailable. Not covered further here.

31.2 Architecture

 Kafka ─► events ─► [feature build, keyed state] ─► AsyncDataStream ──► model server (HTTP/gRPC, autoscaled)
                                                        │  timeout / retry / capacity
                                                        ├─► scored events ─► sink
                                                        └─► fallback score + flag ─► metrics; failures ─► DLQ side output

Keep the model server outside Flink: it scales and deploys independently, and a model rollout does not need a savepoint upgrade (Chapter 9). Compute features inside Flink (keyed state, Chapter 5, 21) and send only the feature vector.

Figure 31.1: Scoring via AsyncDataStream with timeout, flagged fallback and DLQ isolation.

31.3 The async function (sketch, not compiled)

public class Scorer extends RichAsyncFunction<Features, Scored> {
    private transient ModelClient client;                       // placeholder non-blocking client
    @Override public void open(OpenContext ctx) {               // verified: javap RichFunction.open(OpenContext), flink-core 2.3.0
        client = ModelClient.create("<MODEL_ENDPOINT>");        // placeholder
    }
    @Override public void asyncInvoke(Features f, ResultFuture<Scored> out) {
        client.predict(f.vector, f.modelVersionHint).whenComplete((score, err) -> {
            if (err != null) out.completeExceptionally(err);    // retry predicate sees this (31.5)
            else out.complete(List.of(Scored.ok(f, score)));
        });
    }
    @Override public void timeout(Features f, ResultFuture<Scored> out) {
        out.complete(List.of(Scored.fallback(f, DEFAULT_SCORE, "timeout")));   // never restart the job for one slow call
    }
    @Override public void close() { client.close(); }
}

DataStream<Scored> scored = AsyncDataStream.unorderedWaitWithRetry(
    features, new Scorer(), 800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, 200, retryStrategy);

Verified (docs page and javap AsyncDataStream in flink-streaming-java 2.2.1 and 2.3.0, identical): unorderedWait/orderedWait(DataStream<IN>, AsyncFunction<IN,OUT>, long timeout, TimeUnit, int capacity) (a variant without capacity also exists) and unorderedWaitWithRetry/orderedWaitWithRetry(stream, fn, timeout, unit[, capacity], AsyncRetryStrategy<OUT>); all return SingleOutputStreamOperator<OUT>. AsyncFunction.timeout(IN, ResultFuture<OUT>) is a default method whose body completes exceptionally with a java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException ("Async function call has timed out."), verified by bytecode. Also verified from the page: ResultFuture.complete(Collection) or completeExceptionally(...) once, first call wins; the function runs sequentially per parallel instance (not multi-threaded) so use a non-blocking client; default on timeout is an exception and job restart.

31.4 Ordered vs unordered, capacity, timeout

Choice Behavior (verified) Pick when
orderedWait results emitted in input order downstream relies on order per partition; costs head-of-line blocking: one slow call delays the rest
unorderedWait emitted as completed; watermarks are order boundaries (records do not cross them) default for scoring; per-key order is rarely needed, and event time stays correct
capacity max in-flight requests per parallel instance; when full, the operator backpressures upstream size by Little's law: in-flight = rate_per_subtask x latency; verify the server can take parallelism x capacity
timeout max time from first invocation to final completion, including retries must be below your latency budget (31.8)

Operational consequence: when the model server slows, in-flight requests fill capacity, backpressure builds (Chapter 11.1), and Kafka lag grows. That is the intended protection; the alternative (unbounded queue) is an OOM.

31.5 Retries

Verified API: AsyncRetryStrategies.FixedDelayRetryStrategyBuilder(maxAttempts, fixedDelayMs) with .ifResult(RetryPredicates.EMPTY_RESULT_PREDICATE), .ifException(RetryPredicates.HAS_EXCEPTION_PREDICATE), .build(). Package: org.apache.flink.streaming.util.retryable (javap flink-streaming-java 2.2.1/2.3.0). The exponential-backoff builder is AsyncRetryStrategies.ExponentialBackoffDelayRetryStrategyBuilder<OUT>(int maxAttempts, long initialDelay, long maxRetryDelay, double multiplier) with the same ifResult(Predicate<Collection<OUT>>), ifException(Predicate<Throwable>), build() methods (verified: javap; delay unit assumed to be milliseconds from the interface method getBackoffTimeMillis). Also available: AsyncRetryStrategies.NO_RETRY_STRATEGY and RetryPredicates.createExceptionTypePredicate(Class). The strategy interface is org.apache.flink.streaming.api.functions.async.AsyncRetryStrategy (canRetry(int), getBackoffTimeMillis(int), getRetryPredicate()).

AsyncRetryStrategy<Scored> retryStrategy =
    new AsyncRetryStrategies.FixedDelayRetryStrategyBuilder<Scored>(2, 50L)
        .ifException(RetryPredicates.HAS_EXCEPTION_PREDICATE).build();   // (sketch; names and arities checked by javap)
// exponential: new AsyncRetryStrategies.ExponentialBackoffDelayRetryStrategyBuilder<Scored>(3, 50L, 400L, 2.0)

Rules: total timeout covers all attempts, so attempts x (call latency + delay) < timeout. Retries multiply load on an already struggling server (retry storm); keep attempts at 1-2 and docs warn queue needs grow with retry rate. Scoring must be idempotent and side-effect free, because restarts replay calls (Chapter 26).

31.6 Fallback and failure isolation

Treat a score as optional data, not as a reason to stop the pipeline:

Failure Handling
Timeout / exhausted retries emit Scored.fallback(...) with a flag scoreSource = FALLBACK (default score, last cached score, or rule-based score)
Server 5xx burst circuit breaker inside the client (your code): fail fast to fallback instead of occupying capacity
Malformed response / poison feature vector (4xx) do not retry; route to a DLQ side output with reason (Chapter 12)
Whole model server down fallbacks flow; alert on fallback ratio (31.10); do not let the job restart-loop

Downstream must see the flag: a fallback score of 0.0 that looks real corrupts decisions silently. Emit tenant id on every metric and DLQ record, and never log feature values containing PII (Chapter 27).

31.7 Batching

The DataStream Async I/O page does not document batching, and the flink-streaming-java 2.3.0 jar has no batching class for it (verified absent). Options you build yourself: - Batch inside the model call: a client that coalesces requests from the same subtask for N ms or K rows and fans results back to each ResultFuture. Trade-off: adds up to N ms latency, fewer round trips, better GPU utilisation; the buffer must be flushed on timeout and close(). - Batch before the async operator (keyed window or timer, Chapters 2, 3) and send one request per batch: simpler semantics, more latency, more state. Both are custom patterns; there is no official Flink DataStream async batching API in the 2.2.1/2.3.0 jars (jar listing).

31.8 Latency budget (worked, assumptions labeled)

Assumption: end-to-end SLA 1 s from Kafka to sink, p99. - Kafka + deserialize + features: 100 ms. Sink: 100 ms. Leaves 800 ms. - Model p99 = 150 ms, one retry with 50 ms delay: worst successful case 350 ms. Set timeout 800 ms only if you accept spending all slack; 500 ms is safer. - Capacity per subtask at 400 events/s and 150 ms mean latency: 400 x 0.15 = 60 in flight; set 100-200 for headroom. Write the budget down; the timeout, retry and capacity numbers are derived from it, not guessed (compare Chapter 17).

31.9 Model versioning, feature freshness, caching

  • Versioning: put modelVersion in the endpoint path or request, return it in the response, and store it on the output record. Roll out by shifting server traffic (canary) rather than redeploying Flink. Reproducibility for replays/backfills (Chapter 24) needs the same model version; otherwise scores differ.
  • Training/serving skew: features computed in Flink must match the training pipeline definition; version the feature schema with the model.
  • Feature freshness: state-based features (Chapter 21) are as fresh as the last processed event; features fetched from an online store can be stale. Record featureAsOf on the output.
  • Caching (optional): keyed ValueState<CachedScore> with TTL (Chapter 5.5) keyed by entity or by a hash of the feature vector. Cache hits skip the call. Caveats: TTL cleanup is not instantaneous (Chapter 5.5); invalidate by modelVersion (store version in the value and compare); state grows with distinct keys, so size it (Chapter 5.6). Async functions cannot use keyed state directly (verified: in the 2.3.0 RichAsyncFunction runtime context every state accessor throws UnsupportedOperationException("State is not supported in rich async functions."), javap bytecode): do the cache lookup in a preceding KeyedProcessFunction that either emits a hit or forwards a miss to the async operator, then write results back in a following keyed operator. Keyed state inside the async function itself is therefore unavailable.

Figure 31.2: Caching scores in keyed state outside the async function.

31.10 Observability (Chapter 13)

Signal Source Use
In-flight vs capacity backpressure / busy-time metrics of the async operator (names verified in Chapter 1: backPressuredTimeMsPerSecond, busyTimeMsPerSecond) capacity too small or server slow
Call latency histogram your custom metric via getRuntimeContext().getMetricGroup() p50/p99 vs budget
Fallback ratio, timeout count, retry count, DLQ count your custom counters, tagged by tenant and model version alert thresholds
Score distribution custom histogram / sampled output drift detection: a stuck constant score means fallback or a bad model
Kafka consumer lag + watermark lag Chapter 1.7 end-to-end effect
Alert on fallback ratio above a threshold for N minutes; this must come from outside the data path (Chapter 1.7, 25).

31.11 Pitfalls / failure modes

  • Blocking HTTP client inside asyncInvoke: throughput collapses to 1/latency (Chapter 11.5).
  • Timeout larger than checkpoint timeout: checkpoints can stall behind in-flight requests (in-flight async state is part of the operator's checkpoint, Chapter 6).
  • Capacity x parallelism overwhelms the model server; add client-side rate limiting.
  • Default timeout behaviour (exception, restart) turns a slow model into a restart loop.
  • Unflagged fallback scores.
  • Ordered mode with a slow tail: backpressure from a single slow request.
  • Retry storm during server degradation.
  • Replays (Chapter 24) hammer the model server; throttle backfills.

31.12 Self-check

  1. Why is unorderedWait still safe with event time?
  2. Timeout 500 ms, 2 retries of 300 ms each: what really happens?
  3. How do you make fallback scores distinguishable and alertable?
  4. Where do you put a per-entity score cache if RichAsyncFunction has no keyed state?
  5. Why can ML_PREDICT not simply be used in this book's DataStream jobs?
